### also known as
# DE FLUCTIBUS <note>Latin: "of the floods," a play on his surname</note>

### Or
# COSMIC METEOROLOGY.

### TO THE REVEREND FATHER AND LORD,
# Master JOHN,
## MOST WORTHY BISHOP OF LINCOLN,
### MOST VIGILANT KEEPER OF THE GREAT SEAL OF ENGLAND,
### AND TO THE ROYAL MAJESTY AMONG THE MORE SACRED COUNCILS;
### A MOST PRUDENT COUNSELOR.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap 'N' containing a figure holding a sword and scales <note>The figure represents Justice, fitting for a Keeper of the Great Seal</note>, surrounded by leaf patterns.</image-desc>

Neither the dignity of your eminent honor, nor the title of splendor of your great place or office—inasmuch as these things are momentary and are accustomed to last only by the pleasure of the Prince; nor your piety and humanity toward the poor who entreat for justice; nor that unexpected duty regarding the public affairs of the state (which is especially fitting and consistent for a man of this place and dignity, as if he were the most certain pillar and support of the kingdom); nor, finally, that divine virtue of Justice, which is held in equilibrium by you, and is liberally dispensed to each according to his right by just scales (with injury banished into exile) and distributed by a right measure; none, I say, of these gifts granted to you by divine providence (Most Reverend Father, President most experienced in the most sublime affairs) is the occasion of this dedication of mine. Indeed, these qualities ought to be present by virtue of office in the sight of the Commonwealth for any excellent Chancellor, Keeper of the Great Seal, and pious presiding officer (although this does not always happen). Rather, two virtues in particular, even closer to your heart and Nature, urge me and persuade me that I should now insist on dedicating these works of mine—these most dear reflections of mine produced with much labor—to your Lordship and Dignity above all others, and to freely and gladly bestow them upon you. The first of these in order is your nourishing charity in the increase and exaltation of the sciences, and your voluntary and by no means coerced love toward students. This love—which the sharp wit of the pen resting on the wings of truth can never sufficiently describe or explain while storing it away for the memory of eternal posterity as your happy deeds and actions—and this zeal of yours toward all learned men, has now [brought forth] two offspring...

<summary>A formal Latin dedication to John Williams, Bishop of Lincoln and Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, praising his judicial integrity and his specific patronage of scholars and the sciences.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the formal dedication of Robert Fludd’s work, likely addressed to a high-ranking church official or academic patron, emphasizing the shared legacy of learning and family ties.</meta>

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

...once brought to light and celebrated characters <note>original: "characteres"; here meaning distinguished qualities or reputations</note> who were by no means different from one another in nature and condition; namely, one of whom rendered that famous and renowned University of Cambridge richer in the instruments of study and science, more ornate with magnificent buildings, and more pleasing and accessible to those eager for learning. Furthermore, he established that magnificent sanctuary of select books, a vast work of architecture destined for the use of a Library—a gift welcome to all the literate, profitable to anyone seeking ample utility, and like sweet milk from the breasts of Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and weaving</note>, abundantly pouring forth and liberally showering upon the thirsty. The other offspring or character of your impregnated charity is that excellent Library in the Monastery most famous among Londoners for the monuments and tombs of Kings, called Westminster. It was erected at no small expense to your Dignity and fortified and adorned with every necessary refinement, and especially with rare books of the highest estimation. This library, celebrated and heralded throughout almost all of Britain as much for the beauty of its structure and arrangement as for the excellence of the books contained within it, is accustomed daily to depict and engrave the praises of its illustrious founder and patron upon the eternal monuments of fame. Thus, it is clearly declared by this sweet and voluntary goodness of yours that your Honor and Dignity were born not for yourself alone, but for others, being inclined and devoted to doing good by a natural disposition of the soul. Finally, the latter order and the reason closer to me, by which a cautious respect has induced me and mature consideration has urged me to celebrate your name and honor through this dedication of my works, is that close proximity of our spirits and the firm bond in consanguinity <note>blood relation</note>, by virtue of which bodies otherwise separated are nonetheless joined, bound, and united together by the firmest chains and by a certain magnetic glue of nature, as it were. Therefore, those things which are offered to your Lordship and Dignity with a sincere heart and grateful mind, may you (Reverend Father, a Presiding Officer most worthy of such a place and office) deign for your part to accept with a serene brow and a placid countenance. I implore you to pursue me—who am most devoted to your Lordship in every duty of diligence as well as obedience—with favor and benevolence, while I, for my part, humbly and from the very center of my heart pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that you may live long and happily, be directed by a favorable and propitious divine power in your life, and finally remain forever in the office of holy goodness toward all.

->Of your Highness and<-
->Reverend Dignity<-

->Most Observant,<-

->Robert Fludd. By the origin of his lineage<-
->a Welsh-Briton.<-

<meta>The catchword "TRACTA" indicates the beginning of a discussion or treatise. This page serves as a structural overview or "table of contents" for a scientific work on natural phenomena.</meta>

<note>The author uses the term "meteors" in the Aristotelian sense, referring to any atmospheric or natural phenomena, including rain, wind, and minerals, rather than just falling stars.</note>

This portion is divided into three parts, which treat the causes of **meteors** <note>original: "meteororum"; refers to natural phenomena in the sky and earth</note> in a manner that is far from common:

*   **The First: Material Causes** <note>The "material cause" refers to the physical substance out of which something is made.</note>
    *   Simple substances, which are discussed in Book 1.
    *   Mixed substances, and concerning these, Book 2.

*   **The Second or Middle: Formal and Efficient Causes**
    *   **Formal causes** <note>The "formal cause" refers to the essential nature or design of a thing.</note>, which Book 3 embraces, having been divided into various members.
    *   **Efficient causes** <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or the agent that brings something into being.</note>, and concerning these, Book 4 with its own small parts or members.

*   **The Third and Final: Final Causes** <note>The "final cause" refers to the purpose or end goal for which a thing exists.</note>
    **of both natures, namely:**
    *   Wholesome <note>original: "salubres"; beneficial to health or the environment</note> phenomena, of which Book 5 treats with its members.
    *   Morbid <note>original: "morbosos"; relating to disease or unhealthful conditions</note> phenomena, and Books 6 and 7 deal with these types and their members.

## SECTION I. PORTION IV. PART I.
### BOOK ONE.

->*On the primary principles of meteorological matters.*<-

<note>The term "meteorological" in this 17th-century context refers to all natural phenomena occurring in the air, including rain, wind, comets, and rainbows.</note>

- The stealthy foundations of the knowledge of pagan philosophers; the palpable errors of those Christian followers of pagan doctrine } Namely, in the Preface.
- The name and essence of the Meteor. Chapter 1.
- The true principles of physics <term>physics: here meaning the study of natural philosophy and the physical world</term>, of which are noted:
    - Their differences, since some are:
        - Substantial:
            - Primary or simple, concerning which see Chapter 3.

            - Simple things derived from simple things.

    - Confirmation, as much Pagan and Cabalistic <note>original: "Cabalistica"; referring here to Jewish mystical traditions often integrated into Renaissance natural philosophy</note> as Philosophical. Chapter 6.

# PREFACE: IN WHICH IT IS DE- CLARED THAT THE CHIEFS OF THE PAGAN PHILO- SOPHERS HAVE, IN A SURREPTITIOUS MANNER,
### falsely claimed the foundations of their philosophy from the High Priest Moses <note>original: "Antistite Moyse"</note>, and have poorly constructed the edifice of their philosophy upon them; and in this also, the gross and palpable error of Christian philosophers is pointed out as if with a finger—those who, having neglected the Holy Bible and rejected the teachers of hidden Theosophy <note>Divine wisdom or mystical insight into the nature of God</note>, flee to the vain doctrine of the Pagans.

HOW varied and mutually disagreeing are the opinions of philosophers, both ancient and modern, concerning the essence, origin, and effects of meteors; how unstable their assertions are, cannot be hidden from those who have devoted their labor somewhat more accurately to reading the books and volumes of philosophy. The reason for this matter is usually readily apparent to men endowed with sharpness of intellect; for where the foundations of the palace of philosophy are found to be based on fables, there a weak structure—hardly different from the shadows of a Chimera <note>A mythical creature; here meaning a wild, groundless fancy</note>—is to be expected, and consequently, one that is stuffed and swelling with the propped-up wings of doubtful probability. What of indubitable truth is to be drawn from a spurious philosophy, produced by the foolish labors of the Pagans? For indeed, it was by no means granted to them by the central light of nature—that is, the Creator of nature and natural things—to truly penetrate the fountain of Christian philosophy or the spring of the sacred scriptures. What is the doctrine of Aristotle, what of Plato, what of Pythagoras; what, finally, of the Greeks, Hippocrates and Galen, and what of Avicenna and the rest of the Arabs—both philosophical and medical—if we look upon the marrow of the Holy Bible correctly and in a mystical manner, or with the eyes of a Lynx <note>Proverbial for keen, piercing sight</note>? Certainly, it is a merely deceptive vapor and vanishing smoke, and a plainly empty figment. Whence it happens that St. Paul <note>original: "D. Paulus"</note> endeavored most earnestly to draw us away from vain philosophy, as being that in which nothing but trifles and scarcely probable things, or any matter as it truly is, can be elicited. Do we not gather from the excellent teaching of the Prophet how impious and profane it is, having left the way of truth, to imitate the doctrine of the Pagans? By this we are taught that the fountain of all wisdom must by no means be abandoned to seek art, science, and understanding in foreign regions, as did the Hagarenes <note>Descendants of Hagar; used here to denote those outside the covenant</note> and those who were in Teman (Baruch 3), who indeed never recognized true wisdom. And although we have it confirmed by the testimony of trustworthy writers that the light of nature and the secret of the philosophers was in some way revealed to some of the Pagan philosophers: nevertheless, because they were ignorant of the divine center of that light—the true Christ, the Word of GOD, and the origin of the Holy Spirit—therefore, having that divine light before their eyes, but not knowing the true reason for it, they erred, and so they vanished into...

<summary>The author argues that pagan philosophers stole their best ideas from Moses but corrupted them, and he criticizes Christian scholars for preferring pagan texts over the mystical truths of the Bible.</summary>
<keywords>preface, Moses, theosophy, Christian philosophy, Aristotle, Plato, Pythagoras, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, St. Paul, Hagarenes, Teman, Baruch, light of nature</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory argument (Prooemium) regarding the divine origin of true philosophy, contrasting it with the errors of pagan idolatry and the derivative knowledge of Greek philosophers.</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

through their own imaginations. From this it happened that they attributed the efficacy of such great miracles and the glory of the results not to God, the sole creator, but to created Nature and the elements, which were brought forth and produced from His womb. Hence the origin of Idolatry: namely, the veneration of the sun and moon; the cult of Osiris and Isis; the adoration of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury; sacrifices to Heaven, Ceres, Vesta, Proserpina, Vulcan, Pluto, and Neptune; and infinite other errors. By these, ignorant men are persuaded to wander away and depart from the contemplation of the true GOD JEHOVAH, rather than approaching a perfect knowledge of their creator. 

The cause of this error was an ignorance of the divine word and the operation and property of the Holy Spirit, as well as a neglect of the Holy Bible—the fountain and origin of all science and wisdom. But the sacred scriptures contain the secrets of most holy Philosophy revealed to us Christians, through which the miracles of the Word are manifested to us by the mediation of worldly Nature. For in these it is explained: *This word was in the beginning (John 1) with God, and in God, and was God himself; and that it was the light of the world, in which was life; and that through this word all things were made, and without it nothing was made.* <note>original: "Hoc verbum fuisse in principio... et sine eo nihil."</note> Therefore, through true knowledge of the Word, we understand the nature of the Speaker, since the Son has a relationship to the Father. Once these two are known, there immediately follows the revelation of the Spirit of holy discipline, as proceeding from both. 

He, therefore, who does not know the word of GOD knows nothing, *since by the word God made all things (Wisdom 9:1)*; and he who does not understand it cannot understand the truth, because Christ is the only truth, the true GOD, and eternal life—or, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 1, *the power and wisdom of GOD.* <note>original: "DEI virtus & sapientia."</note> Hence it follows that those who do not know Him cannot centrally know the things created by Him and their essences. *From him, in him, and through him are all things (says the Apostle), to whom be praise and honor.*

How great, then, is the madness in us Christians to venerate those pagan authors of philosophy and Medicine like deities? To read their writings with such diligence and confidence? To hold their inventions and arts in such immense esteem? To defend their opinions in public Schools with such obstinacy? Indeed, to cite their authorities so steadfastly and firmly in writings and disputes, as if they had been poured out and distilled onto the earth divinely from the heavens and immediately from GOD himself? Since the sacred writings testify that Christ is the only truth, and all truth of things is from Him—the power and wisdom of GOD teaching all things. 

Who, then, among all the Philosophers can demonstrate the nature of a thing or a natural object by *a priori* <term>a priori: reasoning from theoretical deduction rather than observation</term> reasons, if he is ignorant of the true and primary cause of things? Are we not also taught that there is no truth of science outside the true gift of the Holy Spirit, who is the only Teacher of true doctrine and science? This may be gathered from many places in the sacred scriptures (Exodus 28:3, Exodus 31:2, and 35:30). Hence the Royal Psalmist says exultantly in *Psalm 119:99*: *I have become more intelligent than all my teachers, because the testimonies of GOD are my meditation.* 

What, then, of that Aristotelian "Nature"? It is certainly either vain or a case of explaining the unknown by the even more unknown, since he himself was ignorant of Desire <note>original: "Cupidinem," likely referring to the divine creative impulse or Eros in a Neoplatonic sense</note>, which is the true and shining spirit of all wisdom, the light of the world, the glory of the truly wise, the life of creatures, the mind of the soul, and the prince of reason, governing in the very center of natural things. 

Aristotle, Plato, Pythagoras, and Hippocrates undoubtedly perceived a great light in nature from afar, having been instructed by the Ethiopians, Egyptians, Hebrews, and certain people of Armenia and Arabia after long and distant travels. Thus, having merely changed the names of the three principles of Moses, they falsely attributed these things to themselves:
<margin>AB</margin>
For what Moses called "darkness" or the "potential principle," Aristotle called "prime matter" <term>materia prima: the primitive, formless base of all reality</term>, Plato called "formless hyle" <note>Greek: hyle (matter)</note> or "invisible and unformed species," Pythagoras called "unity," and Hippocrates called "deformed Chaos" or a "disturbed universal mass." What Moses designated as "the waters," Aristotle called "secondary matter," Plato called "spirit," and Pythagoras called "Diadem"; Hippocrates, along with Anaximenes, called it the "vast and universal air of the world." So also Light, the third principle of Moses...

<summary>The author argues that true scientific and philosophical knowledge must be rooted in the Christian Word of God rather than pagan Greek philosophy. He claims that thinkers like Aristotle and Plato merely renamed the Mosaic principles of creation to claim them as their own discoveries.</summary>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critique of pagan philosophy. The opening word "pium" is the conclusion of "principium" (principle or beginning) from the previous page. The author is arguing that Greek and Roman philosophers stole divine truths from Moses and the prophets, renamed them, and then obscured them with human imagination.</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

...principle <note>original: "principium"</note>, Aristotle called it his **Form**, Plato the **Soul of the World**, Pythagoras the **Triad**, and Hippocrates that immortal thing which he called **Heat**; all of which, when they became throw into confusion, receded to that highest region which the ancients called the **Ether**. Is this not a monstrous theft among the Pagan teachers, by which they do not blush to falsely and through subtle ways claim for themselves the principles of the Divine Overseer and His doctrine? 

And yet we Christians, who are the possessors of the doctrine of Moses—indeed, of all the other prophets and writers—and who have been truly instructed in them as if by a sacrosanct finger, are nevertheless moved by I know not what madness. Deserters of the divine fountain and neglectful of the mirror of truth, as if intoxicated by a lethal cup, we do not cease to be immersed in the deceptive filth of the Pagans. I speak of a Philosophy erected upon firm enough foundations, but poorly arranged insofar as it is fabricated and linked together by the various imaginations of its inventors—nay, rather, it is defiled and contaminated. For what does it profit to find stable and firm bases for a structure where the members of the house are joined from reeds or straw, subject to every wind? 

Therefore, the more learned of the sects of Pagan Philosophers perceived the formal light from afar with the shadowed eyes of their minds, but they were by no means able to penetrate to the deep fountain of all wisdom from which that form flowed. Wherefore it must be considered an extreme madness in us Christians to dwell instead in darkness and to extract a bastard Philosophy from the dung-heap and filth of the Pagans, rather than drawing the subject of a sacred, naked, true, and clear Philosophy from the bright spring of life arising from the Holy Bible. 

Let us therefore reject those profane books of the Pagans and flee to the sacred lights and remains of the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, true Philosophers, and mystical Theosophers <note>A 'theosopher' refers to one who gains knowledge of the divine through mystical insight or direct revelation rather than mere logic.</note>, in whom we shall find the virtues of the spirit of holy discipline (whose role alone it is to teach all things) and the truth of all sciences. 

It shall be my task (with God's favor) in this volume of mine to speak of the essences of **meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, clouds, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>, as they are the mothers of all composite things. I shall also strive to compare the positions and axioms of the ancient philosophers, as well as those of their modern disciples, regarding these "imperfectly mixed" things with the testimony of the Holy Bible. I do this so that you may clearly perceive the difference between them and the holy scriptures, and consequently, so that you may choose whether the sacrosanct Bible or the vain, uncertain writings and truth-wandering sayings of the Pagan philosophers and their Christian sects are to be embraced.

The aim of this entire volume of ours is to show that meteors are produced daily by God in the world in a mystical manner. They are the immediate causes of both health, restoration, and preservation, as well as of diseases and death, in both the **Macrocosm** <note>The 'Great World' or the universe as a whole.</note> and the **Microcosm** <note>The 'Little World,' referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>. This I shall attempt to prove with testimonies derived from the sacrosanct fountain and to support upon Atlantic shoulders <note>A metaphor for a massive intellectual undertaking, referring to the Titan Atlas who held up the sky.</note>. Hence, I shall endeavor to extract and fish out the principles, differences, causes, and prognostics of both good and bad meteors—as well as the cures for their worst effects—from the deep spring of the Bible and of the Theosophers or Hebrew and Egyptian Doctors. I will reveal and publish these according to the smallness of my talent, with my loins girt with the belt of truth, and with a favorable and propitious divinity smiling upon me.

A 2

# THE FIRST CHAPTER OF THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FIRST PART OF THE FOURTH PORTION OF THE FIRST SECTION, CONCERNING THE PRIMARY PRINCIPLES OF METEORS.

->*In which various opinions of both ancient and modern philosophers regarding the name and essence of the Meteor are discussed.*<-

---

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting two scholars, one seated at a desk and one standing, within a circular frame surrounded by decorative foliage.</image-desc>
Although I have written quite copiously throughout the entire seventh book of our physical treatise on the various natures of meteors—treating them both physically and metaphysically—and also throughout the "History of the Preternatural World" <note>original: "De præternaturali vtriusque mundi historia"</note> in the second portion of the first section of the third part, the profound contemplation of this subject now in my hands and the necessity of our purpose nevertheless compel me to penetrate into their centers with a somewhat more accurate inquiry in this place. For whoever desires to reach the marrow of meteors, and does not attempt to bring such a business to a happy conclusion, will surely confess that he has not reached even the smallest secret of GOD and nature. First, therefore, before I descend into the depths of such a difficult work, I shall explain briefly and clearly what the Philosophers, both Ancient and Modern, have devised regarding the general name, essence, and origin of the meteor.

The Greeks assigned the name "meteor" <note>from the Greek *meteoros*, meaning "lofty" or "raised up"</note> due to the loftiness of its position in the region of the air. Among our own thinkers, however, they are called "impressions" <note>original: "impressiones"</note> because for the most part they are seen to be imprinted and formed in the high—that is, the lofty—regions of the air. Yet truly, this name is attributed to them not from their essence or constitution, but rather from their location. With respect to their consistency, philosophers call them "imperfectly composed" and "imperfectly mixed" bodies—or, as some prefer, they are so named because of their sudden generation, seeing as they are observed to form in an instant or a moment of time. Others maintain that they are called "imperfectly composed bodies" because their composition does not seem to occur according to a change of substance or an alteration of qualities. Some call them "imperfectly mixed" insofar as they are compared to animate and perfectly mixed bodies <note>such as plants or animals</note>. Finally, there are others who assertively say that these "impressions" are called "imperfect mixtures" because a perfect form is not acquired in them, nor is a great alteration of parts found in such a composition; rather, the parts, being only slightly altered, are confused among themselves. And this is the reason why the parts of such an imperfect mixture are so easily dissipated from one another and dissolved into their primary elements, from which they were previously coagulated without any perfect mixing or transmutation having taken place.

As for what pertains to the existence of these "impressions," all agree that two things are required: one, namely, in which they are made, which is the air—acting as the medium or the lowest "spirit of the world" <note>original: "spiritus mundi infimus"</note>, which is the womb <note>original: "matrix"</note> of all meteors; and the other, from which they are made. They conclude this second thing to be vapor or, as others prefer, smoke <note>original: "fumum"</note>, rising fundamentally from either the earth or the water. In this upward motion, they identify a celestial heat as the more principal and primary agent, and an aerial heat as the secondary one; then, they believe this matter, having been elevated upward, is gathered together and given form by the nature of a "coagulum" <note>a thickening agent, like rennet in cheesemaking</note> that is partly celestial and partly elementary.

In the matter of the "material cause," however, some seem to disagree. While one chooses only vapor as the universal matter of meteors, others assert that vapor and exhalation are their material subjects. They say that vapor is hot and moist, and thus they believe aqueous meteors <note>such as rain or mist</note> proceed from its substance. On the other hand, they maintain that fiery impressions <note>such as lightning or comets</note> arise from exhalation because it is hot and dry according to the nature of fire. Thus, in place of vapor, they made smoke the common matter of meteors, since it participates in the nature of every element; it is sometimes hot and dry, and sometimes hot and moist, so its matter is as fit for the procreation of aquatic impressions as it is for fiery ones. But Robert of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), a famous English scientist and Bishop of Lincoln</note>, supported by the authority of Aristotle, seems to include "exhalation" under the dimension of "vapor," as he established that vapor is tripartite according to Aristotle's opinion: namely, hot and dry, hot and moist, and cold and moist. He asserted that the first of these is extracted materially from the earth or earthy things, the last from water or watery things, and the middle one from both (though with water dominating). Hence it was that he defined vapor as a subtle substance from any one or two of the lower elements...

# ON THE PRIMARY PRINCIPLES OF METEORS.

...derived or exhaled from the lower regions, refined by celestial action, and raised to one of the three regions of the air. However, those who established a "general smoke" as the material of these impressions claimed it arose from water or earth, and for this reason, they devised a twofold smoke: namely, **Vapor** and **Exhalation**. They described the former as a hot and moist smoke, watery and non-flammable, arising from both earth and water; the latter they described as a hot and dry smoke, terrestrial, flammable, and drawn out from the earth. Thus, they called earth and water the "remote" material causes, while vapor and exhalation were the "proximate" or immediate causes.

But indeed, as we come to the opinions of the philosophers regarding the efficient causes of meteors, we shall find no small discrepancy among them. Some have been of the opinion that the efficient causes of these impressions are heat and cold. They made this heat twofold: namely, the heat of the location and the heat of the sun. Furthermore, they distinguished the sun’s heat into that which "calls forth," which evokes and lifts the smokes extracted from the earth or water, and that which "scorches," which burns the smokes that have been raised, depending on the directness or indirectness of the solar rays. They also devised a twofold condition for cold: namely, the cold of the location and external cold. Again, they made external cold "constricting" and "prohibiting." They say this constricts the pores and surface of the earth so that the solar rays, approaching from a distance, cannot extract the smokes; they assert that this is the reason why there are few "ignited" meteors <note>Such as lightning or shooting stars.</note> in the winter time, but more numerous and abundant "aquatic" ones (such as rain and snow). Others, making no mention of cold, established the heavens, the light of the sun and the other stars—and especially the hidden influences of the planets—as the efficient causes of meteors. They argued that these produce various and differing impressions in a hidden manner according to their various positions, relationships, and conjunctions. Some have supposed a hidden warmth of the air, working together with that celestial warmth, to produce these "imperfect mixtures" <note>A term for phenomena that do not have a stable, permanent physical form, like clouds or rainbows.</note>. Thus, different men have produced different efficient causes of meteors according to their differing fantasies; we shall bring the opinions of all these to the **Lydian stone** <note>original: "Lydium seu igneam probationem"—a touchstone or "fiery trial" used to test the purity of gold, here meaning a rigorous test of truth.</note> or fiery trial in its proper place, the divine power assisting us.

They recognized the formal cause of these impressions—by means of which different phenomena are adorned with various shapes—as being varied according to the diversity of the location, the motion of the matter, and the efficient heat.

Those well-versed in Natural Philosophy are also quite anxious and uncertain in their opinions regarding the **final cause** <note>The purpose or "end goal" for which a thing exists.</note> of meteors. Nevertheless, all of them, taught by outcome and experience, recognize a twofold effect of meteors in nature: namely, the good and healthy, and the evil and unhealthy. For they have learned through observation that the final effect of these tends toward the universal health of living plants and other bodies, as well as the convenience of every particular thing. They confess themselves to have experienced that each of them has its own manifest and hidden virtue—just as the duty of rain is to water and fatten the earth, and the duty of **Comets** is to consume the corrupt and poisonous smokes of the air, and so on. That they also sometimes achieve the worst and most mournful effects is taught to us not only by the more skilled Astrologers, but even by those immersed in the "mire of common philosophy." Daily practice has instructed them on how heavy floods are produced by immoderate rains, and how much terror of war, famine, and plague a Comet portends; the same must be judged of other meteors, both watery and fiery, according to the disposition of their mass and quality. Indeed, on the testimony of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer and geographer.</note>, meteors have more obscure significations regarding both the benefit and the harm of the lower world and its creatures than the stars themselves; nonetheless, he confesses that these can be observed and judged in some sober way by men endowed with prudence.

Such, therefore, are the opinions of the Philosophers, both ancient and modern, regarding the general essence and existence of Meteors. If we compare these with the sense of the Holy Scripture through diligent observation, we shall clearly perceive—or it will be very easily brought into the public view—whether there is any relationship between the two or not. For whatever is seen to clash with the fountain of all truth is false and deceptive.

### CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the principles of Nature in general, according to our design.

The principles of natural things are divided into two kinds: namely, into **simple** and **mixed**. Again, we divide the simple principles into **substantial** and **accidental**. We call those "substantial" which subsist by themselves, and we call "accidental" those qualities whose essence is to exist within some substance. As for those which are substantial, we make them either **absolutely simple**, or **comparatively simple** (that is, those which arise immediately from simple things). Those substantial things that are absolutely simple flowed forth from the divine power immediately at the beginning of creation, such as **Light** and the **Waters** out of the **Darkness**. But the "simple things born from simple things" are called the **Elements**; in a more general sense and in imitation of the simple principles, we establish only three of these: namely, **Fire** from Light, the **Sphere of Humidity** from Water, and **Earth** from Darkness. Moreover, simple...

...however, we call those accidental qualities active which are derived, as if they were effects, from the opposing actions of simple principles. There are two in number: namely, **Heat**, springing from the motion of light; and **Cold**, sent forth from the dark abyss to repel the assault of heat. <note>original: "à tenebrosa voragine caloris, insultus repellendi gratia, emissa" - The author suggests cold is a reactive force sent from the darkness to check the power of light/heat.</note> Furthermore, those simple accidents propagated from the opposing actions of these simples are called **moisture** and **dryness**. From these principles—both material and formal—by the mediation of those accidental qualities which emerged from them, the world was created in a physical manner. Through their firm permanence, the world will remain in the same state without evident alteration until the very end, when it shall perish.

But truly, in the **Microcosm** <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>, as with other perfectly mixed things, it is recognized that matters behave far differently. This is because their principles are "imperfectly mixed," being the more immediate origins of these things. To these principles, it is granted to be altered by constant changes, inasmuch as they are in perpetual motion toward either generation or corruption, as is more clearly demonstrated below in its proper place.

Therefore, "mixed principles" are either **primary**—namely, those which are drawn immediately and most closely from the substantial principles of nature of the second order (the elements)—and of this kind, two are reckoned by Philosophers: namely, **Vapor** and **Exhalation**. Or they are **secondary**—that is, those flowing immediately from the primary ones, such as **Meteors** <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> or "imperfectly mixed" things. From these, composite bodies are immediately produced, and through their dissolution, they result again in their primary elements. For the sake of a more succinct method, we have condensed these principles in this manner:

-> **Physical Principles are either:** <-

**I. Simple Things**
*   **Substantial**, which are either:
    *   **Primary** (absolutely simple), being three: Darkness, Water, Light.
    *   **Secondary** (simple things from simples, such as the elements), being three:
        *   Earth.
        *   The Sphere of Humidity, which in its nature is either: **Thick** (as Water) or **Thin** (as Air).
        *   Fire.
*   **Accidental**, and these are either:
    *   **Simples of the first order** (two in number): Heat, Cold.
    *   **Simples from simples** (of the second order): Moist, Dry.

**II. Mixed Things**
*   **Of the first order**: Vapor, Exhalation.
*   **Arising from primaries**, such as **Meteors**:
    *   Fiery.
    *   Watery.
    *   Mixed.

We shall deal with all of these more extensively (God willing) and separately, so that we may arrive by a smoother path at the effects of the **Macrocosm** and **Microcosm**, both the healthy and natural ones, as well as the unhealthy and preternatural.

# On the Primary Principles of Atmospheric Phenomena.

In my history of the physics of the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole.</note>, and later in Book 9, Tract 1, Chapter 9 of the *Natural History of the **Microcosm*** <note>The "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>; as well as in the first and fifth chapters of the first book of the first section of the second part, regarding the **cabalistic** <note>Referring to the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism often adapted by Renaissance Christian philosophers to explain the secrets of creation.</note> and physiological discourse of both worlds (where the primary elements of Nature are discussed); and finally in Part 3, Section 1, Portion 2, Chapter 1 of that same discourse, where the threefold principles of the Macrocosm and Microcosm are clearly explained—it is my purpose in this place to briefly re-examine and recite those same matters for the sake of fresh memory and a more certain method.

We say, therefore, according to the doctrine of the High Priest **Moses**, that there are three primary principles of all things, and consequently of atmospheric phenomena: namely, **Darkness, Light, and the intermediate Spirit** which participates in both. Its "sublunary" part <note>The region below the moon; the earthly realm.</note> is more familiar with the earth and darkness, which is why it is subject to constant alterations. Its "empyrean" <note>The highest, most heavenly part of the universe, associated with pure fire and light.</note> and super-celestial part is observed to have a greater fellowship with the source of light, as it was the receptacle of the light created on the first day, over which the Spirit of God is said to have moved. Finally, its middle portion participates equally in both extremes. For this reason, the "sphere of equality"—which is the solar path, or rather the way through which the Sun passes daily—is recorded by the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, who often emphasized the mathematical and symbolic structure of the heavens.</note> to be drawn in its very center. From this, it is called **Ether**.

Moses called this worldly Spirit "the waters." The subject of these waters is "secondary matter," arising from the bowels of "formless darkness" (which is the primary or potential matter itself). The provider or beneficial "midwife" of this birth was that fiery power emanating from the Spirit of the Lord—that fiery love by means of which potential matter, hiding in the bowels of formless **chaos** or **hyle** <note>original: "hylæ" - A Greek term used by philosophers to refer to raw, unformed matter.</note>, was brought into the "act" of being water. 

**Water**, therefore, is the daughter of the hidden God (the darkness); **Light**, however, is the offspring of the divine power or splendor—that is, the manifest God. The midwife of both is the **Word** or **Divine Spirit**. Hence the wise man said: *God created the world from formless*—or as Jerome has it—*invisible matter* (Wisdom 11:18). And Saint Peter says: *That the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and through water by the word of God* (2 Peter 3:5). From this it is clear that the first matter of the world was formless matter, which was called "darkness" or the "dark abyss" by Moses; and its secondary matter was water, from which the heavens and the earth were later made. The worker or operator of all these miracles was the Word with the Spirit of the Lord (Psalm 33:6). And hence the Royal Psalmist <note>King David.</note> sings: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth.* 

Here, then, we have confirmed from Holy Scripture the "potential" or "privative" principle—namely, darkness or formless and invisible matter; which is why it is said that the earth was "void." We also have the "positive" principle—namely, Light, or the effect of divine power, by whose presence the invisible, formless, and potential matter was made visible and active. Finally, we have the intermediate subject or object of both: namely, **water**, from which the heavens and the earth were fabricated by the mediation of **form**.

Because of this, natural philosophers, when describing the breadth of all beings, place "Pure Act" <note>Pure form or God, possessing no material limitation.</note> without matter at the summit, and matter without form (namely, darkness) at the bottom. Everything in between is shown to be a mixture of form and matter: specifically, water mixed with life-giving light. For this reason, we conceived the origin of our **formal and material Pyramids**. <note>The author is famous for illustrating the universe as two overlapping pyramids: one of light descending from God, and one of darkness/matter ascending from the earth.</note> 

From these things, it is clear that **Earth** is nothing other than thick water and the "dregs" of the spirit remaining after its extraction from the formless chaos. **Air**, on the other hand, is universal water that is thin and subtle, or an invisible spirit extracted from chaos. Finally, the intermediate substance of water, participating in both extremes, is visible water—the sea, springs, and rivers. Because it is thicker and slower in its motion and heavier than air, it appears to have a commerce with the earth; but insofar as it is clear, mobile, and not as heavy as the earth, it seems to taste of the nature of air and stand apart from the laws of the earth. 

Therefore, when Saint Peter said *the heaven and the earth consisted of water and through water by the word of God*, he understood "heaven" as the universal air (the base of which is visible water) and by "earth" he seems to imply everything dark, opaque, and dense. The order of these principles is also best denoted by those "regular bodies" of Geometry, where the **Cube** is defined as the extreme and most ample body, because it is the first-born and contains the reason of the whole.

This body [the Cube] is held by the more occult philosophers to represent **Chaos**, or **hyle**, or opaque, dark, and formless matter, from whose lap or womb both light and water emerged—that is, the formal and material principles of all things. This is **PAN**, or universal nature, produced from formless chaos by a "Virgin birth." <note>A symbolic reference to nature arising spontaneously from the first matter through divine will.</note> When philosophers said that the **Tetrahedron** <note>A four-sided pyramid shape.</note> was the first-born from the cube, they meant that **Fire** (or the primary bright form) emerged from the immense darkness as if from the greatest and most opaque body. For then, formal light immediately appeared in the moist nature; then, I say, the Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters, imparting fiery vigor to them, which was followed by the completion of the first day of creation. And so, according to that saying of the wise man: *Wisdom was created before all things* (Ecclesiasticus 1:4)—that is, the divine light flashed out of the darkness before any other creature. King Solomon also seems to confirm this in these words: *Jehovah possessed Wisdom in the beginning of his way, before his works, before any time: before the beginning of the earth; when there were no abysses I was brought forth (says Wisdom), when there were no fountains, when God strengthened the clouds above, when he fitted the heavens I was there, when he established the circuit upon the*

Sect. I. Port. IV. Part I. Book I.

...upon the face of the abyss, when he established the heavens above, etc. Proverbs 8:22. <note>original: "superficie abyssi, quando firmabat coelos desuper"</note> And so the **hidden GOD** became the **manifest GOD** <note>original: "DEVS latens factus est DEVS patens." A central theme in Hermetic philosophy where the unknowable Creator reveals Himself through Light.</note>, the divine splendor of which produced a created light within the moist or watery nature. From this birth, therefore, we have the **Tetrahedron** <term>Tetrahedron: A four-sided triangular pyramid, associated in Platonic philosophy with the element of Fire.</term>, or the first fire, generated from the **Cube** <term>Cube: A six-sided solid, associated here with the "dark father" or the element of Earth.</term> of its dark father. Then, from the "bowels" of the Tetrahedron—that is, from the illuminated spirit—the **Dodecahedron** <term>Dodecahedron: A twelve-sided solid made of pentagons, associated by ancient philosophers with the Aether or the Heavens.</term> is extracted. For once the luminous spirit was created on the first day, the Heaven or the Firmament was created from its womb or matrix on the second day of creation, as Moses testifies. This Dodecahedron is formed from pentagonal surfaces, and for this reason (as I believe) heaven is called the **fifth essence** <note>The *Quinta Essentia* or Aether, a substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>, arguing that it is a fifth element distinct from those four sublunary ones. The work of the third day, however, is the gathering of the thick or sensible waters into the place designated for them by God; their symbol is the **Icosahedron** <term>Icosahedron: A twenty-sided solid, associated with the element of Water.</term>, from whose belly the air immediately flew forth, symbolized by the **Octahedron** <term>Octahedron: An eight-sided solid, associated with the element of Air.</term>; for water became air through a process of thinning. The remainder of the dark **Cube** settled into the earth, and thus it obtained the name of "fertile earth," which was previously called "void" by Moses. Therefore, according to the image of these three principles—namely, darkness, water, and light—the entire spirit of the world is divided into three elements, differing from one another in nature and disposition: namely, into Earth, the Sphere of Moisture, and Fire, as has been more than sufficiently explained in the second book of our *History of the Macrocosm*.

From these things explained here, a great discrepancy has arisen among the leaders of the ancient philosophers regarding the principles of natural things; nevertheless, their opinions do not seem to differ much from one another if we consider the matter a little more accurately. For **Thales of Miletus** placed Water as the principle of all things; **Anaximenes** said that infinite air was the cause of the existence of things (wherefore **Anaximander** even made air GOD). But **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary Persian prophet, often cited in Renaissance texts as a source of ancient "prisca theologia" or primordial wisdom.</note> thought that all things were made from fire or light, and the **Pythagoreans** said there was a single fire throughout the whole.

And certainly, as has been said, if we consider the matter well, we shall find that these men did not stray far from the path. For fire, first emerging from the darkness, suddenly revealed the invisible waters by its splendor; the subtle vastness of these waters is the airy spirit. Thus, both Thales and Anaximenes seem to agree in a certain way. Yet both of them explained nothing but the material or passive principle. But **Zoroaster**, preferring fire to the others, not without merit frequently called it the primary principle, inasmuch as it preceded moist matter, just as action precedes passion, or an act precedes the thing to be produced into action. And yet he himself erred in a way, since an active principle cannot exist except insofar as it relates to a passive principle.

Wherefore **St. Peter** said the heaven and earth were made of water and through water by means of the Word—that is, by the agent or the "first act." Hence, **Diogenes** spoke with more mature discourse concerning the principles of things, saying that air, possessing divine reason, is the principle of things: that is, the air or the created moist nature, and the divine light. It is as if he wished to say with Moses: the spirit of the Lord carried over the waters was, with the waters, the principle of created things. And **Zeno the Stoic**, being more cautious in his opinion and attempting to make his judgment on the principle firmer, says that the substance of Fire, converted through air into water, is the principle of all things. **Empedocles**, proceeding in a coarser manner, established the four elements as the principles of all things. Finally, the error of all these men in their judgment of principles was immense because they did not notice that the divine power, or the most holy Word, was a more ancient beginning than all of these. Indeed, if they had understood this with more mature meditation, they would have said with Zoroaster (equipped with *a priori* reasoning) <note>Reasoning from cause to effect.</note> that the divine light was the **Monad** <term>Monad: The "One," representing unity and the source of all being.</term> or primary author of all things, being the source and origin of acts and forms, by whose revelation the number **Dyad** <term>Dyad: The "Two," representing the first step into multiplicity or duality.</term> was produced—namely, the dark Monad (which was water) alongside the luminous Monad.

### CHAPTER IV.

->On the simple accidental principles of atmospheric phenomena—that is, on the origin of the two active qualities of nature, and how the two passive qualities (which we therefore call "simples of simples") are derived from them.<-

Regarding qualities of this kind and the reason for their origin, we have spoken quite extensively in Chapter 7, Book 1 of our *Physical History of the Macrocosm*. Here, however, we think it will be worth the effort to say a few things about them: namely, how their effects caused a progression from the aforementioned principles to the "principled" things <note>Things derived from the principles.</note>, involving both the thickening and thinning of elements. Through these qualities, mixtures (both imperfect and perfect) are gathered in a homogeneous way, digested, ripened, and fixed, and are led to the goal of perfection. Likewise, heterogeneous things are cut, separated, dissipated, driven away, and beaten back—a duty which **Heat** completes, insofar as it comes from the most noble and subtle spirit...

...is directly derived. Both heterogeneous and homogeneous things are also gathered, restrained, and condensed by cold; things of the same nature are rendered obscure and dark, in greater or lesser degrees, by a sticking together <note>original: "agglutinatione"</note>, just as is clearly and extensively explained in the place cited above. We say, therefore, that since two acting qualities are reckoned both from the Holy Scriptures and from the doctrine of the Philosophers, and just as many passive qualities arise from the intermediate actions of the agents, it will be ours to know: that just as heat is the immediate offspring of created light—and nothing other than the effect of the motion of light itself, or of the lucid or fiery air—so also, conversely, cold is the immediate progeny of darkness. Cold is excited and brought from potentiality into an action that is, as it were, involuntary and coerced by the power of heat springing from the lucid source. Thus, the life or act of the cold exists within the act of the heat, and its action is, as it were, accidental and not natural. Indeed, it is accustomed to be made and procreated by "creatance"—that is, by resisting. For just as the proper life of darkness is rest—as may be seen in the dark nature of the earth—so also the nature of cold, 
<margin>Cold †</margin>
springing as it does from the womb of darkness, is to rest and to be moved as little as possible, unless it is urged for the sake of resisting the assaults of heat. And from this it happens that, just as the empyrean <term>Empyrean: The highest, most celestial part of the heavens, thought to be composed of pure fire or light.</term> of the world and the fiery sphere of the elements is the hottest, so also the center of these—insofar as it is the dark seat of the earth and most remote from the circumference—is the coldest. For just as light is in every way opposed to darkness, both in appearance and quality, so also the qualities leaping forth from them are greatly contrary to each other. Whence the rays of light tending downward into the earth and water are observed to act continually by their heat in thinning <note>original: "subtiliando," the process of making something less dense or more "subtle."</note> that which is dense and dark. Therefore, to repel these actions, the earth and water immediately emit their cold vapors, stirred up by the heat, by means of which the forces of the pursuing heat are repressed and struck back.

But as for the origin of the two passive qualities, we describe the same thing in this place as was expressed in Chapter 7, Book 1 of the *History of the Physics of the Macrocosm* alleged above: namely, that from the meeting of the actions of the two aforesaid qualities—heat from the extreme fiery agent, and cold from the extreme earthy resistant—a third temperature or quality is procreated in the middle motion or the midpoint between these two opposite terms. This third quality participates in both the earthy and the fiery nature; hence it is neither intensely hot (for the sharpness of the heat is blunted by the force of the resisting cold) nor intensely cold (since in the middle path, the vigor of the resisting coldness is depressed by the pursuing heat). Whence it is necessary that this procreated quality be some third thing, and consequently neither hot and dry, nor cold and dry, but an intermediate between these two natures. That is, it is a meeting of two things producing a middle moisture <note>original: "medium humidum"</note>. For the subtle spirit of the world, by the opposite actions of such agent and resistant qualities, passes into a moist nature in the middle by a kind of homogeneous application. For in this way the material or passive substance of the world was produced—namely, by the action of uncreated light and the resistance of deformed darkness. By the effect of these contrary actions, the universal moist nature or water was produced, from which the heaven and the earth were afterward procreated. This, then, is the reason that the moist nature of the world is passive, and consequently that its quality also suffers <note>In this context, "suffers" or "passive" means it is acted upon by outside forces rather than being the force itself.</note>, as those things which are produced by the effects of the active qualities of a double condition; and so by its nature, it is apt to suffer the actions of both cold and heat. For we are taught by experience that just as it is the nature of heat to thin and dissipate moisture, and even to summon it away from those places where it is, so also from the region of cold it is the office of cold to condense, gather, and constrain moisture, to draw it back down toward the center, and to retain it in the lowest places. Again, in the middle region of the air, clouds are condensed and united by cold, just as they are dissipated into air or rain by the faculty of heat. Thus, we can see more clearly than light that just as the quality of moisture is produced by the mutual action and resistance of the primary qualities, so also it is ordained to suffer the action of both. Hence it is that, just as the two aforesaid qualities are primary and were produced into the world immediately with light and water, so they are not unaptly called "simple qualities" by Artetius <note>Likely referring to Artephius, a famous medieval alchemist and author of *The Secret Book*.</note>, just as both moisture and dryness are called "simple" by the simples, because they are produced from the mutual actions of those very simples. For dryness in its nature is nothing except in respect to moisture, since where moisture is absent, there dryness is said to abound. And for this reason, dryness is rightly defined as being nothing other than the absence of moisture. Therefore, just as the natural position of moisture is between earth and fire, or darkness and light, so also the seat of dryness is in either extreme: namely, in the earth or darkness, where the effect of heat (which must necessarily concur for the generation of moisture) is most absent; or in the fire, or primary light, where the resistance of cold (whose power is also required for the essence of moisture) is absent. And in this way, the four primary qualities of things were produced, from whose ordinations the various elements in the world are procreated, as we shall show more extensively below. Moreover, Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna established these qualities as the primary
->principles of their medical Art.<-

## CHAPTER V.

### On the progression in Nature that occurred from these primary principles to the structure of the three Elements: which are the secondary principles of natural things.

Having produced these simple qualities, and those derived from them by the aforementioned principles of Nature, the motion of nature then immediately tends toward the generation of the secondary principles, which they call elements. In this limit of simplicity, Nature seems to rest in its absolute fabrication of the world, so that in such a state it might remain without any evident change or alteration until the very end. However, those things which follow these in the order of nature—pertaining both to the generation of a perfectly mixed body and to its corruption—are subject to daily changes and alterations in this sublunary <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, the region below the orbit of the Moon, which was traditionally thought to be the only place where change and decay occur.</note> world, and they can never rest long in the same state. These are called "meteors" <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and clouds, not just falling stars.</note> or "imperfectly mixed" things, which we have not unadvisedly made into "tertiary principles," as was declared in its place in Part 3, Section 1, Portion 2 of the *Physiological Discourse of Both Worlds*, and as will be more copiously explained below. It was concerning these principles subject to change, as well as those simple and least corruptible ones, that the Wise Man <note>A common reference to King Solomon, the traditional author of Ecclesiastes.</note> understood when he spoke in these words: *One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever* <note>Ecclesiastes 1:4</note>, arguing from this that the elements are immutable—that is, they are not to be resolved back into their primary principles—but that all "Generable" things (such as meteors and the things procreated from them) are subject to alterations.

Therefore, just as three principles presented themselves in the first moment of the world's creation—namely Darkness (or Chaos), Light, and Water—so also in the production of these secondary principles, three parts of the said universal water, distinct from one another in nature and quality, are seen to concur. Each of these has a very close relationship to one of the aforementioned primary principles. The highest portion of this moist sublunary nature is benevolently "enkindled" by the act of light and its heat; and since heat is excited by the vehement motion of light (for light is more mobile than all things, as you will find abundantly in Chapter 1, Book 1 of our *History of the Macrocosm* <note>original: "Macrocosmo historia". This refers to Fludd’s magnum opus, "Utriusque Cosmi Historia".</note>), and its nature is to thin and disperse the moist nature, it therefore drives the moisture of the waters of that place downward from its own region. From this, it happens that that place becomes very dry. 

Furthermore, that moist vapor so driven downward is naturally denied the ability to tend toward the dark place of the earth, because it participates in the heat of light, which is in every way contrary to the terrestrial darkness and its coldness. Thus it happens that between these two extremes, a very vast sphere of moisture is gathered, participating in some way in both. From this, it follows that the base of this sphere is thickened and rendered visible because of its commerce and proximity with the earth, and it borrows its cold disposition from the earth. Thus, that portion of this sphere is called "cold and moist," just as, conversely, the part nearer to the lucid or fiery orb is very thin and not as moist as the middle portion, which is nonetheless called "moist and hot" along with the whole invisible portion.

<insert>
And it is from this that Philosophers, both ancient and modern, have divided that sphere into two distinct elements, which they made into Water and Air. But my purpose in this discourse leads me to consider these two as nothing other than a single "Moist Element," which we call the Sphere of Moisture. In this way, we may better arrange these three principles according to the pattern and order of those first three. For Moses did not say, "He divided the air from the water," but rather "He divided the waters from the waters" <note>Genesis 1:6</note>, etc. We therefore align this sphere of moisture with the created waters; and just as in the first creation the Spirit of the Lord (or Fiery Love) was carried over the waters, so also the lucid orb (or Fire) is carried over this sphere. Finally, the Earth, which is the lowest of the secondary principles, is compared to Darkness—indeed, it is the gathering of that very darkness into the center of the universe. From this, Cold has its offspring ready in its bowels to attack any invasion of its son, the Heat of Light.
</insert>

Thus far, then, we have reached the completion of the structure of the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" is the "Great World" or the universe as a whole, often contrasted with the "Microcosm" or man.</note>: namely, from the circumference of deformed shadows divided from the infinite darkness (out of which the moist or watery matter of the world emerged) all the way to the center of the periphery, in which all darkness settled.

But lest you think these things were fashioned by me and invented from my own brain—these things which have now been brought forth by us concerning the production of the first principles and the procreation of the primordial qualities (which serve the principles themselves like handmaidens), and also concerning the origin of the three Elements from them as secondary principles—I wish for you to observe with a diligent gaze and a somewhat more accurate speculation how these assertions of mine are defended by the consensus of the Sacred Scriptures, as well as by those skilled in Theosophy and the mysteries of the Kabbalists, and how they seem to be supported as if by Atlantean shoulders <note>A reference to Atlas holding up the heavens; here meaning his theories are supported by massive, ancient authorities.</note>.

### C H A P T E R VI.

**A**lthough these three principles of ours, and those things which proceed from them, are sufficiently demonstrated from what has already been said and from several passages of Holy Writ, nevertheless, to fundamentally remove the objections of both the envious and the ignorant who contradict them, we shall produce certain other testimonies from the Holy Bible to confirm these primary principles. *He reveals (says Job) the foundations out of darkness, and brings the deadly shadow into light. Job 12:22.* By this speech, he seems to argue that God led the waters—which (according to the opinion of St. Peter cited above) were the matter or subject of the world's structure—out of the darkness. Thus, the water, which he called a "deadly shadow" insofar as it was destitute of all form or appearance, was brought back into light with its splendor now made manifest; that is, it took on the form of waters. Hence Moses said, *The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters.* Here, therefore, Job recognizes that darkness is the subject of the world's matter, and that God himself, or the divine light, is the efficient cause of so great a miracle. For darkness was the "first matter," the "revealed foundation" or water was the "second matter" brought from potentiality into act, and light was the formal principle—which is indeed declared by its effect. For the further manifestation of the matter, it is said, *And he brings the deadly shadow into light. Job 26:7.* <note>The author uses "deadly shadow" to describe the primordial, unformed state of the universe before God's light gave it shape.</note> Furthermore, in the same author we read, *God extends the North over the empty and void*, arguing from this that He extended a visible and actual spirit in the Northern region, where there was nothing but shapeless darkness. And indeed, it should be noted that the cold winds seem to breathe from this region; these are the offspring of darkness, due to the gloominess of the place. Hence he made mention not of the South, nor of the East or West, but only of the North. But more on this below. Finally, to roll the same stone again <note>A Latin idiom meaning to labor at the same task or repeat an effort.</note>, we find in the Book of Wisdom, *Wisdom 11:18*, that the hand of the Almighty created the world out of formless matter (or as Jerome prefers, from invisible matter). From this it appears that the first matter of the world was formless and invisible—that is, dark—from which the world was nonetheless fashioned, brought into act by the power and, as it were, the "hands" of God—that is, by the appearance of ineffable light. Here, then, we have formless matter as the first and potential principle; we also have that matter produced into act, which according to St. Peter was water; and we have God the operator, who is the father and source of light. It follows that by His appearance or lucid power (or as the author speaks in this thread of discourse, by His "hand") He operated as the formal principle and first act. Moreover, in Deuteronomy we find these things written: *Jehovah spoke to your whole congregation on the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness with a great voice, etc. Deut. 5:22.* <note>The text cites verse 28, but the quote corresponds to Deuteronomy 5:22.</note> Here the Prelate <note>Likely referring to Moses or the biblical authority.</note> seems to hint at darkness by "thick darkness," at the waters by "the cloud," and at light by "the fire." But let us hear for a moment what those more skilled in the Cabala <note>Jewish mystical tradition involving the interpretation of the Hebrew alphabet and divine emanations.</note> say concerning these beginnings of things. These men indeed mention a double <term>Aleph</term> <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, signifying unity or God.</note>, that is, a double species of unity, one of which they call the *Dark Aleph*, the other the *Bright Aleph*. Yet they made each of these a symbol of divinity: for by the *Dark Aleph* they signified the "Hidden God" or the potential principle, in which state they believed God to be before He shone forth from the darkness for the creation of the world. And this is the very thing they intended by "divine power." Of such a unity or Monad <note>The number one; a single, indivisible unit representing the source of all things.</note>, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Egyptian sage thought to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus, central to Renaissance alchemy and magic.</note> makes mention when he speaks in these words: *The Monad generates a monad, and reflected its heat into itself.* and in the Holy Page: *He made darkness his secret place, and surrounded his tabernacle with very black waters and thick clouds. Psalm 18:11.* The Cabalists therefore estimate this divine power, thus contracted in the dark abyss, to be as if idle and remaining without action, or, as they say, "looking at nothing"; and for that reason it is called by them <term>Ein</term> <note>original: אִין; a Cabalistic term meaning "Nothing" or "The Infinite" before manifestation.</note>, that is, "Nothing," or "non-being," or "no-end," because we, being so impoverished in our understanding of divine things, judge of those things which do not appear no differently than of those things which do not exist. But where it has so extended itself that it becomes something and truly subsists, then they assert the *Dark Aleph* is converted into the *Bright*. They hold the *Bright Aleph*, therefore, to be Wisdom, the "first creature" as the Book of Sirach says in *Chapter 1*; or the Divine Word sent forth from the Father, at whose presence the darkness fled, *according to that saying of David in Psalm 77:16: The depths feared at the presence of the Lord and were troubled.* The presence of this Word (according to John) was the light of the world, *by which and through which all things were made, and without it nothing. John 1.* The heavens and the earth consist of water and through water (as St. Peter says), and as the Psalmist testifies, the heavens were made firm with all their powers; and the foundations were revealed out of darkness, as was said before, and brought forth into light. And in the Royal Prophet <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> we find that in the splendor of the divine essence the clouds vanished, and the springs of water were made visible, and the foundations of the round world were revealed. *Psalm 18:15.* Here, then, we see that those more skilled in Cabalistic science recognize a "dark principle," in which they acknowledge the divine power to have dwelt under the symbol of the *Dark Aleph*, and also a "bright principle," under the symbol of the *Bright Aleph*, by means of which they confess all things were created. Afterward, he makes mention of the act from the first act, or the "informing form," namely the holy splendor, at whose command the elements were produced, while the heavy and dark matter, which was the murky dross of the waters, was driven back to the center of the periphery. Finally, Plato himself recognized that a certain primary species, invisible and formless, was the "first matter" of all things.

that is, he constricts and condenses both the clouds and the waters, according to that saying of the royal Psalmist alleged above, *he made darkness his secret place, and with very black waters and thick clouds he surrounded his tabernacle*, from which it is clear that the clouds are made very black and condensed by the cold which proceeds from the hidden God, inasmuch as his hut is a thick cloud. From this it happens that when God intends to hide and conceal himself in darkness, he then uses his cold breath, with which he is accustomed to condense. But this is also best signified by David, where it is read:

> That God gives snow like wool, scatters frost like ashes, and casts down his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold? Psalm 147:16.

From these things it is clear that cold is, as it were, the breath of the divine power—that is, of the hidden God—since with such a breath he produces snow and ice. Furthermore, on the opposite side, heat comes from the presence of the divine splendor—that is, from the Word or the bright emanation from God in the darkness. Whence it is clear that just as coldness is a congealing quality exhaled from the hidden God, so its opposite, heat, is as it were an essential essence immediately poured forth from the manifest God as he reveals himself from the darkness. Which is indeed evidently declared from those things said above.

> God (says the Psalmist) gives snow like wool, and disposes frost like ashes, he casts down his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold? Psalm 147:16, 17.

But just as both of these simple qualities proceed from the divine breath (whence they are active agents), so also two other secondary qualities are observed to emanate from these, produced by the various changes of the moist nature which it undergoes due to the variety of actions of the opposing simple qualities. Thus water, or spirit, or flowing vapor, in the presence of intense cold, becomes accidentally dry, as may be seen in ice, snow, and hail. Again, that same accidental dryness is reduced back into its natural humidity by the presence of intense heat, as is explained more clearly than light itself to those who observe diligently in the testimonies cited above.

### *In which the progression of these simple principles from divine power is explained by both Arithmetic and Geometric demonstration.*

The nature of the order in the progression of the aforementioned principles can be most aptly delineated and explained both by the successive movement of the Arithmeticians and that of the Geometers into a fourfold multitude. For in the first place, just as in arithmetic nothing is argued or signified before the expression of unity, so when unity is expressed, it seems to emerge out of nothing. But indeed, once unity is expressed, immediately by its light or potential presence, a certain unity comes to be considered, from which this manifest <term>monad</term><note>A "monad" refers to a single, indivisible unit; in this philosophy, it represents the primary unity of God or the first point of creation.</note> originally progressed, just as a man (though invisible) is included in a human act. Therefore, Nothing, or the potential unity, which was unseen before the revelation of the actual unity, is revealed by the presence of the bright or actual unity—not unlike how a father is known through a certain relationship to his son. Thus the darkness, from which the primary light emerged, is uncovered and indicated by the emergence of that light from its very bowels. Whence it happens that by the revelation of the One, the source of that unity is immediately considered, which produces a <term>Dyad</term><note>The "Dyad" (dualism or the number two) represents the first departure from unity toward multiplicity.</note> or duality, which number the Pythagoreans quite deliberately called the "number of confusion," inasmuch as it intends two extremes with no intervening medium. But for all perfection, three terms are required: namely, *from which*, the *middle* or *through which*, and *to which*. Hence, following the example of the three persons in the most Holy Trinity, a third or middle thing must be elicited from both the potential unity and that bright unity. And so, by the action and passion of these extremes, the universal <term>Pan</term><note>In this context, "Pan" refers to the totality of the created natural world, often personified in Renaissance philosophy as a "Universal Spirit."</note> was produced, or the airy spirit, or the moist nature so-called, because it is more inclined to receive the dark effects of its cold parent, and seems to become wet by liquefying from the warm act of light; although in itself it is neither cold nor hot, nor moist nor dry, but is moderate in its nature, being a participant in both the cold of the dark extreme and the heat of the other bright extreme, yet uniform in its Being, as indicated by us below. We have, therefore, through the emanation of the bright unity out of the darkness, three things manifested and detected: namely, the light itself or the first wisdom of creatures (as <term>Ecclesiasticus</term><note>A book of the Biblical Apocrypha/Deuterocanon, also known as Sirach.</note> says), the darkness, and the invisible or spiritual waters (for according to the testimony of Paul <insert>↓</insert> visible things are procreated from invisible ones). But truly, since those spiritual waters are like <term>Mercury</term><note>In alchemy and natural philosophy, Mercury represents the fluid, changeable principle that can take on different forms.</note> in their readiness to put on the forms of either extreme, their extreme part near the darkness is most fit to incline toward their disposition, so that they are condensed by the cold of the earth or darkness into visible water and a vaporous nature, and they even desire to imbibe and retain the quality of cold more or less. Conversely, their other extremity, closer to the source of light or fire, is more fit for a fiery disposition, and because it is imbued more or less by the act of coldness, it seems to taste somewhat of humidity. Hence it is that because of the division of this creature of a double nature, the ancient Philosophers made two distinct elements, namely air and water; both of which we, following the doctrine of the wise <term>Artesius</term><note>Likely referring to a specific authority on natural philosophy or a variant spelling/pseudonym used in meteorological debates of the era.</note>, have compressed into a single sphere, which we have called the sphere of humidity because (as we said above) it is originally familiar with coldness, whose impressions heat makes somewhat moist by its action. Thus, therefore, the Arithmetic demonstration shall stand: 1. 2. 3. 4. These are called <term>meteors</term> <note>original: "meteora".
