Thus it is necessary, according to the teachings of the philosophers, that the final simple principles (the "simples derived from simples") are the immediate sources of smoke, vapors, and exhalations. These, in turn, are the closer origins of meteors. Since these are "imperfectly mixed" bodies, they follow the same progression of nature toward the procreation of all composite (that is, "perfectly mixed") bodies. Thus it happened that in the circuit of nature, from darkness, water, and light—acting as primary principles—the three elements immediately arose: namely earth, the sphere of moisture (both the visible kind called water and the invisible kind of an airy nature), and Fire. Up to this point, the progression has moved toward the complete production of the material and formal world. Because of the simplicity of their substance, the structures of this world will remain firm and unchanged in the same state until the final Day of Judgment. From this it follows that the elements are the simple principles from which nature proceeds as a starting point toward the <term>generation</term> <note>The process of coming into being or being born.</note> of any composite or mixed creature; they are also the end point toward which nature tends in its progress from generation to <term>corruption</term> <note>The process of decaying or breaking down into constituent parts.</note>. The "middle way" between these points is the meteor—either growing (like the Moon) during generation, or decreasing and scattering the parts of the composite during corruption. Thus, in generation, the starting point is the elements and the end point is the "perfectly mixed" body—such as the human body, which is our primary focus in this section.

Therefore, it is necessary that in the corruption of a composite body, the starting point is conversely that "perfectly mixed" body; likewise, the point toward which nature veers in the act of corrupting is the simple element. From this element, nature can then progress again toward the generation of either perfect or imperfect mixtures. Beyond the elements, there is no further progression of corruption because of the simplicity of those primary subjects. The intermediate term—the "pathway between"—is the meteor. Since it is impossible for any progression to occur from one extreme to another without a medium intervening, it is necessary that between the simple natures (where there is no mixture) and composite bodies (where mixture is perfect), an "imperfect mixture" must intervene. This is called a "meteor" based on the location of its procreation, whether in the heavens or on the earth. Consequently, it follows that both life and death, as well as health and disease, are brought about through the mediation of meteors. Just as a meteor is the middle point between perfect generation and complete corruption, so too is the movement in a living creature a withdrawal of health toward the goal of corruption or dissolution (which resides in the elements). Thus, disease is like a reduction of a healthy, generated thing back toward the nature of a meteor—that is, toward the "middle path" of dissolution. Therefore, that healthy nature which was once a "perfect mixture" has now become "imperfectly mixed," since its nature is diseased and positioned as if on the middle road between the point of complete generation and that of absolute destruction. A human creature at this middle station is equally capable of moving backward toward the point of health from which it withdrew, or moving forward toward the extreme limit of destruction (which is to pass into the nature of the elements, especially air, from which it first arose). Thus, the more nature tends in its motion beyond the middle point toward simplicity, the more the composite creature gradually approaches its end; but by taking the opposite path, it begins to grow stronger and recover. In this matter, we must diligently observe that the conjunction of a "worst meteor"—that is, a nature that is dissolutive and destructive—with the middle nature of a thing that had reached complete composition, is the cause of death or destruction, unless it receives aid from a "salutary meteor" through divine assistance, as will be explained more broadly and clearly below. ## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the material or substantial cause of meteors; what the Author’s opinion on this is, and how it appears to differ from the view of the ancient philosophers in this matter.

The matter of meteors (says Aristotle, along with the other philosophers of his sect) is clearly the fumes arising from water and earth. These fumes they divide into a twofold nature: either **vapor** or **exhalation**. They assertively claim that vapor is hot and moist, aquatic, and non-flammable, arising from earth and water; whereas exhalation is hot and dry, terrestrial, flammable, and summoned forth from the earth. They seem to show by the following reasoning why the remaining elements—namely fire and air—do not yield such thick fumes as those which constitute the substance of meteors: they argue that those higher elements are much more subtle in their substance than fumes, and therefore they believe that air and fire cannot produce such fumes. 

Such are their views. But it shall be our task to destroy these arguments using their own mouths. For every one of them acknowledges in his writings that air, through condensation, becomes water, and much more so becomes **Vapor**, which by its nature and constitution stands between pure air and visible water. Furthermore, they acknowledge—and we have experienced—that this same water is reduced into earth by thickening. Does not Aristotle also refute himself with his own mouth when he says: <term>The stellar body is the denser part of its own sphere</term>? <note>original: "Corpus stellare esse densiorem sui orbis partem". Aristotle argued that stars were simply denser concentrations of the celestial ether.</note> That is to say, a visible substance fashioned from condensed, invisible ethereal spirit. From this, it seems possible to infer that a comet, a cloud, or any other meteor can be brought forth from the condensation of the air.

Therefore, this assertion of the ancients is weak—that air cannot be the immediate cause of vapors because it is more subtle than vapor. For in the seventh book of my physics in the <term>History of the Macrocosm</term> <note>A reference to Robert Fludd’s own work, "Utriusque Cosmi Historia" (1617), where he discusses the origins of the universe.</note>, where the generation of clouds is discussed, we demonstrated by infallible arguments that clouds are made immediately from the composition and condensation of air by opposing winds. Consequently, that cloud—as a substance midway between water and air—takes its origin not from the watery extreme, but from the aerial one as its primary principle. Whence we say that the air brings forth the matter of the cloud from its own womb, and by the operation of the divine power, administers it centrally to the world by way of rain, snow, or hail. 

We also gather this from these passages of the Holy Bible (the fountain of all truth, neglecting the writings of the Heathens in this matter). In the Pentateuch of Moses, we find written: <term>Jehovah will open to you his best treasure, the heavens, by giving rain to your land in its time. Deut. 28:12.</term> And GOD himself, addressing Job, says: <term>Have you entered into the treasures of the snow, or have you seen the treasures of the hail? Ibid. 38:22.</term> And a little later he continues: <term>Who is the father of rain? Or who begot the drops of dew? From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven? The instruments that GOD uses for the production of such meteors are His winds—I mean the angelic winds of Jehovah. # On the Material Cause of Meteors.

...are they deprived [of their senses]? Nay, indeed, in our own times it has been observed that several people from the multitude, staying in the fields during stormy and sweltering weather, and holding the effects of thunder and lightning in contempt and derision, were suddenly killed and struck dead by the spirit of that same sun, while others among them escaped the danger. Among these was a certain woman, moved by a horrendous audacity and unspeakable obstinacy toward God the Creator, who, while scorning the thunder and lightning, turned her backside <note>original: "anum"</note> in derision toward that quarter of the world from which the sound was coming; she was suddenly struck by lightning, and the member offered in contempt was miserably torn asunder in every part. What do the wretched philosophers of this world respond to these things? Do you believe that this creature, so possessed of divine reason, received its life from earthly and watery smoke? Is it not said everywhere in the sacred scriptures that *thunder is the voice of GOD*? <margin>Psalm 103:4 <note>In many English Bibles, this is Psalm 104:4.</note></margin> Psalm 103:4. Are not the *winds called the Angels of Jehovah, doing his pleasure*? Has it not been said, *that GOD has placed thick clouds as his chariot, who walks upon the wings of the wind, and makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire; at whose rebuke the waters fled, and from the voice of whose thunder they hastened their flight*? What? Is it to be thought that such wonders of GOD consist in the accidental generation of watery vapor and earthly exhalation? Far be it from a Christian man, aware of the divine mind, to believe this.

But so that we may approach somewhat closer to the empty trifles of the vain philosophers, we shall examine a little more strictly their opinions: first concerning the origin of winds, then the generation of clouds, then afterward the procreation of fiery <term>meteors</term> <note>In this period, "meteors" included any atmospheric phenomenon, such as lightning, comets, or rainbows.</note> in the highest region of the air, and finally the beginnings of hail, snow, and ice.

### CHAP. III.

->*In which the trifling vanity and improbability of the opinions of the ancient philosophers regarding the origin of meteors is discussed.*<-

To begin with the opinion of the ancient philosophers concerning the origin of winds, they seem to hesitate and disagree among themselves in this matter. Those who embrace the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, whose theories dominated natural philosophy for centuries.</note> sect and uphold the opinion of Aristotle in this regard define wind as a hot and dry exhalation, difficult to ignite, raised as far as the middle region of the air. From there, it is driven downward by the cold of that place, and then, striving upward again by the inclination of its own nature, it moves laterally over the earth in the lowest region of the air—partly due to its own lightness and partly because of other exhalations encountered from below. They say it agitates and fans this air so that it does not rot, as it were, through perpetual sluggishness. Others (among whom I name <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer.</note>) wish for the wind to be a wave of air, with an uncertain overflow of motion. <margin>Vitruvius, Book 1, ch. 6.</margin> Vitruvius, Book 1, ch. 6. [This occurs] when heat encounters moisture, and the onset of the heat turns the force of the blowing spirit [into wind]. And the first group, who support the Aristotelian sect, say that the material cause of wind is a breath or smoke or hot and dry exhalation, having in itself nothing of the "fatness" <note>This "fatness" or "oiliness" was thought to be the fuel for atmospheric fires.</note> that can be ignited; because of this lack of fatness, it can neither be set on fire, nor reduced to a mist by condensation, and much less thickened into a cloud. And they said that this emerges from the earth, although <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist.</note> says that some winds breathe out from the waters.

But let us now ask what these Peripatetics (who seem to so excel in the inspection of nature) feel about the origin of a Comet: for they say this arises from an earthly smoke or exhalation—thick, fatty, and viscous, and made of densely compacted parts—which is raised by the power of the stars from the bowels of the earth into the supreme region of the air, and there dilated, set on fire, and inflamed, etc. Thus, there is this difference between the windy exhalation and that which generates the comet: namely, that the former is light, hot, and dry, and difficult to ignite, as it has no fatness in it; while the latter is earthly, thick, fatty, and viscous, made of densely compacted and easily ignitable parts.

Therefore, these Peripatetics fall into <term>Scylla while wishing to avoid Charybdis</term> <note>A classical metaphor for trying to avoid one mistake only to fall into a worse one.</note>, for in the description of the generation of both meteors, they show both materials to be false and not at all true. For what is the reason that one exhalation—though it is not fit for inflammation, and consequently less opposed to cold, and though it is lighter in its substance than the other—is nevertheless hindered in its ascent by the force of the cold in the middle region of the air, and is beaten back down to the place from which it was raised? Yet, nonetheless, the other exhalation—which is thick, fatty, and ignitable, and consequently most opposite to the cold of the middle air, and less suited for upward motion due to its heavy thickness—has a path through the middle region of the air into the highest region without any opposition from the cold? How poorly these things agree, and how adverse they are to the laws of Philosophy! Namely, that heavy and more compact things should ascend more easily by natural appetite and tend upward by their nature than those that are light? And then, that those things further removed from inflammation in their nature should be more infested and attacked by cold than those that are ignitable and of a purely fiery disposition? Hence it is clear that when they say the coldness of the middle region of the air is the cause of the impediment to the ascent of the windy exhalation (since it is hot and dry but not ignitable), they are in every...

### Section I. Portion IV. Part I. Book II.

...in such a way that they contradict themselves, denying the very logic for the generation of a comet that they have presented elsewhere. For the material cause (as the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking about the "Peripatos" or covered walkways of the Lyceum in Athens.</note> themselves maintain) is a hot and dry exhalation, yet one that is flammable, thick, and compact—and consequently less suited for ascending and penetrating into the <term>middle region of the air</term><note>In ancient and medieval science, the atmosphere was divided into three layers: the lowest (warm), the middle (extremely cold), and the highest (hot, near the sphere of fire).</note>. Furthermore, in what Aristotle says—that a hot, dry, flammable exhalation, being very compact and viscous, can pierce the middle region of the air and reach the highest region—he again seems to oppose himself, asserting elsewhere that a windy exhalation cannot penetrate that middle region because of the local cold. Thus, in asserting both extremes, he and his followers seem to imply a negation of both; for what they are eager to affirm in one case, they are forced to deny in the other.

Furthermore, how frivolous is that reasoning for the "lateral" (sideways) motion of wind over the earth—namely, that it occurs partly due to its own lightness and partly because of other exhalations encountered from below. This is proven false by the fact that winds, during the time they blow, are stable; they do not blow spirally or circularly from every direction at the same instant. They are stable, I say—that is, they persist firmly from one quarter of the world to another. Such perseverance could hardly occur if the cause of lateral motion were of the sort they recount. Finally, what our own opinion is regarding the material origin of the winds, we shall explain more broadly below, where we shall also describe the errors of the Peripatetics more clearly.

But now let us look for a moment at what these Peripatetics feel regarding the generation of clouds and rain. They define a cloud as a vapor raised from the earth into the middle region of the air, where they think it is hemmed in by the force of the local cold, frozen, and driven hither and thither by the various motions of the winds. If this were indeed probable, we would perceive clouds being procreated in the air more frequently in the summer time than in the winter. For in summer, common and visual experience seems to indicate that springs, rivers, torrents, ponds, and lakes are reduced into vapors by the power of heavenly heat (as they themselves have admitted) and dispersed everywhere in the air—although the matter stands far differently than they supposed, as we shall declare in its proper place. And who among the Aristotelians would deny that the air is far thicker in its summer state than in its winter state, due to the abundance of vapors which (according to their opinion) it receives from the water and the earth? This air is only later condensed by winter cold and reduced into clouds. From this it follows that the ponds, lakes, torrents, and earthly springs which the summer sun exhausted are filled again in the winter time; and yet, clouds and rain are sent down abundantly from the air into the earth and water at that very time when the air is thinnest in its substance. I am speaking now according to their opinion, although we think otherwise and shall show something else hereafter. 

But let us proceed: if vapor visibly gushing from the earth or water is the cause of clouds, from where, I ask, does it happen that the <term>South Wind</term><note>original: "Australis"</note> is a constant extractor or gatherer of vapors, since at its blowing, rain clouds are usually procreated in great numbers? And vice versa, when the <term>North Wind</term><note>original: "Borea"</note> blows, are we not taught that snowy and haling clouds are generated? What? Is it not easier for these winds, by their opposing blasts, to compress the thin substance of the air into a vapor—or rather a cloudy mass—and then into a cloud, thicker or thinner according to the violence of the compressors, than for them to extract vapors from the thick and corporeal earth and water, which must then be condensed by the cold of the middle air region? Why then do the other winds not perform this same thing, if this is accomplished not by the nature of the winds, but by the origin and motion of vapor? 

Furthermore, if it were granted by me that the vapors of the earth and water passed into the nature or substance of the air, it does not follow from this that either thick water or compact earth are the beginning of air. Rather, it follows that both thick water and earth are made from subtle and invisible water—of which kind are air and <term>ether</term>—and not that subtle water comes from them, as St. Paul testifies in these words previously alleged:

<margin>Hebrews 11</margin>
> *By faith we acknowledge that it has always been so dealt with the world through the word, so that from those things which could not be seen were made those things which can be seen. Hebrews 11.* <note>original: "Per fidem agnoscimus, quod semper ita actum sit cum mundo per verbum, vt ex iis quæ videri non poterant fuerint ea quæ possunt videri."</note>

For in the natural proceeding of things, creation does not happen from the "posterior" (the later/complex) but from the "prior" (the earlier/simple); things that have a beginning or mixtures are not made from other complex things, but from simple things and first principles. Therefore, thick water and earth were made from air as their proximate matter, but air was not made from them in turn. For we have it confirmed in Genesis that heaven was first instituted and established in firm harmony before any mention was made of dry land or thick water. 

We say, therefore, that vaporous matter—such as cloudy smoke—is like a medium between a cloud (or thick water) and the air. Indeed, we recognize air to be the *starting point* <note>original: "terminum à quo"</note> from which vaporous matter proceeded, just as the watery cloud is the *endpoint* <note>original: "terminus ad quem"</note> toward which it progresses by thickening. And indeed, since it is certain that the word of GOD is the hidden operator of these things (as is explained clearly enough in the places cited before and to be alleged below), it is certain that just as clouds were produced in an abstruse manner by that Divine Wisdom—which was the "Beginning" according to the testimony of Solomon and St. John—so vapor immediately begins its motion and act from the first material principle. This principle is more fit, because of its simplicity, to receive the actions of such an abstruse source, which undoubtedly does not begin its motions from the "posterior" (since it is itself the first of all creatures) but from the "prior." From this it is clear that it acts upon the air to produce cloudy smoke, inasmuch as air was prior to thick water or earth. Finally, as pertains to the origin of clouds, we have explained that abundantly in Book 7, Chapter 4 of our *History of the Macrocosm*, where the generation of clouds is discussed; there we demonstrated that it is caused by the compression of air, and not by the extraction of vapors from the earth and water. There I also produced an infallible argument, derived from my own practice and experience, for the better confirmation of this our opinion—

# On the Material Cause of Atmospheric Phenomena.

...we have brought forth: therefore, I would wish to refer those of you who desire to be somewhat more precise in the investigation of such matters to that part of our work. Furthermore, you will find me, God willing, expanding somewhat more on this same subject in the following pages. What has been said concerning the generation of a cloud can also be said concerning the origin of hail and snow, since the <term>Philosophers</term><note>Meaning the followers of Aristotle and the scholastic tradition.</note> have imagined that both these <term>meteors</term><note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon (rain, snow, wind, etc.), not just falling stars.</note> are formed from hot and moist vapor. They claim the cause of the freezing of hail and snow is the cold surrounding the vaporous matter, which penetrates it due to the variety of the subject, and thickens it by expelling the heat. Although we see a visible difference in the form of each, they nevertheless attribute the same material and form (or active quality) to both. Therefore, as far as the origin of this material is concerned, we say that it is the same as that of a cloud; consequently, we affirm that it does not originate from the earth or the water, but is "brought to birth" from the womb of the air by divine power and will. We maintain that the northern winds, stirred by the divine spirit, are the causes of freezing: for, according to the <term>Psalmist</term><note>Referring to the author of the Psalms in the Bible.</note>, *God gives snow like wool, and scatters the frost like ashes; who can stand before His cold?* (Psalm 147:16). And Job says, *By the breath of the mighty God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen* (Job 37:9). And there it is again implied that this comes from the North wind. But concerning these things, we shall speak elsewhere in their proper place.

Finally, what has been said regarding the material origin of a comet must also be said concerning the matter of any "simple ignited meteor" (such as shooting stars): namely, that according to its substance, it is procreated from the compression of the fiery part of the air itself, and not from exhalations springing up and rising from the earth, as will be shown more clearly below.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Where the wondrous nature and arrangement of the air is clearly discussed.*<-

<margin>What is Air?</margin>
If, therefore, it is asked by the curious: what is the material origin of atmospheric phenomena—or of all things "mixed," whether perfectly or imperfectly—or what is their immediate cause derived from simple substances? We say that it is the substance of the air itself, altered from its simplicity. For this reason, <term>Anaximenes</term><note>A pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 585–528 BC) who taught that air was the primary substance of the universe.</note> did not blush to boldly assert, and not without foresight, that air was the cause of all things. Indeed, air is such an ancient principle that <term>Anaximander</term><note>Anaximenes' teacher, though the author suggests he was "inconsiderate" for deifying air directly.</note> did not hesitate to regard it as God, though quite inconsiderately. The vast dimension of this history of ours, and the hidden depth of the subject, compels me to treat and discuss its nature and occult properties in this place.

Concerning the essence and consistency of air, it is called <term>RUACH</term><note>original: "RVACH." The Hebrew word for breath, wind, or spirit.</note> by the Hebrews, by which name "spirit" or "wind" is also understood. From this, these three do not seem to differ from one another in the least with respect to the word *Ruach*, which denotes them in many places of the Holy Scriptures: for all these things agree in the same essence. *Ruach*, or Air, is therefore that great spirit occupying the vast cavity of the world with its mass, which encompasses heaven and earth in its embrace and fills all things that are in the world. Indeed, it exists within and permeates all beings: angels, stars, men, beasts, plants, earth, water, and stones. In its substance, it is not double or multiple, but uniform; not divided, but a single spirit, and a single perfect life, acting as the <term>spirit of the world</term><note>original: *spiritus mundi*. A vitalist concept of a soul-like substance that connects the physical and spiritual realms.</note>. In its existence, it is thin, slender, subtle, invisible, incomprehensible, impalpable, and spiritual; and in its essence, it is not inaptly compared to the spirit and soul of man. For just as the human soul or spirit (which is also derived from the air) is the tabernacle of the Spirit of God, and also of other spirits of God (whence it is called the "temple of the Holy Spirit" by the sacred writings), so too is the Air the habitation of the Holy Spirit of God, and of other spirits. For we are taught throughout the Holy Bible that "thick clouds are His pavilion," that He "walks upon the wings of the wind," and that His "spirits or angels are the winds and His ministers a flaming fire." From this it is clear that the Principle of this world dwells in the air. From the air, therefore, and through the air, all creatures live, grow, and move by means of the <term>Word</term><note>Referring to the *Logos* or divine creative command.</note>, since they are primarily constituted by air and filled with air, which rejoices in its own likeness.

For this reason, those more skilled in Philosophy maintain that air is a spirit of an incomprehensible nature and the most ancient foundation of things, which occupies the vast cavity of the universal world. It is observed to perpetually circulate through all things contained beneath the heavens—visiting, cultivating, breathing life into, transforming, binding, keeping in vigor, nourishing, and miraculously sustaining them. Hence, the Hebrews did not count it among the number of the [four] elements, but rather made it the firm bond and connection of all higher things with the lower. The opinion of the <term>Pythagoreans</term><note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their belief in the "music of the spheres" and the mathematical harmony of the universe.</note> is not far from this; they thought that the air was a certain great divine organ or instrument that perpetually resonates both on earth and in the heavens, maintaining the higher and lower things in union and concord. This is also the reason why the Egyptians imagined the air to be the messenger of the gods: for as soon as it receives the rays and breath of the celestial bodies, it communicates them...

...to the insensible regions of water and earth, as if it were a legate or messenger sent from the higher worlds to the lower, predicting accidents that are to occur on the land, in the water, and to the creatures within them. It is as if the planets and stars—using their rays like living colors and a painter's brush—have depicted upon the air, as if upon a most polished table or tablet, rains, snows, hailstorms, thunders, winds, tempests, and the like. It also displays the most evident signs of drought, cold, earthquakes, fertility, sterility, and other matters concerning both the ruin and the health of mankind. Thus, God has figured into the air, by means of His celestial creatures, a reading and knowledge of future things, which is granted to be read and understood only by those men who are truly learned and fortified with wisdom. For example, Comets do not appear in the air for nothing or in a vain manner, nor do the infinite other <term>meteors</term><note>In early modern science, a "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or rainbows, not just falling stars.</note> and particular wonders.

From these things we are clearly taught (by the testimony of the ancients) that the air, with the help of the celestial bodies, indicates to us—much like a mirror or a pointing finger—the beginnings of common calamities, the deaths of illustrious persons, the cruelties of wars, the changes of seasons, famine, plague, and all kinds of diseases and other such things.

Hence **Robert Grosseteste**, the Bishop of Lincoln, says, *The air is the matrix of all impressions*, <note>original: "Matrix omnium impressionum est aer"</note> inasmuch as by grace of its moisture, it takes the place of a spiritual mirror. It most easily either receives or emulates the forms and natures of things placed before or cast into it, and it readily receives and represents the likenesses of all shapes and colors. Thus he spoke.

From this he concludes that the air is the matrix of all impressions, because it is the medium, whether in its own proper region or in the bowels and depths of water and earth; it is also the very material of meteors, both the healthy and the unhealthy.

Indeed, and <term>what</term> is more, it retains within itself invisible and insensible impressions which are the effigies <note>In this sense, "effigies" are subtle spiritual images or "ghosts" of physical events.</note> of manifest and visible things. This is why it happens that if someone passes through a place where a man has been killed, or where a fresh corpse is hidden, he is immediately shaken by fear and stupor. This occurs because the air in that place is filled with the specters of the killing—horrible images or "seeds" of the homicide—which disturb and affect the spirit of the man passing by and breathing that air with similar images, inciting great dread.

Similarly, through these kinds of hidden impressions in the air, various dreams and multiform impressions are procreated in the human spirit through icons of "idols," likenesses, or species. These arise from those things which originate from speeches or actions, whose forms are multiplied in the air.

This "species" of invisible or hidden meteors is therefore the reason why such miraculous cures are brought to a happy conclusion by the **Weapon Salve**, <note>original: "Vnguento Armario." This was a famous and controversial medicinal ointment believed to heal a wound by being applied to the weapon that caused it, rather than the body.</note> as has been explained more than enough in our treatise on *Mystical Anatomy*.

Also of this kind—the species of meteors reigning hidden and invisibly in the air—are the origins of Epidemic diseases or those that spread among the people, namely the plague and pestilential diseases. These diseases are the effects of a Comet or some other meteor (whether fiery, watery, windy, or mixed) that was visible in the past, but which has now been dissipated everywhere through the air into invisible parts after its dissolution. When this enters the human or terrestrial spirit along with the air through breathing, it defiles them everywhere in the manner of the external air, as will be demonstrated more extensively below.

As for what pertains to the disposition or <term>complexion</term><note>The balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a substance's nature.</note> of this spirit, a huge difference appears to arise concerning it among the leaders of the Philosophers, <note>(Galen, *On the powers of simple medicines*, book 2, chapter 20.)</note> who notice that they are by no means consistent with one another in their writings.

For **Aristotle**, and those who follow his opinion, think that the air is hot; the **Stoics**, opposing them, confidently say that it is cold.

But if we explore the matter a little more accurately, we will perceive that it is neither hot nor cold, nor moist nor dry through itself, but stands as if in a middle point between these qualities. From this it follows that the air is judged fit and suitable for receiving any of these accidental impressions, even though the air itself exists with no certain or manifest quality of its own. And from this it is observed to be sometimes hot, sometimes cold, sometimes moist, and not infrequently dry. Therefore, it is not improperly compared to the celestial **Mercury**, the messenger of **Jupiter**, as was said above; for Mercury is accustomed to take on the nature of the quality of whichever planet he is joined with. Thus, he is observed to be cold and dry with **Saturn**, more hot and less moist with **Jupiter**, hot and dry with **Mars**, but to a lesser degree with the **Sun**, more moist and less hot with **Venus**, and cold and moist with the **Moon**. The air is observed to provide this same function, being eager to receive a varied temperature according to the variety of celestial influences and the difference of the blowing winds.

Therefore we say that the air, considered simply and in its own nature, is neither hot, nor cold, nor moist, nor dry. However, insofar as it withdrew from the vortex of dark <term>primordial matter</term> <note>original: "hylæ tenebrosæ"</note> during the first creation under the name of "the waters," it is more apt to participate in the quality of darkness, which (in the absence of light) rules especially as coldness. But insofar as it participates in the luminous form, to that extent it is made ready to receive hot and fiery influences.

Hence it is clear that in its own proper nature, without respect to other influences, its aptitude for coldness is removed by its inclination toward the heat of the informing light; therefore, it cannot be called hot or cold originally and in its essence.

Since, however, moisture and dryness are simple qualities derived from other simples—that is, arising from heat and cold—it follows that air by its nature is neither cold nor hot, and consequently neither moist nor dry. But indeed, insofar as...

Its potential existence in <term>hyle</term><note>The Greek term *hyle* refers to the "prime matter" or the raw, unformed substance from which the universe was created.</note> or dark chaos was naturally a companion to potential coldness, which then later flowed out with the water from the darkness at the creation of the world. We conclude, therefore, that the air is fit to receive any of the four aforementioned qualities, and it is accustomed to bring this fitness into actual reality according to the nature and condition of the wind that happens to blow. For example: Northern winds render it cold and dry; Southern winds, hot and moist; the Eastern and South-Eastern winds, hot and dry; and Western winds, cold and moist. From this, it happens that the quality of the air can be changed at any moment: according to the ordinance of GOD, who disposes it according to His will; indeed, the air receives whatever is poured into it, and yet it nonetheless retains and preserves its own spiritual and uniform essence.

### CHAP. V.

->*Where the active reason for changing air from one quality to another is explained.
Here also is related how it is daily altered and changed from a thin
to a thick and visible constitution.*<-

**A**lthough the air (as has already been said) is single and simple in its nature and existence, it is nevertheless moved from one quality to another by means of the Word and the <term>angelic ministers</term><note>In early modern natural philosophy, angels were often viewed as the "middle management" of nature, physically carrying out God's commands to move the winds or stars.</note> who blow and stir it with various winds. Consequently, it is accustomed to migrate from a dense substance to a thin or moderate one, and conversely from thin to dense—and this happens daily. For who, having any common experience, does not see that clouds are composed of air? And consequently, that the very substance of the air is condensed into hail, frost, and hoarfrost by the boreal cold? The Holy Scriptures teach us that this cold flows from the divine breath. For (says Job, chapter 37, verse 9):
> The mighty GOD produces ice by his breath; by the blowing of GOD the frost grows, <note>original: "Glaciem DEVS fortis edit flatu suo, flante DEO crescit gelu"</note>

and it is said elsewhere that when He sends His command to the earth, His word runs very swiftly,
> who gives snow like wool, and scatters hoarfrost like ashes; He casts down His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? # Section I. Port. IV. Part I. Book II.

Do we not see the terrestrial clot—that is, the human body, and indeed that of any animal or plant—return, by the testing of common fire, first into smoke (as an intermediate meteor), and finally into air (as the simple beginning or end of those meteors, or imperfect mixtures) from which they first departed?

Do we not also see, for confirmation of this matter, that common Quicksilver (which for this reason the common Alchemists called Mercury <note>original: *Argentum vivum* / *Mercurium*</note>) joined or amalgamated with any of the other fusible metals, converts its nature into the nature of the metal with which it is joined? But because thinned air requires a wider space for its expanded existence, it is necessary that either the glass breaks, or that as much air as exceeds the dimensions of the space is condensed into water. This is clearly demonstrated in our experimental instrument.

## CAP. VI.

->*How meteors are also generated in the earth and waters, and the reason for them.*<-

**IN** the preceding sections we have declared that all things, regarding their substance, are originally forged from air, and nothing exists without its benevolent breath <note>original: *afflatu*</note>, since nothing can live without it. For thin air nourishes the spirit of things; in its moderate substance, it feeds humors; and it daily refreshes gross, solid bodies. By these differences of air, those things remain as they were created. Air therefore abounds, and that most fluently, in every thing—namely in the earth, in the water, in rocks, in stones, in man, and in other animals, and even in every plant. 

Just as we see every animal filled with air and spirit, breathing in air daily for the sustenance of its life, so too the life of the earth, the sea, and the waters consists in air, through which they subsist and are perpetually revived. Indeed, air is not only present in the empty spaces of the earth itself (just as it is in the spaces and cavities of the human body), but it is also certain that it penetrates the pores of the earth, stones, and metals everywhere, filling them spiritually. Furthermore, the substances of the waters are full of air, since they originally proceeded from air, just as we have blood—both arterial and venous—filled everywhere with aerial spirit. 

Therefore, just as we said that in the space between the sphere of the Moon and the earth, the air (which is uniform in itself) is ordered into parts of different quality, so also the air contained in water or earth observes a similar order. It is thicker and denser near the center of the earth, where minerals are generated from thick and heavy water. However, in the middle of the earth <note>original: *meditullio*</note>, the air is thinned and grows together into stones; a little higher up it turns into spring water and is condensed, upon which plants primarily depend; and on the surface of the earth, it turns into vapor along with the open aerial sea of the world, useful for the generation of animals. # CHAPTER VII.

## On the material cause of meteors in Man.

We have said that Man is composed of spirit and body—that is, of heaven and earth—in no other way than the world itself is composed; hence, Man is not without reason called the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: "Small World." The ancient and Renaissance idea that the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</term> by the Philosophers. But truly, since (as Hermes Trismegistus testifies in *Pimander*, Book 8) man is the image of the world—which in another place he called the "son of the world"—it is therefore necessary that his dark body be derived from that earth of the world, and his airy spirit from the heaven of the world. Both are sustained and nourished in succession by means of terrestrial foods and the perpetual drinking of the "airy cup." <note>This refers to the act of breathing, viewed as a form of nourishment for the vital spirit.</note> Hence Moses testifies *that GOD created Adam from the mud of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life.* From this it is clear that whatever the state of the external air may be, the human spirit must have the closest relation to it, because the Macrocosmic spirit constantly mixes with that of the Microcosm through various inspirations (breathing). Thus, it is inevitable that air affects air, just as water colored with blood, snow, or saffron converts other water into its own disposition; so also the foul air of one place makes the sweet and kindly air of another place smell most foul, and consequently, air tainted by rot and pestilential "seeds" converts healthy and clean air into its own nature.

And this is what Hippocrates and Galen <note>Hippocrates and Galen were the foundational authorities of Western medicine until the early modern period.</note> sang of in various parts of their writings, such as *Introduction to the Art of Medicine*, chapter 85, and *On the Differences of Fevers*, book 1, chapter 4. For Galen recognized that our bodies are necessarily altered by the surrounding air. And elsewhere he says: *The hotter states of the surrounding air, such as occur mostly around the rising of the Dog Star, <note>The rising of Sirius, associated with the oppressive heat of summer.</note> clearly heat the heart through breathing; moreover, being poured around the body from the outside, they make the whole body hotter. But especially the arteries, as they draw in something of the substance of the surrounding air itself, from all of which it is necessary for the heart to be affected.* Similarly, Hippocrates (Aphorism 12, book 1) teaches us that through the surrounding air we can arrive at the knowledge of diseases. And elsewhere he says that at the beginning of winter, bile decreases because it is now cooling, and **phlegm** <note>original: *pituita*</note> increases anew, both from the following rains and from the length of the nights. Hippocrates himself seems to recognize this same thing in his book *On Nature*, chapter 37, and throughout his first book *On Common Diseases* (Epidemics), where he is seen to declare and predict the subsequent effects of epidemic diseases from the blowing of the winds, depending on the rising and setting of the stars. This is seen in Hippocrates, *On Common Diseases*, book 1, along with Galen as his commentator. And Galen, in book 8 of the same work, recognizes that the bodies of animals are altered by the air, so that they become wetter through rain, and drier through heat or summer warmth. He says that when the heat is strong, the head will be firm; but when cold abounds, the head will be very light, but the chest and lungs will suffer. Furthermore, he speaks elsewhere in these words: *Of those things which happen to bodies from the outside, one is certainly such that it cannot be separated from them, as it adheres to them perpetually like a kinsman—namely, the surrounding air, which harms us either because it makes us excessively hot, or cold, or wet, or dry* (Book 1, chapter 3, *On Preserving Health*). There are infinite other passages in both Hippocrates and Galen by which we are warned that the internal air has an inseparable union with the spirit of animals. Moreover, the manner in which air drawn into the lungs is "cooked" by them is demonstrated by Galen in book 7 of *On the Use of the Parts*, chapter 8. Similarly, how the air which is drawn in by breathing is carried in two directions—partly to the heart by means of the lungs, and partly to the brain with the assistance of the nostrils—is shown in Galen's *On the Causes of Respiration*. Finally, in the notable booklet titled *Whether Blood is Naturally Contained in the Arteries*, he admits that the inspired air is diffused through every single member of the whole body by means of the lungs, heart, arteries, and nostrils.

But now we shall make a brief discourse concerning the air or spirit contained within man, and concerning its origin, seat, and motion in the human body; in the center of which we have elsewhere declared the living soul dwells, just as the bright influences of life sent down from the sun into these lower regions dwell in the innermost parts of the worldly air...

Whence some, being deceived, thought the humor of the blood was the soul; it clearly escaped these people that first it is necessary for the spirit to flow all the way to the soul, then for the blood to congeal, and the hollow veins and arteries to be extended, and finally for the animal to be dissolved—which resolution is the death of the body.* <note>Hermes Trismegistus was the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus was attributed; his writings were central to Renaissance alchemy and philosophy.</note> These are his words, in which he truly denotes the dominion of the spirit or air in the body, inasmuch as he makes it the vehicle of the soul. This is according to that saying of Hippocrates mentioned above: *at the beginning of winter, bile grows cold and decreases, and phlegm [pituita] is increased anew.* <note>original: *bilis ineunte hyeme frigescit & decrescit, & pituita de integro augetur.*</note> From this it is clear that the air, with its internal essence, is the cause of the variety of humors, or the change of one humor into another. These humors take on the appearance of <term>meteors</term>; <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric or internal vaporous phenomena, including winds, clouds, and bodily fluids, not just falling stars.</note> indeed, upon the "dissolution of the animal," the blood is accustomed to migrate into its internal spirit, just as the meteors of the heaven migrate into the air. Whence also Trismegistus says: *The soul returning into itself, the spirit is contracted into the blood, and the soul into the spirit, etc.*

Do not the Holy Scriptures also confirm that the seat of the soul is the blood? From which it follows that blood is nothing other than "tempered air," <note>original: *aer temperatus*</note> reduced by thickening into that bloody mass, like a natural meteor, according to the laws of mixing. Therefore, this air, dispersed everywhere through the body and carrying the soul through all the parts of the body (in the way Philosophers say the soul is "in the whole and in every part"), is that sublime place in which meteors—or "imperfectly mixed" lofty things—are procreated. It is also the place from which various meteors, both healthy and unhealthy, are produced in man by a thickening caused by "Microcosmic winds," <note>Internal movements of gas or spirit within the body, mimicking the winds of the external world.</note> made in imitation of those of the Macrocosm. Of these meteors, those that are more spiritual and invisible bring good or bad passions to the soul, according to the nature of the meteor (whether favorable or unhappy) which is procreated in and from that airy medium.

Wherefore, regarding the internal efficient cause of these meteors, the same thing must be said sincerely as was said of the meteors of the "great world": namely, that the primary cause is the "essentializing" property of the ineffable name of GOD, <note>A reference to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter Hebrew name of God, believed in esoteric traditions to hold the power of creation and governance.</note> turning either toward clemency or toward punishment. By this name, those things are ordained which are afterwards committed to execution by His angelic ministers who do His word, by means of the air, which they change and convert into this or that nature and constitution according to the will of the divine Creator—a point we intend to demonstrate more openly and copiously elsewhere.

And in this way, you have placed before your eyes an Anatomy of the human spirit, as well as its necessary relationship with the spirit of the Macrocosm. Now, let me be permitted to speak—and indeed briefly—concerning the comparison between the body and the human spirit (of the "lesser world") and the spirit of the earth in the "greater world." For between these most noble creatures of the sublunary world, there is a maximum and very necessary commerce and reciprocation at every moment of time.

And yet, this huge and gigantic creature was created for human use, according to that word of the royal Psalmist: *GOD made the earth and gave it to the sons of men.* From these things it is right to gather that man himself is the end [purpose] of all creatures, and consequently a creature of exquisite height.

The earth, however, is next to him in dignity, as it is not only the basis for the external man, but it also produces, contains, and nourishes all creatures required for human life and sustenance. And certainly, there is a very great relationship in their composition between these two creatures (if we explore the matter a little more curiously). For just as we observe man to be compacted of body and spirit—in which spirit a certain divine soul, or a certain internal acting principle, holds its habitation—so the matter stands with the mass of the Macrocosmic earth. For she was compacted and formed by the Creator out of an external body and an internal spirit, in which spirit there dwells a certain "Solar soul," which the wise have not without reason called the "Central Sun." <note>original: *Solem centralem*. An alchemical concept suggesting a vital, spiritual heat at the center of the earth that mirrors the sun in the heavens.</note> Both of these exquisite creatures are therefore "animals" (so to speak), endowed with the same life functions and duties—both bodies, I say, are vehicles, receptacles, and matrices for the influences of both the super-celestial, celestial, and sublunary realms. These bodies contain similar spirits cut from the universal sublunary air (as if from a great cliff or spiritual sea), in the same way we see the lunar circle or sphere embrace the entire mass of the sublunary air. And this kind of air or spirit, enclosed both in man and in the earth, has as much fellowship and commerce with the universal worldly air as a single drop of water has to its whole; for they are joined by an inseparable "glue" with the air, or the "great worldly spirit," just as a drop of sea water, when applied, is joined in inseparable union with the whole of that water. By the successive administration of these spirits, they are daily refreshed and live. He did this so that one, in a rapacious manner, wandering and running out from its own homeland or beyond its proper limits, would not rashly or unjustly invade the limit or portion granted to another by the creator, and thus set fire to war and discord within the bowels of a peaceful world. This is why the stars and the earth always claim the same station for themselves. 

Therefore, the entire space of the aerial region between the Moon and the earth is appropriated to both the moon and the earth, but especially to the earth; without the breath of its spirit, it is impossible for either the earth or any of its creatures to endure. Whence, beyond all doubt, the earth breathes in and breathes out this kind of aerial spirit—filled with the grace of divine life—no differently than a human, or any other animal, or even a plant. 

In man, therefore, we see that the <term>heart</term> <note>original: *cor*; the author views the heart not just as a pump, but as the central sun of the body's anatomy.</note> is that noble organ whose duty is to purify the spirit attracted centrally by breathing, and then afterwards to emit the superfluous and sooty air through exhalation. Does not the earth also have its own <term>heart</term>, namely the central sun? By its operation, the celestial benefits of life are attracted through the pores by a certain magnetic virtue, carried by the aerial spirit. Then, afterwards, by a certain contraction or tightening, that which is superfluous is emitted in the form of vapors. On its path, that vapor is congealed in the "veins" and changed into water, from which springs arise. However, that which is useful is reserved in its belly and shared abundantly with the creatures it nourishes, like a devoted mother. 

By the same reasoning, the <term>human heart</term> offers and scatters in every direction its portion of Manna or celestial honey—newly collected or drawn from the air—through the arteries to all the members of the entire body, and especially to its spirits. That which is superfluous, however, it emits outward; and if the place into which that vapor is exhaled be sooty, narrow, and cold, it is condensed into drops of water. For example, if someone breathes into a vial, or a mirror, or marble, we perceive that spirit first as a mist, then as dew, and finally coagulated into drops. 

But someone (I know) will object that breathing in and out is not at all proper to the earth, or at least is entirely hidden from men. To this we respond: if we consider the order and motion of the ebb and flow of the sea with a diligent gaze, we will perceive that it was not made in vain by <term>creative nature</term> <note>original: *natura naturante*; a philosophical term referring to God or the creative force of the universe acting as a dynamic principle.</note>, but was rather ordained for the inhalation and exhalation of the giant earth itself. Thus, in <term>Diastole</term> <note>The phase of a heartbeat when the muscle relaxes and the chamber fills with blood; here, the author equates it with the earth "inhaling" the sea.</note> the earth seems to dilate, as if by a retreating tide, and in that time it absorbs subtle water and also air into its bowels. But in <term>systole</term> <note>The phase of a heartbeat when the muscle contracts; here, the "exhalation" that causes the tide to rise.</note>, by contracting itself in a certain way, or by the hidden virtue of nature, it expels the superfluities—both through its "marine mouth" and through its pores—thus making the sea flow. 

Nor is it enough for those who will reply that the ebb and flow is not universal; for by the same respect, it is well known that the lungs in a human are not in the entire body, but in a single place of it more convenient for respiration and exhalation. We see a similar motion in the gills of recently caught fish, which they now contract and now dilate like the ebb and flow of the sea. 

But now I know it will be objected against us: if this is probable and consistent with reason, let the reason be shown why there is not as much of an interval between <term>Systole</term> and <term>Diastole</term> as there is between the ebb and flow of the sea? We respond that the larger the animals are, the slower is their motion in breathing in and breathing out. But the earth is an animal of immense magnitude, so that a long time is required for the complete inhalation of its spirit, its dilation through all its limbs and interior members, and likewise for its exhalation. But even this seems to be proven by its effect by Solomon, who asserts:

> that all rivers enter into the sea and the sea does not overflow; to the places from which the rivers come, they return, so that they may flow again. Ecclesiastes ch. 1.

From which it seems to be argued that the thinner part of the sea, free from all saltiness, is drawn like an inhalation into the bowels of the earth along with the air dispersed everywhere in those waters. There, what is pure and suitable for the sustenance of terrestrial creatures is reserved by the <term>Archaeus</term> <note>original: *Archæo*; in Paracelsian alchemy, the "Archaeus" is the internal "chemist" or vital force that separates the useful from the waste in an organism.</note>, the minister of nature. The rest is converted into vapor, which is condensed into drops during its path or motion through the veins and pores; from a multitude of these joined together, springs are procreated for the benefit of creatures, and especially of man, who is the end of all creatures. From the union of springs and rivulets, rivers result, which hasten their way to the sea from whence they arose. And in this sense, there will be a hidden agreement (though it does not appear so at first glance to all philosophers) between that opinion of Aristotle—which is that the origin of springs is from terrestrial vapor congealed into water—and that of Solomon—which is that springs arise from the sea and tend toward the sea from which they were derived. ### Concerning the Material Cause of Meteors.

Neither Aristotle nor Solomon could fully perceive the origin of those vapors; nor would I wish the readers of our writings to think that my opinion regarding the breathing in and breathing out of the earth is vain, simply because, as far as I know, it has been devised by no one before this time. This theory consists in the mystery of the ebb and flow of the sea, since it is certain beyond all doubt that more things still lie hidden from humans than have been revealed to them. However, what the difference is between the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> and Holy Scripture, we shall declare more than sufficiently in what follows.

But let us proceed in this comparison of ours between the external man and the earth. We find in the spiritual or airy—that is, the internal—man, three regions of air differing from each other in purity, thinness, and composition. For the **animal spirits** <note>In early medicine, these were "spirits" responsible for sensation and movement, centered in the brain.</note> are formed from the purer air, the **vital spirits** <note>Spirits responsible for life and heat, centered in the heart.</note> from the middle grade, and the **natural spirits** <note>Spirits responsible for nutrition and growth, centered in the liver.</note> from the denser air. In respect to these, the air expanded universally through the vast cavity of the world reflects this hierarchy: the first or "animal" air is likened to the substance of the Empyrean world <note>The highest, most heavenly realm of fire and light.</note>, whence it is the vehicle of reason and sense; the middle or "vital" air is likened to the ethereal spirit, which is between the highest and the middle; and the lowest or "natural" air is likened to the sublunary spirit, which is commonly called "air." Furthermore, regarding the sublunary air, the animal spirits are referred to the highest region of sublunary air, the vital to the middle, and the natural to the lowest. For it is the lowest region of air that contributes to the nutrition of the body; the middle region regards life and the procreation of arterial blood; and the highest region contributes to the senses and the interior faculties of the soul.

Does not the earth also contain within itself as many grades or regions of its internal air or spirit, in imitation of the worldly and human air? For in its highest region, the animal kingdom is found, which is of a more fiery and Empyrean nature according to the intentions of all Philosophers; then the middle region is occupied by the vegetative power, which participates in the nature of air and ether, or of thinner water; and the lowest region is the mineral and metallic, which consists of gross water from which metals are procreated—for in this same way, the natural power in man procreates solid parts. These spirits, or "double air"—namely, both the human and the earthly—were infused into them by the Creator from the womb of the universal sublunary air at their creation. Thus, there is no difference between this particular enclosed air and that universal air expanded everywhere in the elementary region, except in its location. They agree, I say, in nature, and are held together by an inviolable bond, not unlike how terrestrial water has an inseparable union with seawater through the rivers. Hence it is that the parts of one and the other are most fit to be bound and mixed together in an inseparable conjunction, just as water mixes with water. 

From this, it happens that the disposition of a smaller portion is easily changed into that of the larger. For we observe that sweet rivers poured into the salty sea migrate and are transformed into its salty nature. In exactly the same way, air that is universally infected is observed to pollute with its breath not only the earth, but also its creatures, both animal and vegetable. From these things it is right to conclude that meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, comets, and lightning.</note>—whether fiery, airy, or watery—disseminated in the vast air, infect the air of both man and earth. Indeed, if the meteors are from the higher region of the open air, they tend to penetrate to the internal spirit of man because of the thinness of their "seeds" <term>seminarium: a "seed" or formal principle that gives rise to physical phenomena</term>. And from this it happens that comets and other such fiery meteors of the highest region of air are said to excite even the rational spirits of men to passions—namely, anger, war, and dangerous imbalances <note>original: "dyscrasias"</note>—and to procreate plagues in the very marrow of the spirits, and so on. 

So too, pestiferous vapors in the bowels of the earth are stirred up from their enclosure, full of the meteorological seeds of the air which the earth is accustomed to draw in through breathing; it also infects fruits and animals with its breath, so that the food of man becomes more deadly than the corrupt air drawn to his heart through breathing. And from this, for the most part, we see epidemic diseases arise, which are more likely to proceed and happen from the corrupted nature of nourishment than from the malevolent aspect of the heavens—though the heavens also contribute primarily to the corruption of food. Man, therefore, has his own "meteors" which are procreated in imitation of those in the world's air in each of his regions. These arise from invisible "seeds" of those things dispersed in the world's air, introduced with the air through breathing (both by the movement of the lungs and the attraction of the pores) and mixed with the human spirit. From this, both diseases (which we call "malignant meteors") and health are procreated by either harmful or beneficial meteors, as will be explained more copiously in its proper place. The earth also has its own proper meteors which, by means of human drink and food, very easily mix their own "sperms"—whether healthy or poisonous—with the human spirit.

That the earth suffers from contagious diseases and various passions, we gather from these facts: for in an earthquake, she herself is heard to groan, and to bellow as if with the voice of thunders, as if she were seen to be afflicted by some contagious and painful disease. From this it happens that, besides her shivering and trembling—by which she suddenly raises the peaceful seas on high and confounds and destroys towers and palaces—she also infects nations and the people of cities with a lamentable plague and devastates them with contagion. We see her also sometimes sterile and languishing as if with **alopecia** <note>Baldness; here used metaphorically for a barren landscape.</note>, sometimes laboring with sulfurous inflammations and reduced to lime and ashes by burning, sometimes corrupted by poisonous waters and turned into a filthy and morbid swamp, sometimes submerged by an inundation of waters and as if suffocated and made slimy and putrid, sometimes dried into dust and wounded with cracks and gashes, and sometimes seething with cloudy sweats and exhaling the manner of sighs...

...affected by such preternatural passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to being acted upon by external forces, like a patient suffering a disease.</note>, all of which accidents <note>Occurrences or symptoms that are not part of an object's essential nature.</note> she has received from the meteorological pollutions of the external air. These infect her internal spirit (which is also derived from the external air), as is testified by philosophers and astrologers, as well as those more skilled in divine wisdom <note>original: "theosophia peritiores"</note>. By all these ailments (I say), the earth is affected; for she, who was first ordained for the benefit of man—healthy and free from suffering—is now rendered cursed and morbid because of the sin of Adam. This was done so that she might afflict man with diseases, painful ailments, and a lack of harvest, thereby punishing him for his disobedience; according to that saying of the Wise Man: *For God is not the author of death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living, for he created all things that they might exist, and the origins of the world are healthful, in which there is no destructive poison, nor the kingdom of the underworld upon the earth. But by the envy of the Devil, death entered into the world. Wisdom 1:13 & 2:24.* 

But there are some, no doubt rising up against this opinion of mine, who will assert that no sensation exists in the earth, and consequently, that she neither suffers nor is affected by pain. To these we shall likewise respond that they are very little practiced in the Holy Scriptures, or have entirely forgotten their teaching. For we are taught by them (as is held in the song of Ananias, Azarias, and Misael <note>Commonly known as the "Song of the Three Holy Children," a prayer of praise found in the Greek additions to the Book of Daniel.</note> delivered in the fiery furnace) that it is the Earth's role to bless the Lord, and to exalt him in praises above all things forever. And we are instructed from that very place that not only the earth, but also the Sun, Moon, stars, heaven, waters, and fire—indeed, even all other meteorological creatures—possess sensation and a certain instinct of reason for blessing God and magnifying him above all with praises. 

Furthermore, the Royal Psalmist says, *Let the Earth praise Jehovah, Psalm 69:34,* and elsewhere, *that the Earth trembled when God looked upon it, Psalm 104,* and *that the Earth, opening itself at the divine command, swallowed Dathan and his associates, Psalm 106.* We could review many other passages establishing this same point, which to review now might perhaps be too tedious for the reader; similarly, we read that the Sun stood still in the heaven at the command of Joshua and prolonged the day, and so it is in other cases. From this it is certain that the earth possesses not only life, but also sensation and a certain hidden reason. Even those most skilled in the **mystery of the Magnet** <note>Early modern scientists believed the Earth's magnetic properties were evidence of its "soul" or internal life-force.</note> have found that the earth has its own poles, its circles, a Zodiac, an Equinoctial, Solstices, and Polar regions. From this it follows that the winds blow in her internal spirit from their own regions no differently than those winds blow from the regions of the world or the open air; but we recognize that such particular winds depend upon those universal ones, as we shall show more clearly in what follows.

We conclude, therefore, that there is a universal aerial sea in the world, giving life to all the bodies of the world by its presence, permeating all beings, providing them with an internal spirit, and courteously imparting to them its own aerial nature. From this it happens that, according to the health or sickness <note>original: "temperiem vel intemperiem"</note> of the universal air, any particular air—that is, the air enclosed within any body—is very easily altered. Consequently, the bodies which are, so to speak, promiscuously drenched by these particular airs, follow the conditions of those airs thus enclosed; they are altered by their health or their sickness. And from this, philosophers and physicians have concluded (and quite maturely so) that the temperament of the body follows the temperament of the soul. Thus it happens that when the internal spirit is disturbed by the external—whether by heat, cold, moisture, or dryness—the body in which it dwells is also disturbed by those same afflictions. 

From these things, therefore, it is clearly declared that, since the entire mass of **sublunary air** <note>The atmosphere between the Earth and the Moon, thought to be the realm of change and decay.</note> is affected by a multiform kind of "meteors" (whether healthy or unhealthy), it is necessary that the particular air of both the giant creature of the earth and the tiny creature of man be likewise affected in the same way. Indeed, when the terrestrial spirit is infected by that mundane spirit, we see that the spirit of man also participates in those same passions. And this is why famine, pestilence, and pestilential fevers are, for the most part, inseparable companions. Hence it is said that when a comet reigns, famine and plague are foretold; for famine proves the sterility of the earth and the pestilential fruits of that same spirit by which they are nourished, as well as impurity, poisonousness, and the corruption of the universal spirit. 

From this it happens that the human spirit also suffers from the corrupted universal spirit drawn in through breathing <note>original: "inspirationem"</note>, and also from the terrestrial spirit by way of nutrition. Indeed, sometimes the particular air is infected by the diseased breath of the earth, as occasionally appears during an earthquake, which a plague often follows. And what is more, we say reciprocally that the human spirit, by its own error, corrupted that terrestrial spirit; whence it happened that, because of the sin of Adam, not only man but also the earth itself (which God ordained from the beginning for the sons of men) was cursed and became deadly to man himself. But concerning these things, we shall speak more abundantly in what follows.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## *On the three stages in the motion of expansion and growth between simple air and meteorological bodies (or imperfect mixtures), and on their mathematical reasoning.*

**I**n the final chapter of the previous small volume, it was explained that a progression was made out of nothing—or from the "womb of matter" <note>original: "hylæ gremio"; *hyle* is a Greek-derived term for the primordial, unformed substance of the universe</note>—by the emanation of light toward unity <note>the Monad, or the number 1</note>. By the revelation of this light, another "potential unity" was produced, opposite to it in nature: namely, darkness. From these, the progression continued from the Monad <note>unity</note> to the Dyad <note>duality, or the number 2</note>, and from the Dyad to the Triad <note>the number 3</note>, through the introduction and production of the "humid spirit." This spirit acts as a glue, joining both extremes together just as a soul is joined with a body. Finally, these progress to the Quaternary number <note>the number 4</note>, reaching the completion of the "simple world." This process brings the four elements into actual existence, which differ from one another and serve as the immediate beginnings of all mixtures. This is no different than in geometry, where square surfaces are the immediate principles of a cubic body. We have depicted this order arithmetically as follows:

Where the number two <note>the binary</note> is the material root from which the first square (indicating the 4 elements) is derived. All these intervening stages are what should truly be called "imperfectly mixed bodies" <note>meteorological phenomena like clouds, rain, or wind</note>, insofar as they are progressing from the simplicity of the elements toward a full mixture. In this order, point **h. 4.** relates to a **perfect mixture** just as **1. a** (or the light of simple progression) relates to **e. 4.** (the four elements). Furthermore, just as **b. 2.** represents **prime matter and form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "prime matter" is the raw, formless stuff of the universe, and "form" is the organizing principle that makes it a specific thing.</note> from which the four elements proceeded through multiplication, so do **e. 4.** (the four elements) denote matter and form within the simplicity of the elements. From these, through further multiplication, bodies proceed that are mixed more profoundly and perfectly as "unity" immerses itself deeper into the "multitude of matter." 

Therefore, just as the luminous unity **1. a.** is the simplest source of all simple things, so too are **e. 4.** (the four elements) the simplest origin of **mixed bodies**. In this progression of mixtures, the **5th order** (the number five) relates to the others as the number 2 relates to "nothing" or darkness in the simple world. Similarly, the **6th order** relates to the 5th as 2 relates to 1; the **7th** relates to the 6th as 3 relates to 2; and finally, the **8th** relates to the 7th as 4 relates to 3. 

As we saw in the first progression—where the number 2 was created as the number 1 shone forth—so too do the four elements gather themselves together in the "womb of the one air." This air is their parent, the **universal spirit of the world**. From this, the first species of mixture is produced: the winds and **invisible meteors** <term>meteors: in the 17th century, this referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or lightning, not just space rocks</term>, both fiery and watery. By the force of the winds, these gradually thicken, taking on a visible fiery nature (represented by the 6th order). This has a relationship to the number 3 of the simple progression, in which water is either brilliantly illuminated by light (signifying fiery meteors in the second degree of mixtures) or water prevails over light (signifying thundering meteors). 

Then, finally, the **seventh degree** shows denser and darker meteors, such as clouds of hail and snow, as well as rain and other things of that kind. If these proceed even further into composition, they coalesce into **perfectly mixed bodies**. For this must be known for certain: all bodies—whether animal, vegetable, or mineral—are nothing other than clouds or "meteors" brought to a state of perfect mixture. Who can doubt that any perfectly mixed thing was first an imperfectly mixed one? It is necessary for "imperfection" to sit between the simple elements and the completely composed ones; it is impossible to find two extremes where the "middle" (the path between the starting point and the destination) is missing. We observe this even in the motion of generation: **sperm** is a kind of imperfect mixture, like a "little cloud of generation" <note>original: "nebulam seu nubeculam generationis"</note>, which proceeds by natural motion until it reaches the production of a complete fetus or a "perfect mixture."

We say, therefore, that a **meteor** is called an "imperfect mixture" because it is "on the way"—a natural motion arising between the simple elements in the womb of the air—and it moves toward the goal of perfection for whichever species it tends toward. If it fails in its motion because of some obstacle in the middle, so that it cannot progress further on the path of perfection, it returns gradually to its simple nature from which it was first derived. 

If it is procreated by **poisonous winds** or malevolent spirits blowing together, it usually infects the air and brings a bad omen. But if it is procreated by benevolent breaths by divine power, it purifies and cleanses the air, bringing a good and favorable omen to the earth and its fruits; it is even proven to be healthy for the lives of animals, if God so wills it. Nor should we doubt that meteors contribute to the production of perfectly mixed things. We are taught by experience that frogs, worms, and monstrous animals—likewise flesh, blood, grain, and other crops, and even stones, sand, and dust—have fallen from the clouds and the air by the blowing of the winds. We must know, therefore, that there are meteors of both generation and corruption...
