# BOOK THREE.

## Member I.

### On the formal cause of Meteors.

#### Chapter I of Member I.

->*This chapter treats precisely the formal cause of the meteors of both worlds,*<-
->*as well as the differences between them.*<-

Since in the preceding book we have discussed the material origin of the **meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, clouds, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> of both worlds sufficiently and even more than enough (as it seems to me), it is my intention here, for the sake of a more certain method, to discourse upon their **formal cause** <note>The "formal cause" is a philosophical term for the specific essence or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is, distinguishing it from the raw material it is made of.</note>, albeit briefly and succinctly. Just as we declared in the previous sections that the material cause of meteors is that substantial part from which all meteors are forged—namely, from a thinner subject of air, more or less contracted and compressed according to the condition of the meteor—so also we affirm that their formal cause is that by which those meteors, as far as their material existence is concerned, are carved out or sketched from the universal and invisible mass of the world’s air. This is to say, they are brought into a visible state, claiming for themselves a name and a peculiar essence. 

This cause is what is accustomed to adorn, clothe, or shape a particular aerial vapor with various and diverse figures that differ from one another. This diversity of figures or images is taught to proceed from the hidden and internal form of the meteors; it is no different than how the outward **image** <note>original: "ico"</note> or figure of a human being, proceeding from their own unique internal essence, makes their structure differ from that of other animals and plants. Because of this, we recognize from afar that this or that being is a human, and neither a beast nor a plant. By a clearly similar reasoning or distinction, we gather and distinguish a dark meteor from a bright one—that is, one species from another. And again, in a more specific sense, we distinguish the bright from the bright, and the opaque or dark from the dark. For example, we have observed that a comet, or lightning, or a **lance** <note>A term for a streaking atmospheric light or fire-phenomenon.</note>, or a burning column is distinguished and differs from a cloud, a mist, a halo, or dew. Even within the same category or species, we see a comet vary from a burning column or from lightning by that same formal difference. Similarly, in the dark kingdom, even the common eye discerns that a cloud differs from a mist, a mist from dew, and rain from frost, and so on. 

Therefore, it is for this reason that in this treatise of ours, by means of these formal causes, we distribute meteors first into their genera, then those into their species, and finally those—after various subdivisions—into infinite individuals. We see this partitioned no differently than the trunk of a tree into branches, and those again into subdivided twigs, which finally end in small shoots, so that you may reach the goal of our intention by an easier method.

And since our purpose in this present treatise leads us to compare the meteors of the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Greater World" or the universe at large.</note> with those of the **Microcosm** <note>The "Lesser World," referring to the human being.</note>—that is, man himself—so that we might more clearly demonstrate the reason for his health or sickness through the effects of the good or bad meteors generated within him, we have therefore followed a thread of progression throughout this work. After every chapter concerning the meteors of the Macrocosm, we have made a correlation and comparison between the parts of the preceding chapter and those of the Microcosm or man, specifically by applying the meteors, **humors** <note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note>, and properties of the one to the other, just as the subject and occasion for discussion presents itself.

On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

## CHAPTER II.

### *In which it is demonstrated that in the universal contemplation of the meteors of both worlds, two things in particular come to be considered.*

In the universal contemplation of the meteors of both worlds, two things in particular come to be considered, namely:
1. The seat or chief place: see **A**.
2. The general difference: see **B**.

We find it written, and not without wise counsel, by **Mercury Trismegistus** <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and scientific writings were attributed. He is the founding figure of Hermeticism.</note>, that most profound high priest, that *the world belongs to God; man, however, is the son and image of the world.* For just as God originally brought forth the substance of the world from nothing, so also He fashioned man from the matter of the already created world: specifically, his external part from the mud of the earth, but his internal part from the worldly spirit—that divine breath previously adorned with the forms of the reason and intellect of God as a most precious gift. 

From this we observe that just as the earth is the dark house or vessel of the vast **Macrocosmic spirit** <note>Macrocosm: The "Great World" or the entire universe, viewed as a large-scale version of the human being.</note>, without which no perfectly mixed thing in the **sublunary world** <note>The region below the moon, traditionally thought to be the realm of change and decay, composed of the four elements.</note> can be brought to completion (for the earth is the matrix or "womb" of the worldly elements as well as the celestial and even super-celestial influences), so also it can escape no one’s notice that the human spirit claims for itself a similar receptacle. This spirit is a vehicle for celestial and super-celestial inflows in no other way than the elemental air is in the Macrocosm. 

From this it is clear how great and how close and necessary is the relation between these two spirits and both these bodies—namely of the Macrocosm and the **Microcosm** <note>Microcosm: The "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>. Indeed, since both the spirit and the body of the "lesser world" are derived from those of the "greater," it must infallibly follow that both the airy and ethereal spirit in man, and his dark body, are sustained and nourished by that of the world, and remain in their state and existence at every moment because of it. They adhere to the worldly parts, both spiritual and bodily, by an inviolable bond, so that they cannot be separated from each other even by death or the dissolution of the composite being. Thus, it has happened from the beginning that when the elements of the greater world become "sick," the airy and terrestrial parts of man are also very quickly infected, as will be described more accurately in the following pages.

## CHAPTER III.

### *On the chief seat or place, both of the procreation of meteors, and of the reception of their seeds in the Macrocosm.*

**A: The chief seat or place of meteors**

1. Where they are procreated:
    * **General:** The universal sea of the sublunary air.
    * **Particular:** The spirit or air enclosed in:
        * The worldly Earth.
        * The human body.

2. In which—as in a most proper vessel or receptacle—their **seeds** <note>original: "seminaria." In early science, "seeds" referred to the hidden origins or formative principles of natural phenomena like rain or disease.</note> are received by inspiration:
    * The Earth of the world.
    * The body of man.
    * (These are the **matrices** <note>A "matrix" (plural: matrices) is a formative cell or "womb" in which something else originates or develops.</note> of every influence and impression of these seeds.)

Those who have applied their efforts to the investigation of **meteors** <note>In this context, meteors include all atmospheric phenomena like wind, rain, and lightning, as well as their equivalents inside the human body.</note> have identified a twofold matter for all such impressions, as you have already seen mentioned before: namely, one from which the meteors are made, which we call by the common name of "air changed into another form," but which they themselves called vapor or smoke...

...remained: the other in which the air, remaining in its nature or state, allows the **meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, lightning, and even certain minerals or diseases believed to "condense" from the air.</note> of both the **great and small worlds** <note>The Macrocosm (the universe) and the Microcosm (the human being).</note> to arise and float. Therefore, the **mundane air** <note>original: "aer mundanus"</note> is the common and general vehicle, as well as the parent and author, of meteors. Yet, there is also a particular air, enclosed either in the bowels of the earth or in the bodies of humans and other creatures, which also contains its own meteors arising from within itself.

We hold it as a most certain truth that all these spirits (which are homogeneous and of the same identical nature) have **matrices** <note>Wombs or molds that give shape to substances.</note> appropriate to themselves. These matrices, by a natural embrace, receive not only the spirits themselves but also the influences—those celestial and super-celestial treasures—floating within them. This is not unlike how the shell of an egg contains the crystalline white or the golden yolk floating within it. Indeed, it is impossible for anything "perfectly mixed" to be procreated in the **sublunary world** <note>The realm below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> unless it is cooked in its own **Philosophical egg** <note>An alchemical term for a sealed vessel or the natural "womb" where a substance matures.</note>—be it the common and universal earth or a specific body, such as animals, vegetables, and minerals—and brought gradually to perfection in its own time.

However, it often happens that due to some impediment—namely **impure and foreign sulfur** <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible principle; "impure sulfur" implies a corrupting influence.</note> or some similar accident—a meteor or "imperfectly mixed" substance cannot reach the peak of perfection. Thus, a thing is procreated that is monstrous, weak, leprous, and contrary to the laws of nature within the spirit or the air it occupies. Those skilled in **Astrology** attribute the reason for this to various planetary aspects, specifically the malevolent ones like the **square and opposition** <note>Astrological angles (90° and 180°) believed to cause tension or conflict.</note>, especially if the "unfortunate" planets look upon each other in these positions. This occurs if **Saturn and Mars** <note>The "Greater Malefic" and "Lesser Malefic" planets, associated with decay and strife.</note> hold dominion, for they operate in an unlucky and preternatural way in both the sublunary world and in the creatures that take in their spirit. That is, they procreate meteors that tend toward destruction rather than generation.

Yet, those more expert in **occult and secret Philosophy** attribute this same thing to the **Angels** presiding over those stars. These angels, following the manner of astrological influences, pour down their powers—and indeed, legions of **demons** under their command—into the elements during their time of strength or dominion in the heavens. At their prompting, the sublunary demons (whether good or evil) who obey them act in the form of **winds**, operating by fate in the air, water, and earth. They work either toward the destruction, sickness, and unhappiness of mortals, or toward their health and preservation, according to the good pleasure of the Creator and the disposition of their primary leader.

Thus, the earth attracts the mundane spirit, whether it is infected with a good or evil celestial "juice." Sometimes no meteor is manifest in it, but is secretly and scattered throughout; other times, the earth attracts the mundane spirit from a meteor that was previously visible but has since dissipated invisibly back into the air. Therefore, the spirit attracted into the earth by "breathing" is fit to procreate similar meteors in its womb, for within it are the **seeds** <note>original: "seminaria"</note> of both the meteors that appear visibly in the mundane air and those that lie hidden.

The same can be said of the human body, which by necessity attracts a portion of the surrounding air every moment through breathing. For this reason, **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician (c. 129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> numbered air among the necessary "alteratives" of the body, as it must be introduced through breathing, whether it is healthy (affected by the seeds of healthy meteors) or unhealthy (polluted by morbid seeds). Furthermore, the spirit in the human body is accustomed to "taste" terrestrial exhalations—both the good, where the seeds of meteors are beneficial, and the bad, where they are preternatural—through both food and breath. But we shall discuss these matters more copiously below.

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

...it is necessary that time precedes things begun, and simple things precede those composed of them; thus, in this methodical division of ours, we must start from the simpler or primary meteorological member, which we call **Wind**. Its beginning or root is so ancient that we have it handed down from the Sacred Page <note>The Bible.</note> that it took its origin from the mouth and nostrils of the Almighty Jehovah. We shall speak somewhat more extensively in this chapter about wind taken generally, since it is a creature of a truly divine condition and a very marvelous nature.

The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking (peripatētikos).</note> assert that wind is a hot and dry exhalation, difficult to ignite, springing from the earth and raised up to the middle region of the air. Repulsed downward by the cold of that region, and struggling upward—partly due to its own lightness and partly because of other exhalations meeting it from below—it is observed to move laterally above the earth in the lowest region of the air, which it agitates and fans, lest the air rot due to a lack of movement and a kind of laziness. We will dwell primarily on this definition of Aristotle here, because the spurious Christian philosophers <note>Thinkers who, in the author's view, followed Greek philosophy too closely over Scripture.</note> have not hesitated at all—almost as if struck by an unbridled madness—to defend and support this opinion of his with all their might, both in public schools and in their private studies, as if it were a divine publication for worldly folk or a decree issued from a most holy oracle.

From the aforementioned definition of Aristotle, they attempt to teach: First, that the matter or substance of wind is a hot and dry exhalation. Second, that the place in which it is generated and from which it is derived is the earth; they say the place toward which it tends is the middle region of the air, which it cannot penetrate; and they make the lowest region of the air the medium in which it moves upward, downward, and laterally. Third, they seem to establish a twofold mover of this exhalation both downward and laterally: namely, the cold of the middle region of the air, pressing that barely imaginable exhalation down toward the earth, and then later other exhalations successively rising from the earth, which, by their upward motion, meet the exhalation depressed by the cold, struggling with it and consequently producing noise in the air. Finally, this definition seems to succinctly outline the end or purpose of this motion ordained by nature: namely, that the air might be refreshed by such ventilation, and be preserved and purged from all rot.

But whoever wishes to place any faith in this pagan definition—especially if they are a lover of true wisdom—we believe it will be worth their while first to examine every particle of that definition. Let them, after a diligent inquiry, see whether it agrees with the laws of divine wisdom or not; that is, whether by the right of firmer reason such an opinion of pagan philosophers ought to be approved by us Christians, or rather rejected. In the first place, therefore, let us ask whether there is any probability of truth in the first part of his definition or not: namely, whether the matter of wind is a hot and dry exhalation springing from the earth? We are taught by Sacred Scripture (to which we Christians must give faith above all things) that wind has its origin from the spirit of Jehovah. From the breath, it says in <margin>*Exodus 15:8*</margin> *of your nostrils the waters were gathered together*. And it continues in <margin>*ibid. 10*</margin> *you blew with your wind, and the sea covered them*. And elsewhere: *God produces ice by his wind; at the breath of God, the frost is frozen*. And elsewhere, in <margin>*Job 27:9 & 28:25*</margin> *God makes a weight for the wind*. And the Royal Psalmist <note>King David.</note> says that the very angels of God are winds when he says in <margin>*Psalm 104:4*</margin> *He who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire*. And it is from here that doctors deeper in the mysteries of nature have said that the manifest or external part of the angels was air or the mundane spirit, but they made their hidden part divine fire; hence, such angels are called *Agalmata* <note>original: "Agalmata"; Greek for "images" or "statues," used here to mean reflections of the divine light.</note> by Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a theologian who wrote on the celestial hierarchy.</note>—that is, the clearest mirrors, receiving the light of God and representing his image. By the Royal Prophet, therefore, in the place cited above, both the hidden wind and the manifest or flashing and fiery wind are described as an angelic spirit, animated by divine fire. For this reason, a commentator on that passage speaks thus:

> For (he says) God uses winds and fire as administrators of His will and judgments, so that they also have the name of angels, where by flaming fire, flashes and lightnings are understood.

Thus he says; but more on the explanation of this matter in what follows, where the supernatural efficient cause must be discussed. It must be confessed, therefore, that either the breath of the nostrils or the treasury of God is an exhalation subject to preternatural passions, coming out of the earth—which is certainly profane to say—or that this part of the Peripatetic definition is most false. But from the examination of what follows, this will be more clearly depicted and debated; we shall therefore hasten to the inquiry of the second member.

The second member is that the place in which it is generated, and from which that exhalation (which is the material cause of wind) is derived, is the earth; that the place toward which it tends is the middle region of the air; and the medium in which it moves upward, downward, and laterally is the lowest space of the air. In this assertion of that pagan, what gross errors and absurdities are found will be clear from the following. We therefore divide this clause of his definition into three parts for better examination: in the first portion, we must explore by diligent inquiry whether the matter of winds is extracted from the terrestrial body or not; in the second, whether that substance makes its way upward only to the convex surface of the middle region of the air; in the third, whether the place in which the wind moves is only in the lowest region of the air. Regarding the first, we say that either the Sacred Page (which is the source of all truth) is not true, or this little part of the second member of his definition is

...this is most false, for the Spirit (as Saint John says) blows where it wills, but you do not know where it comes from, or where it goes <note>John 3:8. The author plays on the dual meaning of "spiritus" as both Holy Spirit and wind.</note>. Either, therefore, Aristotle the Pagan <note>original: "Ethnicus"</note> saw more into the mysteries of GOD and nature than the Evangelist, who was a true and sincere Christian; or John is plainly a liar in his doctrine—to assert which, for the love of Aristotle, would be the greatest impiety in a Christian. Aristotle himself affirms that the wind is moved from the earth and ascends to the middle region of the air, and from there is driven downward again. But Saint John says it moves not by compulsion or accidental impulse, but voluntarily according to its own pleasure; and that, although its voice or sound is familiar to the ears, where it comes from or where it goes remains unknown. This very doctrine of the Evangelist, which disagrees in every way with that of Aristotle, is established in various places of the Holy Scriptures; for the Royal Psalmist says:

> He brings forth the wind out of his treasuries. <note>Psalm 135:7.</note>

That the earth is not the seat of divine treasuries is clearly taught to us by the prelate Moses in these words:

> Jehovah has opened to you his best treasury, the heavens, by giving rain to the earth in its time. <note>Deuteronomy 28:12.</note>

He does not say "the earths" but "the heavens," between which two there is as great a difference as between day and night, light and darkness. For it is the heaven, or the air, which is the treasury-chest of GOD, and not the earth; from the heavens (I say) proceed the meteors <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note>, which finally rain down upon the earth either for its blessing or its curse. Hence David says:

> He opened the doors of the heavens and rained down Manna for them to eat, he gave them the grain of the heavens, etc. <note>Psalm 78:23-24.</note>

And elsewhere:

> GOD covers the heaven with thick clouds, who prepares rain for the earth. <note>Psalm 147:8.</note>

But even to this doubt—namely, whether the origin and passage of the wind is from the earth into the heaven—a man far more learned and wise in natural things than Aristotle responds directly in these words:

> The way of the wind (he says) man knows not, man knows not the work of GOD himself, by what way He does all these things. <note>Likely a paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 11:5 or Job.</note>

Yet Aristotle was a man—indeed, a Pagan—to whom it was consequently much less granted to judge rightly concerning such abstruse matters. Hence Jehovah, as if mocking the audacity of such a man and rebuking him, speaks thus:

> Do you know where the way is in which the vapor <note>original: "exhalatio"</note> is divided, which scatters the wind upon the earth? <note>Job 38:24.</note>

Thereby arguing the impossibility of this thing to a man to whom divine wisdom (which alone teaches all these things) has not been granted by the Creator. And yet Aristotle seems to answer Him impudently: "I know it; for the path of such an exhalation is from the earth upward, where—partly through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>A philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being compressed by surrounding cold.</note> by the cold driving it downward, and gradually by other exhalations striving upward—it is dispersed and driven laterally over the earth." But we shall immediately show the impossibility of this very reasoning in what follows.

Regarding the second and third parts of this clause, we say that the medium through which the winds move is far more vast than what Aristotle busies himself ascribing to them. For the wind does not blow only in the lowest region of the air, but also in the middle, and likewise in the highest—indeed, even in the Empyrean and Ethereal world. But the actions of the wind in any of these regions of the world vary according to the different actions of resistance—that is, the thinness or thickness of the moved air—as will be clearer in the following chapter. If, therefore, the wind blows in the middle region of the air, the vigor of that Aristotelian definition will be utterly destroyed, the efficacy of which consists chiefly in this: namely, that the exhalation is not permitted to penetrate through the "diaphragm" <note>The dividing layer between the lower and middle atmosphere.</note> of the middle region of the air, but is reverberated downward by the force of the cold resisting the heat of the exhalation. For the cause of the wind—if any exists in the middle region of the air—is totally taken away from him, because it is not driven downward by cold, but is observed to blow in the very center of that region.

Yet it is manifest that the clouds—both the higher ones, which are more light, bright, and colored, and the lower ones, which are observed to be darker and heavier—are driven by the winds from any quarter of the world to its opposite and fly as if on their wings; which indeed cannot happen without the presence of the winds in that middle region. Do we not also see with open eyes the South wind sometimes blowing strongly in one horizon, while at the same time the North wind holds dominion in the horizon next to it? From this it happens that at the boundary of both horizons we see a huge mass of clouds accumulated, and clouds moving against clouds, bringing with them horrendous thunders and astounding lightnings, striking out fire like flint against flint—which indeed cannot happen unless the winds moving them in opposite ways are also impetuous and violent in the middle region of the air.

This the Holy Scriptures also seem to confirm in many places; for in one place it is said:

> Smoke ascended from the nostrils of Jehovah, coals were kindled by Him, and He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under His feet; and He ascended upon the Cherubim and flew, and He glided upon the wings of the wind; He placed darkness in His circuit as a hiding place, sieving the waters from the clouds of the heavens; at His brightness and sight the clouds were kindled; the Lord thundered from heaven. <note>2 Samuel 22:9-14 (often cited as 2 Kings 22 in older texts).</note>

From which we gather that not only are clouds, thunder, and lightning moved by the winds, but even GOD Himself, surrounded by dark clouds in the middle region of the air, is carried upon their wings. And elsewhere it is said that the mighty GOD from His breath produces ice, and for irrigation He wearies the thick cloud <note>Job 37:9-11.</note>. From which it follows that it is necessary for the wind and its effects to be stronger in the middle region of the air than in the lowest. Does Aristotle not also speak against himself by confessing that the stormy wind, called <term>Ecnephias</term> <note>A Greek term for a hurricane or storm-wind that bursts forth from a cloud.</note>, together with the whirlwind, are sudden winds driven downward from a cloud? And yet, does he think there is any passage for a windy exhalation in the middle region of the air? But let us immerse ourselves a little deeper into this absurdity of his. He himself admits that the causes of ignited meteors <note>Such as shooting stars or comets.</note> are hot, dry, inflammable, and oily exhalations, and yet the path or passage for them through the middle region of the air is permitted by the nature of the place...

### On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

...acknowledged to be sent. For who in Philosophy can be so ignorant as to not know that coldness resists an inflammable and actually fiery thing more than one which is neither actually inflammable nor fiery in itself? Furthermore, the material cause of ignited meteors <note>In the early modern period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including lightning, rain, and clouds, not just "shooting stars."</note> is heavier than that of the wind, insofar as it is more compact and oily, and consequently not as fit for ascending or tending upward as the matter of the winds, which is quite light and rare. Therefore, it would be more impossible for the matter of ignited meteors to ascend into the middle region of the air, and through the middle into the supreme region, both because of the resistance of the cold in that place and because of the heavier and more compact composition of its substance (whose inclination is to tend downward), than it would be for the path of the winds to be denied by the cold in the middle position of the air. For cold obstructs an actually fiery and inflammable thing more than that which is only potentially so; and that which is light by its nature ascends more quickly than that which is compact and more ponderous.

But we shall now hasten to the examination of the third part of his definition, where he describes the twofold action of the winds, which he treats as accidents. It is as if one were to say that the wind is not moved and excited by an internal principle, but rather by external accidents—namely, by the cold of the middle region of the air, which drives the exhalation downward through <term>antiperistasis<note>original: "antiperistasin"; a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by the opposition of its contrary, such as cold air compressing and pushing down warm vapors.</note></term>, and by other ascending exhalations which meet those thrust downward, and by such an encounter hinder their direct motion. From this, he seems to assert that the wind is compelled by force and chance to move to the side, and by such lateral motion to agitate the air or the medium in which it moves, which causes the noise and sound to be emitted. How beautiful is this lie, and how very similar to the fictions of the poets! As if the wind were nothing other than something accidental? 

Yet the Holy Bible stoutly defends that the wind proceeds primarily from the divine breath. Indeed, it even calls it an "angel," which it acknowledges is spread everywhere by the divine spirit. Hence Moses says in the passage cited before, *By the blast of your nostrils the waters were gathered together (Exodus 15:8)* <note>original: "a flatu narium tuarum coaceruatæ sunt aquæ"</note>. And elsewhere, *You blew with your wind, and the sea covered them;* and elsewhere, *By the breath of God frost is given.* Does not King David also say in *Psalm 103:20, Bless Jehovah, you his angels, who are mighty in strength, who perform his word and listen to the voice of his word;* of whom it is said elsewhere, *Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire (Psalm 104:4).* And in the prophet Baruch, *chapter 5 verse 60: The wind performs the command of God;* and elsewhere, *O you winds, bless the Lord, and exalt him above all forever,* in the Song of Ananias <note>This refers to the "Song of the Three Holy Children," a deuterocanonical addition to the Book of Daniel.</note>. 

And yet, nonetheless, this Pagan of ours [Aristotle] wishes the wind to be something merely accidental. He does not blush to assert that it has its motion from external principles and not from an internal one, which is the "first act" of all things. He makes the motion of the wind involuntary (I say) and proceeding from contraries in nature, rather than voluntary; and yet we are taught by Saint John that *the spirit blows where it wills (John 3:8)* <note>original: "spiritus vbi vult spiret"</note>. This means its motion is voluntary, and by its indwelling nature, it is ready and always prepared to serve every command of its Creator. Aristotle extracts this dead fiction of his from the earth according to his own fantasy, whereas, on the contrary, God brings forth this living creature of His from His treasuries by means of His breath in truth, as the Royal Prophet and Jeremiah testify. 

But in this part of his argument, he seems to conclude that the lateral motion of the wind is caused by the resistance and hindrance of ascending exhalations. O, the poorest of all arguments! As if anyone would prudently say that a motion so constant as that from the North to the South, etc., proceeds from such an uncertain and varied cause. I mean to say, that the North, South, East, and West winds have their lateral motions from such frivolous and uncertain accidental struggles! What, I pray, my <term>Peripatetic<note>A follower of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle used to walk about ("peripateo") while teaching.</note></term>, was that reason for the struggling exhalations, and the order of their gushing from the earth, when the Prophet, by divine admonition, said to the spirit: *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live (Ezekiel 37:9)*? To me, they—and indeed their Christian followers—seem plainly mute and destitute of tongues with which to respond. The Wise Man says: *Awake, O North wind, and come, O South wind, and blow upon my garden (Song of Solomon 4:16)* <note>original: "Euigila Aquilo, & veni Auster, & perfla hortum meum"</note>. How deaf would that invocation of the Wise Man be if the material and life of such winds were as Aristotle describes them! 

And finally, how does it happen that there is such great variety in the condition or quality of the winds, so that one is hot and moist, another cold and dry, a third hot and dry, and the last cold and moist, if the Aristotelian opinion remained in its vigor—namely, that all winds were created in a single way and are moved laterally by the same accidents?

Finally, regarding the last clause of his definition, in which he placed the "end" or purpose of the winds (namely, for the purification of the air and preservation from putrefaction), we say, taught by experience, that this is most false. We observe with Galen and Hippocrates <note>Two of the most influential physicians of antiquity, whose works formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries.</note> that the Southern winds are very contagious and pestilential, insofar as they thicken the air and render it putrid with their malevolent heat and moisture. We have this confirmed by the Holy Scriptures, which support us in this matter. *Fear not (says the Psalmist) the plague or the demon that wastes at noonday (Psalm 91:5)*. And Habakkuk says in his prayer, *When God came from the South, his glory covered the heavens and the earth was full of his praise; the pestilence went before him and burning coals went forth at his feet.* Indeed, the Holy Page teaches us in *Job 37:14* that the winds in general, as well as the other meteors of heaven, were ordained by the Creator as much for a scourge as for doing a benefit. Therefore, Aristotle erred across the whole heaven no less in the "final cause" of the winds than in the others, along with his disciples. We conclude, therefore, that the definition of that Pagan Philosopher, which Christians venerate and follow with such devotion, is in every way false and—

and false, since winds are creatures by nature far more excellent and divine than Aristotle or any of the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> ever understood. For they are not inanimate things endowed only with an accidental motion—that is, exhalations springing by chance from the earth and stirred up by the cold of the upper regions and ascending vapors—but, as the Angel taught Zechariah (*Chapter 6:1* <note>Likely referencing Zechariah 6:5: "These are the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth."</note>): Winds animated by an angelic spirit go forth and stand before the Ruler of all the earth. But I confess there will be some Christian followers of Aristotle who, in the common manner, will want to argue that in a dispute one should not jump from one art to another <note>Original: "ab arte in artem... progressionem," a logic rule that one shouldn't mix disciplines like physics and theology.</note>, and that it is therefore irregular to move from Philosophy to Theology or to use the authority of one to disprove the other. To these we easily respond that Theosophy <note>Divine wisdom or "God-knowledge."</note> and Sacred Philosophy do not differ from one another in the least. Furthermore, if the laws of Philosophy disagree with those of Theosophy, that Philosophy must be considered false and spurious, and consequently must be entirely rejected and consigned to eternal oblivion by Christian men; for the Bible, which is the true source and origin of Theosophy or Theology, is the only truth, and whatever is discordant with it is false and Diabolical. Of such a kind are those deformed inventions of the Pagans, which will vanish of their own accord like shadows, whereas, on the contrary, the characters of the divine word—carved in the everlasting monuments of memory and inscribed as if by the finger of GOD—will remain until the very end. For in this word the spirit of all truth is to be found, which, as the most holy scripture testifies, will teach all things; and without it, nothing can truly be learned or acquired.

It is well: perhaps someone will say, let it be as you say, but I wish to know, what then is wind? How should it be defined or described according to the consensus of the Holy Scriptures? To which we say that this can be provided in many ways under a single essence. We think it should be described in these ways quite pertinently:

->**Wind is an aerial spirit, of moderate consistency, inspired or animated by the breath of Jehovah, which He Himself brings forth from His treasures according to His will, whether for the purpose of a scourge or for a blessing.**<-

Every part of this definition is proven from many passages of the Holy Scriptures. That its internal substance is air, in its moderate consistency, is clear from the fact that air, spirit, and wind are called by the same Hebrew word *Ruach* <note>Original: רוּחַ, meaning breath, wind, or spirit.</note> in many places of the Holy Scriptures. Furthermore, that its internal part or moving soul is the divine breath is shown by those passages of the Holy Scriptures previously cited, namely: *by the blast of your nostrils the waters were gathered together* (Exodus 15:8). And again: *You blew with your wind and the sea covered them.* And elsewhere: *The mighty GOD produces ice by his breath.* It is as if he were saying that GOD inspired the air with His mighty spirit, so that there is no difference between an angel and air inspired by GOD; for air is the external or manifest form of an angel (whether evil or good) animated by the divine spirit for either benevolence or a curse. Just as its hidden part is the immediate breath of GOD, they are also called *Agalmata* <note>Original: ἀγάλματα, Greek for "images" or "statues." In Neoplatonism, these are mirrors that reflect divine light.</note>, that is, the clearest mirrors receiving the light of GOD, as has been told. And hence it is said that the name of GOD was in the Angel who preceded the Israelites, who also moved in the pillar of cloud and fire; this was composed partly of dense, moist air (as if from a thinner substance) and partly of a subtle fire. This angel, as we read elsewhere, was called Wisdom: for we read in Ecclesiasticus <note>The author cites Ecclesiastes 9, but the quote is actually from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:3-5.</note>: *I, Wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High, and covered the earth as a mist. My throne is in a pillar of cloud; I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep, in the waves of the sea, in all the earth, and in every people and nation I rested.* For this reason, the Kabbalists and the more skilled of the Hebrew Doctors called this angel Metatron [Mitattron], whom the Platonists made the Universal Soul of the world. Thus, the universal spirit or air of the world, animated by the divine emanation called Wisdom, is that great angel or spirit and wind whose heart or center is in the Celestial Sun; hence the Royal Psalmist says, *He set his tabernacle in the sun.* And this is the reason why the angel preceding the Israelites is sometimes called an angel (that is, a creature) by the sacred text—specifically in respect to the external spirit or air, which was created—and is sometimes called Jehovah, in respect to the name of GOD, or the divine and uncreated light that animated him. From this it is clear that GOD is the center of every spirit, and air is its vehicle; air so inspired is the soul of the cloud and of every other meteor <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, such as wind, rain, or lightning.</note>, and indeed even of a perfectly mixed body, as it is the internal soul moving all things where it wills, *for the Spirit blows where it wills.* Hence the wise man says, *The incorruptible Spirit of GOD is in every thing, moving internally.* And this seems to be the same as what the deeper scholars of the Kabbalah hold (*Reuchlin in Cabala* <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a pioneering Christian scholar of the Kabbalah.</note>), asserting that an Angel is a mediating power between GOD and nature, by which operations are performed in things that their nature either would not do, or would do in such a way that others say they proceed from a "hidden property" or "because it is so." This great angel, called Wisdom, therefore seems to be the one who appeared to John in the Apocalypse, who was said *to be like the son of man in the midst of seven golden candlesticks, whose eyes were as a flame of fire, and in his right hand he held seven stars, and his voice was as the sound of many waters or winds; under whose command the other angels were seen to be subjected, as it was given to him to command the four Angels who had power over the winds, ordering them not to hurt the earth or the water, etc.* (Revelation 1 and 3). We conclude therefore, that just as GOD is Identity—namely, pure uncreated form—so also an angel is Alterity <note>A philosophical term for "otherness" or the first departure from divine unity into created multiplicity.</note>—na-

The author argues this verse proves that angels and winds are essentially the same substance.</note>, in which discourse he seems to explain both the hidden and the manifest nature of angels.

For the Royal Prophet says: *He brings the wind out of his treasuries, Psalm 135:7*. Furthermore, the Prophet tells of its use in general: *The wind performs the command of GOD: Baruch 6:60* <note>The original cites Baruch 1:60, but this likely refers to the "Letter of Jeremiah" found in the Book of Baruch in the Vulgate Bible.</note>. And that royal one: *The spirit of the storms, which fulfill his word: Psalm 148:8*. And elsewhere: *Angels, most powerful in strength, doing his pleasure: Psalm 103:20*. Finally, the wind, the whirlwind, cold, ice, frost, clouds, rain, and lightning are prepared; for whatever GOD has commanded these to do upon the surface of the orb of the earth—whether for a scourge, or for terror, or for the performance of a kindness—He causes them to be ready at hand: *Job 37:13* <note>The original cites Job 38:8, but the context of "scourge or mercy" matches Job 37:13.</note>.

In our aforementioned definition, therefore, we have first expressed the nature of the wind's material cause: we said, namely, that it is air of a moderate existence. Next, we noted its internal form: that it is the bright breath of GOD, animating, agitating, and illuminating the airy matter. We have also indicated the place in which this creature is reserved and stored: the treasury-chest of GOD, namely the heavens or the air. Finally, we said its use is to be prompt and ready to fulfill the will of its Creator, either through the manifestation of its hidden part—that is, in its fiery or flashing form—or through the concealment of its internal part—that is, in its airy or invisible form (which is its body).

From these foundations, therefore, we have described the wind in another way, after this manner:

**Wind is an invisible spirit or air, animated and quickened by divine light from the face or sight of Jehovah, issuing like a breath from His nostrils, to execute His pleasure both in the heavens and on the earth.**

Or thus:

**Wind is a certain angelic spirit, or subtle air, inspired and animated by the fiery spirit of Jehovah—sometimes visible and manifest, as in lightning and flashes, and sometimes invisible and hidden, as in that which is heard but not at all seen—emitted by divine power in a secret manner from some quarter of the world to execute the divine will, whether for salvation and benevolence, or for punishment and a curse upon the earth.**

Or thus:

**Wind is an invisible and hidden spirit, endowed with a fiery soul, and inspired by GOD in the manner of an angel; it flies here and there on invisible wings according to the pleasure of the Inspirer, and sometimes delights to carry the Inspirer upon its pinions. For it is said: *Jehovah ascended upon the Cherubim, and flew, and glided upon the wings of the wind. 2 Samuel 22:11*.**

Or thus:

**Wind is a certain angelic creature, produced by Jehovah the Creator, made of air as its agitated matter and inspired by divine light as its moving central soul; it is brought forth from His treasuries at His will and sent here and there, whether for benevolence and mercy, or for a scourge and punishment.**

Or thus:

**Wind is an angelic spirit, breathing here and there, secretly and invisibly, according to the hidden good pleasure of the Creator; although its sound may be heard, the boundary of where it comes from or where it goes is unknown to mortals: *John 3:8. The Spirit <note>The Latin word "Spiritus" can mean both "Spirit" and "Wind."</note> blows where it wills, and a man hears its voice, but knows not whence it comes or whither it goes.* Furthermore, the sacred writings testify that the way and place of GOD are unknown to men.**

Or thus, from the mouth of the Savior:

**Wind is a spirit that blows where it wills; though its voice may be heard, the goal is unknown and the place uncertain from which it comes or whither it goes.**

Or thus, as we perceive or gather from the passages cited above:

**Winds are the angels of GOD, most powerful in strength, fulfilling His word, hearkening to the voice of His speech, His flaming ministers, doing His pleasure: *Psalms 103 and 104*.**

Here, therefore, we see how opposed that Ethnic <note>The author uses "Ethnic" to mean "Pagan," referring specifically to the Ancient Greeks like Aristotle.</note> doctrine is to this one, which is drawn from the fountain of all truth. From this it follows that he who firmly adheres to Aristotelian doctrine cannot be radically engaged in the Christian faith. *You cannot faithfully serve two masters*, says our Savior; and St. Paul warns us not without reason *to abstain from vain philosophy* <note>Colossians 2:8.</note>. For in truth, that philosophy is the primary instrument or organ of the Devil himself, by which he is accustomed to distract worldly men from GOD and to draw them with sophisticated deceits toward his own antipathetic harmony, inciting them to give credit to his otherwise vain temptations. This, therefore, is the reason why the men of this age—who should be possessors of the divine mind but have forgotten their illustrious origin and nobility, led as they are by illusions and shadowy lights—are so crude and unskilled in both true theosophy and the sincere arts, that they understand neither GOD as He truly is, nor His creatures...

### CHAPTER V.

->*In which it is proved that the world and all things contained in the world are originally wind, and consequently from wind, no less than a thing begun is from its beginning.*<-

God, the best and greatest, the uncreated spirit and as it were uncreated wind, the primary source of all spirits and winds, breathing into the world His breath of life, brought its universal spirit (previously existing in potential) into a living and actual air or wind. For His lucid spirit or breath was carried over all the spiritual waters, imparting to them a fiery vigor or life, and thus He animated the entire mass of the mundane air by His breath, and reduced it into the wind of created nature. Hence, the primary spirit or wind, breathed from the mouth of the GOD of Gods and the spirit of spirits, from which the world and all its creatures are forged, is called in the Sacred Scriptures (as expressed in the Hebrew context of *Genesis 1*) **Ruach Elohim** <note>original: **רוח אלהים**; usually translated as "The Spirit of God" or "The Wind of God"</note>, that is, the wind of the Lord, which elsewhere they also call **Hochma** <note>original: **חכמה**; "Wisdom"</note> or Wisdom. They describe this as the holy spirit of intelligence, and a certain flux or emanation of clarity—that is, of the spirit or lucid breath of eternal light, and a mirror without stain of the majesty of GOD. The Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics whose traditions were often integrated into Renaissance Christian philosophy</note> have not unadvisedly called this spirit the *soul of the world* <note>original: "anima mundi"</note>, which they understood through the great angel **Metatron** <note>In mystical tradition, Metatron is a supreme angel who acts as the celestial scribe and mediator between the divine and the created world</note>. From this, they argue that the universal created spirit of the world (which we call general air) is animated by the spirit or breath and as it were the divine and uncreated emanation. Therefore, they also thought this angel was the one who preceded the Israelites in the desert, of whom God spoke thus: *Behold, I send my angel before you; beware of his face, for my name is in him, Exodus 23:20.* And hence it is that, with respect to the created spirit, which is its external part, he is called an Angel and a creature of the first degree; but with respect to the name of **Jehovah** bestowed upon him, which is his central character, he is accepted as the Creator. Whence it happened that in the same chapter, he is sometimes called an "angel"—that is, with respect to his external, which is a creature—and sometimes "Jehovah," insofar as his divine and internal nature is regarded. He was made as a type <note>A "type" is a symbolic model or precursor in theological study</note> of our Savior, who was called both GOD, with respect to that internal and immortal spirit or divine name, and also man, with respect to His mortal flesh. The Poets also called this spirit the **Bread of God** <note>original: "panem DEI." This is that spirit or breath and divine blast or wind, the **Ruach Elohim** proceeding from the mouth of the Most High (according to that saying in Ecclesiasticus: *I, wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High* <note>Sirach 24:3</note>), by which God inspired the potential spirit of the world with the actual spirit of life. From this, first of all, the **Empyrean** <note>The highest, most refined part of the heavens, associated with pure light and fire</note> spirit or wind, the thinnest of all creatures, was informed and animated, and was moved by the divine will in the manner of gently stirred elementary air. Then, this angelic composition is as it were the form informing the ethereal spirit produced on the second day of creation, in whose center this spirit of God's forms placed its tabernacle—namely, in the sun. # On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

Thus, by both a super-celestial and celestial inspiration, the wind—or the air of the lowest region of the world—is animated, no differently than we see a body being moved by a soul. Furthermore, the wind thus animated is the soul of all meteors. From these winds, or portions of air inspired by angelic powers, all the meteors of the world, both visible and invisible, are procreated. For example, we see that clouds and other meteors, both bright and dark, are not only moved centrally by the winds but are also materially fashioned from the air.

<margin>The incorruptible Spirit of GOD is in every thing, Wisdom 12.</margin>
From these things, we see that the divine breath is the central and internal principle of every worldly thing—the simplest and primary agent, according to the words of the wise man. By its blowing, the angelic spirit or wind is moved and animated; the aerial spirit, in turn, is moved by the angelic wind; the elementary or ethereal spirit by the ethereal wind; and the meteors (or imperfect mixtures) by the aerial wind. This aerial wind, along with its souls—namely the empyrean and ethereal—drives and moves all composite things. These are nothing other than "spermatic" meteors <note>The author uses "spermatic" to mean things containing a seed or life-principle, like a developing organism, rather than just inanimate matter.</note> brought to the perfection of maturity. Their destiny is either to be returned to the air from which they came—that is, from an imperfect mixture back to simplicity—or to proceed toward the completion of a perfect composition. This occurs through the constant movement and mediation of internal forces which, according to their own nature as governed by the divine will, work either toward generation by maturing or toward destruction by putrefying and corrupting. 

We observe, however, that the uncreated spirit or wind blows in diverse ways, though it is one and the same spirit. In the same way, we see that the same fire can act either kindly and naturally by providing warmth, or harmfully, either preternaturally by drying or heating excessively, or unnaturally by totally consuming and burning the subject. These varied effects are not due to the agent, but rather to the resisting subject that receives it poorly. And hence it is that, just as GOD is the first and principal act in every creature—whether His intention is directed toward destruction, affliction, and the infliction of suffering, or inclined toward generation and beneficence—so too a different name is attributed to Him in the Sacred Scriptures for each of those properties. Thus, according to the various arrangements of the ten Kabbalistic *Sephiroth* <note>In the Jewish mystical tradition of the Kabbalah, the Sephiroth are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals Himself.</note>, ten names are ascribed to GOD. Nevertheless, all these seem to tend toward two ends: namely, either toward severity, by which He is accustomed to punish sinners and corrupt the elements for the sins of men, or toward kindness, as will be said more broadly in our discourse on the efficient causes of meteors.

And this was the reason that the wise Greeks called Him *Dionysus* <note>original: "Dionysius"; likely referring to the myth of Dionysus Zagreus, who was torn into seven pieces.</note> during the nighttime, when He is said to tear apart the seven composite parts. But during the daytime, they called Him *Apollo*, as he is thought to reconstruct those seven parts and rebuild them through generation—parts which he had decayed through putrefaction under the name of Dionysus during the night. But since GOD is thought to act through ordination, while the angels (as His ministers) act through execution, those versed in the deeper mystery of *Theosophy* <note>Divine wisdom or mystical insight into the nature of God and the world.</note> attribute the execution of His severity to the angels: *Gabriel*, presiding over the Northern Winds, and *Samuel* or *Uriel*, governing those of the south. Hence it happens that effects preternatural to the world are often produced by the spirits of these angels, as you have explained more fully in our treatise on *Mystical Anatomy* and more copiously in the section on the efficient cause of meteors. On the other hand, the angels provide evidence of divine clemency and mercy: *Michael*, holding dominion in the east and breathing benevolent breaths of life and generation from that quarter; and *Raphael*, to whom the guardianship of the western quarter is attributed, as he has dominion over the winds of that region—for the name *Raphael*, by its very designation, denotes the "Medicine of GOD." From these winds, under the dominion of the Archangels, all meteors in the sublunary world are procreated, whether they reach the goal of a composite generation or retreat to the simple end of corruption. 

For in the center of any "seed" <note>original: "spermatis"; used here in the sense of a biological or elemental starting point.</note>, a certain wind is seen to animate the seed-mass, inflating it and making it swell—as experience teaches us—since a seed is nothing other than a cloud or thickened air. It is centrally inspired and animated by the spirit of life and moved toward the point of perfection in no other way than we see air being reduced by an angelic wind or spirit into vapor, from vapor into mist, and from mist gradually into a thick cloud. Its flashing soul sometimes appears to our eyes and sometimes is hidden; finally, the substance of the cloud is observed to transform into hard stone through the action of that lightning-like and formal wind. In a similar manner, for the generation of a man, the will of the father—which is also a wind—stirs the paternal mind. Then the animal, vital, and natural winds are enclosed in the seed; within a few days after its infusion into the womb, they raise up with their breath three "bubbles" <note>In early embryology, the three "bubbles" (ampullae) were thought to be the precursors to the three primary organs: heart, brain, and liver.</note> from which the heart, brain, and liver are formed. Then, like an inflated bladder, these winds are observed to gradually fashion the mass into the likeness of a fetus, and finally into the human form. Indeed, the whole life of man is spirit and wind, whose duty it is to breathe in and breathe out at every moment. Does not the Holy Scripture call it the *breath of life*? Furthermore, every passion of the soul—whether violent and unnatural, or according to the laws of nature—is driven by winds. Thus anger, madness, fury, fear, and other things of this sort are the effects of stormy and tempestuous Microcosmic winds, like the *Typhon*, *Ecnephias*, and *Prester* <term>Ecnephias and Prester: terms for specific types of violent whirlwinds or fiery storms described in ancient meteorology</term>, as well as thunder and earthquakes. Of this kind also are diseases such as epilepsy, vertigo, "suffocation of the womb" <note>original: "suffocatio matricis"; an old medical term for hysteria or uterine disorders believed to be caused by internal vapors.</note>, and so on. Which is indeed confirmed by the testimony of the wise man—

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the types of Macrocosmic winds, and first concerning the Cardinal winds.

There are two types of Macrocosmic <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the great world or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "Microcosm," which is the human being.</note> winds. Since some are:

*   **Cardinal, which are four in number, namely:**
    *   **Boreas**, blowing from the Northern pole of both heaven and earth.
    *   **Auster**, breathing from the Southern pole of both heaven and earth.
    *   **Subsolanus**, leaping out from the eastern equinox of heaven and earth.
    *   **Favonius**, blowing from the western equinox of both heaven and earth.
*   **Collateral. See G.** <note>Collateral winds are the secondary winds that blow between the four main directions.</note>

The ancients recognized, or rather focused upon, only the Cardinal winds from among these types, because they are accustomed to blow from each distinct quarter or fourth of the world, in whose power and naming all those called "collateral" winds were contained. They are called Cardinal, principal, and primary, both from their varying duties—since each is observed to blow a breath different in position and condition—and from their site and location, as we shall show below in its proper place. The cardinal number is fourfold, according to the four quarters of the world from which they are observed to emit their blasts. For **Boreas** [the North wind] has its place and dominion from the arctic pole, namely from the seven northern stars <note>A reference to the Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note>; hence it is entirely contrary to **Auster** or **Notus** [the South wind] in both location and nature. Conversely, **Auster** is said to blow from the Southern pole, which likewise is opposed to the nature or condition and location of Boreas. **Subsolanus** [the East wind] is accustomed to breathe out its breath from the eastern point of the equinoctial line, just as **Favonius** [the West wind] does directly from the opposite western point. 

We have this confirmed by the Bible of all truth. For in the prophet Jeremiah we find these words: *I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and I will winnow them into all those winds, Jeremiah 49:36.* And from Revelation: *I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the winds of the earth, so they should not blow upon the earth, Revelation 7:1.* And in the Prophet Ezekiel: *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, Ezekiel 37.* And in the Prophet Daniel: *Behold, the four winds of heaven fought upon the great sea, Daniel 7,* and also in many other places. In the specific naming of these winds, the Holy Scriptures seem to differ slightly from modern writers; for what the moderns call **Boreas**, the Scriptures call **Aquilo** [the North wind]. Likewise, what the moderns call **Subsolanus**, the Scriptures call **Eurus**, which is generally taken for every wind blowing from the East. If it leans more toward the South, it expresses a stormy and furious force, wherefore the Psalmist testifies that *the tempests of the sea are stirred by the East wind [Eurus], and by the East wind you break the ships of the Ocean, Psalm 48:8.* And Job: *By the East wind [Eurus] he brought in a whirlwind in the manner of a storm; by the East wind [Eurus] he brought the Red Sea back to dryness, Job 27:21; Exodus 14:21.* If it leans more toward the summer solstice, they assign it greater powers of heat and dryness; thus in Genesis we find *fruits scorched by the East wind [Eurus], Genesis 41,* and also herbs dried up, as is found in the Prophet Jonah. If in its middle disposition: *By the East wind [Eurus] light is scattered over the earth, and by the East wind [Eurus] Jehovah brought locusts, Job 38 and Exodus 10.* So also they take **Aquilo** for every Northern wind, where it is said by the wise man: *The North wind [Aquilo] brings rain, and, the North wind [Aquilo] produces cold, Proverbs 25:23; Job 37:9. And, Arise North wind [Aquilo], and come South wind [Auster], blow through my garden, Song of Solomon 4.* Finally, **Favonius** [the West wind], and all other winds of that quarter of the world...

### On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

They seem to include it under this common term: *With a wind from the West* (says *Moses*) *in its strength, GOD took up the locusts, Exodus 10.*

It is not without cause that in the division of the cardinal winds, we mentioned the poles and the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note>, and consequently the winds blowing from them both on earth and in heaven. For we are taught by the experience of the magnetic stone (which is also called a *terella* <note>original: *terella* — literally "little earth." A spherical magnet used by early scientists to model the Earth's magnetic field.</note>) that the earth itself has an excellent proportion to the heavens and its circles. It even lives and breathes in imitation of its celestial parents by an aerial-like spirit, through the mediation of that world-spirit from its four quarters, no differently than the heavens. This world-spirit also seems to be emulated by the human body in every respect; for the human—being a child of the world—possesses his own poles, circles, and winds proper to each of his quarters, as was explained in *Our Mystical Anatomy* <note>Refers to Fludd’s earlier work where he maps the human body to the structure of the universe.</note>.

The experiment of the magnetic *terella*, by whose arrangement we are also accustomed to judge the nature of the Macrocosmic <term>Macrocosm: the "Great World" or the entire universe.</term> and Microcosmic <term>Microcosm: the "Little World," meaning the human being as a reflection of the universe.</term> earth, is as follows.

First, it is certain and proven by experience that the magnetic *terella* emits its forces from its center into a sphere. This same thing is undoubtedly observed in the earth, of which the magnet is a tiny offspring, possessing the disposition of the whole no differently than any drop of water possesses the nature of the great sea. For in the center of the earth is a **central Sun**, having within it an exactly magnetic power by which it draws its like to itself. Indeed, just as we observe two poles in the mathematical heaven that rotate the machine of the world, so too do we find natural poles endowed with Macrocosmic power in the terrestrial globe: one tending toward the arctic pole, and the other declining toward the opposite part of the world. This can be most easily demonstrated by the nature of a round magnet (a small portion of the earth, just as a drop of water is to the element of water). When this stone is fashioned into a spherical shape like the earth, it reveals not only poles but also the equator and other circular lines at various latitudes through its effects. For the closer the parts of the magnetic sphere are to its equator, the more obliquely the magnetic pieces (namely iron) are observed to be attracted and lured to it. But the parts of the spherical body are observed to draw iron or a needle to themselves more directly the closer they are to the pole. We have expressed the figure of the spherical stone with its various formulas of attraction here.

A similar magnetic force is also present in the human body, which is also a *terella*. Its magnetic spirit is observed to be so strong that the Sages were well aware that it could attract not only elemental but also celestial virtues in a wonderful way, and join earthly things with celestial ones through the mediation of this magnetic faculty of spirits. Indeed, just as a pure and clean spirit is able to attract clean things to itself from the heavens and the elements, so also a malignant and impure spirit, by the opposite reasoning, attracts spirits similar to itself from the heavens and the earth—namely, the good attract divine inspirations, and the evil attract diabolical ones. And by this kind of magnetic power of spirits, not only those most true in natural magic, but even witches themselves, are accustomed to produce such stupendous and hardly imaginable things; through this kind of occult mastery, they are known to malignantly infect the spirits of men from a distance.

### *The relation or application of the aforesaid Macrocosmic distinction to the human microcosm.*

The same thing must be said regarding the cardinal winds of the human body—or the "human earth"—as was said of those of the <term>Macrocosm: the "Great World" or the universe.</term>. Therefore, we divide the Microcosmic winds in this manner:

<margin>The cardinal or principal winds in the Microcosm—which blow in imitation of the cardinal winds in both the heaven and earth of the Macrocosm—are either:</margin>

- **Cardinal winds**, which are understood as a set of four:
    - **Boreas** <note>The North Wind.</note>, blowing from the region of the **spleen**, or the microcosmic North.
    - **Auster** <note>The South Wind.</note>, breathing from the region of the **liver**, or the microcosmic South.
    - **Subsolanus** <note>The East Wind.</note>, emitting its life-breaths from the station of the **heart and the spiritual organs**.
    - **Favonius** <note>The West Wind.</note>, breathing from the **reproductive vessels, the viscera, and the stomach**, as if from the West.
- **Collateral winds**. I.

Just as we see the earth—following the example of the magnetic *terella* <note>original: *terella* — a "little earth," or a spherical magnet used to model the planet's magnetic field.</note>—containing its own quarters of the world, namely the Poles, the Equator, and the Tropics, so too the "little earth" of the human body undoubtedly possesses its own quarters and principal regions. The various spirits of these regions attract the world-spirit to themselves in different ways through a magnetic virtue. 

From this, it follows that just as certain parts are found in iron that seek out one part of a magnet or another due to their essential properties and a certain natural inclination (as is clearly shown in the experiment mentioned above), so too in the world-spirit drawn into the human body through breathing, one may find various portions that naturally adhere more to this or that part of the human body's spirit, according to their condition and nature. 

For example, that portion of the world-spirit introduced into the human body through breathing has some northern parts, some southern parts, others eastern, and finally some western. However, in its general inclination, it participates more in that wind whose dominion was strongest at the time it was inhaled. Thus it happens that a certain spirit or wind makes the spirits of men more "fluid" and prone to <term>catarrhs: excessive buildup of mucus or "runny" conditions, traditionally associated with the damp South wind.</term>, namely the **Southern wind** (*Austrinus*); and so it is with the others. Even the spirit attracted at the first moment of birth—or rather, at the hour of the fetus's life—causes one to have a phlegmatic, melancholic, sanguine, or choleric <term>complexion: the "four temperaments" of ancient medicine, believed to be governed by bodily fluids (humors).</term>, according to the nature of the wind first inhaled at that time.

Similarly, the spirit of natural life is derived from all the winds (as Ezekiel seems to assert, who prophesied to the bones, saying: > *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe into these slain, that they may live* < <note>original: *Adueni spiritus à quatuor ventis, & insuffla istos mortuos vt viuant* — Ezekiel 37:9.</note>). From the inhaled Macrocosmic spirit, it divides those parts proper to each wind of the Macrocosm and distributes them by magnetic virtue into their own "quarters" within the human *terella*. That is, the Northern part of the Microcosmic spirit is attracted by that of the Macrocosmic North, both for its sustenance and to perform those duties in the human body which must be provided by the styptic <note>Astringent or contracting.</note> and cold temperament of that part—namely, to restore the Melancholic humor, which is the food of the Spleen. 

In the same way, the Southern portion performs this same task in the "sanguine" duty for the sustenance of the liver and the creation of blood. Likewise, the portion destined for life performs its work in the heart and arteries. For like always rejoices in like, and by a certain magnetic attraction, they embrace one another closely in the bonds of love, because "nature rejoices in nature and exults." 

Do we not have this very thing most accurately tested and proven by us in the "anatomy" of Wheat and Bread? <note>Fludd frequently used laboratory distillation of wheat to prove that solid matter is actually "thickened" air or spirit.</note> In this experiment, we divided the substance into its distinct elements, which, when examined by the test of fire, we found to be nothing other than wind and air. For when subjected to a very slow heat, they dissolved into a smoke very much like atoms. 

From these things we can argue—and clearly so—that a composite body relates to its internal animating spirit just as a cloud relates to the wind. For just as a cloud was formerly air, which is condensed into mist and cloud by the breathing of winds blowing from opposite directions, so too an opaque composite body was nothing but a cloud, brought into a perfect mixture by the benevolent breath of the winds. This is proven in this way: namely, because every thing is resolved back into that from which it was originally created. Wood, wheat, and the animal body are reduced by the violence of fire into smoke or a thick vapor, much like a cloud, which then gradually dissipates into invisible air—the very air from which all things are seen to depart. 

From this, the axiom of Plato is verified: *The source upon which the beginning of any thing depends is the same source in which its growth shall be.* Since no creature deprived of air can either grow or live, we say therefore that the whole composite body is nothing other than air of various conditions, [blown] into that which it is...

...composed; I mean air of various conditions, insofar as it includes the seeds <note>original: *spermata* — here used to mean the fundamental essences or "germs" of qualities</note> of different winds, namely the **choleric** from the Eastern winds, the **phlegmatic and watery** from the Western, the **melancholic and earthy** from the Northern, and the **sanguine with putrefaction** from the Southern. And this is why the fiery oiliness of wheat is air containing the seed of the South-East wind <note>original: *Euri*</note>, and why its ethereal part—which is the central salt of life—is the East wind <note>original: *subsolani*</note>, as that wind is the airy instrument of growth. Its air, containing the seed of the Southern winds, and its earth, which binds everything together, partakes of the Northern winds; likewise, its phlegm or watery substance is nourished by the Western winds.

It is for this reason that from the same substance, the oil or choleric humor is separated by the natural chemistry of man and stored in the **gall bladder** <note>original: *cistam fellis*</note>; the aerial part is processed in the **liver** and changed into blood; and the earthy part or "gluten" is transported to the **spleen**, as if to its own natural home. Sweet phlegm is carried to the stomach and the hidden passages of the viscera, while the salty serosity <note>the watery part of bodily fluids</note> is sent to the kidneys and the bladder. And yet, all these parts of bread or wheat are nothing other than air, "infected" by the different natures of the winds blowing from the four quarters of the world. This is evident from the fact that, as has been said, they are gradually converted back into air or wind by a light fire.

By these things, therefore, it is clearly explained that there is a **magnetic force** in the spleen that attracts to itself those things from both nourishment and inhaled air which are of a Northern nature. In the liver, it attracts those that participate in the Southern winds; in the heart, those which, by the natural power of life, descend from the ether; in the gall bladder, those from the bilious winds (such as the East-North-East and South-East winds); and finally, in the stomach and viscera, those which receive their life from the Western winds. Therefore, from these effects on the parts of man, we can determine the points of the poles and the equinoctials (both East and West), just as we determine the equinox, the poles, and the vertical axis of a magnet by applying iron to its parts, through the experiment described earlier. Is it not also established by similar reasoning that air is converted into a cloud by the application of various winds, containing within itself bodies of diverse natures, namely stones, flames, waters, and so on?
