### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I.

For example, the **North-East wind** <note>original: *Aquilo*</note> carries with it the cold and dry nature of the **North wind** <note>original: *Boreas*</note>—the direct polar wind—in every way, except that its coldness is mitigated in some small, though barely perceptible degree by its proximity to the place of the rising sun, which is intensely hot. Thus, it is observed to differ in certain qualities from the nature of the North wind; for while the North wind's role is to drive away dense clouds, the North-East wind does not drive them away or dissipate them, but rather binds and constricts them. This can be understood from the very etymology of its name: for as Isidore, Constantius, and others argue, *Aquilo* is named as if it were "binding the waters and clouds" <note>original: *aquas & nubes ligans*</note>. In the Holy Scriptures, this wind seems to be understood generally as any wind blowing from the northern quarter.

Another wind collateral to the North wind, situated opposite the part of the arctic circle called **Circius** <note>the West-Northwest wind</note>, leans somewhat away from the dryness of the North toward the moisture of the **West wind** <note>original: *Favonius*</note>; hence it is observed to differ slightly in its condition from its principal, the North wind. So too does the **South wind** <note>original: *Auster*</note> have the **South-East wind** <note>original: *Euro-Austrum*</note> on its right side, whose humidity is somewhat mitigated by the dryness of the East; just as on the left side of that Cardinal direction, the heat of the **South-West wind** <note>original: *Austro-africus*</note> is somewhat—though insensibly—blunted by the cold of the West. Thus it happens that these winds produce effects somewhat different from those of their Cardinal principal.

By a clearly similar logic, the collateral winds of both the **East** <note>original: *Subsolanus*</note> and the **West** <note>original: *Favonius*</note> differ. For that wind which is North of the East, called **Caecias** <note>the North-East wind</note> from its "wickedness" and **Hellesponticus** from the region of the earth where it blows, increases its dryness because of its proximity to the Northern region; in this respect, it sometimes puts on a "cold garment," for it is very inconstant and changeable in its nature. It does not drive away clouds like the North wind, but rather attracts them because of its dryness. Hence the proverb regarding a greedy man: *he draws money to himself as Caecias draws the clouds.* On the southern side of the East wind, however, is **Eurus** <note>the South-East wind</note>, which, insofar as it faces the South, participates slightly in its humidity.

In the Holy Scriptures, this wind named **Eurus** is generally taken for every wind blowing from the eastern quarter.

Among the collateral winds of the West, the humidity of the northern one, **Coridictus** <note>the North-Northwest wind</note>, is slightly altered by the dryness of the North, whereby its condition varies from that of its principal in certain ways. So too the **South-West winds** <note>original: *Africi*</note>, named after the region from which they blow, are seen to vary in some respects from the disposition of the West wind, shifting from cold to southern heat. But concerning these various qualities and natures of both the Cardinal and collateral winds, we shall discourse more copiously below in the treatise on the final causes of meteors.

## The Relation to the Microcosm.
<note>The "Microcosm" is the human body, viewed as a small-scale reflection of the entire universe.</note>

I.
The wind in the Microcosm (the human being) corresponding to each Cardinal's collateral wind is as follows:

**The Northern or Spleen Region** <note>original: *Lienis*</note>
*   **The Eastern wind** is the offspring of the North-East wind <note>original: *Aquilo*</note>. It appears to blow from the region of the **spleen** through the **short vessel** <note>original: *vas breve* — a vein connecting the spleen and stomach</note> and other insensible passages into the stomach, and from there (as well as directly from the spleen) through the branches of the **portal vein** <note>original: *ramus portae*</note> into the rest of the internal organs, and especially into the intestines.
*   **The Western wind** is the child of **Circius** <note>the West-Northwest wind</note>. It is observed to blow from the lowest region of the spleen and as if from the left kidney and its contiguous region, partly into the viscera and stomach, but especially into the right **hypochondrium** <term>the upper abdominal region just below the ribs</term>, which is the cavity where the **liver** <note>original: *hepar*</note> is located.

**The Southern or Liver Region** <note>original: *Hepatis*</note>
*   **The Eastern wind** is the offspring of the **South-East wind** <note>original: *Euro-auster*</note>. It blows from the right kidney and the region situated around it toward that part of the hollow of the liver where the small veins conduct **bile** to the **gall bladder** <note>original: *vesicam fellis*</note>. From there, it usually blows into the stomach, the intestines, and through the entire **hypochondrium** by means of the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: *venis meseraicis* — veins that drain blood from the digestive system</note> and other passages, both hidden and those noted by common observation.
*   **The Western wind** is of the lineage of the **South-West wind** <note>original: *Austro-Africus*</note>. It is observed to blow from the right viscera located immediately below the liver to the left **hypochondrium** (in whose cavity the **spleen** <note>original: *Lien*</note> is situated).

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

->**Eastern region, or the region of the heart and spiritual organs**<-
> The Southern wind is **Eurisoboles** <note>descendant of the East wind</note>, which strives to disseminate its fiery and sulfurous blasts from the gallbladder into the intestines and veins—both the *vena cava* and the portal vein—and indeed, even into the arterial spirits.
> The Northern wind is **Caecius** <note>the North-East wind</note>, and this one blows from the left cavity of the Diaphragm, sending blasts or winds that are sometimes hot and sometimes stiffly cold to the lower hypochondria <note>the upper abdomen below the ribs</note>.

---

->**Western region, or the region of the lower viscera and the spermatic vessels**<-
> The Southern wind is the **offspring of Africus** <note>the South-West wind</note>, which seems to blow upward into the stomach and the left region of the Diaphragm from the right seminal vessels and the organs situated around them—namely from the region of the cecum <note>the beginning of the large intestine</note> and the flanks.
> The Northern wind is **Corifilius** <note>literally "son of the Northwest wind"</note>, which blows from the region of the left seminal vessels and from the organs placed around them into the stomach and the right part of the Diaphragm.

---

It has been sufficiently and abundantly declared before that in the wind or air inhaled by man, as well as in the "juice" of nourishment (which was also derived from the winds), there is a portion of every wind, both cardinal and collateral. It has also been shown that there is a certain **magnetic force** <note>original: *vis quaedam magnetica*</note> in the human spirit, implanted in it from the fetus's first breath, which attracts things similar to itself by a certain natural instinct from any quarter of the human world—whether equinoctial or polar—from the air of the macrocosm <note>the "greater world" or universe</note>. Whether it extracts from the simple sea-air or from its waves within compound nourishment, a sound mind observes it uniting these with its own substance.

Thus, the internal power of the **Spleen** <note>original: *Lien*</note> is to attract and preserve styptic <note>contracting</note> and acidic humors, as well as the muddy and earthy substance of the blood or prepared chyle-juice, by a connatural appetite. In the same way, it is the nature of the **Liver** <note>original: *Hepar*</note> to gather "chyle-clouds" and convert the chyle-juice into the nature of hot and moist blood, and sometimes to procreate "catarrhal rains," in the manner of the **South Wind** <note>original: *Auster*</note>. There is also a point of magnetic attraction in the intermediate places, whose role is to draw the intermediate parts of the air—those infected by the side-winds—toward itself.

By this reasoning, the whole portion of the human spirit, constructed from infinite particles, is permeated by the governing power blowing in the macrocosm. This power comes from the "seeds" of all the winds, though in an unequal proportion. This, therefore, is the reason why (according to the rules of **Galen** and **Hippocrates**) the bodies of men and their airy spirits are necessarily altered by the surrounding air. For this reason, the most skilled physicians have not hesitated to prognosticate <note>predict the course of a disease</note> the types of future illnesses based on the dominance of malignant winds.

We say, therefore, that the "offspring" of the world’s collateral winds exercise their powers and blasts within the human air no differently than their "parents" do in the greater world. For this cause, we call them the offspring, sons, and descendants of the world's collateral winds, since they are procreated and exercise their powers within the human body from the "seeds" of those winds, which are dispersed everywhere in the open air and drawn in through the lungs and pores. 

But as we see in female birth, not all wombs <note>original: *matrices*</note> are fit for propagation: some are too cold, and the seeds are killed and do not move toward the desired goal of the fetus; others are too hot and either scorch the seeds or absorb their radical moisture; others are almost suffocated by a mass of superfluous humors and are hindered in their generative motion by infinite other obstacles. In the same way, the "seeds" of the winds—both malignant and benevolent—are dispersed everywhere in the air. When they are drawn into the human body (as if into a womb), whether by breath or by animal or vegetable food, if they find matter in the body that is contrary to the nature of that wind, they are perceived to operate neither maliciously nor beneficially. This is because the growth of such seeds is hindered and almost extinguished by the quality of the contrary wind predominating in that same body. 

For example, we do not see everyone infected by the plague during a pestilential time, and yet we perceive that everyone inhales that contagious air. Therefore, we see that the natures of some men are not at all fit for nourishing such "seeds" received into their bodies, because they abound in the disposition of a wind of the contrary condition. He is, I say, that very solar soul, the ruler of life and health, acting kindly to protect health in no other way than the office of Raphael is ordained to drive away diseases (as is evident from the etymology of his name <note>Raphael means "God heals" in Hebrew</note>). **Classification of Secondary Meteors**

Concerning secondary meteors—found in both the Macrocosm <note>The universe or "Great World"</note> and the Microcosm <note>The human being or "Little World"</note>—which are airy bodies contracted by the winds and formed both secretly and openly, two things must be considered:

*   **1. The principal parts in their composition, which are:**
    *   **Acting Light** <note>original: *Lux agens*</note> or the internal principle, which is either:
        *   Supernatural
        *   Natural, and this is either:
            *   Celestial
            *   Elemental
    *   **Passive Water** <note>original: *Aqua patiens*</note> or the material part, which is either:
        *   **Invisible**, like air:
            *   Divided into: Highest, Middle, and Lowest Consistencies.
        *   **Visible**, and this is either:
            *   Transparent and thin, like water commonly understood.
            *   Dark and thick, and this is either:
                *   Dry, like earth.
                *   Moist, like mud and slime.

### Chapter I. Of Member II.

->Where meteorological bodies produced from the winds are treated in general.<-

The condition of meteorological bodies <note>The author uses "meteors" to mean any atmospheric phenomenon, such as clouds, wind, or rain</note>, in both substance and form, is the same as that of "perfectly mixed" bodies. Previously, these were "imperfectly mixed" bodies arising from the movement of airy simplicity; in that state, they took on the form of meteorological bodies—namely, between the "starting point" <note>original: *terminum à quo*</note>, which is the state of simple air, and the "ending point" <note>original: *illum ad quem*</note>, which is perfect composition. This has been sufficiently demonstrated to you in the preceding pages. From these things, it seems clear enough that everything which exists is originally one and the same in terms of consistency—namely, air. Furthermore, there is no composite thing in the world that is not either a meteor or made from a meteor. I say "a meteor" if it is an imperfect body, and "from a meteor" because it is through the nature of the meteor that a transition must occur from a simple nature to a perfectly composed one.

For it is impossible for a progression to occur from a starting point to an ending point unless a "middle" is placed between them. In the number two <note>The Dyad</note>, no perfection is found, since only two terms are present; thus, it is not absurdly called a "confused and imperfect number" by the Pythagoreans. Therefore, they most rightly attributed the dignity of perfection to the number three <note>The Triad</note>, because in it three terms are found: the beginning, the middle, and the end. In a composition, these terms act like an imperfectly mixed or meteorological body. 

We see this in how dough is made from impalpable flour—as if from air—serving as the middle term or the "composition in motion" between bread and flour. By the decrease of moisture and by cooking <note>original: *coctio*; a term also used in alchemy for ripening or processing</note> and the hardening of that imperfect composite, it is then reduced into the perfect species of bread. Does this not also appear in the examination of wood, or an animal body, or even metals like lead, iron, copper, etc., in the cupel? <note>original: *cupella*; a shallow ceramic dish used in refining precious metals</note> Through the violence of fire, those bodies first turn into thick smoke or a cloud...

### Chapter 2. Member 2.

->Concerning the principal parts in composition, and first concerning Light.<-

Since it is certain and beyond all doubt that two things are required for the constitution of bodies—both meteorological and perfectly mixed (which also comes from a <term>meteor<note>Here, "meteor" refers to any atmospheric phenomenon like clouds, rain, or wind, not just falling stars.</note></term>)—I believe it will be worthwhile to diligently investigate the nature of these parts. But because it is impossible for anything in the nature of things to be produced without action (which comes from the "Form") and passion (which comes from the "Matter"), we must inspect the natures of these two in composition, as without them no thing in the world can exist. 

We find that **Form** is a single, simple thing: the first act, the central agent, the offspring of primary light, forming and effecting all things. In its origin, it is supernatural and uncreated; but when clothed in a natural spirit and effect, it is natural and created. Hence, the Book of Ecclesiasticus says: *Wisdom is the first creature* (Eccl. 1). And because light was created on the first day, it is seen in one respect as the garment of the spiritual world which it put on. In respect to the soul, it is called an "angel," or simply the formal name of the **GREAT GOD** inscribed in the Angel, which is **Jehovah**—the immediate emanation of God, the fountain of light, into the world, through which His spirit (previously existing only in potential) was formed. And so it is said that light was created on the first day; that is, the spirit shining with divine light, or the divine act, was clothed and invested with the spiritual substance of the world, illuminated by His presence. 

Whence it was said by David, *GOD is clothed in light* <note>Psalm 104:2</note>, which is to say, in an illuminated spirit; that is, the glory of God shines forth in His creature. So also in His anger, *GOD is called a consuming fire.* And this light or "Form" sometimes takes the name of its "garment" in form, where we find it written: *Wisdom was a covering for the Israelites by day and the light of the stars by night,* and elsewhere, *I, Wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High, and like a mist I covered the earth; my throne is in a pillar of cloud, etc.* (Wisdom of Solomon 10:17 and Ecclesiasticus 24). 

This divine Wisdom, therefore, is the "act of acts" and the central mover in every creature. Thus the wise man said: *the incorruptible spirit of GOD is in every thing* (Wisdom of Solomon 12). This luminous spirit of God is the central power of the thing itself, without which it can neither live nor exist. That this spirit of Wisdom is the innermost light of meteors and the "soul of souls"—indeed, the secret mystical soul of anything, whether imperfect or perfect—is evident from three points: 
1. In its perfection it surpasses all things, insofar as it is divine, incorruptible, and uncreated. 
2. It is more mobile than all noble things, simpler and more subtle than any spirit, and more powerful than any act. 
3. It is in every thing, as has been said: that is, in every element and every thing composed of elements. 

We can easily gather this from the words of the passage mentioned before: *I, Wisdom, covered the earth like a mist; my throne is in a pillar of cloud; I alone compassed the circuit of heaven and walked in the bottom of the deep; I stood in the waves of the sea and in all the earth; I took rest in every people and nation.* Therefore, it is divine Wisdom, which the wise man clearly describes with these words as being the holy spirit of understanding: single (or simple), manifold, subtle, undefiled, certain, sweet, free from suffering, sharp, kind, humane, having all virtues, overseeing all things, containing all intelligent spirits, more mobile than all mobile things, reaching everywhere because of its purity, a vapor or emanation of the power or brightness of God. Since it is one, it can do all things; and remaining in itself, it makes all things new, and conveys itself through the nations (Wisdom of Solomon 7). 

This, I say, is the central life or principle and the most internal "being" of any thing existing in this world. It is *not* that fictitious or imaginary "form" of **Aristotle**, which is a mere mental construct, attributing all things to its own nature and not immediately to **GOD**. Through the **Word**, says the Evangelist <note>The Gospel of John</note>, all things were made, and without Him was nothing made; *In Him was life, and that life was the light of men; the world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not.* 

How foolish, then, is that distinction made by Christian Philosophers, by which they wished to distinguish and separate God from His power and virtue! They say that God is everywhere "virtually" (by His power) but not "essentially," as if anyone of sound mind or consistency would say that the Virtue of God could be separated or divided from His Essence, any more than the rays of the sun can be separated from the sun itself, for they are in every way inseparable. **Hermes Trismegistus** also seems to confirm this in the *Poimandres* (Chapter 12) with such a discourse: *Mind indeed is of the very essence of GOD, if indeed He has an essence; it is born from it, wherefore it is by no means divided from the essence of GOD, but is rather connected to it in the same way that light is connected to the body of the Sun.* 

This "Worldly Mind" is that immediate emanation, or the *brightness of eternal light, the unspotted mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of His goodness* (Wisdom of Solomon 7), by means of which we know God "from behind"—that is, through His creatures. It is that very Wisdom which we described above through the testimony of Holy Scripture.

# Concerning the Formal Cause of <term>Meteors<note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including clouds, wind, and rain, not just falling stars.</note></term>.

We find this confirmed in the same text of the Book of Wisdom, Chapter 7. Concerning this, <term>Trismegistus<note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note></term> speaks thus, following the revelation of his good spirit: *The Mind, the soul of GOD, rules over all things, and even over law and all else; nor is anything that belongs to fate impossible for the mind.* <note>original: "Mens anima DEI dominatur omnibus..."</note> *Pymander*, Book 12. Therefore, the human mind is superior to fate, yet it does not neglect those things which are subject to fate. This Mind, then, is that from which all souls in the whole world obtain their life and being, no differently than how innumerable candles are lit from a single candle and receive, as it were, their life. Whence the aforementioned High Priest says: *Universal souls throughout the whole world flow from the single soul of the whole world, as if distributed and running about; of these souls, however, there are many changes, partly indeed for the better and more happily, and partly into the contrary.* *Pymander*, Book 10.

And this same idea does not seem to differ from the Sacred Scriptures, where it is left written: *That GOD created all things through Jesus Christ*, Ephesians 3:9. And elsewhere: *He who previously descended to the deep parts of the earth ascended, and he who descended is the very same who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill all things in this way*, Ephesians 4:8. And also the spirit of wisdom (says Solomon) fills the whole world, Wisdom 1. Furthermore, it is said that GOD made thick clouds his vehicle and his dwelling, Psalm 104:3 and Job 22. Therefore, this luminous act of GOD is present everywhere in the air, even if it is not manifest to the eye. So also he placed his tabernacle in the sun.

Finally, this divine power or essence is present everywhere, as the royal Psalmist testifies: namely, in heaven, in hell, in the furthest parts of the sea, in the night, and in darkness, Psalm 139:7. Hence it is said: *Know therefore and recall into your soul that Jehovah himself is God in the heavens above, and on the earth below, and there is no other*, Deuteronomy 4:39. From these things we gather that there is one light which is supernatural—that is, in its sole and absolute essence, without any regard for created things—which is also "super-celestial," meaning it is exalted beyond the limits of nature. There is another light which is natural, which is again distinguished into "celestial" and "elementary" due to the variety of its location, or the thinness or thickness of the air. It is celestial insofar as this light placed its tabernacle in the center of heaven, namely in the sun, from which it imparts its luminous power and life to the stars and ethereal creatures, such as <term>daemons<note>In this context, "daemons" refers to mediating spirits or intelligences that govern the natural order, rather than evil demons.</note></term> ordained for the execution of fate. It is elementary insofar as it radically informs everything in the region of the world, whether simple or composite; for it is the Word, in which the life of things consists.

For the incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing, as it reaches everywhere because of its purity; and since it remains within itself, it renews all things—that is, it causes them to flourish, grow, and multiply. Whence it is said: *heaven and earth shall pass away, but the word of GOD shall remain forever*, for the spirit of GOD is incorruptible, and consequently is subject to no corruption, whence it exists into eternity.

## CHAPTER III.

### Concerning the universal Water and its species, and that it is the passive matter of any mixture, whether perfect or imperfect.

Just as the form of all things, whether mixed or simple, is an internal uncreated light, or a certain incorruptible spirit implanted in them by God from creation—without whose presence they could not live, nor indeed even exist—so also that spirit is the immediate garment or vehicle of this light. By this spirit, the invisible air (namely, the wind) is moved at the command of this God-like spirit dwelling in the center. Its distant covering, however, and the one closest to the air carrying it, is invisible water, both thick and thin, from which the bodies of creatures are forged.

From this it follows that all things in the world were created primarily from water and through water, by the operation of that central spirit; and secondarily from heaven (as the internal and spiritual part) and earth (as the external and corporeal part), since these two are what fill and complete the vast cavity of the world. And this is confirmed by St. Peter, in the passage cited by us many times previously, who says: *That the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and through water by the word of GOD.* From this it follows that those things which are forged immediately from heaven and earth mixed together are originally made from water and through water—yet not from waters alone, which are the passive parts in the composition, but by the mediation of the active divine Word, without which (as John testifies) nothing was made, as the life of the creature is within it. Or, as was said before, it is through the mediation of Wisdom, which was the brightness of the eternal light emanating from the mouth of the Most High before any creature, and which (by the testimony of the Wise Man) was assisting her Father in his works. Or, as the leader Moses intends, it is by the mediation of the Spirit of the Lord, which moved over the waters, providing them with fiery vigor or life.

We see, therefore, that the waters first created from mundane creatures are everything that is called "heaven" and "earth," and consequently, it is certain that they fill the vast concavity of the world. Whence also, just as the heavens or the air, expanded everywhere in their spiritual nature, are of an invisible consistency, so the thin earth is visible water. The thick part, however, or the dregs and the "dead head" <note>original: *caput mortuum*; an alchemical term for the useless residue left after distillation.</note> of the whole, is the opaque earth itself, whether of a moister substance like mud and mire, or of a drier and harder one. So also we think it is not absurd to distinguish between visible and invisible waters—namely, into celestial and earthly. But it is certain that the invisible waters preceded the visible ones in creation, both in time and in order, since the heaven was established in them before any land or sea appeared.

# Book 3. Member I.
## Concerning all dark Meteors.
### Chapter I.

->Concerning the twofold species of <term>meteors<note>In this historical context, "meteors" refers to any atmospheric phenomena, such as wind, rain, or clouds, rather than objects from space.</note></term> formed from the winds.<-

| Meteors, both of the microcosm (man) and macrocosm (the universe), differ from one another in species depending on the winds from which they are composed, which are either: | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | **Simple**, and those are either: | **Dark** (See H) or **Bright** (See I) |
| | **Arising from simple ones**, which are also twofold: | **Tempestuous** (See K) or **Peaceful** (See N) |

We say that secondary meteors, or those arising from the winds (that is, born from primary meteors), are derived for many reasons. For in the first place, the external or mundane winds, with their opposing blasts, compress the air—the universal matter of creatures—and condense it into the "seed" of the creature. Just as we see, led by experience, that the visible seeds of things have their own invisible seeds within them which serve as central souls to those seeds, so also do the said winds breathe their spiritual seeds into the aerial or meteorological bodies. It is established that the seeds of creatures are spirits or winds included within them, by means of which the mass of the seed (with the addition of its like) is extended by a certain internal breath into the species or image of the creature to which the seed belongs, and thus the fetus is formed. 

So also in a cloud procreated by opposing winds: we see the spirit leaping forth from the winds and included within them in the manner of a soul. By means of this spirit, the cloud is seen to thrive, grow, and be driven and fly through the middle region of the air from one region of the world toward its opposite. #### The first part, concerning dark aqueous [watery] meteors in the Macrocosm.

Dark meteors of an aqueous consistency are either thinner or thicker in their substance. Indeed, we call those meteors "thinner" which are more spread out, softer, and less compact in their parts; these are the types which exist midway, as it were, in their movement from simple and invisible air toward what is commonly understood as water. We call those "thick" which are either liquid water or frozen, or which are compacted with earth, which we shall discuss below. Aqueous meteors of a thinner consistency are various degrees of vapors or fumes, of which one is denser or heavier than another, or closer to the water toward which they tend. These include the Halo, the Mist, and the Cloud, which we will treat here in more detail—first by explaining the opinion of Aristotle <note>The "Peripatetics" mentioned later are the followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> regarding the origin or generation of such meteors, and afterwards considering how that aligns or disagrees with the testimony of Holy Scripture. 

Aristotle, along with the rest of the Peripatetics, defines the **Halo** as a circle appearing white at the edges with black surrounding it, appearing around the Sun, the Moon, or a luminous star. It is formed from a moist vapor rising from the earth and waters, condensed into a thinner little cloud or mist, which creates a circular shape in the eyes of the onlookers beneath the star. This is usually a sign of rain if it gradually turns black and becomes thicker overall; but if it breaks with a great crack on one side, it portends winds from that region where it first opens and bursts apart. These are their views. Pliny also recognizes that the circle of a Halo is sometimes of a blood-red color, due to the density of the cloud surrounding the sun (Pliny, Book 30, Chapter 2).

**Mist** <note>original: *Nebula*</note>, according to the opinion of the Peripatetics, is a kind of "sterile" cloud—that is, one without rain—which remains as a residue of the vapor welling up from the earth and waters that could not be raised high enough or condensed into a cloud. Or it may be defined thus: Mist is vapor drawn upward from the waters and earth by the heat of the sun; but because the solar heat is not strong enough to lift that vapor into the middle region of the air (so that it might be contracted into a cloud by the cold of that place), the heat allows it to descend gradually back to the earth after a slight condensation.

A **Cloud** <note>original: *Nubes*</note> (which is the most general category for the others mentioned) is vapor raised from the lands and waters into the middle region of the air by the force of solar heat, and there contracted and as if frozen into the consistency of a cloud by the power of extreme cold; afterwards, it is driven here and there through the middle region of the air, partly by the heat of the sun and partly by the force of the winds.

Finally, they define a **Little Cloud** <note>original: *Nubecula*</note> as a tiny cloud contracted by the union or addition of a vast magnitude of vapors flying successively into the heights; hence the common proverb: *from a small cloud a great storm can often arise.*

In conclusion, therefore, all these meteors seem to differ not only in their material cause but also in their external form, since some are more or less compact than others, and some are either smaller or thinner in quantity. Therefore, once the matter and form of one have been investigated with diligent intuition, the others will reveal themselves even more clearly from that light, since they are all of the same nature and condition.

In the definition of the condition of any such meteor, three things are worthy of observation: namely, the **matter**, the **place**, and the **efficient cause**.

Aristotle makes the matter of the halo, the mist, and the cloud the same: namely, a moist vapor welling up from the earth and water as the places appropriate for its generation. But let us hear what the Sacred Page <note>A traditional term for the Bible.</note> tells of the origin of such little clouds and clouds, so that we may see the testimony of the whole truth.

# On the Formal Cause of Atmospheric Phenomena. #

<note>The term "Meteors" in this period referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including clouds, rain, and wind, not just falling stars.</note>

The experience was of this sort. While I was traveling from Venice toward Augsburg, Germany, among the mountains and Alpine crags, I perceived on the summit of a certain cliff of immense height, which the solar rays were striking vigorously, a very thin mist appearing at first, almost like a vapor scarcely visible on its forward side. By thickening more and more, it was gradually reduced from a barely visible vapor to the consistency of a mist, and finally a cloud, clinging to the front face or peak of the mountain. Meanwhile, I observed that the other parts of the cliff and even the surrounding air were free of clouds, as if dressed in the garments of the clearest weather—that is, shining everywhere with solar rays. Being somewhat curious to investigate the cause of such a sudden appearance of this atmospheric phenomenon, I dismounted my horse, and having grabbed some grass and tossed it into the air, I noticed that a wind blowing quite strongly against that side of the cliff or mountain peak was the cause of this arriving phenomenon. Specifically, the wind, pushing the thinner air before it with its blast, compressed it against the resistant substance of the perpendicularly upright cliff. Thus the air, unable to flee further because of the hard resistance of the rock, was successively held back, united, and gathered; that is, the following parts of the air, propelled by the force of the wind, were added to the preceding parts. In this way, by such compression, they gradually and little by little escaped into and were transformed into the consistency of a dense cloud. Finally, the solar rays striking the peak of the cliff dissolved this cloud into drops, bringing on rain. From these things we can gather that the substance of a cloud is nothing other than air, transformed from its moderate and invisible substance into a visible atmospheric phenomenon by gradual addition and compression.

But perhaps someone will object that clouds arise where mountains and cliffs are not found at all. To this it must be answered that the condensation of air is produced by similar compression, though by different efficient causes. For two opposing winds blowing—even if one is stronger than the other due to a void of dominance—are very often accustomed to compress and condense the thinner air into the appearance of a cloud of any consistency. These winds, if they act and react against each other very strongly, produce a sound in the air similar to that which two rivers make when falling violently into the same bay or abyss with contrary motion.

Yet some will undoubtedly reply that two winds rarely blow at the same time, futilely revolving that old axiom of the inconsistent Philosophers: *That every greater thing contains the lesser within itself, and a greater force repels and overcomes a lesser.* Nevertheless, we see, taught by experience, that a small force resists a stronger force in proportion to its mass; for a candle is not deprived of its power simply because it is inferior to the light and clarity of the sun and reduced to nothing in the human eye. Indeed, I remember when I was in a ship plowing the sea with sails spread and a stronger wind blowing on the way to England, and also from Marseille toward Italy; even with a prevailing wind serving our journey, I observed an opposing wind blowing somewhat more feebly and pushing the sails back, until that wind favorable to our navigation again overcame the one adverse to us and finally carried us happily to our desired goal. During that time, I perceived various clouds gathered in the air, sometimes sweating out rain. Is it not also apparent to the common eye that a cloud armed with lightning, appearing on the furthest edge of the horizon, moves against the motion of the wind of that horizon? From this it happens that thunder and tempests are procreated from the clash of two clouds moving in opposition, as is shown more clearly in the said chapter.

But lest anyone believe these things are reported by us futilely or untruthfully, we shall proceed to establish our assertion with the testimony of the sacred fountain of all truth. Did not Ezekiel, by divine command, call upon the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritum"; in both Latin and Hebrew, the word for "spirit" also means "wind" or "breath"</note>, that it might come at the same time from the four winds of heaven and breathe upon the slain that they might live again? *Ezekiel 37.* And the Prophet Daniel said: *Behold, the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea. Daniel 7.* And in Zechariah we have: *These four horses are the four winds of heaven, which go forth and stand before the ruler of all flesh. Zechariah 6:1.* Furthermore, we have in Jeremiah: *And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds. Jeremiah 49:36.* From these it is quite clearly established that not just one or another wind, but all four at once are sometimes given to blow at the same time, by which clouds and tempests, whirlwinds and thunders, and such things are stirred up for the destruction of the impious. This same point that divine poet Homer also seems to argue in these verses, where he is understood to sing of spirits struggling in the air (as Daniel said) and fighting among themselves in the aerial sea:

->*Such a great rumor spread through the heavenly hall,*<-
->*When the gods rushed into savage battles one after another;*<-
->*Phoebus Apollo fought against Neptune,*<-
->*Pallas Athena strove against Mars, etc.*<-

Where, by Neptune, he seems to mean the western wind which is cold and humid, and by Phoebus, the eastern wind or the spirit presiding over it. Similarly, Ovid is eager to reveal the contest between Boreas <note>The North Wind</note> and the other winds with verses of this sort, speaking in the person of the North Wind:

->*I likewise, when I have found my brothers in the open sky*<-
->*(For that is my field of action) struggle with such great effort,*<-
->*That the middle air resounds with our shocks,*<-
->*And fires leap out, forced from the hollow clouds.*<-

# Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I. #

...where by "brothers" he understands the <term>South Wind (Auster)</term> and the other cardinal winds, which the North Wind (<term>Boreas</term>) encounters in the air, usually stirring up tempests such as thunder, whirlwinds, and other such stormy things. Therefore, there is very little doubt that two or more winds emit their blasts in the open air during the same tempest, either from opposite directions or crosswise; by their compression, clouds are generated from the air itself and are driven here and there by the winds, as was declared before according to that passage in *Job 37:21*: "Suddenly the air is forced into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away." <note>The author uses a Latin translation of Job that emphasizes the "forcing" or "thickening" of air into clouds, supporting his compression theory.</note> Therefore, it follows that the assertion of <term>Aristotle</term> is completely false—namely, that the vaporous substance of a cloud is formed into a cloud by the constriction of the cold in the middle region of the air. This can also be made clear from the fact that the southern winds (which are the primary parents of clouds and rains) are quite warm; consequently, the vapors emitted from that region should instead dull the power of the cold in that middle region. As a result, they would produce either no clouds or at least much thinner ones than the other winds. Furthermore, the blasts of the <term>East Wind (Eurus)</term> are the hottest of all, yet experience teaches us it is far otherwise, since those winds are noted for thickening the air and producing clouds far denser and wetter than the others. Indeed, these winds thicken the middle air so much that they usually make objects appear larger to the eyes than other winds do, as <term>Isidore</term> <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), an influential encyclopedist of the Middle Ages.</note> testifies.

To arrive now at the resolution of the final doubt—namely, whether clouds are moved here and there (that is, away from a center) by an external motion such as the winds and the sun and only superficially, or by some internal principle? To this doubt we respond that the halo, the mist, the small cloud, and the cloud itself (all of which are <term>meteors</term> <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, from rain to rainbows, not just falling stars.</note> that differ neither in matter nor in internal form, but only in shape) enjoy their own internal and "moving-from-the-center" principles. By means of these, they move here and there according to the will of the Creator. For since that Divine Spirit (which they call Wisdom) is present in the <term>World Spirit</term>—by which the world is animated—it is necessary that this luminous soul be dispersed everywhere through the air. This is no different than how we observe the soul to be expanded through the smallest parts of the human spirit and body—namely, in the whole and in every part, as the Philosophers teach.

Hence, because the condition of this luminous soul is to be stationed around the center of any "mixture" and not just on the circumference (though it also emits its rays from the center to the circumference, which is why it is said to be in the whole and in every part), the entire portion of that **World Soul** <note>original: *animae mundanae*</note> (if it be permitted to think of it as divisible) which moved in the air before its contraction to inform it, now reflects and contracts itself into the center or heart of the air converted into a cloud. There it breathes through the mediation of its angels or spirits, sent from the quarters of the winds to execute the will of that incorruptible Spirit. It moves where it wills, here and there, according to the will of the King residing on His central throne, either for the benefit or the curse of the earth and its inhabitants. Therefore, this eternal spirit, thus hedged in by its own will within its **black hut** <note>original: *tugurio suo nigro*; a metaphor for the dark interior of a storm cloud.</note>, partly attracts the air from the center to its circumference by a magnetic virtue, and partly the angels (who are His "windy" ministers) apply the air from all sides with their breathing-holes, so that suddenly and almost in a moment they may build a hut for their Creator, which they do not cease to carry here and there according to the Emperor’s pleasure.

Do we not also have this very same thing vividly depicted by the Holy Page in these express words? *He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet; and he ascended upon the cherubim, and flew, and glided upon the wings of the wind. He placed darkness round about him as a hiding place, sifting the waters from the clouds of the heavens; before the brightness in his presence, the clouds were set on fire, etc. 2 Kings 22:8-13.* <note>The author is citing the song of David, also found in Psalm 18.</note> And we have it written in the Psalmist: *The thick cloud is the vehicle or chariot of GOD, who walks upon the wings of the wind, Psalm 104.* And elsewhere it says: *Jehovah spread a cloud for a covering, Psalm 105:39.* And in Job we find: *Thick clouds are the hiding place of GOD, who walks the circuit of the heavens.* Indeed, even Jehovah Himself affirmed that He dwells under darkness. Did not this Spirit of Wisdom also say: *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and like a mist I covered the earth; my throne is in a pillar of cloud; I alone have circled the circuit of the heavens, and walked in the depth of the abyss, etc. Ecclesiasticus 24.* <note>Ecclesiasticus, or the Wisdom of Sirach, is a book of the Biblical Apocrypha/Deuterocanon.</note>

Therefore, it is this incorruptible Spirit sitting in the heart of the cloud who gives rain to the earth when He wills, and again restrains it according to His pleasure, as in: *He so restrains the waters that they dry up, and He so sends them out that they overturn the earth, Job 12:15.* Or this: *I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon the earth, Isaiah 5.* And elsewhere: *The heavens over your head shall be brass, Deuteronomy 28.* And elsewhere: *Jehovah is so kindled with anger against you, that He shuts the heavens so there is no rain, and the earth does not yield its fruit, Deuteronomy 11:17.* And elsewhere: *With thick clouds GOD covers the heavens, which prepare rain for the earth so that the mountains bring forth grass, Psalm 147:8.*

This, I say, is that Spirit of Divinity which is centrally within the clouds, but not "included" (confined) within them, as He who is present everywhere and breathes where He wills. His glory sometimes reveals itself in the brightness of a bursting cloud; sometimes He leads the cloud here and there in His invisible essence. His "windy" ministers follow His will or appetite, for they go out and stand before the Ruler of the whole earth, as the prophet testifies in *Zechariah 6*. Hence it is said: "Wisdom was a covering to them by day"—that is, a cloud or mist by day and the light of stars by night. For just as Wisdom is accepted in its angelic nature (insofar as it is "otherness," that is, clothed in a created spirit), so it is called a "creature" by Ecclesiasticus, and the **Angel Metatron** by the Cabalists, and the **Alpha and Omega**, and that **Great Angel** having the appearance of the sun and holding seven stars in his hand, speaking with a voice like the murmur of waters or winds, whom the four angels presiding over the winds obeyed (as is held in the Apocalypse), and He who went before the Israelites, in whom the name of GOD resided. But truly, as Wisdom is considered in itself, it is called the brightness of the divine majesty, an emanation or flow of the light...

# On the Formal Cause of Meteors #

...eternal, and God himself; wherefore Wisdom, in respect to its angelic garment or contracted air, can be called a mist, a pillar of cloud, and likewise a fiery spirit, or light leaping forth from the cloud or covering of Jehovah. It is even called smoke from the nostrils and mouth of Jehovah—that is, from the cloud with which he is clothed (just as the soul is clothed by the body). > *The sacred page says,* **"Smoke rose from his nostrils, fire flew from his mouth, coals were kindled by him, the Lord thundered from heaven, etc."** *2 Kings 22.* <note>original: "Ascendit, inquit pagina sacra, fumus è naribus..." In modern Bibles, this passage is found in 2 Samuel 22 or Psalm 18.</note>

This spirit is that first emanation from the Father, *Wisdom 10:17*, present everywhere, which is the "spirit of spirits," insofar as all spirits of every kind, whether angelic or otherwise, are formed by its presence, and consequently, all worldly spirits offer it obedience. It is the "wind of winds," for it blows where it wills, and all winds—inspired by its breath—strive to carry out its commands as if from a supreme commander. Nor can anyone of sound mind deny that it is the prince of winds, seeing that it appeared to the Apostles in its windy nature; by its presence or most powerful breath, they were granted the power not only to command created winds, but even to calm tempestuous seas, extinguish the rage of poison, drive away diseases by a mere touch or word, and bring many other stupendous miracles to fruition. The history expands upon this in these words: ***"And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing blast, or a violent wind, which filled the whole house where they were sitting, etc."*** *Acts 2.* ***"By the breath of your nostrils,"*** says Moses, ***"the waters were gathered together,"*** *Exodus 15.* And elsewhere: ***"By the breath of God frost is produced, and snow is given forth like wool,"*** *Job 37.* <note>The comparison of snow to wool is a common biblical metaphor for the gentle but thick covering of the earth.</note> This was that spirit by whose virtue Elijah produced a tiny cloud, like a man's hand, rising from the sea: whence it happened immediately that the heavens were darkened with clouds and wind by the virtue of that spirit of immense strength sitting in the center of the little cloud, drawing the air to itself from every side, *1 Kings 18*; of which spirit Solomon also speaks thus: ***"By his wisdom the depths broke open, and the heavens drop down the dew,"*** *Proverbs 3:20.*

We conclude, therefore, against the doctrine of <term>Aristotle</term> and the other <term>Pagans</term> <note>original: "Ethnicorum" — the author uses this to refer to non-Christian Greek philosophers.</note> that neither earth nor water are the sources of watery meteors, but rather the air or heaven itself, which is the treasury-chest of God. Nor is the cold of the middle region of the air the cause of the compression of vaporous substance into the substance of a cloud; rather, it is the central spirit floating in the cloud. At its pleasure, and by means of its windy ministers, this spirit expands the cloud as a covering, that it may dwell beneath the gloom. This happens not by solar heat or action, but by the divine light centrally implanted in them, which sits like a commander upon the <term>Cherubim</term> <note>The author interprets Cherubim here as "airy and windy angels" who serve as the mechanical agents of God's will in the weather.</note> and flies upon the wings of the winds. That spirit inspires them with its primary breath, by means of which they move and blow wherever it wills. It is, I say, the spirit of Wisdom, which is far nobler than the sun (being the soul of the sun) and more excellent than light. It is the chief actor in this kind of business, and not any other of the host of heaven. It is, I say, a creating spirit, not created, which is the <term>First Act</term> <note>original: "actus primus" — a philosophical term for the primary cause or prime mover of a process.</note> in the motion of meteors, assisted by its angelic ministers breathing in the world to execute its pleasure. It is, I say, a wind blowing from the center of the cloud, which blows originally—and not the created winds, which move at the motion of the primary breathing-hole, which is the prince of spirits. Whence this spirit said in the place previously cited: ***"I, Wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High, and like a mist I covered the earth; my throne is in a pillar of cloud, I alone have compassed the circuit of the heavens, and walked in the depth of the abyss, etc."*** <note>This quote is from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24.</note> It did not say: "I compassed the circuit of heaven driven by the violence of the winds," but it performed this voluntarily and of its own will, as one at whose nod the winds are always ready. For by the divine presence alone, as an internal agent, the clouds and the earth itself are moved; which David also seems to confirm in these words: ***"The waters saw God and were afraid; the depths also were troubled. The clouds poured out water, and the upper clouds gave forth sounds,"*** *Psalm 77:17.* And elsewhere it is said: ***"When Jehovah sends his word to the earth, his word runs very swiftly, he who gives snow like wool,"*** *Psalm 147:15.* From this it is clear that the principle of the motion of clouds is in the very heart of the cloud, in which this spirit has its throne—that is, from an internal princely wind, and not from an external agent. Although external winds are also always ready to move and blow according to the disposition of the universal spirit, let every Christian set aside all doubt in this controversy and consider first the words of Saint John: namely, that ***"all things were made or created by the Word, and without him nothing was made."*** Since the question now concerns the daily creation of clouds, I would like you to tell us seriously: is the creation of this kind of meteor by the uncreated Word, as the sacred scripture teaches us, or by creatures—namely, the Sun and the cold of the middle region of the air compressing and constituting it? How can you thoughtlessly refer the reason for the cloud's constitution to an external accident and not to an internal and central principle? If, therefore, we agree with the Pagans, the doctrine of the sacred page must be rejected, and thus falsehood embraced instead of truth.

Here, then, one may see with open eyes how inconsistent is that doctrine of the Pagans concerning clouds, and how fragile and filthy are the foundations of those who, neglecting the Holy Spirit moving centrally everywhere, ascribe the motions of meteors to external acts and not to internal principles. By this, they seem to make those things arise plainly by chance and not at all naturally or supernaturally and divinely; indeed, they falsely attribute to creatures those things which sacred scripture teaches us are derived proximately and immediately from the Creator. Nevertheless, their Christian disciples are so stuck and entangled in the "birdlime" of their erroneous doctrine that they do not hesitate to hold the things brought forth by them as if they were oracles sent from God and from heaven. From this it happens that, being intoxicated by the delusions of such Pagan fictions, they cannot rightly engage in any science—indeed, not even in sacred theology—nor can they [perceive] God in his creatures...

But if they should finally say: "If this definition of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who sought purely natural/physical explanations for weather.</note> is false and erroneous, show us a definition of a Halo, a mist, and a cloud that is more fitting and in agreement with the truth."

## CHAPTER IV.

### *In which the Halo and clouds are described according to the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures.*

A **Halo** is invisible air, compressed into the consistency of a thinner and transparent cloud by the magnetic attraction of Divine Wisdom (which presides centrally within it) and by the squeezing of its ministers, the winds. Through this air, the rays of the Moon, the Sun, Jupiter, or Venus—prepared and adapted for this reception—penetrate in a circular fashion, typically prefiguring a crown or a circle of various colors within it. Or thus:

A **Halo** is the direct and voluntary application of the incorruptible spirit of Wisdom—which has its throne in the heart of the mist as if within its vaporous covering or garment—to the orbicularly diffused rays of a particular star; or, it is the peripheral reception of those rays.

<margin>Deuteronomy 28:12</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 18:41</margin>
<margin>Psalm 103:24</margin>
<margin>Job 28:25</margin>
In these definitions of the Halo and other species of the same kind, we understand first of all what their primary matter is: namely, invisible air. Hence it is said (as you have seen reported in the preceding pages): *The Lord shall open to thee his good treasure, the heavens, to give the rain unto thy land.* This means that from the air, which is the "heaven" or "expanse," clouds of every consistency are procreated, from which rains are produced by resolution. This is also why Elijah heard the "sound of an abundance of rain" before any cloud appeared—that is, he heard the motion of the invisible spirits in the air, the winds who are the ministers of Wisdom. By their agitation, the air was first forced into a mist "the size of a man’s hand," and then immediately afterward the heavens were agitated by winds and darkened by clouds. Thus, it was necessary for the winds to precede the appearance of the clouds, as the clouds were to be gathered by the blowing of the winds. For the wind, or the motion of spirits in the air, began first as a noise, by whose agitation the mist was procreated; then the winds grew, and that little cloud was increased to an immense size. All these things, however, were done by Wisdom, hiding as if on its throne, centrally and primarily in the heart of the air (which was first invisible and then contracted into clouds), perfecting all things according to its pleasure. Even the Psalmist seems to confess this generally when he speaks thus: *Your works are wonderful and vast, which you have made in wisdom.* And Job says: *God by his wisdom fits the weight for the winds and weighs the waters by measure; he makes a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder.* This means that Divine Wisdom sometimes converts the air into the consistency of either a Halo, or a mist, or a cloud, or some other meteor. For this spirit is everywhere, though invisibly dispersed in the air, serving it in the place of a primary form. For just as the moist nature of the world (which we call the universal air) is first a universal passive...

<meta>This page continues the author's philosophical and theological exploration of the atmosphere. ...[created] spirit, so eternal light emanating from God, and proceeding as if from His mouth, is an uncreated act that gives form to that created or passive spirit. This is further confirmed by the Holy Scripture, which says: *By His Spirit He garnished the heavens* <note>original: "Spiritu suo cœlos... ornauit"</note> (that is, the whole air), *Job 26:13*. This spirit is the central light, dwelling in inaccessible light, whereof it is written: *GOD is clothed with light as with a garment*. This light, appearing with its garment, is sometimes visible, as in lightning and the sun; for this reason, it is sometimes called a *consuming fire*, the *fire of GOD*, and so on. This is, therefore, that hidden spirit which performs all things in the heavens and on the earth. In its power (as stated before) is the ability to open the heavens—His finest treasure—at His pleasure: that is, to bring forth from His treasury mists, clouds, and all other meteors <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, rainbows, and clouds, not just falling stars.</note>. Hence it is said elsewhere: *He opened the doors of the heavens, raining down manna, Psalm 78:24*. We conclude, then, that air is the primary matter of the Halo as well as of other meteors (of which more will be said in the description of mists and clouds). Wisdom is the primary efficient cause, and her ministers are the secondary or rather instrumental causes, as will be explained more fully below.

As for the consistency of the Halo, it takes the form of a translucent mist; that is, a vaporous substance through which stellar rays can very easily penetrate. This consistency is applied in a denser or thinner measure according to the will of Divine Wisdom, in whose power it is *to give weight to the air, and to weigh the waters or vapors by measure, Job 28:25*. Thus it happens that, according to the variety of density and thinness, He produces various effects as the Creator wills, as will be more clearly explained in our treatise on the final cause. It is necessary, therefore, that the consistency of this kind of meteor is not of the purely natural constitution of air—since air is invisible and consequently cannot visibly receive such impressions—nor of a dense mist or cloud, since a stellar body <note>i.e., a star or planet</note> could hardly, if at all, be seen through such bodies, and consequently could not print its coronal image upon them. Rather, it is an intermediate state between corporeal darkness and that incorporeal state in which air is rendered invisible. It does not obscure the light so much as to be opaque, yet this transparency must not be without some shadow; otherwise, the reflection of an image cannot occur, and consequently there would be no visible impression of the rays or the received image, just as one may see clearly in glass or in the air itself. Hence Algazel <note>Algazel: The Latinized name for Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian philosopher whose works on optics and logic were influential in Europe.</note> rightly says in *On the Nature of the Mirror*: *That no part of the celestial sphere is visible to the power of sight, nor receptive and retentive of received sunlight, except for its denser part, which we call the star itself; because,* he says, *the rest of that sphere, being rarer, does not become bright when light is projected toward it, because it is not subject to color; indeed, it is not visible.* This also seems to be confirmed by Haten <note>Haten: A reference to "Ibn al-Haytham" or Alhazen (c. 965–1040), the medieval pioneer of optics.</note> in Book 1 *On Perspectives*, saying: *that which has no color is not visible, because* (as he says) *a thing is not visible except according to the light in the thing seen; for visible light only occupies what is colored.* From this it is clear that the substance of a Halo must be misty, with a consistency midway between invisible spirit and an entirely opaque body, so that it may better receive the forms of the stars. Thus Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on the natural world.</note> says that the images of bodies can very easily be expressed in humid air, no differently than in a mirror or its reflections. It is even recorded that it happened to a certain person that, due to the weakness of his sight, the nearby air in humid weather served as a mirror for him; the rays could not perfectly penetrate the air but were partially reflected. This same thing often happens to those afflicted with the most destructive and dangerous illnesses and pestilential fevers: because of the weakness and lack of their visual faculty, they see their own faces in the air and, struck with terror, imagine they are seeing demons and foul shapes. But I shall now proceed to the description of the Mist.

# CHAPTER V.

## On the description of the Mist.

A MIST [Nebula] is a transmutation of air from its natural and invisible consistency into a visible and thick vaporous substance, created by the light of wisdom acting centrally—that is, from the inside, contracting the air toward itself from all sides—and by its windy ministers from the outside, lightly compressing it with contrary blasts.
->Or thus:<-
A Mist is the primary species of dark visible meteors, created and procreated from the first degree of air contracted into vapor, by the divine will operating from the center and the circumference.
->Or thus:<-
A Mist is the vaporous dwelling-place of God-like wisdom, fused and contracted from air by the magnetic attraction of the Lord inhabiting it centrally, and by the external compression of His winds.
The Mist is therefore made of the same matter as its body, and shares the same form as that of the Halo; the only difference is in its thinness and density—that is, in the formula of its composition.

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member II.

As for the matter of this subject, although we have spoken quite abundantly in the preceding pages, something still remains to be explained in this place which was not clearly demonstrated before. We have said, therefore, that **air** is the immediate origin of the first stage of meteors—namely, **vapor**—which, by thickening more and more, is reduced into the consistency of a **cloud**. This invisible spirit is that from which all visible things were made, according to that verse so often cited before: *through faith we understand that the world was framed by the word, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear; Hebrews 11:3.* <note>The author uses this famous biblical passage to argue that the physical world arises from an "invisible" spiritual substance, which he identifies here with the air or "spirit."</note> It is as if he were saying that from a "nothing"—that is, an imperceptible spirit—something, or a thing subject to the senses, was created. Thus the world was created from nothing, and likewise its creatures were produced from a thing that (according to our meager capacity) almost does not exist, but is to be commemorated by faith alone. This thing exists in "potential" through the mediating Word or the Spirit of Wisdom, which first shone forth before all things, and is then brought into "actuality" for us. 

Does not Saint Paul seem to acknowledge this same point in these words: *God hath chosen the base things of the world, and things which are despised, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are: That no flesh should glory in his presence; 1 Corinthians 1:28-29.* By these words, he seems to argue that things of no apparent value or existence are the cause, through the mediation of Wisdom, of both the existence and the abolition of those things that do exist. For all generation and regeneration, all corruption and resurrection from corruption, comes from that invisible source through the mediation of that Christ, who is called by the Apostle *the power of GOD and the wisdom of GOD*; whence it follows in the next verse: *Christ Jesus is made unto us wisdom from GOD, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption; 1 Corinthians 1:30.* Therefore, the Apostle says elsewhere: *Of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory and honor; Romans 11:36.* 

But this same point is also excellently expressed by the mystical Doctors and the **Cabalists** <note>Cabalists (or Kabbalists) are practitioners of Jewish mysticism; here, the author uses their theories of the Hebrew alphabet to explain the mechanics of creation.</note>. For **Rabbi Bahir** says that there is no principle except **Wisdom**; which, contracted in darkness or invisibly, or in an invisible spirit—according to that saying of **Hermes Trismegistus**: *The Monad generates the monad and reflected its heat upon itself* (that is, it shone back upon itself)—remained as if idle and devoid of action, having regard for "nothing." In such a state, it is called by the Hebrews **Ein** (**אין**), which means "Nothing," or "Non-being," or "Without End" <note>Ein Soph is a Kabbalistic term for the infinite God before any manifestation.</note>. So sterile is our apprehension, and so meager and powerless is our capacity in the contemplation of divine objects, that we judge those things which do not appear as if they did not exist at all. 

But truly, when it appears in some real form or subsistence, then the Cabalists say that the "dark Aleph" is converted into the "lucid Aleph." <note>Aleph (א) is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing unity or God.</note> And as **Aleph** is held by them to be a hieroglyphic for God, representing unity and simplicity, they understand the "dark Aleph" as the hidden God, and the "lucid Aleph" as the revealed God. From this, they even call the lucid Aleph **Beth**, which is the second letter in the Hebrew alphabetical order, just as Aleph is the first. Therefore, if Beth is added to the letter Aleph, it is read as **AB** (**אב**), which is interpreted as **Father**, who always has a relationship to a Son. Thus **AB** denotes the Father of all generation, where Aleph is the sign of the Father, and Beth the sign of the Son, proceeding from the Father by divine emanation. 

This order is esteemed by the Cabalists as the first deduction in divinity and the primordial beginning of all alteration, which Moses called **Bereschit**—that is, the "Beginning," or the immediate emanation of light from infinity. This is the second "numeration" <note>The "numerations" are the Sephirot, or the ten attributes/emanations of God in Kabbalah.</note> of the Cabalists, called **Hochma** or **Wisdom**, over which the benevolent name of God, **IAH**, presides. Through the mediation of this divine property, all things were made from "nothing"—that is, from an unknown, invisible, or formless matter—according to that verse in the Book of Wisdom: *The hand of the Almighty made the world out of formless matter* according to **Pagnini's** interpretation; or, as **Tremellius** has it, *created the world from formless matter*; or as **Jerome** prefers, *created the orb of the lands from invisible matter; Wisdom 11:17 (or 18).* 

This passage agrees with that of the Apostle cited from Hebrews 11, where we find that visible things, such as all bodies are, come from a thing that is invisible, or unseen, or formless, or unknown—namely, from the **mundane spirit**, which is called the heaven and the air, distinguishing it from visible corporeal things of earthly composition. Hence it is said: *The Lord shall open unto thee his good treasure, the heaven, to give the rain unto thy land; Deuteronomy 28:12.* It does not say He will open His treasure of "earth and water," as **Aristotle** would have it, but the "heavens," and this through the mediation of His wisdom. 

Does not Moses also make a difference between the **vapor** of the earth and the **cloud** of the heaven, where he says: *For the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, nor had any vapor gone up from the earth to water the face of the ground; Genesis 2:5-6.* Furthermore, it is said: *Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail? Job 38:22.* And elsewhere: *He bringeth the wind out of his treasuries; Psalm 135:7.* And elsewhere: *He opened the doors of heaven, as if of the air, raining down manna, etc; Psalm 78:23-24.* 

From these words of Holy Scripture, the general place of origin is elicited. But truly, what that thing might be which is shut up and hidden in the recesses of that invisible treasury-chest of God is beyond the grasp of the common man to understand—except that it is within the power of Divine Wisdom to uncover and reveal at her pleasure those things now kept secret and hidden in that mystery. I speak of the **seeds** (*seminaria*) hidden in the air, which, while existing only in potential, are brought into visible act for us. For through the mediation of the Word, all things were wonderfully created out of "nothing," as it were, according to that saying of King David: *O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all; Psalm 104:24.* And elsewhere: *Remember (he says) his marvelous works that he hath done; his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth; Psalm 105:5.* 

Hence it is said to Job: *Hearken unto this, O Job: stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God. Dost thou know when God disposed them, and caused the light of his cloud to shine? Dost thou know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him which is perfect in knowledge? Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong, as a molten looking glass? By what way is the light parted? Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it? Where is the way where light dwelleth? and as for darkness, where is the place thereof? Job 37 & 38.* 

But truly, the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, often criticized by early modern mystical philosophers for being too focused on physical "causes" and ignoring the spiritual/divine origins of nature.</note> in their vain manner boast that they know all these things. And yet, the wisest of all men thus...
