# On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

->He speaks<-: *I have perceived that man cannot find out all the work of God that is done under the sun; however much a man labors to seek it out, yet he shall not find it; yes, even if a wise man thinks he knows it, yet shall he not be able to find it,* **Ecclesiastes 8:17** <note>The original text cites Ecclesiastes 9:2, but the quote corresponds to 8:17. This emphasizes the theme that human effort alone is insufficient to grasp the complexities of creation.</note>. By this, Solomon understands the striving of man by himself, without the attainment of divine wisdom—which indeed he seems to verify elsewhere: *For what man can know the counsel of God? For the deliberations of mortals are timid, and our thoughts are uncertain,* **Wisdom 9:13-14**. *For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind full of many cares. And we hardly guess at the things that are upon the earth, but who has tracked out the things that are in heaven? And who has known your counsel, unless you have given wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from the highest places? For so the paths of those who dwell on the earth were corrected, and they were saved by wisdom.* From these words it is evident that human or worldly wisdom is vain; therefore, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> teaches us to beware of the vain philosophy of the Heathens and to look diligently into the fountain of all truth. And we are taught by the Prophet Baruch that we should by no means leave the fountain of all wisdom to seek art, science, and understanding in foreign regions—that is, from the Heathens—as did the Hagarenes and those who were in Teman, **Baruch 3** <note>Baruch 3:22-23 refers to regions famous for worldly wisdom that ultimately failed to find the way to true knowledge.</note>. Since they never knew the way of true wisdom, wisdom must first be acquired, and then through it we shall understand all things. *Seek first (says Christ) the kingdom of God and all these things shall be added unto you.* Hence Solomon confesses that through the enjoyment of wisdom he attained certain knowledge of the constitution of the world, the forces of the elements, the beginning, end, and middle of times, the changes of the solstices, the varieties of times and seasons, the circuits of the year, the positions of the stars, the natures of animals, the rages of wild beasts, the violence of winds, the thoughts of men, the differences of plants, the powers of roots, and the understanding of all things, both hidden and manifest, **Wisdom 7:17-21**. By this it may be seen that although the human spirit cannot by itself elicit the mysteries of <term>meteors</term> <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including clouds, wind, and rain, not just shooting stars.</note>, nor know how to search into divine mysteries, yet a man can perform all this in the light of wisdom; but let us return to the matter at hand.

That the matter of **mist** is air, condensed into a thick vapor, is clear from what has gone before. And although someone might object that the vapor leaping up from the earth's surface is the cause of mist, yet it was declared by us above that the earth itself is necessarily filled with air no differently than a man or any other body—whether animal, mineral, or vegetable—which it constantly breathes in through its pores, like an animal or plant, for its own sustenance. For there is in the air a hidden food and spiritual nourishment for every creature. Here also, when wisdom is at work with its ministers in the earth (*for the spirit of discipline fills the world, and the incorruptible spirit of God is in all things,* **Wisdom 1:7 and 12:1**), it is seen to procreate smokes, vapors, clouds, and waters in the earth through various degrees of condensation. For wisdom *sets a weight for the air* according to its appetite *and weighs the waters by measure*, both in the earth and in heaven, **Job 28:25**. Whence the earth enjoys all its meteors, and even the human body does as well, no differently than the Macrocosmic heaven, since the air is present in them, which is of the same nature as the worldly air, as was more fully discussed by us previously. From this, therefore, we discern that there is another species of mist besides that which rises from lakes, rivers, and even valleys—namely, that which is suddenly made from the coagulation of the universal air in a wonderful and hidden manner by the operation of wisdom, which fills the entire lower region of the air. Hence it is written in the Holy Scripture: *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth as a mist. I dwelt in high places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud. I alone compassed the circuit of heaven and walked in the depth of the abyss; in the waves of the sea and in all the earth, and in every people and nation I had a possession,* **Ecclesiasticus 24:3-6**. Furthermore, wisdom—which made the cloud its tabernacle <note>original: <note>tabernaculum</note></note> (no differently than the body is held to be the tabernacle for the soul, whence "man" is taken for soul and body, and in the sacred page "living soul" is sometimes taken for the whole composite)—is sometimes called a cloud. Whence it is said: *Wisdom was a covering for Israel (that is, a pillar of cloud) and a light of stars by night,* **Wisdom 10:17**. But in the Psalms it is said: *That God led the Israelites with a cloud by day, and all the night with a light of fire,* **Psalm 78:14** <note>The text cites Psalm 73:15, but the verse matches 78:14 (or 77:14 in the Vulgate).</note>. And in Exodus: *The Lord went before the Israelites in a pillar of cloud by day,* **Exodus 13:21**. *And yet God said, Behold, I send my angel before you: beware of his face and listen to his voice, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him,* **Exodus 23:20-21**. That is, "my essential power." Those who are versed in angelic mysteries say, therefore, that an angel is forged from air and fiery light; whence it is called a duality, as there concur in its composition a created spirit (which is its external part, serving in place of a body) and an uncreated light (which is its internal part, acting in place of a mind). Whence, in respect to its external part, it is called in that same chapter an angel or a creature, but by reason of its central internal part, it is there called <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The author is explaining a common mystical view that angels are "envelopes" for the divine presence.</note>. This angel, called <term>Metatron</term> <note>A powerful angel in Jewish Kabbalistic tradition, often considered the celestial scribe or the "lesser YHWH."</note> by the Kabbalists and <term>Anima Mundi</term> <note>Latin: "Soul of the World," a Platonic concept of an intrinsic force that animates nature.</note> by the Platonists, was that wisdom proceeding from the mouth of the Father: which uncreated emanation, insofar as it was mixed with the worldly spirit, is called a creature. The words are as follows: *The Creator created wisdom before the world in the beginning, and unto the world to come it shall not fail; in the holy tabernacle I ministered before him,* **Ecclesiasticus 24:9-10**. But indeed, this emanation in its simplicity is called the Creator and the Word; whence Saint John said: *By the word all things were made, and without him was not anything made, for in him is life.* And this is the reason that the divine Plato not unwisely called it the soul or life of the world, and the royal Psalmist in **Psalm 33**: *By the word of the Lord were the heavens made firm, and all the host of them by the spirit of his mouth. From him, in him, and through him are all things.*

Let praise and honor be given to Him, as St. Paul testifies. We conclude, therefore, that just as the uncreated light in an angel (which was the essential Name of Jehovah that was in the angel) was the central point in the angelic composition and the first mover within it—wherefore Wisdom is said to do all things according to the Father's pleasure, and is the soul or mind to its external form—so indeed this good and incorruptible spirit of God is the internal mover and actor of the cloud and of every <term>meteor</term><note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or clouds, not just falling stars.</note>, directing it wherever He wills. For this reason Job says: *The clouds scatter their light, which wanders round about everything, wherever the will of the governor directs them, for everything he commands them upon the face of the world; whether for a scourge, or for the sake of doing kindness and mercy,* **Job 37:11-13**. Finally, a mist is nothing other than a cloud of medium consistency, between the vaporous substance of a <term>Halo</term><note>A luminous ring around the sun or moon, here considered a very thin vapor.</note> and that of a dense cloud. We have now arrived at the description of the dense cloud.

### Chapter VI.
### On the Christian description of the cloud.

A cloud is air, first compressed and condensed into the degree of a dense or misty vapor, and from that gradually into a thicker and darker consistency, by the blasts of two winds—whether opposing or transverse—God so willing it and operating centrally to fulfill His will. Or thus:

A cloud is a revelation of the <term>worldly spirit</term><note>The *spiritus mundi*, a subtle substance thought by philosophers to permeate the universe and act as the medium for divine influence.</note> hidden in God’s treasure chest (that is, in His heavens) by divine wisdom operating centrally, and by His ministers, the winds, compressing it from without at God's nod: that is, a heap of mist gathered together by the divine breath, which Jehovah spreads out as His covering, and which He holds as a tabernacle or vehicle to fulfill His will both in the heavens and on the earth. Or thus:

A cloud is a vaporous and dense mass of air, which divine wisdom, expanded everywhere through the spirit of the world, made as if out of nothing—that is, produced into common light and revealed publicly to the world from the invisible and unknown sanctuary or treasure chest of the air, to execute His will both in the heavens and the earth.

In these definitions, or rather descriptions, we have the **material cause**: namely, the dense and vaporous mass of air, or the misty heap, in which the **formal cause** is also depicted. We also have its **efficient cause**, both the central one, acting primarily by its own will—namely, Divine Wisdom—and the external and superficial one—namely, the ministers of wisdom, compressing and moving it. We also have the "mine" or treasure chest from which the matter of the composition is drawn: namely, the heavens, which are the treasury of God. Finally, the **final cause** is expressed in the last place: namely, the effect of the Creator's will, whether healthy and inclining toward mercy, or unhealthy, destructive, and tending toward the quality of divine severity.

To defend the first part of our definition, we have several testimonies from the Holy Scripture, in which we find *that God by his wisdom assigns weight to the air, and weighs out the waters by measure, makes a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder,* **Job 28:25**. That is, according to the will and ordination of the divine spirit, the air is changed from a lighter state or weight into a denser or heavier one; the degrees of this change are explained in what follows: namely, into clouds (which he calls waters), and from clouds into rain or common water. He makes the lightnings, however, the internal formal light of the cloud, which is not revealed except by the dissolution of the compound—that is, the removal of darkness—which happens by means of the blast of the winds. Thus it is said: *As soon as he sends out his wind, the waters flow,* **Psalm 147:18** <note>The Latin text cites verse 18; in modern Bibles, this is often Psalm 147:18.</note>. That is, it rains, or the snow, clouds, and ice are dissolved. And elsewhere: *Now men do not look at the light when it is bright in the upper clouds, which the passing wind has cleansed,* that is, separated from the waters or dense clouds, **Job 37:21**.

The efficient cause of the cloud in the definition is also confirmed by the authority of the fountain of all truth, where it is written: *God weighed the waters* (that is, the clouds) *in a measure,* **Job 28**. And elsewhere in the same place: *Who made the sapphire clouds by wisdom?* And elsewhere: *God covers the heavens with dense clouds,* **Psalm 147:8**. And elsewhere: *God spread out a cloud for a covering,* **Psalm 105:39**.

Furthermore, the "mine" or treasure chest from which the matter of the cloud is drawn is expressed in this passage of the Holy Bible: *Jehovah shall open his best treasure, the heavens* (or the air), *giving rain to your land in its season, etc.* **Deuteronomy 28:12**. As it is also said of the "mine" of the winds: *He brings the wind out of his treasuries,* **Psalm 135:7**. And of the treasury of snow and hail it is said: *Have you entered into the treasury of the snow? Or have you seen the treasury of the hail?* **Job 38:22**. Now, the storehouse or sacred apothecary for all these things is one and the same, in which the general matter of the world was originally extracted: namely, the spirit or <term>Universal Mercury of the world</term><note>In Hermetic philosophy, "Universal Mercury" refers to the primal, fluidic substance of all matter, capable of taking any form.</note>, which, at God's command and with His wisdom assisting, is transmutable into any form like <term>Proteus</term><note>A shape-shifting sea god from Greek mythology, used here as a metaphor for the changing states of matter.</note>. # On the Formal Cause of Meteors.

->I 3<-

By the truly Christian Philosopher, this spirit—taken in a general sense and endowed with the power of wisdom—is defined as an infinite nature. It procreates like from like, generating and increasing all things, and holds within itself the names of all things. Because it is a living being by nature, everything we see—stones, wood, trees, and all bodies, whether they are imperfectly or perfectly mixed—is animated by this kind of spirit of divine wisdom and stabilized by its bond. It is the "bond of the elements" <note>original: "ligamentum elementorum"</note> and the power of mixing which, by means of its central soul in every thing of this world, effects the mixtures of the elements and imprints the form appropriate to its species. Through this form, one thing is distinguished and separated from any other. Yet, this hidden nature is not of any one color, though it shares in and creates all colors; it has no weight or quality of its own, yet it produces all weights and qualities and is the fertile mother of all things. It was for this reason that Anaximenes <note>Anaximenes (c. 585–528 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that air was the primary substance of the universe.</note> boldly asserted that air was the cause of all things, and Anaximander <note>Anaximander (c. 610–546 BCE) was another Pre-Socratic who believed the primary substance was the "Apeiron" or the Infinite.</note> wished it to be held as God, as the first author of all things. But that good man did not realize that this universal spirit is merely the vehicle and receptacle of divine and god-like emanation, at whose nod this spirit is accustomed to be transformed into this or that species. Therefore, in the manner of the Heathen and Idolaters—looking only at the circumference and ignoring the center—he foolishly held the creature in place of the creator, and erroneously offered divine worship to the external body instead of the internal soul. Finally, the "final cause" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "final cause" is the purpose or end for which something exists.</note> proposed in our definitions is also supported by the authority of Holy Scripture. For in them we read: *With moisture he wearies the thick cloud; he scatters the light of his cloud. It turns round and round by his guidance, to do whatever he commands them on the face of the habitable world, whether for a scourge, or for his land, or for mercy, he causes it to happen.* **Job 37:11-13.** <note>The Latin text cites Job 37:40, but the content matches verses 11-13.</note> And in the Prophet Baruch we read: *When the clouds are commanded by God to go over the whole world, they do as they are bidden.* **Baruch 6:60.**

But without a doubt, someone—or rather, many people—will object that God and His wisdom did not always influence the clouds, mists, and other <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, a "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or snow, not just shooting stars.</note>, but only occasionally in a prodigious and miraculous way. They will argue that in the present time (all miracles having ceased), and indeed even in those times from the origin of the world to the birth of the Savior, God or the Divinity only influenced the clouds in an extraordinary manner; and that at other times, the clouds were procreated by the order and disposition of nature and produced their fruitful effects by a natural progress.

To these people we certainly respond, in the first place, that miracles—however much some are accustomed to babble with open mouths and claim with a profane spirit that they have ceased—will remain as divine in their efficacy as long as God, the author of miracles, has the power of acting in this world. For the Word of God (by which all miracles are perfected) shall remain in its vigor forever. But let those infidels, who have dared to put an end to miracles, read the prophets; let them read Joel especially, let them read the Apocalypse, and then afterward let us see with what face or what audacity they dare to defend an error of such great importance. But let us now make a more specific inquiry into Holy Writ, so that it may appear more clearly whether or not God acts immediately through His wisdom in the production of clouds and other meteors. We find, therefore, in the place cited before: *That God opens his good treasury, the heavens, to give rain to the land in its season, and by blessing every work of the hand of the righteous.* **Deuteronomy 28:12.** And elsewhere it is said: *God covers the heavens with thick clouds, which prepare rain for the earth, which makes the mountains bring forth grass, and gives food to the cattle.* And elsewhere: *By his wisdom the depths were broken up, and the heavens drop down the dew.* **Proverbs 3:20.** And elsewhere: *God withholds the waters so that they dry up, and he sends them out so that they overturn the earth.* **Job 12:15.** And elsewhere: *He who gives snow like wool, and scatters the mist like ashes; who can stand before his cold?* **Psalm 147:16-17.** <note>The text cites Psalm 147:5, but it corresponds to verses 16-17.</note> And elsewhere: *He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, so that the cloud is not rent under them; he covers the face of his throne, and spreads his cloud over it.* **Job 26:8-9.** These passages are not to be understood as referring to miraculous events, but to how God acts commonly through His wisdom in the production of clouds in this world. Hence elsewhere: *Who has numbered the sapphire clouds by wisdom? and who can tilt the bottles of heaven?* **Job 38:37.** To which question it is answered elsewhere: *God by his wisdom prepares the weight for the air, and weighs the waters by measure; he makes a decree for the rain, etc.* And elsewhere he asks concerning this: *Do you know the balancings of the thick clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge?* **Job 37:16.** From these places it is explained clearly enough that all these wonders do not arise centrally from any created nature, but have been from the wisdom of the Great Creator from the beginning, are daily in the present time, and will be made and procreated in the future until the final "Let it perish" <note>The end of the world.</note>: according to that of the Royal Psalmist: *How manifold are your works! In wisdom you have made them all.* **Psalm 104:24.** <note>Cited as Psalm 103:24 following the Vulgate numbering.</note> And elsewhere: *Not one jot of the word of God shall fall to the earth.* Nor is it indeed a wonder that these and all other things are effected in this divine wisdom, since by its spirit—more effective than any other thing—that "world spirit" <note>original: "spiritus mundanus." In this philosophy, the world spirit is a bridge between the divine and the material.</note> is animated and quickened, without whose presence it would vanish into nothingness, in which state it was before the creation of the world. But indeed, the presence of the word of the Lord shall remain forever. Hence it is said: *By his spirit he has garnished*—that is, formed with beauty—*the heavens, etc.* **Job 26:13.** We conclude, therefore, that it is impossible for any meteor, whether visible or invisible, to be procreated without the presence and assistance of the Creator, who acts principally and primarily from the center in this world. For the incorruptible spirit of God (as the wise man testifies) is in all things, **Wisdom 12:1**, and consequently in meteors, which are the "seeds" <note>original: "spermata"</note> of things. That spirit is defined by him elsewhere as *a spirit having all power in itself, comprising all intelligible spirits,* **Wisdom 7:22-23** <note>The text cites Wisdom 9.</note>, as being more mobile than all movable things, and reaching everywhere because of its purity, insofar as it is a vapor of the power of GOD, or a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty GOD, and the brightness of eternal light, and a spotless mirror.

## CHAPTER VII.

->***On the different types of clouds, according to the testimony of Philosophers, Pagans, and Christians alike, as well as the Holy Scriptures.***<-

Those who were well-versed in Aristotelian Philosophy proposed many different types of clouds. Primarily, they distinguished one from another by a general difference: namely, by <term>substance</term> <note>The actual material the cloud is made of.</note> and <term>quantity</term>. Then, they divided each of these members into their own species. They categorized their substance into "dense" and "rare," insofar as dense, thick clouds or thin, subtle ones are procreated within and from the spiritual medium of the lower world. They claim the former are composed and forged from many thick, earthy <term>fumes</term> <note>original: "famis" / "exhalationibus." In Aristotelian meteorology, "fumes" or "exhalations" were dry and earthy, while "vapors" were moist and watery.</note>, while the latter come from a more subtle and less dense vapor. 

In this opinion of theirs regarding the difference in the density and thinness of clouds, they did not err in the least, as they were skilled in common experience regarding the varying consistency of clouds. However, in claiming that the material cause of a cloud's density is a thick and earthy fume, they are altogether deceived. This is because the consistency of a cloud, in both rarity and density, is <term>homogeneous air</term>, accumulated in either a larger or smaller mass and constricted in a more compact arrangement. For do we not see that the rainwater from the blackest and densest cloud is of the same homogeneity and clarity as that from a thinner, whitish cloud? Therefore, an earthy disposition of "fume" is not the cause of the density or gloom of a cloud, but rather the density of the air itself, or rather the gathering of its vaporous consistency into a deep mass. In a mist, we see the matter of the mist is the same—namely, condensed air—but its diversity lies in its depth of composition and its compact union. 

But let us proceed. They were also accustomed to distinguish clouds according to their color. Thus, they said black clouds arose from earthy smoke, or from something thick and packed together. We, however, confess they arise from air that is strongly and deeply thickened. Those clouds that are reddish or yellowish with blackness, they said arose partly from stellar light or fiery exhalations, and partly from thick, earthy smoke. We, on the other hand, affirm they are made by the various spirits of the winds compressing the air, along with luminous or fiery lights spread everywhere through the air, without any exhalation from the earth. Furthermore, they say those reddish clouds that turn green with blackness are procreated from exhalations with thick and copious vapor, as well as a great quantity of water and moisture. We assert those are born from various vapors or air gathered into one mass according to the various winds blowing from different quarters of the world to produce them. For we see from this that opposing winds tend to produce clouds and lightnings of various colors. Finally, they say white clouds are made from a scarcity of vapor; thus, because of the thinness of the subject, the stellar light very easily penetrates the mass and makes it bright.

They also have another distinction of clouds, for they make some "empty" or "void"—those which are dispersed through the sky like tufts of wool. The Aristotelians want these to be forged more from hot, dry exhalations than from moist vapors or those drenched in wetness. But we, following the Holy Scriptures, say that "luminous clouds" are purged of their liquid substance by the passing wind. For the Holy Page speaks of them thus:

> And now men do not look upon the light when it is bright in the higher clouds, which the wind has cleansed. Job 37:21 <note>The original citation says "Job 37. 38.", likely a reference to a specific commentary or a non-standard verse division; the text matches the meaning of Job 37:21.</note>

From this passage, Aristotle’s opinion on winds (mentioned above) is also refuted—namely, that the matter of winds, which he calls "exhalation," does not penetrate the middle region of the air. Yet by this testimony, the wind seems to blow in the highest part of the middle air, specifically where the "superior clouds" have their positions. Other clouds they call "abounding in water," namely those that dissolve into rainy matter. But we, following in the footsteps of the Holy Bible, divide clouds first by their different positions into "superior" and "inferior." Hence it is said:

> Men do not look upon the light when it is bright in the **superior clouds**. Job 37:21.
> And elsewhere: The **superior clouds** gave a sound. Psalm 77:17.
> And elsewhere: He commanded the **superior clouds** of heaven, and opened the doors of heaven. Psalm 78:23.
> And elsewhere: The **superior clouds** were established on high. Proverbs 8:28.

And in many other places. By this, it is signified that there are also "inferior clouds" which are thicker and denser in their substance.

Furthermore, by the authority of Scripture, clouds appear to be distinguished from one another in respect to their substance—namely, into "dense" and "thin." Into "dense," I say, because we find it written in that place:

> GOD covers the heavens with **dense clouds**, by which he prepares rain for the earth, etc. Psalm 147:8.
> And elsewhere: **Thick clouds** are his hiding place. Job 22:14.
> And elsewhere: A **thick cloud** is the chariot of GOD. Psalm 104:3.
> And elsewhere: Jehovah binds the waters in **thick clouds**, so that the cloud is not torn under them. Job 26:8.

Furthermore, the thinness of a cloud is argued by this passage: Behold, the Lord ascends upon...

In the preceding pages, it has been demonstrated how necessary the relationship is between the Macrocosm <note>The Great World or Universe.</note> and the human Microcosm <note>The "Little World"—Man.</note>; for indeed, the latter is shaped according to the pattern of the former, just as the former was fashioned after the image of the Creator. Both of these are said by those skilled in both <term>theosophy</term> <note>Divine wisdom or mystical insight.</note> and Philosophy to have been created in the divine image. For just as the world was created by God out of a dark nothingness and divided into heaven and earth by the mediation of the Spirit of God which moved over the waters, and is distinguished into four elements; and finally, by the inspiration of that universally breathing and acting Spirit, meteors of every condition are procreated both in heaven and on earth: so similarly, man was formed by GOD in the image of the world—and consequently of GOD himself—from the mud of the earth. He is inspired by the Creator and divided into heaven and earth, which is to say, into body and spirit. These are again distinguished into their own particular elements, in which meteors—both bad (that is, for punishment) and good and health-giving—are produced, namely both in his aerial heaven and in his earth or body.

Therefore, just as meteors both humid and dry are found in the aerial medium of the earth in the Macrocosm, as well as in its lowest heaven; so also are similar things found and procreated in the Microcosm, both in the body and the spirit or aerial heaven. But truly, since man, considered in his integrity, is "composed of the composed" <note>original: "compositus de composito." A philosophical concept meaning man is a complex mixture of things that are already mixtures, making him the most condensed part of creation.</note>—that is, made from the parts of the composed world—it follows that man has immersed himself more deeply than the world into a multitude of compositions. From this it happens that his elements, as well as his "meteors," are far denser and more compacted into a glutinous substance than those of the world, which are more simple. For example: blood, which is the ethereal element of man in which that worldly spirit lies hidden, is visible because of its density; as is that bilious humor <note>Yellow bile or choler.</note> which is related to fire and is the natural receptacle of the worldly fire. 

For (as was said before) the worldly spirit exists in man as his heaven, in the center of which nevertheless dwells the divine spirit, which provides man with reason and intellect—something the worldly spirit cannot achieve on its own. Thus it is written: *There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding, Job 32:8.* <note>The text cites Job 9, but this is Job 32:8.</note> By this we see that the divine spirit is the central actor in both the worldly and human spirit; it breathes and incites the created spirits of both wherever it wills, and makes them forever ready and prompt to perform its pleasures. It is not the heat or cold of the creatures, which are only the effects of the divine action or breathing, as will be declared elsewhere.

### CHAPTER VIII.
#### On the Halo, the Mist, and the Cloud.

Since air is the medium in which watery <term>meteors<note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon like rain, clouds, or fog, not just falling stars.</note></term> are produced—both in the <term>macrocosmic<note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe or the world at large.</note></term> heavens and throughout its earth—it is necessary that these same types of meteors are also produced in every part of the "human air," whether solid or fluid; that is, every degree of a cloud. Furthermore, because the eyes in the highest heaven (or the head of the <term>Microcosm<note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being, viewed as a miniature version of the universe.</note></term>) have a strict relationship to the two great lights of the larger world <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, as it is through them that the rays of the human spirit emit their sight, every species of cloud—namely the **Halo**, the **mist**, the **cloudlet**, and so on—can be very easily distinguished by their effects in the eyes.

For just as in the larger world we sometimes see a **Halo** or a very thin mist positioned between our eye and the sun or moon, and sometimes a thicker one, and sometimes a very thick cloud that is not at all penetrable by solar rays, so too in the ocular medium—specifically within the <term>humors<note>The fluids of the eye.</note></term> as well as in the membranes or between the membranes of the eye itself—we sometimes see these meteors mixed between the visual rays and the objects seen. These are called **mists**, **white spots**, and **suffusions** or **cataracts**.

*Mists* in the eye are said to be thin and superficial whitenesses, or "darknesses" of either membrane of the eye. Such a disease is called a **cloudlet** <note>original: "nubecula"</note>, because a certain thin humor exists there, much like a thin and tiny cloud imprinted in the air, clinging to the <term>cornea<note>The transparent front part of the eye.</note></term>. Because of this, the sufferer thinks they see all things through a mist, or vapor, or smoke.

But indeed, if this humor or vapor becomes even thicker, it coalesces into the "second degree of a cloud" and is then called **Albugo** <note>A white spot or opacity on the cornea.</note>. In this state, all clear sharpness of vision is dimmed, and everything is seen as if in a dark shadow—just as in a very dense mist in the greater world, we see the image of an object that was once visible completely removed from our sight. Furthermore, sometimes due to the excessive thickness of the corneal membrane, vision is rendered dark, which is why this occurrence is called **darkness** <note>original: "caligo"</note>.

There is also another species of cloud produced in a deeper place, namely in the <term>crystalline humor<note>The lens of the eye.</note></term> or the vitreous humor, which causes that humor to change into a sea-green or dark color. People affected this way believe they see through smoke or mist; such an alteration of vision is called **Glaucoma**.

Finally, we have another species of these meteors which produces that effect in the eye called a **suffusion** or **cataract**. This is produced by a "nebulous thickening" of the air, occurring either in the seat of the pupil, or between the <term>uveal tunic<note>original: "Rhagoidem tunicam"; the pigmented middle layer of the eye.</note></term> and the crystalline humor. This happens slowly and gradually, so that in the beginning it can scarcely be discerned. Thus, in the creation of a celestial cloud, we observe various stages: a progress from air into a barely perceptible vapor, from that into a very thin mist, from that into a thicker one, which finally thickens into a dense cloud.

Furthermore, when the air is condensed to the first degree around the circumference of the pupil while the center remains untouched (or obscured only by the thinnest smoke), it is observed to take on the appearance of a **Halo**.

Whatever the case may be, we see here that the process of converting air into a thin or dense mist, or to the consistency of a cloud, is the same as we have in the world's atmosphere. Indeed, we have even observed that when such air is compacted into a dense vapor and thickens into "dew," it nourishes the waning watery humor of the eye and preserves it in its full state. We are taught in two ways that this created vaporous substance was originally air: first, because it proceeds gradually from invisibility to being visible to the onlooker; and second, because it could not have penetrated through the spongy and porous substance of the optic nerve unless it were in an airy and spiritual condition.

The reason why this airy substance sometimes thickens in the aforementioned places is due to the various ways air penetrates that seat—namely, because of its "central force," which can be converted into various dispositions. It receives this force from some "constricting wind," by which it gradually contracts itself into a mass. However, air from a wind of the opposite nature remains dissolved in its own nature, so that it may better perform the roles and duties of the watery humor according to the laws of Nature.

In the ventricles of the brain, airy whirlwinds, vapors, mists, and clouds are also generated, either by natural paths or against the laws of nature. Just as the vapors of air drawn through the nostrils are stirred by the good and healthy spirit of nature, they thicken into a sweet and natural mist through circulation. By lightly condensing, they are dispersed partly into the dewy moisture of the front ventricles, and partly into the invisible spirit through the passages of the <term>choroid plexus<note>A network of blood vessels in the brain that produces cerebrospinal fluid.</note></term>. These are called the **animal spirits** <note>The vital "refined" air believed to travel through the nerves to control movement and sensation.</note>. Their superfluous part, however, is contracted into the state of thick water, which is excreted through the "basin" or **infundibulum** and the **pituitary gland**, and finally through the openings of the sphenoid bone, distilling into the palate.

In the same way, this air—filled with the "seeds" of unnatural meteors—is observed to be reduced into a misty or cloudy substance during inhalation and exhalation through the olfactory processes. This is how **Catarrh** <note>A head cold or excessive mucus.</note>, **Scotomia** <note>Dizziness accompanied by dark spots in the vision.</note>, **Vertigo**, and other such effects of "meteors" are produced in the ventricles of the brain. These occur according to the nature of the airy substance and the qualities of the winds predominant in it, as well as the position and place in which they are formed—

From this it follows that the air, filled with the seeds of turbulent wind, is once drawn in and disposed such that its central mover, stirred by natural heat, rotates it in a circle—much like a whirlwind or the effect of clouds clashing with other clouds, or a river forcefully meeting another river—within the **anterior ventricles of the brain**. From this, all things appear to the imaginative faculty as if they were spinning in a circle like a wheel; for this reason, this affection is called **vertigo** <note>From the Latin *vertere*, "to turn."</note>.

But if the inhaled air, due to a different arrangement of these "seeds," is rendered into a misty matter—even darker and thicker—and remains more stable in the anterior part of the brain than the air which produces vertigo, then objects appear dark or like **flies and bedbugs** <note>original: "muscarum ac cimicum." This refers to *myodesopsia*, or "floaters" in the vision, which the author interprets as internal mists.</note>. This is due to the loose and disconnected constitution of the "cloud" appearing thus to the imaginative sense. Indeed, all physicians acknowledge and freely admit that this type of affection or effect is generated by dark vapors existing in the brain, yet nearly all are either entirely ignorant of where it originates, or perceive it only vaguely. But we shall discuss the efficient cause of this type of preternatural meteor more extensively elsewhere.

Such is also the origin of **catarrh** or **rheum** <note>Mucus or discharge from the nose and throat.</note>: which can be very easily discerned from the fact that we perceive thick air, resulting in "tears of marble" <note>likely referring to condensation on cold stone</note> and a heaviness of the head, caused by the blasts of cloudy winds. Thus it happens that unless a person’s nature is strong enough to resist the impressions of air altered into a damp disposition and overcome its nature, they are very easily overwhelmed by impressions similar to that air. On this point, **Hippocrates** (*Aphorisms, Book 5, Aph. 3*) and **Galen** agree in this opinion: namely, that when the **South Wind** <note>original: "flatu Australi"</note> dominates for a long time, hearing is dulled, the vision is clouded, the head becomes heavy, dizziness of the eyes and brain occurs, the intellect becomes sluggish, and the **falling sickness** <note>original: "morbus caducus," meaning epilepsy</note> and similar conditions are procreated in men. This is because the damp spirit of that wind introduces thick and dark clouds; it is the function of that wind to make the air thick and gross, and to produce corruption and rot because of the wickedness of the "seeds" it sends into the universal air. However, since this wind produces warm dampness, it is apt to produce all watery meteors of that same condition, inclining toward either destruction or benevolence according to the disposition of the Disposer <note>God or Nature</note>.

Furthermore, such meteorological impressions—both natural and preternatural—are generated in the **stomach** <note>original: "ventriculo"</note>, as it is the place in the human body that primarily plays the role of the "middle region of the air" <note>In ancient meteorology, the atmosphere was divided into three regions; the middle region was where clouds and storms formed.</note>. The seeds of these meteors are derived both from terrestrial winds and from those of the elementary heavens in this manner: For just as we see that the seeds of the world's meteors are drawn through inhalation to the left chamber of the heart and then scattered through the arterial vessels into the members of the entire body—and even dispensed everywhere through the brain's vessels via the <term>mammillary processes<note>Olfactory bulbs/nerves, thought to be channels for vapors in early anatomy.</note></term>—so too are vapors, mists, and clouds generated in the stomach. Whether these are healthy or unhealthy, they arise from the varied nature of fruits, foods, or sustenance (both liquid and solid) according to the various disposition of the winds that predominated in the air during the time of the vegetation, growth, and nutrition of those animals and plants.

From this it follows that when **South Winds** preside over the air during the growth or vegetation of plants—namely grain, herbs, fruits, and roots—they organize the temperament of the air according to their own disposition, making the plants prone to their own nature and filling them with putrid seeds. For plants receive the hidden food of their life from the air at every moment; indeed, in both the celestial and terrestrial air, there is a hidden food for the life of every thing. Plants possess a **magnetic virtue** implanted centrally within them, by means of which they constantly attract an "airy life" similar to themselves. As explained in our history, *The Anatomy of Bread and Wheat*, through this faculty and succession, they daily acquire more and more growth, both in their spirit and their physical mass. 

Similarly, such vegetation—grasses, fruits, grains of wheat, etc.—render the animals that eat them (both land-dwellers and birds) into the same condition as the plants themselves, since the temperament of the nourished follows the temperament of the nourishment. For that which makes a thing such, is itself even more such. Thus, the air which contributes to their nutrition and growth is condensed into their substance. When it is later restored to its original freedom through dissolution and refinement [digestion], it always retains the seeds of the wind that predominated during its growth. Therefore, that vaporous air extracted from food in the stomach by the "circulation of the first concoction" <note>The first stage of digestion</note>—which is then reduced by compression into chyle and later into blood—always contains within it the spirit of the wind that presided over it. Consequently, it gradually brings the entire body it nourishes back into its own condition from its previous constitution. For this reason, **Epidemic diseases** and those spreading among the people are so varied and diverse in succeeding years, according to the different disposition of the winds blowing in them. Thus, if the winds most frequent in those quarters of the world are healthy and suitable for animal life—such as the **North** and **East winds**—they announce a healthy year, because plants and animals are nourished by such air and such "seeds" of the winds, and even the brains and hearts of animals are rectified through inhalation. But conversely, the **South winds**, because of their corrupt disposition, affect the fruits and grasses with a foul breath through their long-lasting blowing...

Indeed, *Galen* says, *“All pestilential fevers take their origin from putrefaction.”* Here, however, it is worth noting—according to what was said previously regarding windy meteors—that the nature of the wind, which holds principal dominion over the harvests or food, inclines toward that part of the body which naturally corresponds to that "quarter" <note>One of the four cardinal directions</note> from which that macrocosmic wind blows. Thus, that specific part of the body is chiefly affected, and its natural spirit is agitated and excited in its breathing by the power of the foreign spirit introduced into the body through nourishment, whether this leads toward health or toward infirmity. But we shall discuss more fully, God willing, the mysteries of winds and spirits within food, as well as their roles as both the efficient and final causes of meteors.

By a similar reasoning, meteors of this kind are produced in both sides or chambers of the heart, though with different respects and through different works of alteration. In the left chamber <term>thalamo; literally "inner room" or "bedchamber," used here for the ventricle</term> of the heart, vapors, mists, and in a sense, clouds are generated immediately from the condensation and contraction of the air inhaled through the lungs. In this operation, the final consistency of the "cloud" and the effect of nature's entire action is **arterial blood**. This blood is animated by the life-giving "seeds" of the air; these seeds of the **vital spirit** <note>The subtle substance believed to sustain life and heat, carried by the arteries</note> swim within the vehicle of the arterial blood like a soul within a body. Hence, this operation—the reduction of air into a misty substance for the restoration of life—is a path *from the prior* <note>original: "à priori"; meaning from the cause to the effect, or from the higher (air) to the lower (blood)</note>. 

However, to produce a cloudy or misty substance in the right chamber of the heart, the operation is the opposite, as it proceeds *from the posterior* <note>original: "à poſteriori"; meaning from the effect back to the cause, or from the dense to the subtle</note>. This involves the reduction and resolution of the thick blood—perfected in the "workshop" of the liver—into a vaporous substance (mediated by preparation and circulation). From that, it is condensed into a liquor or blood far more subtle than it was before (so that it is better adapted for the nutrition of the light and delicate substance of the lungs) and is finally condensed there. 

From this it is clear that the first circulation or "rotation of elements" completed in the left ventricle proceeds by condensing simple celestial air. The latter proceeds by altering terrestrial air (or the "elemental" part) first into thick blood, and then into a subtler form through **Nature's Alchemy**. This is further refined by a higher degree of **Alchemy** into an invisible spirit, combined with the **quintessence** <term>The "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated medicinal or spiritual force</term> of the air drawn in through the nostrils. From these, the **animal spirits** are later formed, acting as the most fit ministers of the intellect, reason, and the human mind. Regarding this progression in human nature, we have spoken more copiously in our treatise *The Anatomy of Our Mysticism* <note>original: "Anatomia noſtræ mysticæ"; likely referring to Fludd's own published works on the divine structure of the body</note>, in the section on the mysteries of the blood, in the chapter where the **Alchemy of Nature** in the human body is discussed.

Besides all this, all degrees of cloudiness are to be found in the **Liver**. For when the most subtle substance of the **chyle** <term>chili; the milky fluid produced from digested food in the intestines</term> is drawn from the intestines through the mesenteric veins, it is transmuted in the workshop or laboratory of the liver. Through circulation, it changes from its white or "tin-like" substance into a golden and ruddy color, becoming refined into a vaporous mist. For in every work of Nature, this must be considered first: that in her paths toward perfection, she always proceeds by purifying; she purifies by thinning; she thins by dissolving; she dissolves by concocting <note>or "cooking" through internal heat</note>; and she cooks and lightens through natural circulation. Finally, that which has been circulated and concocted returns once more to perfection or the preservation of the parts (through application, union, and assimilation) to which it is assigned by nature. 

*For example*, the "bloody nature" is perfected in the Liver; in this completion, the misty substance of the refined matter is coagulated into fibrous blood, so that, in a further progression of nature, it is transmuted into flesh and solid parts through condensation. Here, therefore, we must consider that air which has been primarily coagulated into a terrestrial mass is made, through dissolution, more suitable and fit for the rectification and nutrition of solid bodies (namely, the air found in nutrients). Conversely, that celestial air, free from all composition, contributes primarily to the rectification and refreshment of the animal and vital spirits. From this, it is very easy to recognize what kind of air is apt to infect the human spirit with diseases, and what kind, in turn, is accustomed to corrupt only the solid parts while the spiritual parts remain well.

Finally, all types of cloudy meteors concur in the perfection of the **semen** contained in the seminal vessels. On the part of the arterial vessels, the internal semen (which is from the quintessence of the arterial blood, containing within itself—though invisibly—the hidden image of the entire species) hides like a soul in a body. The quintessence of the "coagulated air" is contracted into an invisible smoke immersed in the arterial blood; it takes the form of an **invisible wind**. This wind breathes into and animates that thick, elemental smoke into the visible consistency of semen, just as the spirit of the worldly winds acts as the soul within the clouds. This air is suddenly and instantly drawn into the previously empty seminal vessels by an inclination of nature, or rather by a voluntary and principal action of Divine Wisdom moving from the center. We see it turn into a fleshy mass, part of which later migrates and is converted into bones, cartilages, tendons, and membranes, and finally into the complete framework of the external man.

And all of this is indeed done by Divine Wisdom acting from the center to execute its will, which we also find confirmed in these passages of Holy Scripture. *Did you not,* says Job, addressing the Lord, *pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese? You have exercised kindness toward me with life, and your visitation has preserved my spirit. (Job 10:10-12).* By these words, it seems clearly declared that the "visitation" and real presence of the Divine Spirit is found in the reduction of the consistency of the body (or the human "earth") from the invisible elemental air, through the path and stages of condensation. That is, it moves through a thin vapor into a white, cloudy substance, and from that into a spermatic cloud, and from this coagulation (in the manner of milk into cheese) into flesh and bones. Indeed, the Spirit is always present, "visiting" every creature, though invisibly, for without its presence nothing can be preserved. Hence it is also said that *when God sends forth His spirit, creatures are recreated; when He hides His face, they are troubled; and when He takes back His spirit, they expire (Psalm 104:29-30).*

Furthermore, our previous assertion is supported elsewhere by the words of the Royal Psalmist: *You are He who drew me out of the womb, making me feel safe at my mother's breasts; I was cast upon you from the birth-canal; from my mother’s womb, you have been my strong God (Psalm 22:9-10).* And elsewhere: *You possess my kidneys <note>original: "renes"; traditionally considered the seat of emotions and secrets</note> since the time you covered me in my mother's womb. My strength was not hidden from you, since I was made in secret, as if in the lowest parts of the earth; your eyes saw my unformed mass, and in your book all these things were written, from the days they were being formed, when as yet none of them existed (Psalm 139:13-16).* By these words, he seems primarily to argue that the central act of man—from the point of his generation until his completion—must be attributed to God and His Holy Spirit acting from within. Secondly, he suggests that the movement in human generation is, as it were, "out of nothing"—that is, from a thing that is barely apparent, which is of the nature of air. Finally, Job says: *The Spirit of the strong God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life (Job 33:4).* And elsewhere: *The hands of God have fashioned the man (Psalm 119:73).*

From these things, therefore, we can conclude that just as air is the principle from which generation begins, so a "cloudy meteor" is the middle stage of the motion. From the manifest part of this meteor (with the addition of its like), the external part or **Body** of the offspring is made. From the internal spirit or wind of that spermatic cloud, the internal part or **Soul** of the offspring is made. This "middle" state progresses toward the goal of a "perfectly mixed" substance, creating a creature similar to the father's species through a various rotation of the elements: namely, of air into a vaporous nebula, of the nebula into a compact cloud, and of this into a dense water, which is again coagulated like milk into flesh and bone in the manner of cheese.

Such will also be the motion when moving backward: from the perfectly mixed body to the cloudy meteor, and from that into the air, which is the final goal in dissolution. For whatever the beginning was in generation, such will be the end in corruption. Hence the King said not unwisely: *Man is flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return; Remembering,* he says, *that they are flesh, a passing wind that does not come back (Psalm 78:39).* And elsewhere: *Man born of woman... flees like a shadow, and does not remain.* This is also taught by common experience; for all flesh and bone alike are resolved by the violence of fire into smoke, and from that into almost nothing—that is, into invisible air. By these things, it is right to see that "meteors" <note>intermediate states of matter</note> are the middle points for both dissolution and generation, for both disease and health. Above all these things, we can consider that the "seeds" of infirm meteors <note>unhealthy atmospheric or bodily states</note>—by being drawn into the body through the air via breathing, or through the attraction of food in which they hide—very easily convert a spirit or body prone to corruption into their own infirm nature through a certain hidden malice. Like a poison, they infect the entire human composition or a part of it; that is, they either disturb it with diseases, or they attempt to tear the vital spirits away from the state of health toward the boundaries of infirmity, and finally toward the ultimate goal of corruption.

# CHAPTER X.

## On watery meteors descending from heaven. And first, concerning those of a more liquid consistency.

| **Watery meteors descending from heaven are either:** |
| :--- |
| — Liquid, such as: |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;— Dew. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;— Rain. |
| — Frozen: See S. |

Those watery meteors which are of a thick and more compact consistency than those that are either cloudy or misty are different from one another with respect to the place or "seat" from which they arise. Indeed, some descend from heaven, some rise up from the lap of the earth, and others draw their origin and growth from the sanctuary of both—namely, from both heaven and earth.

Those which descend from heaven are observed to differ evidently in their consistency. Some take on a liquid and flowing form, while others are frozen by the <term>Northern cold; original: "frigore Septentrionali"</term> and become somewhat fixed and hardly fluid at all. Those which rain down from heaven in a fluid and liquid form are Dew and Rain, which we propose to treat primarily in this section. First, therefore, we shall express the opinion of Aristotle and the <term>Peripatetic school; the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</term> regarding the nature of these two meteors; and then afterwards, we will declare in a few words what the opinion of the Holy Scripture is concerning them.

According to the opinion of the Peripatetics, therefore, **Dew** is defined as a vapor, mixed with a small amount of earthy matter, condensed in the lowest region of the air, which they confidently say is dissolved into water as soon as it settles. Or they define it thus:

> Dew is a vapor which, in the spring and autumn seasons, is attracted on high by the power of the sun during the daytime; but because it does not reach the <note>Aristotelian physics divided the atmosphere into three regions; the middle region was thought to be perpetually cold.</note> middle region of the air, it is frozen by the nocturnal cold in the lowest region of the air and is forced to descend in the form of water droplets. Or thus: That which is generated from a weakly warm, thick, and moist vapor, not raised much from the earth into the lowest part of the air, condensed by the nocturnal cold and resolved into water. **Rain**, however, they define as a liquefied cloud, resolved into water, dripping down drop by drop. Or otherwise thus: Rain (they say) is a warm, smoky, and thick vapor, raised from moist bodies by the heat of the sun and other stars, as far as the middle region of the air, by whose coldness it is there condensed and converted into a cloud; which cloud is again liquefied, resolved into water falling to the earth for the safety of living and growing things.

Rain falling more abundantly with force they call a <term>Heavy Shower; original: "Imber"</term>.

From these definitions of Dew, the Aristotelians seem to place no difference between the matter of a cloud and that of dew. For they assign a warm, moist, and sufficiently compact vapor, rising from earth and water and attracted upward by the force of solar heat, to the composition of both; hence they have not hesitated at all to attribute the same agent to both. Therefore, they placed the entire difference they make between the constitution of each in the diversity of locations—namely, in the varying disposition of the cold found in them. For if that vapor had been raised into the middle region of the air, it would follow from their doctrine that, due to the intense cold of that place, it would be condensed into the consistency of a cloud...

...it would be condensed by the cold; but in truth, since it is not raised above the summit of the middle region of the air, it is raised only by the light cold of that place and the nighttime through a gentle constriction. Then, falling downward little by little by its own weight, it is transformed into drops clinging to the herbs. For this reason, they <note>Referring to the classical philosophers.</note> have defined dew as nothing other than a small rain, but without clouds.

Certainly, they assign a very beautiful and, at first glance, a quite probable description of the <term>meteor; original: "meteoro"</term> <note>In the 17th century, a "meteor" was any atmospheric phenomenon, such as rain or dew, not just a falling star.</note> of dew. But indeed, if we look at the matter a little more deeply, we will perceive it to be otherwise, and as far as possible from what they believed. For first, we look back at those things said about the origin of a cloud, and we will discern that the whole matter from its origin, as put forth by the Philosophers, is closer to external probability than to central truth. Furthermore, we add in this place that the cause of dew is not originally from the earth, but from heaven or the lowest part of the air; and if any air or vapor is exhaled from the earth, it is only by way of "expiration," following the "inspiration" of the common air. It does not follow, however, that the air breathed out by a living creature must be condensed into a dewy substance in the nighttime by the nocturnal cold, even though this sometimes happens with an icy or <term>Northern blast; original: "flatu gelido seu septentrionali"</term>. By the same reasoning, we affirm that although vapor exhaling from the bowels of the earth is sometimes congealed into dewy drops, it does not follow that all dew is created from vapors rising from the earth. 

For just as air is accustomed to penetrate everywhere, even to the very center of the earth—since it provides life and spirit—so it is necessary that, because it is of the same nature as the universal world, it has the capacity to be both condensed and refined by that "sea of air." Indeed, let us boldly affirm that the "treasury" of the dewy substance is the universal sea of air, and thus there is no need for it to be exhaled by necessity from the cavities of the earth. The greater contains the lesser within itself, as you will see confirmed below by the testimony of the sacred font. The reason for its condensation is the will of the centrally moving and contracting Wisdom, at whose command the winds—namely the North and South—blowing most sweetly and lightly (the latter more strongly, the former more weakly), very easily condense the nocturnal air by a light compression. This condensed air, drawn into the pores of the earth by "inspiration," adheres to the herbs and grasses and appears in the form of little drops. 

Does it not seem that Aristotle, contrary to the goal of his own description of dew, acknowledges a great truth (though hidden) regarding the South winds' role in the makeup of dew? Taught by experience, he says that there is no dew unless the South wind is blowing; upon which words of the Philosopher, <note>Bartholomew the Englishman (Bartholomaeus Anglicus), a famous 13th-century Franciscan encyclopedist.</note> Bartholomew concludes thus: 
> *Since* (he says) *dew is a tiny rain, and rain is a great dew* 
and in this respect, he concludes that the southern wind generates dew because of its humidity, just as conversely the northern wind, with its dryness, licks up and consumes dews, or condenses and freezes their substance by means of its cold. Furthermore, in this doubtful resolution—namely, what is the origin of dew?—many have written many and contrary things. For <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), an influential Bishop and theologian.</note> Ambrose attributes the generation of dew upon the earth to the moist nature of the moon, 
> *since* (he says) *the Moon is the mother of dew;* 
In these things, one may see that the Philosophers are by no means consistent with themselves concerning the procreation of dew, inasmuch as various men have spoken of it in various ways.

What the Holy Scriptures think about dew and its origin, we shall now show in a few words. We find the Holy Scriptures speaking thus about dew in general, in the person of GOD to man: 
> *Gird up now your loins like a man* (says Jehovah, addressing Job from the whirlwind) *and what I shall ask you, make known to me, etc. Has the rain a father? Or who begot the drops of dew? From whose womb did the ice come forth? Or who begot the frost of heaven?* 
He argues there that it is beyond human grasp to explain such mysteries without the revelation of the divine spirit. And yet the <term>Peripatetics; original: "Peripatetici"</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> nevertheless seem to answer Jehovah’s objection boldly, asserting that the womb or matrix of dew is the earth with water, and its father is the solar rays, acting through nocturnal cold and humidity. 

But we shall approach a more particular explanation of this: from a twofold consideration of the holy letters, we have observed that there is a twofold difference of dew in the world. We gather that one springs from the earth, as it is said: 
> *No vapor had ascended from the earth to water the whole surface of the earth; Gen. 2.* 
But <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> Jerome has it: 
> *A fountain ascended from the earth which watered the whole surface of the earth,* 
but let the exposition of the text be made in the following manner: we say (as before) that "meteors" are generated in the spirit or air enclosed in the earth no differently than in the open air. We have also said that Wisdom is everywhere—in heaven, in earth, in the depths of the sea, etc. And we say that the earth, at the command of that terrestrial Wisdom (which is a single and simple spirit, existing everywhere throughout the world, enclosed nowhere), has its own "expirations" and "inspirations," which we call vapors. However, that vapors of this kind are condensed into dews is a mystical and secret work of divine wisdom; it does not require matter from the earth. For in Wisdom's hands are the universal spirits of the world, and all bodies which are animated by it, whence it is said: 
> *GOD of the soul and the body, GOD strong in spirits, GOD of all flesh, Num. 16:22.* 
But since by His command and breath the air—both celestial and terrestrial—is changed into this or that state: indeed we say that heaven is the father of the earth, inasmuch as it was created from it from the beginning, whence it is said that GOD created heaven and earth, and not earth and heaven—arguing from this that after the perfection of the Heavens, the earth was created. But just as GOD is said to be in heaven, so we acknowledge Him to be in the earth; consequently, it is certain that heaven is found even in the "dark earth," which is also the tabernacle of God. We conclude, therefore, that the matter of dew is principally from the celestial spirit, although that spirit is also inspired and expired by the earth for its own quickening. Therefore, the air is the Ark of God...

<meta>This page continues the argument that atmospheric phenomena (meteors) are not merely physical accidents as the Aristotelians claim, but are governed by Divine Wisdom. It picks up from the previous page's discussion of the "treasury" of the air.</meta>

### On the Formal Cause of Meteors

...treasury, from whose womb both dew and ice and frost are generated in a most secret manner. Although vapors rising from the earth by exhalation are sometimes the cause of a greater thickness in the dew, nevertheless both the matter and the hidden disposition of dew are primarily rained down from the heavens. This occurs by the will of Wisdom acting within, contracting the air into a denser and visible substance. Hence it is written: *I came out of the mouth of the most High, and covered the earth as a mist; I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep.* <note>Original Latin: "ex ore altissimi prodii, & tanquam nebula cooperui terram, rotunditatem cælorum circumiui sola, in profunditate abyssi ambulaui." Ecclesiasticus 24:3–5.</note> And also: *By his Wisdom the upper clouds drop down the dew.* <note>Proverbs 3:20.</note> Therefore it is clear that dews are rained down from the heavens or the upper air, and are not formed from the weakly elevated exhalations of the earth. This is also confirmed elsewhere: *He commanded the upper clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven, raining down manna,* <note>Psalm 78:23–24.</note> Moses explains that <term>manna; original: "manna"</term> <note>The miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert.</note> was nothing other than liquid dew frozen into the form of coriander seeds. <note>Exodus 16:14.</note> He also recounts elsewhere that it proceeded from the mouth of Jehovah, saying: *He fed thee with manna... that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the Lord.* <note>Deuteronomy 8:3.</note> Hence, from the place of its generation, it is called "heavenly bread," just as common bread is called "earthly bread."

Yet I would have you know that heaven is in the earth, and God is in heaven—both the terrestrial and the celestial heaven. Thus, there is a celestial Sun and a terrestrial Sun; there is a celestial air and a terrestrial air; and finally, heaven is in the earth, and earth is in heaven; *for that which is above is like that which is below.* <note>This is a reference to the famous Hermetic maxim from the Emerald Tablet: "quod est superius est sicut & illud quod est inferius."</note> We have, therefore, an internal agent in both dew and frost—namely, Wisdom. At her command, when a thin South wind predominates and a North wind blows more weakly against it, the air is dispersed everywhere into liquid dew for its procreation. But when a thin or stronger North wind blows, with the South wind blowing weakly and secretly in opposition, frost is rained down everywhere upon the earth like ashes. This is also confirmed by the royal Psalmist: *God scatters the frost like ashes; who can stand before his cold? He sends out his word and melts them; as soon as he makes his wind blow, the waters flow.* <note>Psalm 147:16–18.</note>

By these words, he seems to denote that frost and ice are created by the North wind (whence he says elsewhere): *By the breath of God frost is given.* And elsewhere: *By his breath the mighty God produces ice; also for irrigation he fatigues the thick cloud.* <note>Job 37:10–11.</note>

By these things it is clear to see that the generation of dew is far different from what that Aristotelian description professes. Its matter is extracted from its best treasury, the heavens—or the universal aerial spirit—while its form is produced by the incorruptible spirit acting from within the contracted air. The winds serve as ministers executing the divine pleasure, and in them the mighty God of spirits operates according to his will. Thus, supported by the testimony of the Holy Bible, we describe dew as follows:

->Dew is the descent of vaporous air from heaven to earth, occurring by the blowing of God and the operation of his Wisdom, and its clumping together there into liquid drops or droplets.<-

->Or thus:<-

->Dew is the condensation or transmutation of somewhat misty air, sent downward from the heavens onto the surface of the earth into the form of clear and spherical droplets, by the operation of Wisdom, without any manifest rain preceding it.<-

We have therefore made air the material cause; we have placed the heaven, or the middle air, as the place where it is prepared; and we have said that the primary author is the Holy Spirit of Wisdom, acting everywhere from the beginning, whose ministers are the winds. You have every part of these descriptions confirmed by the sacred page. We come now to the description of rain, which cannot differ much in matter from that of dew, since the ancients observed that dew is like a tiny rain, and rain is like a great dew. The <term>Peripatetics; original: "Peripatetici"</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> define rain as a melted cloud, resolved and dripping down drop by drop into water.

->Or otherwise thus:<-

->Rain is a hot, smoky, and thick vapor raised from moist bodies (whether earthy or watery) by the heat of the sun and other stars, all the way to the middle region of the air; by the cold of that region, it is condensed there into the consistency of a cloud, which cloud melts again, resolved into water, falling onto the lands for the health of living and growing things.<-

As for the first definition, it does not seem to wander far from the doctrine of the sacred scriptures, where it is said: *The clouds poured out water; the upper clouds gave a sound.* <note>Psalm 77:17.</note> And yet we find elsewhere: *That God binds up the waters in his thick clouds, so that the cloud is not rent under them,* <note>Job 26:8.</note> as if he understood the cloud to be the receptacle of the waters or the matter of rains. Whence also elsewhere: *God by his wisdom prepares a weight for the air, and weighs the waters by measure,* <note>Job 28:25.</note> by which it is right to notice that thick waters are contained even in the clouds, which were previously the misty substance of the air. God retains these waters by his wisdom so that they may dry up, *and he sends them out so that they overturn the earth,* <note>Job 12:15.</note> restraining them, I say, with the North wind, and sending them out with the South wind. Whence it is said: *He who gives snow like wool, scatters the frost like ashes; he casts forth his ice like morsels; who will stand before his cold? He sends out his word and melts them; as soon as he makes his wind blow, the waters flow.* <note>Psalm 147:16–18.</note> By these words it is clearly explained how clouds are broken, and how they become liquid and flowing—namely, by means of the Word or Wisdom of God. Hence it is said: *The upper clouds by his wisdom drip dew,* <note>Proverbs 3:20.</note> and elsewhere, *God by his wisdom weighs the waters...*

Hence, in such a discourse, Jehovah addresses Job: *Who has numbered the sapphire clouds by wisdom? and who can tilt the water-skins of heaven?* <note>Original Latin: "Quis sapphirinas nubes effecit sapientia? & vtres cœli quis prosternit?" Job 38:37. The "water-skins" is a metaphor for clouds.</note> *Have you known the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge regarding the balancing of the thick cloud? We proceed, therefore, to our own definition of rain according to the sense of the Holy Bible.

**Rain** is a cloud-like substance contracted by the power of Divine Wisdom into aqueous and dewy drops or droplets through dissolution; these GOD tilts like the water-skins of heaven, either for the punishment of mortals or for their benefit.

I say "for punishment," whence it is said: *GOD sends forth the waters so that they overturn the earth,* *Job 12:15.* It is also sent upon the earth as a benefit: for it is commanded in the scriptures, *That Jehovah will open to the righteous man his best treasure, the heavens, giving rain to his land in its season, and blessing every work of his hand,* *Deuteronomy 28:12.* Finally, we read in Job: *That the cloud, the rain, the lightning—whatever GOD has commanded them to do on the face of the world upon the earth, whether for a scourge or to perform an act of kindness—they bring it to pass.* *Job 37:12–13.*

Or it is defined thus:

**Rain** is a certain sieving of waters from the clouds, inasmuch as Jehovah, by His Word or Wisdom, melts those clouds into aqueous drops or droplets, and makes them flow downward or drip by His breath or the spirit of His wind to fulfill the Divine Will.

In these descriptions of rain, we have first revealed the location or the "water-skin" from which rain is accustomed to gush forth as if from its own natural source; then its substance is described as being made into an aqueous form from the consistency of a thick cloud. Then afterwards, the primary acting cause is expressed: the Word or Divine Wisdom which (according to the Apostle in *1 Corinthians*) is the power of GOD; and finally, in the last place, the final cause is expressed—that is, to fulfill the Divine Will here on earth, either as a scourge or as a kindness.

Therefore, if the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> attribute the material cause of rain to the vapors of the earth or water, or the efficient cause to the sublimating heat of the heavens, or to condensing cold and the dissolving heat of the stars, and finally the final cause to the health and growth of animals and plants alone, they seem to err in all these things. For the material cause of a cloud is condensed air; the efficient cause is Wisdom, condensing the air with its windy ministers and resolving it at its pleasure; and finally, the end is as much for punishment and ruin as for human utility and benefit.
