But now we have arrived at the proposal at hand: namely, the exposition and explanation of the forms, locations, and qualities depicted in our **Meteorographic Mirror** <note>The "Mirror" (Catoptrum) refers to the author's specific scientific diagram or visual model used to illustrate these phenomena.</note>. Regarding their location, we find that it is either common or specific. We call the "common location" the entire space of air between the ethereal heaven and the earth. We establish three specific regions of this entire common air, the upper of which we see filled with **comets** of various kinds and differing shapes, along with the **chasm** and the **burning beam** <note>original: *chasmate trabeque ardente*; these were historical terms for types of Auroras or light pillars</note>, which we mention only briefly here because they are treated more fully elsewhere.

Just as there are various species of comets, the Philosophers have also given them names suited to their appearance.

The **Flaming Lance** <note>original: *Lancea ignita*</note> is the name given to the first species, as it is stretched out in length.

The **Sword** <note>original: *Xiphias*</note> is a shorter lance, and this species of comet is tapered to a sharp point.

The **Mercurial** <note>original: *Mercurialis*</note> is a comet that is somewhat blue in color, small in size, and has a thin, long tail.

The **Soldier** <note>original: *Miles*</note> is so called because it has a Martial <note>reddish, like the planet Mars</note> color, and this comet is also tailed, as you have it drawn in the Mirror.

The **Morning Star** <note>original: *Aurora*</note> has the appearance of a star, but excels every star in its clarity and splendor.

The **Rose** <note>original: *Rosa*</note> is a comet large in size and round, which seems to bear and carry a human face.

The **Hook** <note>original: *Tenaculum*</note> is a comet which, as if standing upon a fiery base, is tailed in a wonderful manner.

The **Black** <note>original: *Niger*</note> is a comet of dark color, endowed with a short and brief tail; it seems to be adorned with a very small amount of hair-like streaks.

The **Horned** <note>original: *Ceratias*</note> is a comet called such because of the appearance of its heat or the horned shape of its fire.

There are also other fiery meteors which are sometimes visible in this region, which nonetheless we do not call comets at all. While they are ignited like comets, they are not quickly extinguished. Other appearances—such as the **Chasm**, the **Beam**, and **flying sparks**—are less stable, originating from a less firm and more inconstant matter or spirit. However, since we have spoken of these before and explained their forms in our Mirror, we have decided not to make our discourse any longer here.

For the other meteors, both bright and dark, without further explanation here regarding their forms and locations, I believe you should refer primarily to the inspection of our Mirror, and for their order, to the table or classification mentioned above for the sake of brevity.

### *On Meteors that are seen and are not what they seem.*

Now, however, we come to those meteors that display a certain form or image in the air, and yet are not what they seem to be. But because this will appear hard and difficult to consider at first glance for the unlearned and those unskilled in the science of optics, we have expressed the logic of those appearances in the manner of perspective in our **Meteorographic Mirror**. We have done this with proper and consistent demonstrations, so that you may more easily reach a certain knowledge of these visions in the air without great fatigue. In this business of demonstration, I confess that I follow and imitate the doctrine of **Witelo** <note>original: *Vitellionis*; Witelo (c. 1230–1285) was a famous friar and natural philosopher whose work on optics was essential to medieval and Renaissance science.</note> regarding the manner of seeing. By this, we are taught that we see through the action of a visible form upon the eye and the reception <note>original: *passionem*; literally the "suffering" or undergoing of an effect</note> of the sight by such a form.

The meteors of this kind, the reason for which we gather from the science of optics alone (since they are not what they appear to be), are the **Mock Suns** <note>original: *Parelii*</note>. These occur when the sun is rising or setting at an angle, in the lower part of a cloud, and specifically in the lowest part of the region of air. They are the shapes or images of the Sun or Moon represented in a dewy cloud, no differently than an image is seen in water or a mirror. We show the logic of this vision through **pyramidal lines** <note>In historical optics, visual rays were often modeled as pyramids or cones with the apex at the eye.</note> from the place of sight to the objects of the Sun and Moon in the lower part of the cloud, just as is demonstrated in our Mirror.

### Of the Meteorographic Mirror

Similarly, the **celestial arch** <note>original: *arcus coelestis*; the rainbow</note> is most often seen at sunrise or sunset, but rarely at midday, except sometimes in the winter season. This occurs by divine power as it is drawn by the moisture of the air to our sight. For our vision is not reflected by lighter things, but objects lighter than colors, which move the sight, stir it. But now, contrary to the common opinion of the **philosophers** <note>The author refers here to "natural philosophers," the historical term for scientists who studied the physical world.</note>, we believe it must first be understood that the rainbow does not form in a cloud, but in the lower part of the lowest region of the air, as we have declared in preceding sections. This is because it is observed to be not far from the eye—specifically, not beyond **three hundred paces** <note>The author is arguing that rainbows are a local optical phenomenon rather than something occurring high in the clouds.</note>. We have proof of this because we can see the rainbow shining in its four colors positioned between our eye and a nearby mountain or forest. Indeed, we have sometimes even seen it descending upon the grass during a dewy rain. 

If you wish to know the clear reason for this, you must carefully attend to what is now to be said—casting aside the vain opinions of many philosophers which are shrouded in clouds and darkness—and understand it correctly. In a thick, bright medium (such as water), a small, round image of the sun is reflected; in a thinner medium, a large round image is seen. When the medium is thinned even further, the image becomes larger, though everything around the center of the image appears bare because the scattered rays are not brought to a single point. Just so, they are scattered there in the lighter air, just as we are accustomed to using **glass lenses** <note>original: *vitris*; "burning glasses" used to focus sunlight to start fires</note> to gather rays to burn objects; and indeed, this has great momentum toward that sudden compression of the air. When the air is further thinned and changed into a humid, misty, and vaporous state, the greatest roundness is seen—not of a distinct image, but of represented light. Thus, by certain steps, we can move from the first and smallest reflection to the largest. It is colored by the light being scattered further into the moisture; only a **semicircle** is seen because the earth stands in the way, but if the viewer is placed in a higher location, it appears as a complete circle. This is proven by experience and demonstrated through the principles of sight and objects explained in the science of **optics** <note>original: *catoptro*; the study of reflected light and mirrors</note>.

The **Corona** <note>A halo or circle of light around the sun or moon.</note> is formed in the same way, except that it is created between the viewer and the sun.

The **magnification of the sun** at sunset occurs due to the refraction of light in the thicker air.

The **discoloration of the moon** without magnification usually happens because of its light passing through vaporous, but not thick, air.

**Perpendicular lines** <note>Likely referring to crepuscular rays or "sunbeams" breaking through clouds.</note> are created by solar light passing through openings due to the unevenness of the clouds.

**Evening redness** arises from the penetration of light through the lower parts of the clouds.

**Temples, buildings, and men walking in the air** <note>A description of complex mirages, such as the *Fata Morgana*.</note> sometimes appear to our eyes, just as the images of bodies are usually seen in a mirror. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author of a famous encyclopedia of natural history.</note> writes that there are some who have such weak vision that they can see themselves in the air as if in a mirror, and this happens especially when the **South wind** <note>original: *Austro*; the *Auster*, a hot, humid wind associated in antiquity with distorted vision and strange weather.</note> is blowing.

Finally, we conclude that although we have provided the reasons for these meteors based on their effects in this place, we nevertheless say that the air itself is the **treasury of GOD**, and we establish God and His Word—or Divine Wisdom—as the unique, simple, and sole actor and author in all these things, working in and through His **Angelic instruments**, as discussed more broadly before and below.

### CHAPTER I.

->*On the efficient cause in general.*<-

It is a wonder that the **Peripatetics** <note>original: *Peripateticos*; followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> themselves established the definition of an **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being.</note> as that from which the principle of motion and rest originates, and yet they chose to remain ignorant of—or at least refused to acknowledge—the "act of acts" or the first mover of all things. Instead, they preferred to understand the "primary qualities" (which they call active) as the cause. Thus, they wrongly mistook the effects proceeding from the Mover—namely the divine Word, creating and illuminating all things—for the efficient cause itself. Some, searching more deeply into the nature of this first mover, concluded that it was the very act of Fate or a kind of internal nature. 

We, however, being instructed by the doctrine of the Sacred Scriptures, say that the sole Actor of all things and the sole Mover in all things is GOD—specifically, the divine Word or the Holy Spirit. *By the word of the Lord,* says David, *were the heavens established, and all the power of them by the spirit of his mouth* <note>original: *Verbo Domini firmati sunt caeli...*; Psalm 33:6</note>. Hence, not only are the world and the parts of the world perfected by Him as the sole Actor, but every act, power, and work within it—whether of the earth, the heavens, or the elements—is perfected through the mediation of His Spirit. 

For this reason, it is said elsewhere: *Come and see the works of GOD; say to God, how awesome You are in Your deeds* <note>original: *Venite videte opera DEI...*; Psalm 66:5</note>. And elsewhere: *Whatever the LORD pleases, He does in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deep places* <note>original: *DEVS quicquid vult facit...*; Psalm 135:6-7</note>. And elsewhere: *Your works are wonderful and vast; in wisdom You have made them all* <note>original: *Opera tua sunt mirabilia...*; Psalm 104:24</note>. 

But perhaps some will respond that these words are to be understood and accepted as referring to things produced during the Creation, and not to the natural production and progression of things; they might argue that the various meteors, which arise according to the state and disposition of the seasons, do not come from God, but from things created by God—acting through heat or cold as the primary qualities in nature. But, good God, how absurd it is to think that heat can be generated except where there is a fiery nature, whose property it is to act... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "indefinen-," likely meaning "indefinitely" or "without end."</note>

<summary>This page argues that God, rather than mere physical qualities like heat or cold, is the primary "efficient cause" behind all atmospheric phenomena (meteors). The author critiques Aristotelian philosophers for ignoring divine agency in favor of natural mechanics.</summary>
<keywords>efficient cause, Peripatetics, Aristotle, divine providence, Holy Spirit, meteors, atmospheric physics, theology of nature</keywords>

--- Page 161 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the argument that natural phenomena are not merely the result of physical elements, but are driven by a divine "efficient cause." The previous page ended by critiquing the Aristotelian view that ignores the primary mover.</meta>

...to move without ceasing, and how can fire or light act if the incorruptible spirit, acting internally and centrally as a form, does not incite it? Hence we find these words written: *God made the fire grow mild so that it would not burn, yet now God makes the fire blaze; for the creature serving you, who made all things, is exerted for punishment against the unjust, and is relaxed for the benefit of those who trust in you. Wisdom 16:24.* <note>The author is quoting the Book of Wisdom, suggesting that nature's forces are flexible tools of divine justice or mercy.</note> Hence also, it is said elsewhere—from which it is clear that fire itself is ruled and moved by an internal agent—hear this, Job: *Stand still and consider the wondrous works of the mighty God. Do you know when God disposes them, so that the light of His cloud might shine? Do you know the balancings of the thick clouds, the wondrous works of God, perfect in knowledge? Job 37:14-16.* And elsewhere: *Will you send forth lightnings and they will go, and returning say to you, "Here we are"? Job 38:35.* And elsewhere: *Bringing up the clouds from the ends of the earth, He made lightnings for the rain; He who brings forth the winds from His treasures.* <note>Psalm 135:7</note> There are infinite other passages which, in clear words, confirm that God Himself, or Divine Wisdom, is the "efficient cause" <note>the active agent that brings an effect into being</note> of hot meteors.

Furthermore, the same must be said regarding cold effects; for the sacred text says: *By His breath the mighty God produces ice and narrows the breadth of the waters. Job 37:10.* And elsewhere: *Sending His word to the earth, His command runs very swiftly; He who gives snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes; He casts down His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? Psalm 147:15-17.* And elsewhere: *Who gave birth to the frost of heaven? Job 38:29.* Shall we respond along with the **Peripatetics** <note>original: *Peripateticis*; the followers of Aristotle</note> that the cause is simply cold, or the north wind, or a hot and dry exhalation? Certainly, if we consider the matter to its very core, we will perceive that all these things must be attributed to God alone, and least of all to His creatures. For in this way we might assert that a sword is the efficient cause of a wound, when it should be ascribed to the hand of the man striking with it; and yet, in truth, neither the sword nor the hand is the ultimate cause, but rather the spirit acting within the man. This spirit acts as a vehicle for that first Actor of all things, who dwells everywhere and acts according to His will, directed either as a scourge for man or for his benefit, moving like the lightnings (which are God's ministers for executing the divine will). Hence the Wise Man says: *God brings every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it be good or evil. Ecclesiastes 12:14.* Yet that which seems so to man must not be considered as iniquity or evil. For as Job says: *Far be it from the mighty God to do wickedness, and from the Almighty to commit iniquity. Job 34:10.* For He renders to a man according to his work, and causes him to find according to his own way. And elsewhere: *God does whatever He wills, and who shall ask Him, "What are You doing?" or "Why do You do so?" Wisdom 12:12.* But concerning the act and operation of the Almighty **Jehovah** <note>original: *Iehouæ*</note>—not only in the wondrous production of meteorological things, but also of perfectly "mixed" <note>meaning complex physical substances like minerals or plants</note> things—and concerning His primary ministers and instruments through which He operates both in the heavens and on earth, we propose to discourse more at length throughout this entire section. In the two final parts of this section, however, we shall speak in a "worldly manner," treating the effects of both God-like and angelic divinity as if they were the efficient causes: namely the sun, moon, and stars, with their hot or cold influences upon the celestial region, and the primary qualities of the elements (fire, air, water, and earth), along with the various types of vapors and fluids among those elements.

### CHAPTER II.

->What God is in and of Himself, without consideration of<-
->created things: in the resolution of this question, the<-
->testimonies of both the Philosophers and the<-
->Cabalists, and finally the Holy Scriptures,<-
->are explained.<-

**Simonides** <note>A famous Greek lyric poet (c. 556–468 BC) known for his wisdom</note>—an excellent philosopher rightly celebrated by **Aristotle** and **Cicero** for the depth of his knowledge—was once asked by the tyrant **Hiero** what exactly God might be. To resolve this doubt, he is said to have requested a period of one day. When the Tyrant returned the following day, he asked again for a certain answer; but then the philosopher requested two days to resolve the question. When that time was up and the Tyrant returned, he doubled the time again, asking for four days, and thus he doubled the duration every time. Finally, when the King asked him the reason for this constant doubling of time, he is said to have received this response: *The more I think about this most sublime matter, the more obscure it appears to my intellect, as it is something that dwells in a certain light which human spirits are unable to reach or attain.* And in this, he seems to agree with the Holy Scriptures, by which we are taught that God inhabits "inaccessible light." Yet that Heavenly Teacher, through the Gospel of St. Matthew, teaches us the way by which we may arrive at a knowledge of both God the Father and the Son, asserting that no one can know the Son except the Father; and again, that no one can attain the knowledge of God the Father except the Son, or he to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him. Therefore, it is certain that to judge such a surpassing essence is a very arduous, even impossible task, unless we are instructed by the Word of God and the Holy Scriptures. And although God is revealed "from behind" <note>original: *à posteriori*; a philosophical term meaning reasoning from observed effects back to their causes</note>—that is, from His creatures and His glory in His bright...

# Section I. Port. IV. Part. II. Lib. IV. Membr. I.

While it may be permitted for us to discern God through His "garments" <note>The "garments" of God refer to the physical world and visible creation which clothe the invisible divine essence.</note>, yet to scrutinize His magnitude is beyond the capacity of human intellect; for His greatness *cannot be grasped* (as the Prophet witnesses) *in Psalm 145:3.* Much less is His pure essence granted to be seen by human eyes or the eyes of the flesh, according to the words of the Prophet and the Evangelist: *No one has ever seen God. Jeremiah 1. John 4.* <note>The author combines references to emphasize that God’s essence remains invisible and incomprehensible to mortals.</note>

Therefore, in our description of God, we shall follow partly the doctrine of the most excellent philosophers and partly that of the Cabalists <note>The Cabala is a tradition of Jewish mysticism that Renaissance scholars like Fludd integrated into Christian philosophy.</note> where they agree with the Holy Bible, and finally, we shall declare in a few words what is to be gathered from the Word of God for a living description of Him.

We gather, then, from the testimonies of divine writers, that God has a twofold nature in relation to us: namely, a hidden nature and a manifest nature. The hidden nature is that in which, before the creation of the world, He seemed to human understanding to rest in infinite darkness and to do almost nothing, but rather to reflect His heat and power back into Himself, and not at all to apply the rays of His light toward the creation of the world. This same thing must also be said of His rays or essence resting and concealed within the opaque and dark things of the world; He is described in such a form by <term>Mercurius Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica," texts on philosophy, magic, and theology.</note> in these words: *The Monad (he says) begat the Monad before the creation of the world, and reflected its heat into itself; that is, it shone only for itself.* By these words, he seems to suggest that the divine nature—the source of light, the act of all active things, the origin of life, the ocean of form—reflected the rays of its fiery and purely formal nature back into itself. From this it followed that before there was any will in Him to create the world, an infinite abyss was overwhelmed with shapeless darkness and was empty. This same point the said Philosopher seems to bring up in another place: *There was (he says) an infinite shadow in the abyss.* In this speech, he seems to agree with Moses, who said that *darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* And this was that matter "in potentiality" of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who described "prime matter" as something that exists only as a potential to become something else.</note>, which they called the "first matter," and for this reason, such a hidden nature is called "divine power" by some, as will be explained below. Just as the Philosophers considered that divine nature—hidden in darkness and gloom and not yet expanding itself—mathematically, they called it "Arithmetical Unity," and sometimes the "Geometric Point." I say "Unity" as it is simple in itself, without any regard to number, and a "Point" with no relation to a circumference; but insofar as they are considered in either art, they are in their simple, indivisible nature, having no quantity, quality, or substance, and yet they are the principle of all these things. For once this unity is expanded, it becomes everything that exists, or everything that can be understood within the ten categories, as will be more fully declared in the description of the manifest God; in which this most simple Unity will be shown to be fortified by its peripheral numbers, just as a point is by its circumference.

In the art of the Cabalists, the more skilled have called this hidden divine power the **Dark Aleph**, just as they called that which is manifested and shining out of the darkness the **Bright Aleph**. <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often used to symbolize the unity of God.</note> But truly, by the **Dark Aleph** they understand a numbering according to the Cabalists, namely *Hochma* <note>original: "Hochma" or Chokhmah; the Sephirah of Wisdom.</note> or Wisdom, or that Monad which the Monad begat before any creation, the heat of which it reflected back into itself. The wise have called this divine wisdom, emanating from the Father and returning to the Father’s bosom before the act of creation, the "Beginning," about which it is written in the *Book of Bahir*: *There is no "Beginning" except Wisdom. Reuchlin, Book 3, On the Cabalistic Art.* <note>Johannes Reuchlin was a 15th-century humanist who introduced Cabala to Christian scholars.</note> For, he says, that infinity of the three highest numberings of the Cabalistic tree—which we Christians call the three Persons in the divine—is the most absolute essence. Since it is withdrawn and remaining in the abyss of darkness, as if idle, or as they say, looking toward nothing, it is therefore called **Ein**, that is, "Nothing," or "Non-being," and "Infinite" <note>original: "Ein" (nothing/naught) and "non finis" (without end/infinite).</note>, because we are punished with such a meager poverty of intellect regarding divine things that we judge those things which do not appear no differently than those things which do not exist. But when it shows itself so that it is "Something" and truly subsists, then the **Dark Aleph** is converted into the **Bright Aleph**. And then, just as the **Dark Aleph** was called the **Small Aleph**, so the **Bright Aleph** was called the **Great Aleph**. So they say. By the **Bright Aleph**, they understood the Word or the divine emanation through which all things were made, concerning which we shall speak more fully in the following chapter, where we will treat the manifest God—that is, the bright and manifest **Aleph**. From this it is clear that the same relationship exists between the **Small Aleph** and the **Great Aleph** as exists between **Alpha** and **Omega**, which was called by the Cabalists the **Small** or **Dark Aleph** and the **Great** or **Bright Aleph**. *I am the first and the last,* as is read elsewhere, but back to the matter.

The **Small** or **Dark Aleph**, being like "Nothing" because it is hidden by darkness, is like unity without number and a point without regard to a circumference. For that "Small" one denotes all things in potentiality, because by revealing itself it also suddenly reveals, creates, and brings into act everything that exists—all of which is contained in this emitted divine light.

Hence it is that in our Cabalistic discourse, in which we made mention of the three fathers—most aptly agreeing with the three Mothers of the Cabalists—we placed the **Mother Aleph** as being in the highest agreement with the **Father Iod**. <note>Iod or Yod is the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often symbolizing the initial spark of creation.</note> For just as **Aleph** represents the mundane darkness, namely chaos itself, so **Iod** is the immediate act of Jehovah, sent out from the whirlpool of the dark Abyss, from which the mundane **Aleph** or the "First Mother" receives its splendor. For as the **Small Aleph** among the Cabalists denotes "Unity" in Arithmetic, so **Iod** signifies the number ten, which is represented by a "one" and a "zero." This shining divine unity creates unity in potentiality—namely, the **Dark Aleph**, which is like "Nothing"—and through the "Zero" <note>original: "Cyphram"</note>, something in "Act" is denoted, by illuminating the shapeless waters

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...and driving back the shadows. The second mother of the Cabalists <note>In the *Sefer Yetzirah*, the "three mothers" are the letters Aleph, Mem, and Shin, representing air, water, and fire.</note> was *Mem*, which we have shown corresponds with the second letter of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, namely *He*. For just as *Mem* is the hieroglyphic for pure waters, so also *He* denotes a clear spirit or aspiration. Finally, we have designated *Vav* <note>original: "Vau"</note> in the four-letter name as the father, and as it were the masculine act, or the uncreated sun of the Cabalistic mother *Shin* herself: for just as *Vav* denotes the degree of emanation in the solar palace—inasmuch as he "placed his Tabernacle in the sun"—so also is *Shin* the hieroglyphic for fire. Lastly, the final *He* of the Tetragrammaton name corresponds to the "closed Mem" <note>original: "Mem clausum"; in Hebrew, the letter Mem has a different shape when it appears at the end of a word.</note>: for just as *He* seems to denote the coarser spirits of the world, so also the closed *Mem* proves the existence of thick and visible waters. But more on these matters below.

Finally, we are taught by the sacred scriptures that God was both hidden in respect to us, when He existed concealed in His own existence before the world was created, and in that respect the proper name of God was *I am*, as is found in Genesis chapter 17. <note>Genesis 17:1 actually states "I am God Almighty," but the author likely refers to the divine self-identification "I am who I am" from Exodus, here linked to the primal state of the Creator.</note>

For it was sufficient for Him that He alone existed, when nothing besides Himself was in the infinite mystery. And hence it is certain that He spoke these things through the mouth of the prophet:
> I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time before it happened, I was there, and now my Lord and His spirit have sent me. <note>original: "Ego non à principio in abscondito loquutus sum..." — Isaiah 48:16.</note>
Which indeed seems to be understood concerning Wisdom or emanation, which the wise man says was created before all things, of which it is said elsewhere: "The power of God, created before all things, is the end and beginning of all," <note>original: "DEI potentia ante omnia creata finis & initium omnium est"</note> Ecclesiasticus 1. By these words, he seems to hint at the very same thing that the Cabalists intended: namely, that this power was the *dark Aleph* <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here representing the first stirring of divine power.</note>, as it had been before all things were created, and that it was the *bright Aleph*, the primary emanation from the source of light, insofar as the name of "end and beginning of all" is attributed to it. Hence Wisdom says in her own person:
> *The Lord possessed me, Wisdom, in the beginning of His way, before His works, before any time, before the world I was anointed; when there were no depths, I was brought forth,* etc. Proverbs 8:22.

We conclude, therefore, that God before the creation of the world shone back only upon Himself, and that He sketched the world in His own Ideal and archetypal <term>Archetype: the original pattern or model in the divine mind from which all things are copied.</term> sanctuary according to the model of Himself, before He willed to forge it into a physical form, as will be more clearly explained in the following sections.

## CHAPTER III.

### *Concerning the Manifest God and His office and power in the creation of things, according to both the Philosophers and Cabalists, as well as the Fathers of Theology, whose opinions are all clearly confirmed by the testimony of the sacred scriptures.*

**T**his wisdom, therefore, which was with God before any thing was created; this most holy Word, which was contracted in the dark beginning before the creation of the world, shining only to itself, was God Himself—or the power, and Virtue, and emanation of God—which is no less to be divided from the God-like essence than the rays of the sun from the sun, as *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary sage traditionally identified as a contemporary of Moses and the author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> witnesses in *Poimandres 12*, whom he himself is accustomed to call *Poimandres* and the *Mind* or God. This is (I say) the God-like spirit, this immediate emanation from the Father, which the said master of divine philosophy calls in one place:
> *an exceedingly sweet light, by which all things are revealed and formed; the Mind (he says) of divine power changed its form, and suddenly revealed the universe, and I saw all things converted into an exceedingly sweet and pleasant light.*
By these words, he seems to prove that the hidden God or the *dark Aleph* (which signifies the divine power) revealed Himself for the revelation of the world and the driving back of the shadows. And elsewhere, he calls this spirit "holy splendor," emanating from the darkness. His words are these:
> *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss, but water and spirit were within the chaos; yet a holy splendor flourished, which led out the elements beneath the sand and the moist nature, and the heavy things submerged in the shadows settled beneath the moist sand.*
By which words the Philosopher seems to declare not only the emanation of that spirit of wisdom from the darkness, but also its harmonic power, by means of which the quarreling members of chaos itself are bound together in concordant peace and arranged among themselves. This, then, is that spirit of fire of which *Plutarch* <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer.</note> speaks thus:
> *God is an intellectual spirit of fire, having no form in Himself, but transforming everything into Himself as He wills, and likening Himself to all things and all things to Himself,*
which indeed He does not effect by means of elemental fire, but through Himself alone or through a seraphic heat which is closest to the divine fire. By these things, the Philosopher wishes to make known that every act in the nature of things must be attributed to the intellectual creative spirit of the highest condition, and not at all to creatures; and above all, he seems to confirm that the existence of the world and of every thing in the world proceeds from a fiery act of this kind of divine spirit, which act he recognizes as being God in His purest state. From this, therefore, *Hermes Trismegistus* seems to conclude that there is nothing in the nature of things that does not represent the image of divinity; and the *Platonists* call this spirit, thus infused into all things, the *Soul of the World* <note>original: "Anima mundi"</note>. Whence also this heat or divine light is defined by another as being the unity containing all things within itself, though they be diverse. And *Zeno the Philosopher* <note>The founder of Stoicism.</note> recognizes it as the ruler...

You have, finally, that spirit whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere, inasmuch as it is outside all things. You have the **Ein Sof** <note>original: "Ensoph"; the Kabbalistic term for God's infinite, unknowable essence before emanation.</note> or the infinity of the Kabbalists, which others have called a sea and an infinite Ocean; you have the soul of the world, which is the life and existence of every single thing; you have the "all in all," and thus, according to the Poet’s sentiment:

But let us now see how these sayings of the Philosophers and Kabbalists agree with the testimony of the sacred font. **Ezra** says, *The power of GOD, created before all things, is the end and beginning of all,* (2 Esdras 6). <note>The author cites the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras.</note> By this power, that priest of wisdom understands that **Monad** <note>A term for the "One" or the ultimate indivisible source of all reality.</note> which, according to the opinion of Hermes Trismegistus, was begotten before all things by the Monad, just as a son by a father; it returned into itself by a reflection of the father’s will and did not yet flow out until the Father of all things had determined the creation of the world—namely, of the heavens and the earth. And then He said **LET IT BE** <note>original: "FIAT"; the divine command from Genesis.</note>, and by this emanation, or by His Word—once hidden and now made manifest and revealed—that which the fatherly arranger willed was immediately done. This power, therefore, was wisdom, strength, and divine prudence, created before all things (as has been said), of which **Jeremiah** speaks thus: *It is GOD who makes the earth in His strength, prepares the world in His wisdom, and by His prudence stretches out the heavens,* (Jeremiah 10). Wherefore, in this discourse are included the three primary and principal trees among the Kabbalists, the **Sephirotic** <term>Sephirot: the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals Himself.</term> numerations, of which the first is called **Keter** <note>original: "Cheter"</note> or the Crown, over which the name of GOD **Ehyeh** <note>Hebrew for "I AM."</note> or the Father presides; the second is **Chokhmah** <note>original: "Hochma"</note> or Wisdom, over which the ineffable name **Yah** and **Jehovah** presides; and the third is **Binah** or Prudence, to which is attributed the name **Elohim**. Of these numerations, the first is given to the Father, the second to the Son or Wisdom, and the third to the Holy Spirit derived from them both. Hence also we find in the Royal Psalmist, *That by the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host or power,* (Psalm 33:6). Here, by "the Lord," he denotes the Father and Arranger; by "the Word," Wisdom and the Son; and by the "Spirit," the Holy Spirit, who is the effector and act of every host, both spiritual and bodily. And yet, although three properties of the divine persons are assigned here, we nevertheless have only one and the same Deity and essence to which all things are attributed, which He Himself even seems to assert in His own discourse, in which there is no falsehood: *I am the Lord your redeemer and your former in the womb; I am the Lord making all things, stretching out the heavens alone, establishing the earth and no one is with me,* (Isaiah 44:24). And yet the wise man testifies, *That wisdom was present with him when he established the heavens above and strengthened the fountains of the deep, like a master workman arranging all things,* (Proverbs 8). From these things it is clearly evident that Wisdom is also GOD, yet distinguished from the Father only by property and not by essence. Hence we also find written: *Thus says GOD, creating the heavens, stretching them out, establishing the earth and those things that sprout from it, and giving breath to the people who are upon it, and spirit to those walking upon it,* (Isaiah 42:5). It is as if he had said: one GOD, but three persons—namely, the Lord the Father arranges, the Word the Son establishes the heavens, and the Holy Spirit from both infuses life, spirit, and power into every created thing, according to the sense of the context of the aforementioned Royal Prophet. Whence also elsewhere: *Thus says the Lord creating the heavens, GOD himself forming the earth and making it, its very Molder; He did not create it in vain, but formed it so that it might be inhabited,* (Isaiah 45). It is clear, therefore, that where one property of GOD is present, there also is the other. ### CHAPTER IV.

#### *What this divine spirit creating all things is, and how it is sometimes called the Word, and sometimes Wisdom.*

We have demonstrated in the preceding sections, from the opinions of both Holy Scripture and the philosophers, that this spirit of immense power is God Himself, being no more divisible from the divine essence or the luminous source than the rays of the sun are from the solar body. We shall now explain in the following pages how, by its emanation from the darkness, the overwhelmed darkness or abyss is illuminated, the waters (both thin and thick <gloss>original: "glossae"</gloss>) are animated, and all things are produced from nothing into act and being. Indeed, we have already stated clearly enough that it is written: *The Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters,* <note>original: "Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas"; Genesis 1:2</note> imparting vigor to them. These waters, before this liquid spirit went forth from the luminous source or the bosom of the Father, were called the "abyss," upon the face of which there was darkness, as it is held in the sacred text. Finally, we are taught by many passages of the sacred context that this spirit is the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end of all, as it is the one from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist: *I am the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord.* <note>Revelation 1:8</note> And elsewhere: *I am the first, and I am the last; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens; I will call them and they shall stand together.* <note>Isaiah 48:12-13</note> And it is established that in God *we live, move, and have our being,* <note>Acts 17:28</note> which is also to be understood regarding every created thing, since *the incorruptible spirit of God is said to be in every thing.* <note>Wisdom 12:1</note> For this reason, and by virtue of this spirit, it was said by the Apostle *that God works all in all.* <note>1 Corinthians 12:6</note> Hence, the same Apostle concludes elsewhere that God is *the father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in us all.* <note>Ephesians 4:6</note> And elsewhere he says, *That God gives life to all things.* <note>1 Timothy 6:13</note> This also seems to be verified by the Evangelist, affirming that *by the Word all things were made, and without him nothing was made that was made, and that in him was life.* <note>John 1:3-4</note> And elsewhere we are taught by the Apostle that *from Christ and through Christ are all things.* <note>Romans 11:36</note> And in another place he says: *Christ fills all things.* <note>Ephesians 4:10</note> And elsewhere: *from him, in him, and through him are all things, to whom be praise and honor;* <note>Romans 11:36</note> in that same <note>large gap in original text</note> epistle he acknowledges that *God created all things through Jesus Christ.* <note>Ephesians 3:9</note> 

And this name "Jesus" is said by the Kabbalists <term>Kabbalists: practitioners of Jewish mysticism who sought to understand the divine through the study of Hebrew letters and numbers.</term> to comprehend all the names of God in its power—indeed, even that most essential name of God, the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often rendered as Jehovah or Yahweh.</term> or "Jehovah." For at that name, namely Jesus, every knee shall bow, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. <note>Philippians 2:10</note> Hence it follows that everything ascribed in the Old Testament to the ineffable name of Jehovah is transferred in the New Testament to the name of Jesus. Thus says Job (understanding this regarding the creating spirit and speaking of its efficacy): *Jehovah stretches out the North over the empty space, and hangs the earth upon nothing. He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, so that the clouds are not torn under them; he covers the face of his throne, and spreads his cloud upon it. He has compassed the waters with bounds, until light and darkness come to an end. By his power he divides the sea, and by his understanding he strikes through the depths; by his spirit he has garnished the heavens, etc.* <note>Job 26:7-13</note> From this it is clear that the work of creation, which is ascribed to God, is assigned to Jesus Christ in the New Testament just as it is to Jehovah. 

Moreover, that this name is the "Word of God," and that this Word is God Himself, is declared by the speech brought forth by the Evangelist: *In the beginning,* he says, *was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him: and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not, etc. That was the true light... he was in the world, and the world was made by him, etc.* <note>John 1:1-10</note> By these words he argues: first, the most exalted lineage of this divine spirit, namely that it is of Divine and God-like origin; second, that the place from which it went forth is darkness, which nonetheless did not "comprehend" it. Thus it is said: *Even the darkness cannot be so darkened that you cannot see through it, but the night shines as the day to you, and darkness is to God as light itself.* <note>Psalm 139:12</note> Furthermore, its essence and pure formality are indicated by the fact that it is the light of the world and a light shining in darkness—indeed, the light not only of the world but of man himself. Finally, its office is explained by the fact that all things were made by it, and the reason is that in it is the life of every single thing. Hence it is written elsewhere, *in God himself we live and move and are,* <note>Acts 17:28</note> and elsewhere, *God gives life to all things,* <note>1 Timothy 6:13</note> and elsewhere: *I am God your redeemer, making all things, stretching forth the heavens alone, establishing the earth by myself.* <note>Isaiah 44:24</note> Hence also the Royal Prophet <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms.</note>: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were formed, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.* <note>Psalm 33:6</note> Finally, all this that we have said is most brilliantly confirmed by St. Peter: *The heavens were of old, and the earth consisting out of water and in water, by the word of God.* <note>2 Peter 3:5</note> By which...

If wisdom is the Word, and the Word is GOD, and GOD is not a creature but the eternal creator, it will seem admirable to us that in many places of the scriptures it is found that *wisdom was created first of all things.* <note>Ecclesiasticus 1:4</note> And again it is said that *I, wisdom, was created from the beginning before the ages, and I shall not cease even unto the future age, and in the holy habitation I have ministered before him.* But truly, if we consider the matter a little more accurately, we shall perceive that this is not to be understood regarding that pure wisdom which emanated from the luminous source—immune from all material constitution—which is indeed Wisdom, the Word, and even Jehovah God himself creating all things; but rather regarding the moist worldly spirit, inspired and animated by the presence of that luminous emanation or the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>original: "tetrogrammati" — the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, and brought into act from potentiality. ### Concerning the Efficient Cause of Atmospheric Phenomena.

Then the waters appeared entirely in actuality, which before were void in shapeless darkness and existed only as something in potentiality; wherefore (says Augustine) that spirit was divine love, imparting a fiery vigor to the waters. From these waters, thus revealed and created by that luminous spirit, the heaven and earth were afterward created—as St. Peter witnesses in 2 Peter 3—by the operation of the same Word. And to this matter, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Corpus Hermeticum*, viewed by Renaissance thinkers as a contemporary of Moses.</note> seems to agree in the most expressive words: *Thus having spoken, Poimandres transformed his shape, and instantly I conceived all things in a moment of time; then I beheld an infinite spectacle, for all things had become a sweet and cheerful light, which I loved as I watched.* And a little after: *A shadow or darkness was carried downward in an oblique revolution, so that I imagined I saw the darkness changed into a certain moist nature, agitated beyond what can be described, exhaling smoke as if from fire and emitting an unutterable sound. Following this, an inarticulate voice was emitted from it, such that one would suspect it to be the voice of light; from the light, the holy Word stood by the moist nature and nourished it.* These are his words; with which vivid colors he seems to depict the manner of the primordial light, the emanation from the dark abyss, and the light sent forth by God, acting as an informing and creating "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the active principle that gives shape and identity to "matter."</note> mixed with matter, which he says the holy Word nourishes and stands by. Then, in that same passage, he relates the creation, order, and disposition of the elements: *Pure fire, he says, leaped out from the moist nature into the heights above, for it was light and sharp, as well as effective. But the agile Air followed the spirit as it ascended toward the fire, leaving the Earth and Water behind, so that it was believed to hang from the fire. Indeed, the Earth and Water remained mixed within themselves.* These, however, were moved by the spiritual Word that was carried over them, etc. We see, therefore, that this high priest of wisdom does not differ from the aforementioned opinion of St. Peter, from which it is clear that this emanation from the mouth of the Most High—or the "Luminous Aleph" <note>The letter Aleph (א) is the first of the Hebrew alphabet; in Cabalistic mysticism, it represents the primordial unity of God.</note> of the Cabalists proceeding from the "Dark and Hidden Aleph"—animates and informs the universal spirit of the world, or the moist nature (which is called water), as a universal soul. It exists in the manner of a soul in a body, within the whole mundane spirit and in every part of it; whence it was written by the Poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid* (6.726–727).</note>, that *a mind agitates the mass.* And elsewhere, *The spirit nourishes from within*, and of this spirit it is written that it fills all things and is present everywhere and in every place. And the Royal Prophet says that *God is everywhere, namely in the earth, in hell, in heaven, in the farthest reaches of the sea, in the night and in the darkness (Psalm 139:7).* And from this it is also said, that *GOD does whatever he wills in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all the abysses (Psalm 135:7).* Wisdom says: *I alone have compassed the circuit of the heavens, and have walked in the bottom of the abyss (Ecclesiasticus 24:5).* From which we conclude that this divine emanation (which is no more to be divided from the divine essence than solar rays from the Sun, as Hermes Trismegistus says) is the life of the mundane spirit, and that this mundane spirit was brought into actuality by that emanation.

Hence it is that this emanation—uncreated in itself, yet considered with respect to the spirit in which it dwells as a vehicle (which in itself is nothing, except in respect to the presence or assistance of this kind of uncreated light)—is sometimes called "created" and a "creature." But truly, in respect to itself, having no relation to any created matter, it can be called *Jehovah*, the incorruptible spirit, the spirit of wisdom, and the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>. But we shall demonstrate this more clearly from the sacred scriptures. First, it is said that on the first day Light was created; and yet it is certain that this light is not to be understood as a simple divine emanation, nor indeed as any other thing apart from said divine emanation, since without it no creation can occur. Therefore, it is certain that by this light is meant the spirit of the world, created by the presence of divine light—or rather animated by the rays of the spirit that was carried over the waters and adorned with beautiful splendor. Thus, the spirit so illuminated is called a creature, or created light—that is, the external name for the whole—whereas if we look at its internal nature, it is indeed the Creator, the informer, the first act, and the first mover in the world: GOD, the Word, Jehovah, Jesus, the Messiah, who is the power of the Tetragrammaton.

Here indeed, in passing, we think it will not be useless to unravel the foolish and vain opinions of Aristotle and Damascenus <note>St. John of Damascus, a prominent Church Father.</note>, who will have it that light is an <term>accident</term> <note>In formal logic, an "accident" is a property that can change without destroying the thing itself (like the color of a coat), as opposed to a "substance," which is the essential core.</note> and not something substantial; the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> of this age vehemently adhere to these opinions. But if they wish to be consistent with themselves, it is certain and beyond all doubt—even according to their own doctrine—that the essence of an accident is "to be in" something else. Therefore, if light created on the first day were an accident, it would be necessary that some body or substantial subject preceded or pre-existed it; which is certainly against the sense of the sacred scriptures, which make light the work of the first day. But to the point:

For it is from this that this uncreated spirit, mixed with the mundane spirit in the manner of a soul with a body, is called by the Platonists the *Anima Mundi* (World Soul); hence the world itself is called a creature, although its internal agent is the uncreated spirit itself, from which the whole world is sometimes named. Whence the poet says:

->Jupiter is whatever you see, whatever moves.<-

Which speech indeed seems to agree with the holy scriptures: *Christ GOD fills all things*, says the Apostle (Ephesians 4:10). But he is hidden from our eyes by a lethal shadow, so that we discern him only from afar and from behind in his creatures; but once those Cimmerian mists <note>A metaphor for thick, proverbial darkness, referring to the mythical Cimmerians who lived in perpetual night.</note> are removed, all things will be God. For those things which are not of God are in truth nothing, and shall vanish into smoke; whence the Apostle says elsewhere: *Christ shall be all in all, when he shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father,* and elsewhere: *When I am exalted, I will draw all things to myself (1 Corinthians 15; John 12:32).*

We say therefore, that with respect to the exterior or the creature in which wisdom dwells, she is said to be as if created, that is, insofar as she inhabits a created thing; thus Christ the man is called a creature—a man, clearly, although...

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...with respect to the eternal spirit who inhabited him, he was called **GOD**, the Word, and Wisdom. Similarly, in the composition of an Angel, we observe two things: namely, the external, which is a most subtle ethereal substance, and the form or uncreated light, which is Jehovah himself or Wisdom. This is why Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian and philosopher whose "Celestial Hierarchy" was highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> calls angels *agalmata* <note>original: "agalmata"; from the Greek for "statues" or "images," implying they are vessels for the divine.</note>, which is to say, the clearest mirrors, catching the light of **GOD** and receiving His image. These are creatures of an airy consistency in whom the divine light exists as a sort of form or central agent. This light we can designate with the ineffable name of the <term>Tetragrammaton<gloss>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</gloss></term>, or the Word, or Eternal Wisdom. Hence, we read this written concerning that great angel who preceded the Israelites on their path through the desert: *Behold, I send an angel before you to keep you on this way, and to lead you into that place which I have prepared; take heed of him and listen to his voice, do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him. Exodus 23:20.* From these words, it is right to gather that the Word, or the uncreated light of **GOD**, or Jehovah Himself, was in the airy constitution of that Angel, like a soul animating his airy body and directing it according to His will. Thus it is clear that with respect to his internal part, that angel was not called an angel, but sometimes Jehovah; that is, with respect to his internal light or the light of **GOD**, which cannot be separated from the Divinity. At other times, he is called an angel with respect to his external part—namely, the creaturely form. Hence it is written in the same chapter: *The Angel who preceded the camps of the Israelites in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night;* and then afterward: *Jehovah went before the Israelites by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud;* from which it is evident that this spiritual leader of the Israelites is sometimes named an Angel and sometimes Jehovah. But when he is marked with the name of Jehovah, then the fiery nature of the pillar is noted, just as in the naming of an angel, the watery and vaporous nature is noted, such as the thin consistency of the angelic body.

Furthermore, it is also said elsewhere that the Angel of Jehovah appeared to Moses in a flame of fire in the midst of a certain bush. Yet in the same chapter, it is said that Jehovah spoke to Moses from the middle of the burning bush, saying, *I am the God of Abraham, etc.* By this, the Author <note>Likely referring to the biblical author or a high priest/authority figure.</note> seems to suggest that where the Angel of Jehovah was, there also was Jehovah—the divine light, the emanation from the Father, or Wisdom. Indeed, it clearly appears from the consensus of Holy Scripture that the angel who preceded the Israelites on their journey through the desert was Wisdom, considering its internal agent. For Wisdom was a covering for them by day and a starry light by night: *She brought them through the Red Sea and through many waters. Wisdom 10:17.* Finally, if anyone reads that entire chapter, they will perceive that this angel was Wisdom, created first before all things. Sometimes it is named for its eternal nature—insofar as it is purely and simply formal light—and sometimes for the whole angelic composition—namely, for the created spirit by which that light is covered, the animating light itself, and the light together, as if one were to say the angelic soul and body together. And certainly, the nature of this Deiform <note>God-like in form or character.</note> angel is so immense that it fills everything in the world, yet extends itself beyond all things. *I came out of the mouth of the Most High (she said) and covered the earth like a mist; I had my tent in high places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud. I alone encompassed the circuit of heaven, and I walked in the depth of the abyss; I rested in the waves of the sea and in every people and nation. Ecclesiasticus 24:3-5.* And elsewhere it is said: Wisdom is higher than the highest heaven, and indeed deeper than the abyss. We say, therefore, that the garment of this angel of incomprehensible and immense strength is the universal <term>World Spirit<gloss>Spiritus mundanus; the vital, subtle substance that permeates the universe, often equated with the "World Soul."</gloss></term>, which is the vehicle for this kind of emanation, most excellent in light and brightness. Thus, everything that the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, particularly Neoplatonists who believed in an "Anima Mundi" or World Soul.</note> took to be the Soul of the World is nothing other than this Wisdom, which is clothed in light as if with a garment (as David says). That is, by adorning the World Spirit and especially the heavens with its shining presence, it placed its tabernacle therein, and by the greater sight of its beauty, it copiously enriched the Sun, adorning it with its flashing riches.

How this Wisdom—the supreme minister in executing the will of its Father, to whose command all other angels and demons are subject—was called by the Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a form of Jewish mysticism.</note> the angel <term>Metatron<gloss>Mitattron; in mystical tradition, a high-ranking angel who serves as the celestial scribe or mediator.</gloss></term>, we shall declare more broadly in the second part of this member. Here, however, we have set forth a certain visual demonstration by which the matter may be more clearly explained to the understanding of the readers.

In the previous demonstration, we delineated the flow of the divine emanation from the Father, who formerly dwelt in darkness. This emanation—or holy spirit of intelligence—we have depicted in the form of a dove, because we read that this spirit descended upon Christ in such a form. From this, it follows that Wisdom, the Word, and **GOD** were sometimes called Jehovah and Wisdom in the same respect as the angel <note>Referring to the previous page's discussion of the Angel of the Exodus.</note>. Furthermore, that this radiant spirit—this emanation, or the brightness and splendor of the eternal light—moved in a circular manner is declared by the fact that the Spirit of the Lord is said to be "borne over the waters" <note>Genesis 1:2.</note>, and that Wisdom herself confessed that "she alone went around the circuit of the heavens" <note>original: "rotunditatem cælorum circumiuerit sola"; from Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 24:5.</note>. And elsewhere: "**GOD**, who makes the earth by His strength, prepares the world in Wisdom, and by His prudence extends the heavens" <note>Jeremiah 10:12.</note>; He turns the heaven in a circuit to its place in one day <note>3 Esdras 4:34.</note>. All of this seems to be suggested by Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, often identified as a contemporary of Moses, believed to be the author of the *Hermetica*, a collection of mystical and philosophical texts.</note> in *Pimander* <note>The first book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, describing the creation of the world.</note>, Book 1, where he says: "When **GOD** had revealed himself, all things were turned into a light pleasant to the sight." And a little later: "A dreadful shadow with an oblique revolution glided down into the moist nature," etc.

->**On Created Fire, and how it is produced in the beginning of the world by means of this divine act.**<-

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...resisting, is produced through reflection, which is also multiform according to the diversity of the resistance. For the resistance that typically occurs in the thicker spirit of the world brings forth a coarser and more sensibly acting fire. For example, the fire of the highest heaven is rendered more sweet, benign, and intellectual because of the cleanliness and purity of the spirit of that place; for this reason, that place is assigned to the most spiritual creatures and is called the Empyrean <note>The "Empyrean" was considered the highest, most spiritual part of heaven, composed of pure light or fire.</note> or Fiery Heaven. 

Then, the fire procreated in the middle region of the world on the second day and dispersed everywhere is created due to the duality of the resisting spirit. Its nature is somewhat more violent because of a greater resistance than that of the first degree. This fire, before the third day, is expanded everywhere in the ether through the spirit of that place, which for this reason is called *ether*, as if it were *aetha aer* <note>original: "ætha aer", a traditional but folk etymology meaning "fiery air".</note>. Finally, this fire of the lowest region is more sensible and "rebellious" than those of the two higher degrees, which is why it consumes, as is demonstrated in lightning and terrestrial fire. 

But truly, the internal act of any of these fires is the true light of the world itself—the uncreated and incorruptible spirit—which converts fire, its creature, into whatever act is necessary to fulfill the will of the Father. Thus it is said of the fire of the higher order:

> *Who makes your angels burning fires.* Psalm 104.

And yet (as was said in the preceding pages), the internal act of the angels is Wisdom itself. So also elsewhere:

> *With a shining fire through the whole night God led the Israelites.* Psalm 78:14.

And yet Wisdom says:

> *My throne is in a pillar of cloud and fire.* Ecclesiasticus 4 <note>Likely referring to the Wisdom of Sirach, though the text mentions the pillar of cloud/fire from Exodus.</note>.

And elsewhere:

> *Wisdom was a covering for them by day, and a starry light by night.* Wisdom of Solomon 10:17.

Has it not also been said of celestial fire that he placed his tabernacle in the sun? But the admirable dominion of the divine spirit in created fire is proven by these words:

> *God softens the fire lest it should burn,* Wisdom 16:18.

Just as God makes fire burn in the midst of water, for (says the Wise Man) the creature serving you who made all things is strained and slackened for punishment against the unjust, and sometimes for benefit, etc. From which it is clear that this Divine and uncreated spirit (which is the center and circumference) is accustomed to move and act from the center of any creature, either by emitting its powers or by centrally contracting them to fulfill his commands. For the incorruptible spirit is in every thing, and his habitation is in the "heaven of heavens"—in the spirit of any particular creature as much as in the spirit of the whole world—that is, in the Holy of Holies, from which, as from an innermost center, he sends forth his gazes or reflects them back into himself according to his pleasure. 

Hence it is that Augustine and others hold that the more light something has in itself, the more it seems to claim God for itself. For God (who is the fountain of light and the light of the world) is said to *have his dwelling in inaccessible fire* <note>original: "habere habitaculum suum in igne inaccessibili"; See 1 Timothy 6:16. The text cites Leviticus 10:2, which describes fire coming from the Lord.</note>, that is, in the center of fire. And for this reason, mention is made in the Holy Scriptures of the "devouring fire of God." And elsewhere God is said to be a "consuming fire," by which is understood the fire from whose center Jehovah, with an angry disposition, looked upon the impious; hence in the same place it is said *that fire was a burning that Jehovah kindled* (verse 6). So also elsewhere: *Fire going out from Jehovah consumed those two hundred and fifty men who offered incense* (Numbers 16). And elsewhere: *That greatest fire of Jehovah will consume us.* Finally, for this reason God is said to be *clothed with light as with a garment* <note>original: "veſtri lumine quaſi veſtimento"; Citing Deuteronomy 5, though this is famously Psalm 104:2.</note>. 

We conclude, therefore, that in the first creation of the world, the central form of created light was the Word or Wisdom, from which the heavens and all things of the world were procreated. This is the immediate "act" in the world, in which Wisdom (the created spirit) puts on the spirit immediately created by it as a garment, and thus light is said to be created, and that heaven is adorned which for this reason is called the Empyrean. So in this simple act, the uncreated spirit is the Mind of the world and, as it were, the center of life, and the light of every thing, whose circumference is infinite. Its spirit or created vehicle is the <term>moist nature<gloss>A Hermetic term for the primordial substance or chaos that receives the divine light to begin creation.</gloss></term>. 

Then later, this composition, penetrating further downward, becomes the created soul of the world; nevertheless, its innermost agent is the uncreated. And finally, the soul of heaven with its denser vehicle is the soul of every element and elementary thing, according to that saying of the Poet <note>Virgil, Aeneid VI.724-727.</note>:

> In the beginning, the heaven and the earth and the flowing plains,
> the shining globe of the Moon and the Titan stars,
> a spirit within nourishes, and mingles with the great body;
> Mind moves the mass...

And this spirit, according to St. John, is that light of the world in which is the life of every thing. We say, therefore, that the rays of the spirit of Wisdom, penetrating downward into the dark abyss, generate fire by the reflection of its rays, rebounding from the thick and dark resisting matter. For this reason, fire ascends from below upward with a contrary motion, according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure used as a source for ancient "Egyptian" wisdom and alchemy.</note>, *Pymander* 1: *The holy Word stood over the moist nature, and pure fire leaped out from the moist nature upward into the heights; for it was light and sharp, as well as agile and effective.*

I have depicted the reason for this kind of primary reflection made in the highest heaven, according to my meager capacity, in this place—where the rays of Wisdom descending directly and penetrating into the chaos are explained, along with the rays reflecting upward by rebounding in a vibrating manner. Those which tend toward the heights are the created fire of the first degree, consisting of a created spirit, animated by the uncreated spirit, and converted into a fiery or light-filled nature.

## CHAPTER VII.

->*Concerning the First Mover, the First Moved Sphere, and the Divine Will.*<-

We have stated that the first mover of all things is Wisdom itself, insofar as she was created before all things. According to her own nature (as the Sage testifies in *Wisdom 7*), she is "more mobile than all mobile things," reaching everywhere because of her purity; for the emanation from God is the most vivid act of all, and the origin and source of all actions. Once the darkness was pushed back to the region of the Earth, she immediately exercised her primary moving force in that first heaven which is called the *Primum Mobile* <note>The "First Moved" sphere. In the traditional geocentric model, this was the outermost sphere of the universe which imparted motion to all the inner planetary spheres.</note>. It is for this reason it is called the "First Moved," because its motion causes the other spheres of the world to receive their own movements from east to west. Hence we find it written that the most powerful God, who is Truth, "turns the heaven in a circle to its place in one day" (*3 Esdras 4*). <note>3 Esdras is a book of the Apocrypha, often included in older Latin Bibles.</note>

And Wisdom herself said that she alone circled the heavens. At the motion of this Divine Will, the spirit created on the first day is constantly moved, just as a body moves by the action of its soul. From this it is clear that Divine Wisdom is, as it were, the will of God, emanating directly from the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the *Logos*, the creative utterance of God.</note>, being continuous with it and not at all divided from it (*Ecclesiasticus 1*). Therefore the Sage speaks in these words: "The source of wisdom is the Word of God on high, and her ways are eternal commandments." Indeed, the Evangelist seems to suggest that the will of God is the effect of the Word itself in these words of our Savior: *I have come down from heaven to do the will of the Father who sent me* (*John 6*). Therefore, as the Word is, so is the will of God, and such is Wisdom. The Prophet says: "The Word of our God remains forever" (*Isaiah 40*). And the Sage says: "The will of the Lord shall remain forever" (*Proverbs 19:22*). The will of God is the Word "Let it be" <note>original: "FIAT"</note>. Elsewhere it is said: *Not my will but yours be done*. From this it follows that because the First Mover [possesses] forces and

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*In what matter the Divine Will agrees with the human will, and in what they differ from one another, and that the latter essentially depends on the former.*<-

Just as two principal and primary parts of man are enumerated by Philosophers—namely the intellect or reason, and the will itself—so indeed we find the will (taught by such experience) to be sometimes governed so much against the laws and direction of reason that it is clearly called an irrational and sensitive or sensual appetite by the "Theologasters" <note>A dismissive term for minor or inferior theologians.</note>. Insofar as it is the means by which man usually differs very little from the beasts, in this state of the human will, it seems to differ in the highest degree from the divine will.

it seems <note>original: "videtur"</note>, since it is always just and inclined toward the good unless it is stirred to punish the wicked; it is eternal in its being and intellectual in the highest degree. From this it follows that the true will of man (inasmuch as it derives its origin from that divine will) is of such a condition and nature that it naturally seeks things that are good and rejects those that are evil.

Therefore, as the Divine Will can be defined—and not ineptly—as the moving power of the divine essence, by means of which God performs whatever He wills both in the heavens and on the earth (all of which He afterwards saw by the effect to be good); so also we say that the true and non-spurious human will is the moving power of the rational soul. By this power, a human being either desires things clearly produced by reason as being good, or rejects them as being wicked. From this it is evident that the human will or appetite ought to obey its own reason, and do, will, or perform nothing unless, being led by reason, it can give a probable cause for its motion. Hence it is clear that the reason or intellect ought to provide the rule or goal for the voluntary act. And although a good intention of the will sometimes produces an evil effect—which indeed is accustomed to happen sometimes because it occurs that the intellect is deceived and wanders astray due to the uncertainty of the senses and the deception of the phantasy <note>In historical psychology, "phantasy" or *phantasia* refers to the faculty of the mind that forms mental images, often considered prone to error if not governed by reason.</note>—it is in this defect that man seems to differ immensely from the Divine Will. 

However, this is that true will of man: namely, the power of the intellectual soul, which stands as a principle to that which physicists call the "natural will." Through this natural will, we either desire things naturally and necessarily desirable to a human—for example: to live, to know, to eat, to drink, etc.—or, on the contrary, we hold them in a kind of hatred, abhorrence, and aversion—namely: to die, to hunger, to be afflicted by poverty, etc. The **Rational Will**, therefore, acting as a prince, is free in its motion, and in this it is likened to the Divine Will. The **Natural Will**, however, is not free, but is swept along by the desiring corporeal nature toward its own perfection. For this reason, it is excluded from the rational category; but let us return to the matter at hand.

Just as we stated in the preceding chapter that the act of the Divine Will exercised its primary force upon the "First Moveable" <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere of the universe in the Ptolomaic system, which moves all other spheres.</note> of the heavens during the creation of the world, and that this act is the moving Divine Will, emanating immediately from the first and highest Intelligence of all as if from a general fountain of acts—which exercises its primary force upon the most subtle spirit of the world, which is more obedient to its act—so indeed does the matter stand in man, or the **Microcosm**. In man, the will, proceeding from the intellectual spirit and governed by the ministry of reason, first rotates the "animal spirit" <note>The "animal spirit" was believed to be a subtle fluid or wind that traveled through the nerves to communicate the soul's commands to the body.</note> as if it were the substance of the Empyrean and intellectual heaven, or the "First Moveable" in man. From this it is manifest that the will in man is the queen of all other faculties, which she leads according to her pleasure in imitation of the Divine, directing the arrows of her appetite toward the good as a desirable goal. 

For just as we see in the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Large World" or the universe.</note> that the starry heaven is exceedingly slow in its motion—inasmuch as it moves through only one single degree over a hundred years (according to the doctrine of Ptolemy) and that the number one hundred is the square of the number ten, which is composed of the parts of the quaternary elemental number (namely 1, 2, 3, and 4, which added together constitute ten)—it is clear that this heaven represents the elemental body. This is because it is filled by the fourfold types of signs according to the nature of the four elements: namely, three fiery, just as many watery, and again three airy, with just as many earthy signs. This partition of the signs is called a "triplicity" <note>An astrological grouping of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> by Astrologers. For this reason, it is not inaptly called the body of the "Great Worldly Animal," whose inner organs are the seven Planets. Hence also the Zodiac is called its "girdle," from the word *Zoon* (animal). Similarly, just as this body is moved immediately by the spirit of the *Primum Mobile* as if by a soul excited by the Divine Mind; so indeed the **Will** in the Microcosm represents the likeness of the mind of the Macrocosmic *Primum Mobile*, sweeping its entire spirit along in a circuit (by whose motion the other internal or interior spheres are led). By means of this will, the entire mass of the human body is moved and swept along, like the eighth or "starred" sphere of the macrocosm, and all its internal faculties and organs are stirred like planetary spheres and elemental regions.

This is also what **Aristotle** himself means: namely, that the will in man is a likeness of the spirit of the first worldly sphere, animated by divine light, since it traverses and turns all limbs and faculties no differently than the *Primum Mobile* turns the other circles. And the **Platonists** maintain that, just as the *Primum Mobile* is the leader of the heavens, moving all lower things by its vigor and virtue, yet is not led by any lower circle but only by the holy Intelligence operating within it; so indeed the human will governs and sweeps along all lower organs and faculties in the human body. It is ruled or moved by nothing else but has its primary act from that **spark of divinity** <note>original: "scintilla illa diuinitatis"</note> which moves all things, whose nature is to perpetually incline toward the good, even though reason is sometimes deceived due to the delusions of the senses and the phantasy. For very often the senses are mistaken regarding their own objects, which is why things that seem good to the sense and the flesh are sought by the will, even though they are judged to be evil by their effect—and this happens because of the figments of darkness and the blindness of igno-
