...of ignorance, or the perverse madness of diabolical error, obscuring the rays of truth and shadowing the sight of truth.

We consider, therefore, the divine will to be the moving act of the divine word or wisdom—emanating from the essence of God—which is never to be separated from its ray. It is eternal, along with the word and its emanation, and is no more divisible from it than heat is from fire or light is from the sun. We make this same divine lineage the "Deiform" <note>having the form or nature of God</note> parent of the divine ray in man, which is the primary act in the human will. For when God said, "Let us make man in our image," here the word *Fiat* <note>Latin: "Let it be done"</note>, or the motive power of the word, was the will of God, or the living signature of His will. From this root, the human will arose; for immediately following that word, there followed an act not only of life, but, along with life, that of the will.

What follows then? Shall we conclude, therefore, that the will of man is the will of God? By no means. Just as we say that the life and sublime mind of man are not at all separated from the essence of God—inasmuch as they are <term>spiracles<gloss>breaths or divine inhalations</gloss></term> from God, and consequently not to be divided from His emanation, for the divine essence is indivisible—so we say that the will of man goes out from that divine will. However, that will of God was for the purpose of shaping the human species, and for continuing, governing, and directing it in this life toward good things, and for avoiding foul things that are abominable before God and human nature. This is according to the words of the wise man: > *God sends wisdom from the holy heavens to man, so that she may be present and labor with you, and may know what is pleasing to Him. Wisdom 9.* And elsewhere: *That she may direct man in his way.* Yet this spark of divinity, because of the perverse error and sin of Adam, is so obscured and clouded by darkness for us, his successors, that although this spark always tends toward the good in its own motion, nevertheless, because of the dark disposition of the body, its impressions are poorly received. The wise man seems to acknowledge this in these words: > *What man can know the counsel of God? Or who can know what God wills? For the thoughts of mortals are timid and our foresight uncertain; for the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind that muses on many things. We hardly guess at the things that are on earth, but who shall search out the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your counsel, unless you give wisdom and send your most holy spirit from the highest? So the paths of those on earth were corrected, and men learned the things that please you. Wisdom 9.*

By this third thread of words, he seems to argue that the heaviness and darkness of the corruptible body is the cause of the uncertainty of the human path. Furthermore, we gather that God immediately infused the ray of life and intelligence into man from these passages: > *In man there is a spirit, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding. Job 32.* <note>The OCR lists Job 9, but the quote is from Job 32:8.</note> And elsewhere: > *The spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.* From these, it is clear that the origin of both human reason and life is the divine spirit or breath. Similarly, we understand from the speech of the wise man that this ray of life and intelligence was the very spirit of wisdom: *God made man by his wisdom (he says) that he might have dominion over the creatures made by Him. Wisdom 9:2.* From this it is said that God made man in His own image. *Genesis 1.* <note>The OCR lists Genesis 5:1.</note> Whence it is certain that wisdom itself (whose act is the effect of the divine will) is the source and origin of the human will no differently than it is of the divine.

But the darkness and corruption of the human body, induced by Adam’s sin through the craft and malice of the Devil, are the occasion of error in life and the cause of the depraved effects of the divine will within man. For God, in man's first creation, gave the Holy Spirit to rule him and lead him in His paths, and to defend him from corruption; hence Man was called the "Temple of the Holy Spirit." This we confirm from these sayings of the wise man: > *God created man to be immortal, and made him in the image of his own likeness; but by the envy of the Devil, death entered into the world. Wisdom 2:23.* And elsewhere: > *Do not seek death in the error of your life, nor bring destruction upon yourselves by the works of your hands; for God did not make death, nor does He rejoice in the destruction of the living. For He created all things that they might exist, and He made the nations of the earth healthy. Wisdom 1.* By these words, he indicates that the gift given to man was an act of health, prudence, and happiness, and that it is overshadowed by the vice of man, procreated by the malice of the devil. Thus man errs in his life unless those shadows are illuminated by the influx of divine wisdom sent from the highest heavens—that is, the ray is increased by rays, all corporeal and diabolical obscurity is removed, and so <note>original: "natura naturâ lætabitur"</note> nature shall rejoice in nature. And for this reason, there is a difference between the human will and the divine: not because they differ in essence, but because the latter is never occupied with vain effects, while the former—though it is always good in itself and possesses the most certain knowledge—sometimes has its good operations converted into evil and vicious effects by the foul and base flesh. It is just as the pleasant rays of the sun are converted into a burning heat by the violent reflection of a <term>burning mirror<gloss>a parabolic mirror or lens used to concentrate sunlight to create fire</gloss></term>. It is not that the mirror or the flesh received evil impressions from that divine act, but that by receiving its good acts poorly, it is accustomed to sin—turning the direct motion of the rays into an oblique path away from truth itself through rebellious reflection. Thus, this perverse and oblique will makes man err through the perverse reception of his flesh.

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors. <note>In the 17th-century context of this book, "Meteors" refers not just to space rocks, but to any atmospheric, optical, or spiritual phenomena occurring in the "middle region" of the air.</note>

Hence it is said that the most just of men errs seven times a day—not, I say, because the good spirit is the cause of evil, but because the "evil object," by perversely receiving the good acts of his rays, very often produces perverse effects. This is much like a man wandering in a dark place; he intends to follow the path of his own freedom and the vision of light, but indeed, led astray by the darkness, he unexpectedly falls into a pit. For the rays of divinity (through which all things exist, and because of whose abundance man is said to rule over all other creatures) do not suffer the attacks of darkness within themselves; hence it is said: *darkness is not darkness to you, but the night is as bright to you as the day.* <note>original: "tenebrae non sunt tenebre tibi, sed tam clara tibi est nox, quam est dies" — referencing Psalm 139</note> But darkness deludes the animal creature, which is overwhelmed by the false vision of the senses, and snatches it toward evil instead of good. At that point, it was said by <term>Hermes Trismegistus<gloss>A legendary Hellenistic figure linked to the origins of alchemy and philosophy</gloss></term> that the divine mind in man is at rest, and does not govern him in an intellectual manner, but usually provides him only with the functions of life. Thus it is said, that *your heavenly Father makes his sun rise on the good and the bad, Matthew 5,* <note>original: "Pater vester cælestis faciat solem suum oriri super bonos & malos, Matth. 5"</note> arguing from this that the Father of all has granted the force and power of life to both the good and the bad, but understanding and prudence only to those pure in spirit and far removed from dark actions.

It is required, therefore, to bring back the <term>spark<gloss>Latin: "scintilla," the tiny fragment of divine light remaining in the human soul after the Fall</gloss></term> of such divine power into its intellectual act in the human body, so that it may be illuminated by the rays of wisdom sent from God. By this, it may have dominion over the diabolical darkness of the body, so that in this way the sensual and brutal will of man may be brought back into such a disposition—namely, a truly intellectual one (to which that central spark belongs in its essence)—so that he may walk in the right way and observe the statutes of GOD, *and discern what is just in his eyes; Wisdom 9.* <note>original: "qua iusta sunt in oculis eius discernat; Sap. 9"</note> Hence Job says: *Your visitation will preserve my spirit, Job 10:12.* <note>original: "Visitatio tua conseruabit spiritum meum, Iob. 10. 12."</note> And elsewhere: *Lift up the light of your face upon us, and it will cause us to see good, Psalm 4:7.* <note>original: "Lucem faciei tuæ attolle super nos, & efficiet vt videamus bonum, Psal. 7. 4." Thus it is exalted by its own likeness above the power of darkness, so that even the body, once dark and covered on all sides by gloom, now shines so brightly that it is sometimes even illustrated by a stellar flashing. Which also the sacred letters seem to confirm in this manner: *He who clings to GOD will become one spirit with him:* And elsewhere it is said: *At last we shall be transformed into the same image:* And indeed, all those sparks in the world will be joined into one essence of divinity and truth—leaving behind the filth of diabolical vanity and falsehood—when Christ comes to judgment. *GOD (says the Apostle) will be all in all, when Christ shall have delivered the kingdom to the father. 1 Cor. 15.*

And although in truth the divine spark in man is no more divided and separated from its shining source than the rays of the sun are from its essence, as Hermes Trismegistus testifies (for the divine essence is indivisible), nevertheless, insofar as it is in the creature whom he created and preserves through generations, it seems to be distinguished from the divine light. It is, as it were, the royal part of the creature; if the name of God was said to be in the Angel, yet the whole composition of the angel was a creature. Whence also his motive power—by which man is said to desire good and refuse evil—is said to be varied and different from that of divine wisdom. For in the Divine will, which the Word produces in act, there is eternity and infallibility, certainty and exact perfection in execution without any resistance. ### Section I, Portion IV, Part II. Book IV. Member I.

of our flesh, Ephesians 2. And Christ himself, having first overcome the narrow straits of his own flesh by praying that God might turn away that cup, nevertheless said, "Not my will, but thine be done," Luke 22; according to that in John 5: "I seek not my own will, but the will of him who sent me." But if the human will is united with that divine one, then it is accustomed to perfect that same will, and of this kind of union John speaks:

> He who does the will of God remains forever, 1 John 2.

That is, he has been made one with God; and so that this might happen in the <term>Royal Prophet<gloss>A traditional title for King David, the purported author of the Psalms</gloss></term>, David speaks thus while praying to God:

> Teach me to do your will, for you are my God, Psalm 143:10.

It is as if he had said: let your face shine upon your servant, and in your light I shall see light; or as he has it elsewhere:

> You, the Sun, giving life and glory, and illuminating my lamp, shall make my darkness shining, so that I may enter the right path to execute your will, Psalm 18:29 and 84:12.

From these things, therefore, one may see that the lamp of man does not differ in essence from the **Spiritual Sun**, who gives grace, glory, and salvation—except in this: that the lamp dwells in a created body as its own peculiar ray, providing it with being and existence, and occupies the place of a creature; whereas the Sun exists in and through itself, attributing being and essence to the mundane spirit. It exists both within and outside all things, whence it is said to fill all things: the Father of all, who is over all and through all, the God who gives life to all, the worker of all in all, Ephesians 4:6, 1 Timothy 6. He is the **center of every thing whose circumference is nowhere**, the unity of the united, the father of fathers, the principle of principles, the source of sources, the root of roots, the star of stars <note>original: "syderum sydus" — likely referencing Synesius’s Neoplatonic hymns</note> (Synesius, *Hymns*), the good of the good, the idea of ideas, immense beauty, the hidden seed of things, the father of ages, the father of the intelligible worlds. Ambrose speaks of him as the "instilling spirit, swimming toward the mass of the body, who now stirs the world." He is **Jupiter or Jehovah**, upon whom all lower Gods depend, as Orpheus and the Pythagoreans maintain. Finally, he is everything that truly *is*; by which statement we exclude from him all things empty, deceptive, and fantastical—those children of darkness who seem to be and yet are not, as will appear in the final examination when all things are to be reduced back to the One.

We conclude, therefore, that God acts voluntarily and not out of a stirred necessity (as the <term>Peripatetics<gloss>Followers of Aristotle, who argued that the universe and its movements were governed by eternal necessity rather than a personal, choosing God</gloss></term> claim), and that nothing has been made in either the heavens or the earth which did not receive the motion of its origin from the divine will. But if the spark within a creature does not produce the desired effects that are pleasing to God and good men, this does not happen because of the incorruptible spirit acting from the center, but because of the deceptive mass of darkness subject to all alteration. This darkness receives the acts of the divine mind poorly, and thus obscures the rays of such great light; and "the darkness does not comprehend" that light dwelling in the darkness within the creature, according to that saying of St. John: *In the Word was life, and that was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.*

We can most aptly compare this light—or the spirit of wisdom—to the nature of the **Sun**. In itself, the sun is simple and always uniform in its action; yet it is manifold in respect to the variety of operations which its rays are accustomed to produce in the world. This does not happen because of any varied action of the sun, but because its impressions are received differently according to the variety of bodies—differing according to their existence, or by the greater or lesser resistance of those things receiving the solar acts. For, as the <term>Wise Man<gloss>Refers to the author of the Wisdom of Solomon in the Apocrypha</gloss></term> witnesses, God composed all things by **number, weight, and measure**, and made one thing different from another by proportion, so that he might produce various creatures, both corporeal and spiritual, by his unique and simple act in this world.

Thus we see that various effects are produced in the world by those solar rays, according to the character of the recipients. For in one place, the sun causes grass and herbs to sprout and flourish; but at another time, it burns and dries them up. Sometimes it cherishes and refreshes animals with its beneficial heat, and sometimes it makes the weak and sickly languid by its presence. Indeed, it compels healthy men to hurry to shady places to escape the persecution of its scorching rays. Again, rays contracted into the center of a **burning mirror** <note>original: "speculi vrentis" — a curved lens or mirror used to focus sunlight to start fires</note> set fire to and consume cities and royal palaces, reducing them to nothing; and yet the sun is not observed to act in the same way upon water. It inflames stones and crags with heat, and yet sometimes it only warms them slightly. At times, therefore, the effects of generation are hastened, and sometimes they tend toward corruption—and yet the sun itself, along with its rays, is the same: permanent and simple in its act. The entire difference lies in the diversity of the object, which receives the solar acts either well or poorly.

The matter is no different regarding the rays of the **Invisible and Intellectual Sun**, which gives life and being to this mundane sun. And so you have my conceptions concerning the divine will with its branches, according to which all things happen in this world, in which it produces various effects according to the variety of those receiving the divine rays—varying by number, weight, and measure. We have depicted in this place, to the best of my ability for the better understanding of the readers, the act of the human will, both obscured and illuminated.

### CHAPTER IX.

->***That, contrary to the opinion of Aristotle and certain other Pagans, God works and acts in his creation and in the preservation of his creatures not out of necessity, but by his own proper will.***<-

We call that "necessary" which indeed cannot be otherwise; but we call "contingent"—which includes both the voluntary and the accidental—that which can be otherwise. However, a great dispute has arisen among the Pagan <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note> philosophers as to whether God created the world and the creatures within it in this way (that is, voluntarily) or in that way (namely, by necessity). The greater part of them have fallen into this opinion: that God acts necessarily and not voluntarily in the world, both regarding its creation and the decay <note>original: "corruptionem," referring to the natural cycle of things breaking down</note> of things generated within it. They speak as if he were driven to such works without his own will, by the compulsion and prompting of some nature that was either co-eternal or pre-existent to him, or at least already created by him. How profane this is, and how far it oversteps the boundary of reason, will become clear from the following. For what is more ancient than God, since he is before all things? What is smaller in measure than a point, or lesser in number than unity? <note>The author argues that God is the "monad" or "point"—the simplest, first principle from which all else follows.</note> Therefore, it is necessary that God be free and voluntary in his actions, insofar as he exists through himself and without regard for other things; he was sufficient for himself before any creation...

<meta>catchword: ...sufficient.</meta>

<summary>This page argues against the Aristotelian view that the universe is governed by necessity, asserting instead that God created and maintains the world through free, voluntary choice. It introduces a section on the "efficient cause" of atmospheric phenomena (meteors), framing the physical world as a product of divine will.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the refutation of the "necessitarian" view of God, specifically responding to the arguments that God's actions are dictated by his nature rather than his choice. It bridges the gap between classical philosophy and Christian miracle accounts.</meta>

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...efficient <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "efficiens" from the previous page.</note> cause. But in truth, the primary reasons of the aforementioned philosophers were these two: First, that God acts through his own essence, and not through an acquired power. Second, because the effects seen in the world seem to be necessary, from which they conclude that they cannot proceed from a contingent cause—that is, from either chance or will. To the first of these, we respond that they seem to argue against themselves; for insofar as He acts in His own substance, it is clear that He is moved to act by His own free nature, and not compelled by any necessity, whether external or internal. Furthermore, in absolute unity, there is no involuntary compulsion or provocation, because the "One" does not suffer <note>In the philosophical sense, "to suffer" (pati) means to be acted upon by an external force.</note>. Moreover, it is impossible that He should be compelled or urged to such work by any foreign cause, because remaining primarily and immovably in Himself and from Himself, He acts as the primary source. 

To the second argument, we say that necessary effects do not imply necessity in the First Cause as the ruler, because the secondary causes (which *Plato* and other wise men call "handmaidens" and "servants") act either by His command and mandate, or by a necessary order, such that their necessity depends on His mandate and the order which He established according to His pleasure. Hence we read in the Book of Wisdom: *God made the fire grow mild so that it would not burn; at another time, He made the fire burn in the midst of water, and indeed in snow and ice, without them melting at all; yet that same fire, on the contrary, forgot its own power so that the righteous might be nourished.* <note>original: "ignem mitescit ne combureret DEVS..." referencing Wisdom of Solomon 16:17-19, 22.</note> From this, it follows that the fire did not consume the servants of God in the glowing furnace of the Chaldeans, and that the Sun in the time of *Joshua* abstained from its course for the space of a whole day and rested in a firm standing position, and that the same Sun in the time of *Hezekiah* moved backward by ten degrees or lines on the sundial. 

Furthermore, without any evident reason in nature—namely, with the moon not being at the "head or tail of the dragon" <note>The "head and tail of the dragon" (Caput and Cauda Draconis) are the lunar nodes; ancient and medieval astronomers knew eclipses could only occur when the moon was near these points.</note>—an eclipse nonetheless occurred (indeed, one that happened beyond the common laws of nature) during the very full moon at the time of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. All of these things could by no means have happened if God acted in the world by necessity; for from these examples it is clearer than light that He operates in created things according to His own good pleasure and free will, and not according to the laws of nature—things which He created, made, and continually preserves by His will and mere mercy.

***

But I ask you to come forward, you Philosophers, who wish to bind God, the ordainer and actor of all things, by the laws of necessity: I pray, what honor or glory do we attribute to God for His command, wisdom, justice, and mercy, if He were forced by necessity not only to create all things, but also to cherish and sustain them? What thanks, what service and adorations do we owe Him if these things are so? Why, O *Aristotle*, according to your assertion, is it granted to the roots of nature to offer sacrifices? Or what benefit will prayers and orations bring to us humans, which even *Plato*, *Porphyry*, *Iamblichus*, and *Proclus* teach us are extremely necessary, if God were not moved to favor by prayers? Or why were *Pythagoras* and *Socrates* (who, by the witness of the oracle, were the wisest of all men of that time) accustomed to pour out their prayers, if God were compelled to perform the works He does? Why does the Prophet say *that God alone is to be called upon and prayed to?* <note>original: "quod Deus solus sit inclamandus & deprecandus, Psal. 30. 8." See Psalm 31:22 in modern numbering.</note> If there were some necessity in God for the doing and preserving of things, then indeed it has been clearly demonstrated from these examples that God is accustomed to be inclined toward mercy through those means, and that in His good pleasure He deals either severely or mercifully with the world and His creatures, and especially with mankind; and consequently, that He is not urged by necessity in His actions.

***

But there are certain other philosophers who conduct themselves more modestly in the resolution of this doubt. For *Avicenna* <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) who was one of the most significant thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age; his work deeply influenced Western Scholasticism.</note> maintains that such actions are neither necessary nor violent, but in a middle state between these two, whereby he places them in the will of the agent. In this resolution, he does not seem to differ much from the sacred source, in which we read: *God has chastised us for our iniquities, and He will save us for His mercy.* <note>Tobit 13:5.</note> Here the chosen man intimates that will exists in God, either for doing good or for doing ill. But this is indicated even more clearly and in more express words elsewhere: *God (says the Prophet) does according to His will both among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth, and there is no one who can resist His hand or say, "Why have you done this?"* <note>Daniel 4:32 (Vulgate translation).</note> And God Himself says: *My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done, calling a bird from the east, and from a far country the man of my will.* <note>Isaiah 46:10-11.</note> By these things it is sufficiently clear that every operation in the world happens by divine will and for His good pleasure, and not by necessity as the Pagan philosophers wished, thereby diminishing the divine prerogative and binding Him to necessity. 

But necessity is undoubtedly in the causes and effects, or in their operations; for example, we have in the Prophet *Baruch* that the Sun, Moon, stars, lightning, wind, clouds, and fire obey God in all things—that is, they are compelled to carry out the will of the commander or creator. They are, I say, compelled by necessity, but it does not follow from this that the one Commanding is urged by necessity to command, but rather that He does so by a voluntary motion. Hence it is said: *Who shall resist the will of God?* <note>Romans 9:19.</note>

***

We conclude, therefore, that it is not only absurd but even impious to proclaim with a hardened mouth alongside those Pagans that He, who was all things and in all things, and finally everything that exists, cannot act voluntarily and freely when, how, or where it pleases Him—especially when we see this same privilege granted to the human soul (which is a flow proceeding from that same divinity), as was most clearly shown in the choice of good or evil, both by ourselves and by our forefather *Adam*.

## CHAPTER X.

### On the property of Divine numbers and names among the Cabalists, and how the various effects of the divine will—tending toward both benevolence and malediction—depend upon their natures.

In our "mirror of causes," which is attached to the end of this section, you have seen demonstrated how each Cabalistic enumeration <term>Sephirah; one of the ten attributes or emanations in Cabala through which the Infinite reveals itself</term> is presided over by a different name of God. This is not because there is any diversity in the essence of God Himself, but because His properties in the world are various, according to His good pleasure and will, wherever it seems good to Him. Some of these properties tend toward mercy and benevolence, while others tend toward severity and punishment. For a fuller understanding of this matter, it must be known that although many names are attributed to God (according to the opinion of <note>original: "Rabbi Moysis Ægyptiaci"</note> Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, also known as Maimonides), all of them except for one—namely the Tetragrammaton <term>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</term>, which is called the <term>separated name</term>—are shared. This name is uniquely appropriate to Him alone because it signifies the substance of the Creator in a pure sense, without any participation with created things. The other names assigned to Him denote Him in participation—that is, in respect to created things—and consequently, they are derived from His works. It was for this reason that His essential name was never spoken, except in the sanctuary by the holy priests of the Lord, and specifically in the priestly blessing by the High Priest on the Day of Atonement. The rank of this name (says Rabbi Moses) is great, and it was not to be uttered rashly by the mouth, as it signifies the very substance of the Creator; through this, God is noted as being above all being, even before any thing existed. The other names, however, denote God as He exists within all being.

For example, when Moses questioned God, He responded: "I.H.V.H." <note>original: "I.H.V.H."</note>; that is, "This is my name forever." Therefore, this name alone belongs to eternity—that is, to the Divine essence in its purity. No such name can be composed by a human voice that could equal the nature of divinity. Although God has various titles derived from His works, this is the only name appropriate to Him before any created thing existed. But insofar as the divine essence is now present within created things as well as outside of them all, the Tetragrammaton is also common and general, acting in every branch of the Sephirotic tree, so that the other various titles of God are merely properties, offices, or different acts of power of that one and indivisible essence.

Thus, among the titles of God inscribed upon the various parts of the Sephirotic tree, <term>Ehieh</term> <note>Hebrew for "I Am" or "I Will Be"</note> signifies the source of all creatures, the first of all clemency and all graces, sparing all, the Father of Mercies, and the God of all consolation, whom Christ teaches us to pray to in this way:

> Our Father, who art in heaven, etc.

And it is said of Him that the Father judges no one; furthermore, it is assigned to the Father as one who is always merciful and benevolent toward His children, just as Psalm 103 teaches how God has mercy on His children. This name, therefore, is assigned as the ruler of the Sephirah (or enumeration, or "shining gate," or first branch of the Cabalistic tree) which is called <term>Cheter</term> <note>Keter</note> or the <term>crown</term>. For just as the *Crown* is like the root of the tree, so *Ehieh* is the father of all creation. From this it is clear that the reasoning for this title of God is taken from His property of clemency and mercy toward creatures—namely, in giving and granting life, and bestowing the gift of being or existence upon the world and the creatures contained within it.

The second title of God in the Sephirotic order is <term>Iah</term> <note>Yah</note>. This also tends toward the benign property of God—specifically, the shaping of the world and the extraction of the waters from the womb of Chaos. The enumeration over which it presides is <term>Hochma</term> <note>Chokmah</note>, which means Wisdom; hence it is written of her:

> He gave the winds weight and measured out the waters, when He set a law for the rains and a path for the sounding storms; then He saw wisdom, etc. <note>Job 28</note>

And elsewhere:

> When He prepared the heavens above, when He strengthened the fountains of the deep, when He gave the sea its boundary, when He established the foundations of the earth, I, Wisdom, was with Him as an assistant, arranging all things. <note>Proverbs 8</note>

From this benign disposition, she is also said to be mild, kind, and a lover of good; and elsewhere, it is said that she is given by God to men to show them what His will is. Nevertheless, as it is certain that *Wisdom* stands in the middle between the *Crown* and *Understanding* (the latter of which denotes severity, while the former denotes clemency), so the title of God *Iah* (or Wisdom) sometimes punishes, though very rarely. Hence Jehovah said, speaking of the Angel or Wisdom: "Do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him." <note>Exodus 23</note>

The third Sephirah or Cabalistic enumeration is <term>Binah</term>, which means Prudence or Understanding. The title of the Tetragrammaton attributed to this is <term>Elohim</term>, which signifies terror and dread, as it is through this name that severe punishments and slaughters come. For in this property, God exercises His power by punishing the wicked. And in this office, He employs angels, who for this reason are called <term>Bene Elohim</term>, meaning the "Sons of Elohim." <meta>This page continues the exploration of the Sephirot—the ten divine emanations—explaining how specific names of God correspond to different qualities of the physical and spiritual worlds, ranging from extreme mercy to severe judgment. Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...[from previous page]... and if it be the North, from which all evil or punishment from sin arises. In the act of creation, the property of this [divine aspect] is to illuminate and give form to matter; in this action, it is necessary that a "privation" <term>privatio; the Aristotelian concept of the absence of a form that ought to be present</term> intervenes, if there were any preceding form.

You see that the effects of these three divine titles, taken from their properties toward created things, are varied. Specifically, the first inclines entirely toward clemency and mercy, the last toward severity, while the middle one participates in both natures, yet is most inclined toward clemency. To this middle one is assigned the essential name **Jehovah**, because it is exercised in this world both in punishment and in beneficence, yet it is much more prone to mercy than to punishment. Whence it is written: *The LORD [Jehovah] is long-suffering, and of great mercy, forgiving iniquity and transgression, who by no means clears the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, etc. Numbers 14.* <note>original: "DEVS Iehoua est longanimis, multus benignitate..."</note>

But let us proceed to the fourth enumeration, which is **Chesed** <term>Chesed; the Sephirah of Lovingkindness or Mercy</term> or clemency, to which are attributed grace, goodness, and mercy. Its presiding divine title is **El**, whose role is to cherish all things and succor everyone with the highest piety and clemency. Under this property, bodies are said to have received their outward forms. From this enumeration, therefore, grace and mercy flow into the lower worlds through its own channel or "shining gate."

But we think it should be briefly objected by some: what use is this Cabalistic science to us, or how is it to be proven that this or that name of the Tetragrammaton has this or that property, or an inclination toward clemency or severity? To this we answer that it is proven by the effect seen in the Hebrew text. Hence, the property of the name **El** is openly explained by Moses in this: that he is recorded to have entreated from God the gift of health for his sister Miriam, who was suffering from leprosy, in this manner: *El na rapha na la.* **El** means "God of grace," **rapha** means "heal," **na** means "I pray," and **la** means "her." <note>original: "El na rapha na la. El id est DEVS gratiæ, rapha id est sana, na id est quæso, la id est est illam." Numbers 12:13.</note>

The fifth enumeration (which is **Gebura** <term>Gevurah; the Sephirah of Strength, Power, or Severity</term>) is presided over by the divine title **Elohim Gibbor**. In this property, God is said to have drawn the elements out of turbulent Chaos; and this denotes power, violence, severity, judgment, and the punishment of sins. This property of God flows into the lower regions—namely, into the world—the effects of plague, famine, war, robbery, and desolation. Whence it is clear that just as the nature of the Tetragrammaton **El** promised every good thing to the creatures of the world, so **Elohim Gibbor** seems to announce every evil and turbulent outcome, such as occurred in the extraction of the elements from chaos.

The sixth enumeration is **Tiphereth** <term>Tiferet; the Sephirah of Beauty, Balance, or Ornament</term>, which denotes grace and ornament, beauty and delights. The name of GOD assisting this one is **Eloah**. From this it happens that all those influences which are poured out from this Channel, or this path, or divine property, give form to the sun, returning to it clarity, life, and light, and they adorn the heavens according to that passage in **Job**: *By his spirit he hath garnished the heavens, Job 26:13.* And also: *By the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth, Psalm 33.* From these influences thereafter proceed minerals, of which the chief is gold; vegetables, among which Bread and wine are the chiefs; and animals, whose head in dignity is man, following the position of the sun in the heavens.

The seventh Sephirah is called **Nezech** <term>Netzach; the Sephirah of Victory or Endurance</term>, namely Triumph, victory. Furthermore, it indicates charity and the love of justice, and from here also follow the influences of multiplication and generation. The name presiding over this is **Jehovah Sabaoth**, the Lord of Hosts.

The eighth is called **Hod** <term>Hod; the Sephirah of Splendor, Glory, or Majesty</term>, namely praise, honor, and beauty. The name derived from its property is **Elohim Sabaoth**, that is, GOD of hosts—not, however, for rigor and war, but for piety, justice, and concord.

The ninth enumeration is presided over by the name of God **Elchai**, that is, the living GOD, or **Shaddai**, GOD almighty, or "sufficient unto Himself." This enumeration is called **Iesod** <term>Yesod; the Sephirah of the Foundation</term>, that is, Basis, foundation, redemption, and rest.

The tenth and final Sephirah is called **Malchut** <term>Malkuth; the Sephirah of the Kingdom</term>, that is, the kingdom, the church, the empire, and the temple of GOD. Hence the Psalmist says: *for the kingdom is the Lord's, Psalm 22.* The name of GOD presiding over this is **Adonai** "the Lord," and this enumeration implies severity and servitude to those upon whom it flows.

From these things it may be seen that in all the properties or operations of the divine essence in the world—whether for punishment and the lash, or for beneficence—GOD is more prone to clemency and mercy than to severity. For in the property of His first title, He extends His charity out of the darkness into the world, just as a father to a son; whence also **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>Mercury Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> calls the world the "son of GOD."

In that of the second [title], through His wisdom, He is more inclined toward creating things than toward striking the created human race with a plague for its sins, just as it is explained from the words of GOD speaking to the Israelites: *Behold, I send my angel before thee, to keep thee in the place which I have prepared; beware of him, etc. Exodus 23.* But I have shown elsewhere that this angel was Wisdom, which was sent to the Israelites for their preservation, yet with that precaution, lest they commit evil, because He says He will not bear your defection. Whence it is clear that God is more inclined in this property of His toward doing good than toward the lash. In the property of the third title, severity and punishment are included, for the title **Elohim** is by its nature terrible. Whence it happens that just as the title of the first Sephirah—namely **Ehieh** <term>Ehyeh; "I Am," the name associated with Keter</term>—related to the Father, is attributed to the Empyrean heaven, the place of the blessed and of rest; so the second, namely **Jah** or **Jehovah**, is attributed to the

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...ascribed to the Son is the ethereal or starry heaven, from which Fate claims its origin, raining down both good and evil things upon lower realms. Likewise, the name *Elohim*, presiding over the third *Sephirah* <term>Sephirah (plural: Sephirot); one of the ten emanations or attributes of God in Kabbalah</term> or enumeration [Binah] and related to the Holy Spirit, looks toward the lowest or elementary heaven. In this realm exists all change, generation, and corruption among earthly things, as well as the violence of winds, thunders, and other meteors in the middle air. 

This is also clearly demonstrated by those who compare the sacrosanct persons of the Deity as creators with the properties of created things. They compare the Father to the solar body, as if to essence and quiddity <term>quidditas; the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term>; they compare the Son, or the Word, to the rays emitted from that essence; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, to the heat or the effect. In this same way, the life or fountain of the ethereal heaven (in whose center He placed His tabernacle) was the Empyrean heaven, just as the Son receives His being from the Father. Furthermore, the soul and life of the Elementary heaven is the power of the ethereal heaven. Thus, you may see clearer than light that the Elementary heaven received its Life and Being mediately from the Empyrean heaven, as from a first father among created things; for the first creature was light. It received this immediately from the starry heaven as if from a son, just as we see in the ideal and Archetypal world that the Holy Spirit, in personal number, had His progress from the Father and the Son.

Hence it is certain that the effects of these sacrosanct persons in the typical world <note>The "typical" world refers to the physical world acting as a "type" or reflection of divine archetypes.</note> are as we have reported. Consequently, it is proved through the effect that primarily the intellectual, angelic, and empyrean heaven is a sweet, mild, and benevolent dwelling assigned to the blessed. This is because, according to the property of the Father, it is a sacred *Zenobium* <note>original: "Zenobium"; a communal religious dwelling or monastery, here used to describe the assembly of angels.</note> or Holy of Holies, appropriated to the Angels of God and holy souls, where they act in this world under the shadow of Jehovah’s wings, secure from every severe property of God. 

But *Keter* <term>Keter; the "Crown," the first Sephirah</term>, the second property <note>The author appears to be using a specific ordering that pairs names and Sephirot differently than some traditional Kabbalistic texts.</note>, as the effect of the second Sephirah, imposes Fate upon the world, bringing both good and evil to sublunary creatures. This denotes that the nature of the divine essence is inclined toward both punishment and clemency. Just as in the Sephirot *Chokhmah* <term>Chokhmah; Wisdom</term> is placed between *Keter* and *Binah* <term>Binah; Understanding</term>—or *Ehyeh* and *Elohim*—so indeed its effects are seen between the Empyrean heaven (the place of rest, grace, and happiness) and the lower abyss of the elementary heaven. In that lower realm, there is almost no rest and much vexation, both in the heavens (that is, the air) and on the earth, for it is where that rebellious spirit reigns, whom the sacred scriptures call the prince of this world, and to whom the empire of the air is assigned. 

From this, it is clear that although it is said that by the breath from the mouth of Jehovah all the power of the world and heavens were created, we must understand that both good and evil are breathed into the creature according to its merits by that same spirit. *The Lord has the power of life and death, who leads down to the gates of death and brings back again, Wisdom 16:13.* <note>original: "Vita (inquit sapiens) & mortis habet dominus..."</note> And elsewhere: *Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honesty are from God, Ecclesiasticus 11.* And elsewhere: *Consider the works of God, that no one can correct whom He has despised; in the good day enjoy good things, and beware of the evil day; for as He made the one, so He made the other, so that man may not find just complaints against Him, Ecclesiastes 7:14.* By these, He seems to hint that the actions of God in this world are various, and indeed opposite in nature. The Father *Ehyeh* <note>Ehyeh; "I Am," the name associated with the highest Sephirah</note> is the author of goodness, which the Son *Yah* executes in wisdom, raining it down from His luminous gate *Chokhmah*. The Spirit *Elohim* from both, terrible to the impious, is assisted in his office even by *Yah*, as one participating in both extremes. And hence it is called *the spirit claiming the power of God, and justice pursuing the unjust, Wisdom 11:20.*

But let us proceed: *El* is the name of the bright gate or Sephirah *Chesed* <term>Chesed; Lovingkindness</term>, pouring clemency and mercy into the lower things. But *Elohim Gibbor* in that *Gevurah* <term>Gevurah; Strength or Severity</term> denotes severity and punishment. In the sixth order, however, *Eloah* or *Jehovah* rains down beauty and grace through the gate *Tiferet* <term>Tiferet; Beauty or Harmony</term>. But because it is in the middle between *Ehyeh* and *Adonai*, it is said to participate in both extremes, since this property sometimes punishes. Thus also *Jehovah Sabaoth*, presiding over the gate *Netzach* <term>Netzach; Victory</term>, proves victory and triumph, not in severity, but in its excellence and in the love of justice, yet it is still opposed to the unjust. *Hod* <term>Hod; Splendor or Majesty</term> also gives beauty and praise, over which *Elohim Sabaoth* predominates. Furthermore, *Shaddai* through *Yesod* <note>The text reads "Iesed," likely a printer's error for "Iesod" (Yesod/Foundation)</note> rains down redemption and rest, and thus its influences are good and beneficial. Finally, just as *Ehyeh* emits paternal grace and clemency through its royal gate, *Keter* or the Crown, at the root of the Sephirotic tree, so indeed *Adonai* from the summit of the same <note>Fludd often envisions the Sephirotic tree as "growing" downward from heaven to earth.</note> through its gate *Malkuth* <term>Malkuth; Kingdom</term> emits servitude, miseries, and punishment into lower things.

From this it is clear that in these branches of the Sephirotic enumeration we have four testimonies of divine compassion and clemency: namely the properties of *Ehyeh* of the first and fourth, *Jehovah Sabaoth* of the seventh, and *Shaddai* of the ninth. We have, however, only three of extreme severity: namely *Elohim* of the third, *Elohim Gibbor* of the fifth, and *Adonai* of the last. Finally, we have three participating in both extremes: namely *Yah* of the second (which nevertheless tends toward clemency), *Eloah* of the sixth, and *Elohim Sabaoth* of the eighth. For the planet to which *Elohim Sabaoth* rains its qualities is Mercury, which experience has noted to be good with the good and evil with the evil. Whence with *Elohim*—that is, with fear and dread, and finally perturbation—*Sabaoth* (or rest) is joined. But it is certain that these properties participating in both extremes are more inclined toward clemency and mercy. Whence the Prophet says: *The Lord is gracious and merciful, patient, and of great compassion, and forgiving over malice, Jonah 4:2.* And again: *You, Lord, are a pitier and merciful, patient and of great mercy and true, Psalm 86:15.* And elsewhere: *God, pious and merci-*

->Concerning the Efficient Cause of Meteors.<-

# CHAPTER 11.

*How the Spirit of Wisdom, spread everywhere in the world, and informing and fostering its moist nature, informs, creates, and preserves all creatures composed of elements within it, until their final end.*

The spirit of divine wisdom, animating, informing, and creating the world, binding and arranging all discordant elements with its breath in harmonious peace, and strengthening and sustaining the heaven and earth by its harmonious spirit and through its will alone, according to that saying of the Prophet: *He who makes the earth in his strength, prepares the world in wisdom, and by his prudence stretches out the heavens* <note>original: "Qui facit terram in fortitudine sua, præparat orbem in sapientia, prudentia sua extendit cælos"</note>, Jeremiah 10. This Spirit (I say), having completed universal things, looked toward particulars, namely stars, animals, plants, and even minerals; which the Prophet briefly indicated to us with these words: *GOD creating the heavens, stretching them out, establishing the earth and what grows from it, giving breath to the people, and spirit to those who walk upon it* <note>original: "DEVS creans cælos, extendens eos, firmans terram & quæ germinant ex ea, dans flatum populo, & spiritum calcantibus eam"</note>, Isaiah 42:5.

But this is explained more clearly and specifically in the first chapter of Genesis, namely that by the word "LET IT BE MADE" <note>original: "FIAT"</note>, first general things and then afterwards particulars were created. Hence the Evangelist says: *By the word all things were made, and without it nothing was made that was made; in it was life, and that life was the light of men* <note>original: "A verbo omnia sunt facta, & sine illo nihil quod factum est, in eo erat vita & illa lux hominum"</note>, John 1. From these passages it is evident that in every creature there is a trace of the Word; indeed, a portion of that actual divine light is placed in every creature, through which—and not without it—each exists as it is. And this is what the wise man seems to imply with these express words: *The incorruptible spirit,* he says, *is in every thing* <note>original: "spiritus incorruptibilis est in omni re"</note>, Wisdom 12. And the Apostle has: *From Him, in Him, and through Him are all things, to whom be praise and honor* <note>Romans 11:36</note>. And elsewhere: *GOD created all things through Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Creauit DEVS omnia per Iesum Christum"</note>, Ephesians 3:9. And elsewhere: *GOD the father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all* <note>original: "DEVS pater omnium, qui super omnes & per omnia & in omnibus nobis"</note>, Ephesians 4:6. And elsewhere: *GOD gives life to all things* <note>original: "DEVS viuificat omnia"</note>, 1 Timothy 6. And elsewhere: *God works all things in everyone* <note>original: "Deus operatur omnia in omnibus"</note>, 1 Corinthians 12. And elsewhere: *In GOD himself we live and move and have our being* <note>original: "In DEO ipso viuimus mouemur & sumus"</note>, Acts 17:28; as one of the poets said.

It is clearer than light from these things that a ray of divinity is in every thing, as without it existence is impossible, nor can a thing be brought from potentiality into act. In truth, a thing is nothing, but only seems to be what it is not, without that divine power which is the only truth, inhabiting every thing centrally. But that which appears commonly and in external form is not reality, but exists in creatures in the place of a false image; in the absence of truth it will vanish into smoke and be swallowed by darkness—its illusory parent—and turned into nothing, that is, deformity. Such is the difference between the acts of GOD and the Devil: the latter's act is illusory, appearing to be but is not, the work indeed of the prince of darkness; while the former's is true, infallible, and seen by none but the chosen, yet truly exists: the work surely of the prince and the source of light.

It is clear from what has been said that without the presence of truth (which is GOD alone) no creation occurs, but all is void and empty. Rather, His infinite rays, like angels, brought forth infinite things varying in species and nature according to the will of the one who ordered and emitted them: namely, stars differing among themselves in species and beauty, as well as in quality and property, in the starry heaven or ether; and animals, plants, and minerals among terrestrial things; and <term>meteors</term> <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> differing among themselves, both in the kingdom of light and that of darkness. Finally, just as we have said with the Platonists that universal wisdom or the emanation of divine brightness is the form and, as it were, the soul of the universal world-spirit in general, so each of its rays or breaths is the life-giving form <term>forma vivifica</term> of any particular thing in its species. And although this splendid wisdom in general, and any of its rays in particular, is invisible and hidden in its nature, yet we gather this uncreated nature through its effects: for (as Holy Scripture bears witness) we contemplate GOD in His works. Hence Plato calls [wisdom] the invisible but uncreated son <note>The Latin uses the masculine "filium" (son), though Wisdom is traditionally feminine ("filia"). This likely refers to the Logos or Word.</note> of GOD, while he calls the sun visible but created. Hence the Psalmist says: *Jehovah GOD is a Sun, giving life and glory* <note>original: "Iehoua DEVS est Sol, vitam & gloriam dans"</note>, Psalm 84:11. And elsewhere: *If you light my lamp, Jehovah my GOD, you will make my darkness shining* <note>original: "Si tu illustras lucernam meam, Iehoua DEVS meus splendentes efficies tenebras meas"</note>, Psalm 18:28; that is, if you inspire my soul with your luminous spirit, etc. Regarding this invisibility of the spirit, the wise man speaks thus: *Wisdom is drawn from hidden places, it is concealed from the eyes of all the living, and it lies hidden even from the birds of the heaven* <note>original: "Trahitur sapientia de occultis, abscondita est ab oculis omnium viuentium, volucres quoque cæli latet"</note>, Job 28.

From which it is clear that it is hidden in this world with respect to its essence, but is manifested to us through its effects.

To these testimonies of the sacred text, some Philosophers (deep observers into the mysteries of nature) seem to agree. For Zoroaster and Heraclitus of Ephesus maintained that nature was fire...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the "Spirit of Wisdom" acting as the life-force of the universe. Section I. Portal IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...a certain **invisible fire**, from which they acknowledge all things were born. It is as if they had understood that Spirit of the Lord (which is a fiery love) when it moved over the waters, imparting to them a certain fiery vigor and, as it were, their very Being. For this reason, the world was called a **living creature** <note>original: "mundus est dictus animal"; a reference to the 'Anima Mundi' or World Soul, a concept where the universe itself is alive.</note> by some, who made the sun its heart; similarly, they called the stars living beings, and understood the souls of all particular things in the world to be participants in the divine mind. They declared, not without reason, that these souls were rays or sparks emanating from that universal luminous nature. For this cause, they recognized that a soul presides over every single thing, and consequently **Democritus** and **Orpheus**, along with many of the **Pythagoreans**, were of the opinion that "all things are full of gods." To these they assigned divine honors, dedicated sacrifices and prayers, and venerated them with various forms of worship.

Furthermore, they traced all such souls back to a single **soul of the world**, and consequently referred all gods back to a single **Jupiter**. From this source proceeded all the errors of the heathens in their adoration; from here, I have no doubt, the fictions of the Poets, demonic sacrifices, and sacrilegious offerings emanated. Thus the land of Egypt worshipped and adored certain animals and other monsters and portents. But concerning these various kinds of Idolatry—where the creature is worshipped instead of the creator—the scriptures speak everywhere: namely, concerning the profane worship of stars, demons, men, and others of that kind.

In this, therefore, those Philosophers were deceived: that they did not distinguish the simple uncreated light (that is, the creating nature) from the moist created nature. Instead, they considered the created light—that is, the whole illuminated moist nature, namely the **Angel** or "**Alterity**" (as the **Cabalists** <term>Cabalistæ: Practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) whose ideas were heavily integrated into Western Hermeticism.</term> have it)—and not that **Unity** which preceded it. Hence some of them said fire was God, others air; some made the earth divinity, others water, and so on.

Yet truly, in saying that "all things are full of gods"—or rather, animated and filled with sparks of divinity, all of which they referred to a single Jupiter—or that all things are endowed with luminous souls which they held to have a relation to the single soul of the world; in this they do not seem to differ from the sense of the Hebrew Doctors, nor even from that of holy scripture. For **Rabbi Breseth** <note>Likely referring to the author of a commentary on Bereshit (Genesis), or perhaps a corruption of a name like Rabbi Bahya.</note> says that the creator daily creates a host of angels, which others call "forms," inasmuch as they are formal substances with which the entire sphere of things that can be born and perish is filled without number. Concerning these Angelic forms, the ***Gate of Light*** <note>original: "Porta lucis"; referring to the 'Sha'are Orah', a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</term> has this to say: *From the earth all the way to the firmament there is no empty place, but everything is full of forms; some of them pure, some capable of grace and mercies, and below there are many foul, harmful, and tempting images, etc.* From which he seems to hint that all forms, both good and evil, are like angels; but of these, we speak elsewhere.

However, let us see that while all these forms in the world are like sparks of divinity and rays of the one spirit, assigned with various properties and images for either the preservation of life or its destruction—as is sufficiently explained in the divine properties of the **Sephirotic Tree** <term>Arbori sephiroticæ: The Tree of Life in Kabbalah, representing the ten attributes/emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself.</term> in the writings—nevertheless, all these pure forms or rays of divinity are no less to be divided from their fullness of essence than solar rays are from the Sun. And although by the divine will they are enclosed in various dark tabernacles, both foul and pure, to execute His various commands, they themselves—as **sparks of truth**—will ultimately return to the fountain of unity from which they went forth. Concerning this matter, the Apostle speaks thus: *GOD will be all in all, when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father.* (1 Corinthians 15). Nor does holy scripture seem to distance itself from the aforementioned opinion, in which we have it that *Christ fills all things.* And elsewhere: *GOD, not being in need of anything, gives to all life and breath and all things* (Acts 17). And elsewhere: *In GOD himself we live and move and have our being* (Acts 17:28). And the wise man gives the reason for this thing, since, he says, *the incorruptible spirit of GOD is in every thing* (Wisdom 12:1), which in another place he calls a sincere emanation or flow of the brightness of almighty GOD, and the whiteness of eternal light, which vivifies all things (Wisdom 7).

We conclude, therefore, that it is certain that the life and being of anyone is from GOD, and is like a **fiery impression** from the character or divine seal of the Word (which the Cabalists call ***Emeth*** <note>Hebrew for 'Truth'.</note>) or a ray from the shining Word, which is more abundant and flowing in one creature than in another: for example, in the sun of heaven and in the Man of earth. Whence the Evangelist says: *In the Word was life, and this life was the light of men.* And of another it is said, *He adorned the heavens with his spirit.* And for this reason also it is said that *GOD saw all things created by Him were good* (Genesis 1): that is, insofar as they participated in the divine essence, which is alone goodness and truth, as the sacred scriptures testify.

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

## CHAPTER XII.

->On the Void and the Fullness.<-

Here we consider it to be of no small value to explain to you what that **void** <note>original: "vacuum"</note> is—which is so avoided by nature—and what is meant by **fullness** <note>original: "plenum"</note>, as the solution to this doubt seems especially relevant and necessary to our present purpose. For the fathers of the Philosophers, as well as those most skilled in Theosophy who adhere to the sacred scriptures, have said that this **Void** is **Nothing**. **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus"; a legendary figure from late antiquity credited with writings on alchemy, magic, and philosophy.</note> calls this a **horrible Shadow**, destitute of all form; the **Cabalists** <note>Scholars of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) who interpreted the spiritual structure of the universe.</note> call it a **potential Principle** looking toward nothingness. **Plato**, in his *Timaeus*, says it is a thing perceptible without the senses, and barely believable by a sort of spurious reasoning, making it out to be like a mere dream. And **Augustine** says: *“When I conceive of something formless, I first understand nothing before I understood it, just as darkness is seen by seeing nothing, and silence is heard by hearing nothing,”* from which he seems to compare it to **Darkness** and **silence**. **Job** says: *“That GOD stretches the North over the empty and the void, and hangs the earth over nothing. Job 26:7.”* And elsewhere: *“He reveals the foundations out of the darkness, and brings out the shadow of death into the light. Job 12:22.”* By these words he seems to argue that **Emptiness**, the **Void**, **Nothingness**, **Darkness**, and the **Shadow** are one and the same thing. They are called **Emptiness** and **Void** because all fullness comes from **GOD**; yet indeed **GOD**, the parent of light, had not yet shone upon the world. Therefore, insofar as the **first matter** of the world was destitute of all grace and deprived of goodness, it was called Emptiness and Void—indeed, even darkness and the shadow of death—insofar as it entirely lacked the rays of life. Thus the earth was called empty and void, and it was said that darkness was upon the face of the deep before the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters. But after the appearance of the said spirit, it was said: *“And GOD called the dry land earth, and GOD saw that it was good, and it brought forth tender grass and seed of every kind, and trees yielding fruit, etc. Genesis 1.”* <margin>☩</margin> Thus now the earth, once empty and void, has been made full of divine grace, whereby it is rendered not empty, but fertile; not void, but filled on all sides with divine fire and incorruptible rays. *“The hand of the almighty created the world from formless matter, Wisdom 11:17.”* <note>The text cites verse 12, but this passage is typically found in Wisdom of Solomon 11:17.</note> By “hand,” he indicates the word or spirit emanating from His mouth. Hence the Apostle **Peter** says: *“The heavens were of old, and the earth out of water and through water, by means of the word, 2 Peter 3.”*—that is, by the holy emanation. Through this light (says **John**), the world was made; indeed, where the rays of that informing divinity are absent, there is the greatest void—that is, the absence of complete form. And this is why the void seems so horrible in the realm of nature, for every thing desires above all else to be **informed** <term>informed: the process of a spiritual or formal essence entering matter to give it shape, purpose, and existence.</term> by a natural appetite. Therefore, not only an individual nature, but also that universal parent of all individual things, is accustomed to abhor and avoid deformity. From this it is clear that all fullness in nature comes from the divine abundance, which therefore fills all things in the world by its power, so that from nothingness and emptiness, something actually formal and relatively existing may be made. This gift of existence they received from **Christ**, or **Wisdom**, whence it is written *“that Christ fills all things, Ephesians 4.”* And elsewhere: *“The holy spirit of discipline fills the whole world, Wisdom 1.”* It follows that unless **GOD** had filled all things in the world, there would be void and nothingness in the world; but because He himself created all things by His presence, it is necessary that nothing in the world exists as a void.

# CHAPTER XIII.

->*That it was the will of GOD that the fixed stars should be created in their own sphere, and that they were brought into being in an instant.*<-

We have stated in the preceding sections that God—acting not out of any necessity, but by His own voluntary and personal impulse, moved by mercy—created the heavens, the earth, and even the stars in the sky, along with the rest of the things in <note>The sentence continues onto the next page with the word "earth."</note>

...numbered [among the things] he created on earth, and this is confirmed by the testimony of the royal prophet <note>referring to King David, traditional author of the Psalms</note>, from whom we have: 
> Give thanks to the Lord of lords, who made the heavens in wisdom, for His mercy is eternal; who established the earth upon the waters, for His mercy is eternal. Who made the great lights, for His mercy is eternal: the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night, for His mercy is eternal. Psalm 135. <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 136.</note>

This is assigned in its specific nature to the first Sephirotic numbering <note>referring to the *Sephirot*, the ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</note>, namely **Ehieh** <note>Hebrew: "I AM"</note>, which is the name presiding over **Kether** <note>Hebrew: "the Crown," the highest Sephirah</note>; and it is also ascribed to fatherhood and mercy. From this, we understand the reason why God, who is free in Himself, willed to create the world with its creatures: namely, out of His pure kindness and mercy toward formless things. That is, out of empty things and those veiled in darkness or deadly shadows, He brought forth good things adorned with divine beauty. He infused into every creature a living soul or a spark from His own luminous source, by which it might live and exist in its own being. For this reason, creatures first desire to return great thanks to Him, and then proceed to perform the duty assigned to each by God and to faithfully carry out the commands of the Creator. Regarding this thanksgiving, we read in the royal Psalmist:
> Praise God from the heavens, praise Him all His angels, all His powers. Praise Him, Sun and Moon, praise Him all stars and light. Praise Him, heaven of heavens, and all the waters that are above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord, for He spoke and they were made, He commanded and they were created. Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit or wind of storms, which perform His word, etc. Psalm 148.

Here he runs through all creatures, both terrestrial and aquatic. But to declare the duty of the stars, we say with the Prophet in the place cited before that He made the Sun to have dominion over the day, and the Moon and other stars—both fixed and wandering <note>planets</note>—to have power over the night, and this because of His benevolence. As for the substance or consistency of the stars, both fixed and wandering, it appears to be exceedingly clean and pure, the better to receive their luminous forms from the Creator; this is also confirmed by these words:
> The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God, much less men. Job 25:5.

From this speech, it appears that they are indeed very pure, though not absolutely pure so as to seem so in the sight of God. Yet, if they were not very pure and polished in their substances, they would be least capable of receiving such splendid forms; for as Plato rightly says, *form is given by the Creator according to the merit of the matter.* But truly, since their substance varies in purity, it is said by the Apostle:
> That star differs from star in clarity. 1 Corinthians 15.

It remains now to discuss in a few words the property and influence of the fixed stars. Among these we read that, as God extended the heavens, He alone made **Orion**, the **Pleiades** or **Hyades**, and the stars of the inner chambers of the South. Job 9:9. <note>The text cites Job 32:4, but the content matches Job 9:9.</note> And elsewhere, mention is made of the path of **Arcturus** or the belt of **Orion**. Job 38. The Prophet also speaks thus:
> It is God who makes Arcturus and Orion, turns darkness into morning, and changes day into night; Jehovah is His name. Amos 5.

Our great God, great in His powers and whose wisdom is beyond numbering, counts all these stars of the firmament; He counts as many as there are stars and calls them by their own names, as David testifies in Psalm 147. To these He undoubtedly assigned names based on their various properties, thereby declaring that many hidden properties reside in them beyond the common and vulgar one—namely, that they have dominion over the night. For it is not likely that He would have assigned them such various figures in splendor and shape if they did not have other faculties over creatures. This is especially true since the Prophet adds: *He calls as many as there are by name, our great Lord, great in many strengths or virtues, whose wisdom is without number.* From this, one argues that He who is great in virtues and of innumerable wisdom also assigned various virtues to the innumerable stars of the firmament. This can also be understood through these words:
> Do you know the laws of Heaven? Do you set its dominion upon the earth? Job 38.

By these words, the Creator seems to indicate that Heaven, through its "army" <note>the stars</note>, is accustomed to work upon the earth in various ways. Hence, by some, Heaven is most aptly likened to a husband and the Earth to a wife; and consequently, every particular star of the heaven or firmament has a specific power of influencing particulars, whether animals, vegetables, or minerals. For example, it has been handed down and proven by experience itself that the **Polar Star**—called **Alracuba** by the Egyptians—having the nature of Saturn and Venus, attracts the magnet stone <note>lodestone</note> to itself, as is seen in the nautical needle. And that same magnet attracts iron to itself, provided that a diamond <note>original: "adamas"</note> is not present; for the diamond by its presence hinders the influences of the said star. And **Cecco d'Ascoli** <note>original: "Cichus Esculanus," a 13th-century astronomer</note>, writing on the sphere in the place where he speaks of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, affirms that each of the twelve signs receives its particular and special name from the nature and property of some animal on earth, the nature of one of which seems to symbolize the nature of the other. And **Moses the Arab** <note>referring to Moses Maimonides</note> says that every living thing claims a peculiar star for itself in heaven, from which at every moment it draws and receives influence to protect and sustain its essence; and he says this was done by divine command and will. Thus, the stars in the body of **Aries** in the sky have a relation to such animals on earth, and the **Scorpio** of the sky to the scorpion of the earth, and so with the rest. For this reason, **Diodorus Siculus**, speaking generally, admits quite sensibly that the lower world is ruled by the higher, and the lower world is continuous with that higher one. This also seems to be confirmed by the words of the **Hebrew Doctors**, saying that all lower things are representative of higher things, and that *as it is done below, so it is acted above*; and in this, all those most skilled in the **Cabalistic** science seem to agree. And **Aristotle** himself says that those who think that the shining and glorious bodies of heaven...

...the heavens signify nothing, as written in the book *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "De cœlo & Mundo," a major work by Aristotle</note>. And elsewhere he says, "He who asserts that nature does not act for a purpose, removes the concern of God for lower things," in *Physics*, Book 2. But Hippocrates, in his book *On Fleshes* <note>original: "De carnibus," a medical treatise</note> near the end, describes these things most excellently in this manner of speech: "Regarding celestial and sublime things, I believe I should say nothing, except insofar as I will demonstrate that humans and the other animals that live on earth are born and have their beginning and origin from there, and that the soul is from heaven, and that pain, sickness, death, and finally whatever good or evil is in man, proceeds from heaven." We say, therefore, that just as the Angelic world is a <term>type</term><note>A symbolic model or foreshadowing</note> of that divine world, so too the celestial world is an image of that angelic one. Thus, as the celestial world receives this influx immediately from the <term>archetypal world</term><note>The original "blueprint" of the universe in God's mind</note> and pours it into the heavens, so also the celestial realm is the likeness of the terrestrial one. Consequently, its "army" <note>the stars and planets</note> immediately directs its influences into the creatures of the earth that are most conformed to them in nature and disposition.

We conclude, therefore, with the sacred Priest in the book of 2 Esdras, chapter 16, that the stars were founded in the word or wisdom of the Lord, who also knows the number of the stars, and assigned to each of them a name most fitting to its property; and that each of them, by its own property, has a regard for terrestrial creatures. Through this mediation, it continually pours its influences into creatures similar to itself under the direction of the <term>Intelligences</term><note>Angelic beings believed to guide the movements of the planets</note> who preside over them and who, by divine will and command, take care of lower things.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### First Part.

### *Regarding the creation of the wandering stars in general, and specifically concerning the Sun and its creation, dignity, utility, motion, and obedience toward its Creator.*

In our discourse *On the physical subject of the macrocosm*, where we spoke quite amply on the origin of the fixed stars, I proposed a certain doubt: namely, whether the fixed stars were created on the fourth day of creation along with the <term>wandering stars</term><note>The "erratic" stars, or planets, which move independently of the fixed constellations</note>, or at least on the second day. We expressed our reasons there, by which we proved it likely that they were established on the second day of creation. Indeed, if we consider the orders of the <term>Sephirot</term><note>The ten attributes or emanations of God in Kabbalah</note> (or the "numberings" of the Kabbalists) and the logic of their influences, we will perceive that just as the influx of <term>Kether</term><note>Hebrew: "The Crown," the highest Sephirah</note>—which is the Crown or first numbering—occurs through the Seraphic order of angels into the <term>Primum Mobile</term><note>The "First Moveable" sphere, the outermost sphere of the universe in traditional cosmology</note>, so <term>Chokmah</term><note>Hebrew: "Wisdom," the second Sephirah</note> flows through the order of Cherubim into the starry heaven. If that heaven were empty and without stars, it would receive those influences from Chokmah in vain. But we shall briefly move to the production of the planets (or wandering stars) and their creation within their orbs.

It is most certain, and must be granted without controversy, that all stars are created by God Himself, as we have confirmed by many testimonies of Holy Scripture. "The Sun," says Moses, "the Moon, the stars, and other things, God created for the service of all nations under heaven." (Deuteronomy 4:19). However, how each of these stars has an Intelligence presiding over it, how they receive influxes from the "shining gates" called the Sephirot, what the duties of said angels are (both in the ethereal heaven and the elementary region), and who is their Prince, we shall discuss copiously in the second member of this part.

In this place, however, we shall chiefly cast our discourse upon that most noble creature among the celestial bodies: the king of stars, the corporeal Emperor of the heavens, the heart of the firmament, and the clearest eye of the world—namely, the visible Sun. So that we may arrive at a better understanding of it, we shall first offer a few words concerning the invisible and uncreated Sun, which is the very life and light of this created sun.

### CHAPTER XIV.

#### Part Two.

### Concerning the Uncreated Sun.

Mercurius Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, Hermes Trismegistus, whose writings blended Egyptian and Greek wisdom and were highly influential in Renaissance occultism</note> seems to acknowledge that the whole and entire world, constituted from the elements, proceeds and is led by Him who is abundantly full of the fertility of all things, of both one and the other sex, containing in Himself all power of generating, without any other assistance. Whence He is called PAN by the poets, as if the Total and Universal <note>original: "Totum & Vniuersum"; the name Pan was often etymologically linked to the Greek word for "all" (pan)</note>, whom the Arcadians—thinking him to be the sun—adored as the true GOD. Their error, indeed, seemed to be this: that they falsely accepted and adored the creature instead of the creator, and the visible and created sun instead of that invisible and uncreated one—that is, the royal palace instead of the King of Kings, who built it and inhabited it centrally. Regarding this uncreated and invisible sun, not only the wiser among the Philosophers but even the sacred scriptures have made rich and copious mention. For among those more skilled in Philosophy, Plato (indicating that admirable harmony which exists between that sun of the world and the one of the highest order) calls the mundane sun the shining son of the highest Good <note>original: "summi Boni," a Platonic concept of the ultimate source of all reality and truth</note>, not the first son, but the second, by means of whom we arrive at the knowledge of the first; for in that glorious work [we see] the glory of the creator...
