<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Sun, specifically distinguishing between the spiritual "Archetypal Sun" and the physical "Created Sun." Having previously outlined the Sun’s utility and dignity, the author now explores how divine glory is manifested through the solar vessel according to both classical philosophers and mystical traditions like the Kabbalah.</meta>

### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...let us behold His glory. And this is why Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who wrote extensively on the divine names and celestial hierarchies.</note> (agreeing with the Platonists in this matter) would say, not ineptly or without consideration, that the visible sun is the statue and image of the invisible God; and Iamblichus, <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized theurgy and the divine nature of the cosmos.</note> supporting him, called it the **Image of Divine Intelligence.** Hence the wise man says: *The sun, as it shines, looks upon all things, and its work is full of the glory of the Lord, Ecclesiasticus 42.* <note>original: "Sol illuminans per omnia respexit, & gloria Domini plenum est opus eius."</note> This glory is the divine essence itself, covered and veiled in luminous garments; which is why the Royal Prophet <note>King David.</note> also said *that God is clothed with light as with a garment, and in another place, that He has set His tabernacle in the sun, Psalm 19.* <note>original: "quod Deus sit lumine indutus quasi vestimento, & in alio loco, quod posuerit tabernaculum suum in sole."</note> In this discourse, one should not think that the Uncreated Sun is physically enclosed within the created one, since He is both within all things and outside them. Rather, He is said to have built the sun as a palace and dwelt in it, insofar as this Divine Wisdom—this **Archetypal Sun** flowing abundantly from the luminous gate of <term>Tiphereth</term> <note>A Hebrew term meaning "Beauty" or "Adornment"; it is the sixth Sephirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, often associated with the sun and the heart.</note> (that is, Grace and Beauty) and filling the world on every side—selected by its power the solar mass in this world. It prepared and purified that mass to be a vessel worthy of receiving its divine rays copiously. Of this, the wise man speaks: *The sun, when it appears, proclaims at its rising: a wonderful vessel, the work of the Most High, Ecclesiasticus 43.* <note>original: "Sol in aspectu annuntians in exitu vas admirabile opus excelsi."</note> Therefore, in this visible palace, the glory of the Divine Sun—the Word of the Lord and the true light of the world by which the world was made—appears visibly and most abundantly. It is beheld by the creatures of the world most clearly in this solar palace, because of all the conspicuous bodies in this world, it is the purest, most refined, and most worthy to receive such an admirable form. From this it is manifest that because this solar vessel is capable of such a preeminent and excellent form, it is more worthy than all other bodies in the world; for, as Plato testifies, form is granted in perfection according to the merit of the matter.

It is certain, therefore, that this Divine Sun is God Himself, primarily illuminating all things both secretly and manifestly, of whom King David speaks: *God is a Sun giving grace and glory, Psalm 84:11.* <note>original: "Deus est Sol gratiam & gloriam dans."</note> From Him, the material sun receives its vast power of life, with which it not only illuminates and warms all things in this visible world with heat, but also rains down the act of generation and vivification upon lower things by the divine will, and does so liberally. We also have this explored and confirmed by the precise words of the Prophet: *In the light of Jehovah shall we see light, Psalm 36:9.* <note>original: "In luce Iehouæ videbimus lucem."</note> This speech is not only to be understood of the hidden and invisible light, but also of the visible light, as if the creature had said: "In the light of Him who set His tabernacle in the sun, we shall see light." Later, we shall discuss the manner in which this invisible light is rendered visible through the properties of this visible vessel. To confirm the origin of its life-giving property, the Psalmist speaks thus: *With thee is the fountain of life, Psalm 36:9.* <note>original: "Vitæ fons penes te est."</note> This is to be understood not only of the life of the soul, but also that of the body, according to the sacred page: *God of the soul and the body, the strong God of spirits, the God of all flesh.*

We conclude, therefore, that this sun in the **Archetypal World** is called God, illuminating all darkness; or the Word of the Lord from whom all things come, in whom is life, and who is the true light of the world (John 1). Or it is Wisdom, which is the brightness of the eternal light of the Almighty and, compared to the Sun, is far more excellent in light. When descending by emanation into the **Angelic World**, it is called the "first created wisdom," and by the Kabbalists the great Angel <term>Metatron</term>, <note>In Jewish mysticism, Metatron is often seen as the highest of angels, the "Prince of the Countenance" who serves as a mediator between the divine and the mundane.</note> by whose rays the Seraphic region of angels is illuminated and animated with fiery love. In the **Celestial World**, it descends from *Tiphereth* into the "heart of heaven" and appears visibly in the solar organ. From this it is clear that in the **Ideal World** (or the Heaven of Heavens), this sun reflects its ardor into itself, in which state it is absolutely formal, without any regard for created matter. In the Angelic World, it appears to angelic and purely spiritual bodies by putting on the clear spirit of the intellectual heaven with its invisible rays; such light is not at all subject to physical eyes. But in the **Ethereal World**, it appears visibly and joyfully as a messenger to creatures, driving away the darkness of night. It is infused and received primarily in a clear place (into which it is immediately poured through the ministry of the Archangel **Michael**) and also in other places, appearing by reflection in both the planetary and elemental regions. Finally, this Divine Sun plunges itself even deeper into the multitude of matter, for He foretold that He would *dwell in the thick darkness*—whether in the dense cloud which He sometimes makes His pavilion (2 Chronicles 6:1 and Job 22:14) or in the fleshy house of man, which is the temple of the Holy Spirit, or the earth itself, which is said to "bring forth a Savior." The Uncreated Sun dwells centrally in such dark places within that sun which the mystical Philosophers called the **Central Sun**, <note>A concept in Hermetic and Alchemical philosophy representing the spiritual fire at the heart of the earth or the center of being, mirroring the celestial sun.</note> which maintains a continuous relationship with the celestial sun, just as the celestial sun does with the supercelestial ones, since they are not at all distinguished in essence.

From this, therefore, arose the error of those in Arcadia, Scythia, and Tartary who falsely adored the visible and created sun as God. Indeed, among the Egyptians, the Sun was held in such reverent worship that not only was a magnificent temple dedicated to it, but also one of the five notable cities of Egypt. Thus it is written that the Babylonian king destroyed the houses and statues in Egypt (Jeremiah 43), and elsewhere one of the five cities of Egypt is called the *City of the Sun* (Isaiah 19). <note>Heliopolis.</note> Their error, he says, is egregious because they celebrated with blind and darkness-shrouded worship the garment instead of the one clothed, the palace instead of the lord, the body subject to change instead of the immortal soul, the thing illuminated instead of the illuminating essence—and finally, the creature instead of the Creator. But if anyone were to look upon that invisible sun, which dwells in the "tent of the sun," with the eyes of the heart and mind, and contemplate the Creator within the solar creature, he would not be deceived in his adoration. For to venerate an angel in place of **JEHOVAH** is a sin—which is why the Angel did not permit John to adore him (Revelation 19:10)—but one may adore the name of Jehovah within the Angel...

<meta>This page continues the theological and philosophical exploration of the Sun as a divine instrument. Having established that God "clothed" Himself in light, the author now explains how the Israelites, and later Christians, viewed the Sun not as a god, but as a "visible sanctuary" for the Creator's power. It moves from the Sun's spiritual significance to its eventual role in the apocalypse and the final purification of the world.</meta>

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...and the Israelites were commanded to revere Him with every effort. *My angel (says Jehovah) will not bear your rebellions, because my name is in him, Exodus 23.* <note>original: "Non feret angelus meus... defectiones vestras, quoniam nomen meum est in eo."</note> This is to say: I wish for you to obey his voice, because my Word—which is your creator—is in him. That is, "do this, because I am in him," or "I will be present," whom alone you must adore and no other. Therefore, it is not to honor the sun that the wise man speaks these words: *It is necessary to precede the sun for your blessing and to adore you at the dawn of light, Wisdom 16:28.* <note>The text cites Chapter 10, but this passage is traditionally found in Wisdom of Solomon 16:28.</note> Nor is it for the sun's sake that the Prophet Daniel looked toward the eastern region while praying, or that it is the custom and habit of Christians to pour out our prayers with our faces turned toward the east. Rather, it is so that we may worship Him with all our might—He who gave form to so excellent a vessel and who established His tabernacle in this **polished vessel** which He chose as His instrument. He did this so that from it, as if from a **visible sanctuary of life**, He might rain down life, multiplication, and visible light upon the world and its parts. In this way, the Creator offers solace and joy both to opaque bodies (to whom invisible light is least apparent) and to the soul sustained by invisible light. Furthermore, by this means, He reveals Himself and manifests the grace of His essence to both earthly and celestial beings, to both bodies and spirits. Thus He is rightly called the *God of soul and body, the God of all spirits, and the God of all flesh.*

Finally, this sun is called in the highest heaven **Ehieh**, <note>Hebrew for "I Am," the name of God revealed to Moses.</note> the Father or God giving grace and glory; in the Empyrean <note>The highest part of heaven, thought by ancients to be composed of pure fire or light.</note> it is **Wisdom**, clearer than the sun; and plunging itself deeper into the matter of the world, it "placed its tabernacle in the sun," flashes in the thick clouds, and speaks with the voice of thunder, *Revelation 22.* In Christ as man, it is called the **bright morning star**; *A star (says the Holy Page) shall rise out of Jacob, Numbers 24.* And elsewhere, the *Sun of Justice, Malachi 4,* who is promised to rise for those who fear His name, with healing in His wings—which is why He is called Jesus. Furthermore, Jesus Christ is called the "Sun" in many places of the Scriptures because of the fullness of His light, life, and all good things; hence He is the **Word**, the light of the world shining in the darkness, *John 1.* But I wish for us to come to the examination of these things, or rather, to the **Lydian stone**. <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here used metaphorically as a test of truth.</note> The wise philosophers say that a thing is usually finished in the same state in which it had its beginning. Thus, if we wish to seek and prove the beginning of the mundane sun, we shall perceive it best from its end. For in the holy writings we have this: *Thy sun shall no more go down; neither shall thy moon withdraw itself: for the Lord shall be thine everlasting light in Jerusalem; Isaiah 60.* And with this passage agrees that of John: *And the city has no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God lightened it, and the Lamb is the light thereof: and the nations shall walk in its light, and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into it, Revelation 21:23.* By these passages it is indicated that in the final days of the world, this celestial sun will strip off its dense and dark garments and will appear exactly as it truly is. For there is no truth except in the true light of the world, which reveals all figments <note>The word "figment" here refers to the outward, temporary physical forms of the created world.</note> and reduces them to nothing by the "Lydian" test. For by such an examination, the moon in the final days will have the brightness of the sun as it lays aside its created garments; and the truly central and divine Sun, by stripping off its dense and created clothing, will exist in its naked and clear nature. It will provide light for the blessed servants of God in their purification and, as it were, their resurrection—not differently (but in a far more exalted degree) than the common sun visible in the sky. Indeed, we can clearly gather this from these words of the Prophet: *The light of the moon (he says) shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, Isaiah 30:26.* That is, seven times as bright. And the Apostle speaks to this same sense, saying: *There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars, 1 Corinthians 15.* From these we may conclude that in the end, everything that is a figment shall be abolished and thrust down into the vast abyss of Nothingness; however, whatever is of the simple truth (with which God filled the entire universe) shall all return to its source of unity through a fiery purification. The Holy Bible seems to confirm these things said above: for it is said that God fills all things; *that from God and through God are all things, Romans 11;* that *God is the Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all, Ephesians 4:6;* and that *God works all in all, 1 Corinthians 12.* Since He Himself is the only truth, it is necessary that nothing be true unless it is of His essence. Wherefore we say finally that just as God was the beginning of solar beauty—that is, if His glory is found in the hidden excellence of the solar creature—once the figment is laid aside, it will be far more beautiful, just as it was in the beginning. This means in its first emanation, when it was called **Hochma** <note>Hebrew for "Wisdom," often personified in mystical texts as the first tool of creation.</note> or Divine Wisdom, which is the brightness of the glory of the Almighty. So it was in the beginning, and its beginning shall be justified by its end, inasmuch as He is the **Alpha and Omega**, *Revelation 1,* the beginning and the end. Hence the Apostle says, *God shall be all in all when Christ has obtained the kingdom of the Father, 1 Corinthians 15.* And as He said elsewhere, *When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself,* that is, everything that is of purity and truth; for nothing is to be considered as "nothing" in its mere nature, nor as void and empty.

But let us move rapidly to the nature of our created sun—that is, the solar creature.

## CHAPTER XIV.
### Third Portion.
### Concerning the creation of the celestial and visible Sun, and those things which necessarily follow from it.

We believe it will now be worth the effort to treat the created sun. *Let there be (says God) lights in the expanse of heaven to bring light upon the earth, and it was so; and God made two great lights, the greater light to rule the day, etc. Genesis 1.* In this speech, it is certain that the Lord ordained the fabrication of the sun, and put His will into execution by means of the Word, according to that saying of the royal Psalmist: *By the Word of the...*

The author continues to use the "Macrocosm" framework to explain how physical light reflects divine reality.</meta>

Sect. I. Port. IV. Part. II. Lib. IV. Membr. I.

...the heavens were made firm, and all their powers or hosts by the breath of his mouth, Psalm 33. <note>original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt coeli, & spiritu ab ore eius omnes virtutes seu exercitus eorum, Ps.33."</note> And Esdras, 그hat eminent high priest, denotes this with these express words: *the stars are established in the word of the Lord, Esdras 4:16.* <note>This likely refers to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Esdras in some numbering systems).</note> But truly, to treat the particular manner of this creature’s origin, and to immerse oneself in its mysteries, will seem somewhat difficult for a man, unless we look deeply into the holy scriptures with <term>lyncean eyes</term> <note>Eyes as sharp as those of Lynceus, a mythological Argonaut famous for his keen sight.</note>. Therefore, regarding its matter, it is certain that it possesses the consistency of the clearest, most polished, and highly spiritual earth. This emerged from the darkness after being struck by the bright rays of divine wisdom toward the center of the world (as was declared in our history regarding the physical history of the Macrocosm). With the help of divine rays, it was exalted in the middle of the heavens in the manner of a spindle <note>original: "more fusi"</note>, and was illuminated on all sides by the rays of divine grace and beauty. Thus the body of Adam was formed from chosen clay, animated and quickened by the breath of life and the bright spirit of the Almighty, and formed in the image of the Almighty. Thus the earth was said to bring forth the Savior, and our Savior, rising from the tomb—emerging from death or the dark abyss of the lethal shadow like the morning star—ascended into heaven, clothed on all sides by the celestial spirit. Why then should the created sun refuse the earth as the parent of its consistency? For the sun is the condensed spirit of celestial nature, in whose center the uncreated light of the world placed its tabernacle, as the royal Psalmist teaches us. Furthermore, we see that just as our Savior rose on the third day from the shadows of death and the whirlpool of the grave, so indeed after the third day in creation—and not before—was the fixation of the earth in the center of the world or its suspension over nothingness achieved. No mention was made of the creation of the greater light until then, from which it is likely that the sun ascended from the earth, having cast off its dark filth, as if from a tomb; for in it is the tabernacle of the invisible and divine sun, which holds itself toward that most polished body in the place of a most bright soul. But however it may be, we read that this ethereal matter is so involved in a spherical manner, in a consistency so pure, that it is called by the wise man a *vessel, the admirable work of the most High. Ecclesiasticus 43.* And in what is announced elsewhere, *The Sun, the work of the Lord, is full of his glory, Ecclesiasticus 42.* And elsewhere, *that he placed a tabernacle in it.* It is clear that it is a vessel in nature, very clean and polished; for otherwise it would not be capable of a form so pure and simple, which is usually given according to the merits of the matter. And yet it is impossible, through the entire created spirit, for matter to be given so exquisitely pure that it could merit a form as pure and simple as that divine essence, which is without any stain or impurity. Hence it is written first of the angels and then afterward of the stars, that in respect to the sincere purity of the divine essence they are not pure; in which sense it is written of these very stars: *The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God, Job 25:5.* Regarding those Angels, we read these words: *Behold, in his angels God found wickedness, etc. Job 4:18.* <note>The text cites Job 14:17, but the passage "God finds folly in his angels" is Job 4:18.</note> For it is impossible that the created thing can be made equal in its Being to the essence of the creator. But truly, among all visible bodies, it is certain that the solar substance is the purest; this is declared because the visible glory of God is indicated more to mortals in it than in any other creature of the world. And from this it is said by Augustine, that as much light as something has in itself, so much more of God it seems to claim for itself. Hence also the wise man says of the sun, *The sun illuminating looked upon all things, and his work is full of the glory of the Lord, Ecclesiasticus 42.* From this it is clear that the presence of that divine glory denotes the purity of the subject into which it enters; for in holy scripture we read everywhere that the Holy Spirit does not descend except into a pure spirit or a clean heart—that is, into a purified subject. For such must be the respect between the <term>Groom and the Bride</term>, between <term>Cupid and Psyche</term>, between Christ and the Church, between the mind and the spirit, or there will be no firm bond and union between them.

Hence, therefore, we ought to gather that insofar as the mundane sun is a creature, and like a shadow of the majesty of the <term>archetypal sun</term> <note>The "archetypal sun" refers to the original divine light of God, of which the physical sun is merely a reflection.</note>, it is in no way to be worshiped as God by mortals who are consistent in themselves and not seized by diabolical madness. For this would be to adore the house instead of the master, just as those twenty-five men did who (as Ezekiel witnesses) stood between the porch and the altar with their faces toward the east and adored the rising of the sun, having their backs against the temple of the Lord. Concerning them, God speaks thus to the Prophet: *Is this a light thing, that they should do these abominations which they have done here, because filling the land with iniquity etc. Ezekiel 8:16.* But the sacred page also rejects this in express speech: *You shall not look at the sun, the moon, or the stars, or any thing of the host of heaven, that bowing down you should worship them, Deuteronomy 4.* <note>Deuteronomy 4:19.</note> As if he had said, Jehovah is the only and unique God the creator; to him alone you must offer worship, and not to the images created by him—that is, to the Lord who creates, and not to the servant or minister who is created. The Sun (says the wise man) has the Lord as the one who made it, at whose words it hastened its journey. And elsewhere this is expressly explained in this manner: *The sun, the moon, the stars and other things God created, for service to all nations under heaven.* Therefore he forbade them to be adored and worshiped, as if he had said, I am the creator, therefore the things I have created are not to be adored, but I alone the creator. But how ridiculous would it be to a wise man to revere the servant with honor and not think of the Lord, or to affect the smaller things with praise while rejecting and neglecting the greater? What, I ask, is the body, or the soul, or the informed thing without its form imparting life and glory? Surely nothing—empty, and plainly a deformed and horrendous shadow, as if someone chose the shadow for the true God, but rejected the true subject as nothing. This indeed is the way of the worldly, overwhelmed by darkness and ignorance, choosing things that are seen and are least real, instead of those things which truly are but are least seen, choosing in the manner of the blind. Open therefore, O blind mortals, those eyes which Adam closed on account of his sins, and close your carnal eyes, which in a deceptive manner think they see those things which are not, but truly are not powerful enough to penetrate to those things which are.

On the Efficient Cause of Meteors. 181 <note>The term "Meteors" in this period referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, rainbows, and comets, not just falling stars.</note>

## CHAPTER XV.

### On the Manifold Power and Utility of the Sun.

The primary power of the Sun consists in its light, motion, and heat, just as its secondary power is accustomed to flow from these same effects; we shall therefore speak at somewhat greater length about both, as they are mixed with one another: and first, concerning Light.

As it is certain, and confirmed by what has come before, that GOD is the fountain of light, this primary light made its first manifestation as an act or primary motion. From this was moved the first <term>mobile</term> <note>The "Primum Mobile" or "first moved" sphere in classical astronomy, which imparts motion to all other celestial spheres.</note> of the world—that is, the highest circle of the thin "world-spirit"—by whose motion all the enclosed orbs are also rotated at their edges. Moreover, the effect of this mobility or mobile act is heat; just as, conversely, the sluggish and insensible act of rest is the parent of coldness. And although it is confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Bible that God is always remaining in Himself and not at all subject to change, yet with respect to His wisdom emanating from His lucid fountain, He is "more mobile than all mobile things," *Wisdom of Solomon 7:24* <note>original: "Sap. 7."</note>. By this, it is manifest that He includes all things in His nature—both those that move and those that rest—and that He ordained and procreated darkness as much as light.

We shall say a few things about how and by what reasoning this solar matter receives visible light from the invisible Sun. It was declared previously that the substance of the sun is pure and clear in its nature, so that the vessel and the work might be worthy to receive the rays of so divine a form. But truly, according to the opinion of *Al-Ghazali* <note>original: "Algazel"; a major 11th-century Persian philosopher and theologian.</note> on the nature of mirrors: if the spirit in the sphere receiving the rays is too thin in its consistency, it does not become bright when light is cast upon it—that is, it is not illuminated—because it does not submit to color. Consequently, it is neither colored nor visible. This is also confirmed by *Alhazen* <note>original: "Hatten"; likely referring to Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), the medieval authority on optics.</note> in his *Book of Optics* <note>original: "lib. de aspectibus"</note>, saying that a thing is not visible if it has no color. For (he says) a visible thing exists only according to the light in the thing seen, but visible light occupies only that which is colored. The reason why a subtle and thin spirit is not seen, even in the presence of light, is that it is necessary for the thing seen to offer resistance to the sight. From this, some may conclude that the substance of the sun cannot be entirely pure, clear, and transparent in its being, but that there is a certain opacity—and consequently a dark condition—without which it could not be seen or appear as a bright, colored object. For we see that the image of a thing does not appear at all in clear water, crystal, or pure air for the reasons stated before. To this doubt we respond briefly, using the words of *Al-Ghazali* in the place cited above, by saying that no part of the stellar sphere is an object for the power of sight, nor a receiver and retainer of the sunlight it receives, except for its denser part, which we call the "star" itself. Thus, if the sun's substance (pure and clear as it is) had been thin in its quantitative dimension, no color would appear on its surface, and no spherical shape would be clearly visible. But truly, because it is immense in quantity and of a globular containment, the light renders it more colored the deeper it penetrates. The rays are gathered together into the center of the globe's body; in this way, we see that waters—though they are very pure and clear in their substance, and consequently receive no impression of a luminous object when in small quantities—nevertheless, because of their density and depth, they receive the likenesses of those standing nearby, as experience testifies (and as is read in the story of *Narcissus*). 

We say, therefore, that the deep center of the solar body is the part of the entire body that is primarily "darker." From this it follows that, because of its depth, that place resists the gaze of the lucid spirit looking upon it. Next, the rays dispersed invisibly everywhere through the margins of the spherical body strike together in the center; like a multitude meeting in a single point or unity, this union creates not only a strong reflection (from which comes solar heat) but also visible light that is most pleasant to the sight. Thus, they say that from the gathering of invisible parts of the ether, the visible stellar body is procreated; and even visible clouds are created passively from invisible air, and visible lightning and comets from a more active consistency of the same—indeed, even the flame of earthly fire. Hence it was said by the Apostle that we ought to believe through faith that "visible things were first from things invisible." <note>Hebrews 11:3.</note> Thus also God, putting on a fiery air, is called a "consuming fire," and Wisdom is said to be "brighter than the light of the sun." We see this confirmed also by the practical use of the common burning mirror: by contracting all the solar rays on its circular surface into the unity of its center, it reveals them—moving from an insensible and barely visible nature—into the likeness of a visibly burning fire. And by directing that ray far off through a powerful reflection, it thus destroys houses and towns from a distance with that fire. 

This, therefore, is the reason for visible light of this kind being procreated and contracted in the solar disk from the rays of invisible wisdom. By means of this work, the spiritual light, which is expanded invisibly through the vast spirit of the world, reveals itself visibly in a colored, transparent medium, in order to direct and govern visible bodies in their paths. And certainly, many utilities of this visible light are recounted both from the sacred fountain and by philosophers. For we read written in the holy scriptures that his splendid countenance, and his arrival into the world after the darkness of night, provides joy, solace, and motion to creatures; it drives out light-fleeing spirits and restrains their violence; just as, conversely, his absence inclines them toward sadness, horror, and from motion toward rest and numbness. Thus we read, as we have it in the words of the wise man: "What is brighter than the sun?" *Ecclesiasticus 17:30* <note>original: "Eccl. 17."</note>. So his presence is very pleasing and useful not only to beasts but even to men themselves. "The sun has risen," says the Prophet, "and the young lions are gathered together, etc." *Psalm 104:22*. And else—

Section I, Portion IV, Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...[he will stir] up. When the sun has risen, what does the beast do? what does man? <note>This is a paraphrase of Psalm 104:22–23: "The sun arises... then man goes out to his work."</note> And in another place we have: *You commanded the splendor of the sun on the fourth day, to serve the man who was to come,* <note>original: "Solis splendorem imperasti quarto die, ad serviendū homini futuro"</note> *2 Esdras 6:40-45* <note>The text cites 4 Esdr. 8, but the creation of the sun on the fourth day is found in 2 Esdras 6 in the Apocrypha.</note>. And elsewhere: *God created the sun for the service of all nations,* *Deuteronomy 4:19*. Regarding its absence, Genesis speaks thus: *When the sun was setting, a dread fell upon Abram,* *Genesis 15:12*; arguing from this that the absence of the sun is a time most suited for dread and fear. Furthermore, the light of the sun is an ornament of extraordinary value, not only to the earth but also to the heavens; it is understood concerning its splendor that *He has adorned the heavens by His spirit* <note>Job 26:13</note>. From this spirit, which primarily gives life to all celestial bodies, both the "erratic" <note>the planets</note> and the "fixed" <note>the stars</note> acquire their beautiful splendors. Although it was the opinion of Cicero, and also of certain others, that all stars—with only one exception, the moon—claim their own light and splendor for themselves; nevertheless, other philosophers seem to perceive more correctly: namely, that the other stars, and especially the planets, do not have light belonging to themselves, but they maintain that these are ignited and illuminated by the Sun along with the Moon. So we also observe that although the earth, in the manner of a lunar body, has a soul appropriate to its own body, it is nevertheless illuminated in the daytime by the sun’s splendor, and is stirred up by it in a hidden manner. And for this reason, Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his focus on fire and change.</note> not without consideration called the Sun the "fountain of celestial light," and others claim it was called *sol* as if *solus* <note>A common Latin etymological pun: "sol" (sun) from "solus" (alone/only).</note>, because it alone of all the stars is so great. Heraclitus says: *If you take the sun out of the world, what is our little body if the soul is missing?* No pulsing vein is felt there, no judgment remains in the senses, no vital breath, nor any respiration. And from this, the Sun is called by some the "Heart of Heaven," because just as there stands in the heart a single fountain of blood, moistening and watering the other members of the human body and infusing vital motion, so in the sun there seems to reside the growth and preservation of all things, both lower and higher, because it breathes life and heat through its light. As such, it is defined as a "simple act," converting all things to itself with life-giving heat, permeating all beings, and leading their qualities and virtues through all things, while dispersing darkness and gloom. 

<margin>1</margin> Therefore, Apollo <note>The Greco-Roman god of the sun, often used here as a poetic name for the sun itself.</note> seems to sit in the middle on the glittering throne of heaven, with golden hair and shining in a glorious manner, imparting his lucid influences to the rest of the world's creatures, both celestial and terrestrial. But the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who emphasized the spiritual and "ideal" reality behind physical objects.</note> have expressed this in few words, and as if in a single breath, asserting that the "Soul of the World" is included in the sun; and as the sacred text has it: *In the sun He has set a tabernacle for that light which gives life to all things* <note>Psalm 19:4: "In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun." The author interprets this as the Divine Light dwelling *within* the solar orb.</note>. If this light were taken from the world, it must follow that the world with its creatures would immediately become inanimate and recede into that "nothingness" from which it was first made; for by that "lucid word" all things were made (*as Saint John says*) and without it, nothing.

Hence the Academics <note>Philosophers of the Platonic school.</note>, following the example of that Supreme Sun <note>God</note>, recognize that the mundane sun is unique in itself—that is, in essence and light—but they nonetheless make it manifold in its rays. This follows the example of the "First Essence," which is unique and most simple in itself, most divine and immobile; yet it is manifold insofar as it is disseminated among its creatures. And just as when the sun withdraws its rays into itself, all things become dark, so likewise when the Divine Sun turns away His face, all things are disturbed and return to their nothingness, as is read in the *History of the World’s Harmony*. Indeed, we draw this in express speech from the sacred fountain: that *Wisdom is a holy spirit of intelligence, unique, simple, manifold, having all power, etc.* *Wisdom of Solomon 7:22*. From this they teach us that although it is unique in its essence, it is nonetheless manifold with respect to the rays which it disperses everywhere and into every subject of this world, without which nothing exists. This is also confirmed in that it is said to contain all power in itself, as in its essence consists the life of every thing: *In Him was life, etc.* *John 1:4*. Upon this foundation Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek figure whose "Orphic hymns" were often cited by Renaissance philosophers to show that ancient pagans recognized a single divine power.</note> fixed his opinion that "all things are full of gods"; but many have referred all these "gods"—as if they were rays of one essence—to that one great God, Jehovah or Jove. For the confirmation of the aforementioned discourse, we have this written by the royal Psalmist: *When God hides His face from His creatures, they are troubled; when He takes back their spirit—that is, that light-filled vital form—they expire and return to their dust, which is to say, nothingness; when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated by His goodness,* *Psalm 104:29-30*. From this it is clear that just as the rays of divine light (or the "Invisible Sun") are the acts of life which it rains down liberally upon creatures from its solar temple, so it is necessary that if those rays are taken away, the creature is suddenly reduced to nothing. Finally, there is yet another use for this mundane solar light: namely, that it distinguishes time into its divisions and subdivisions. Hence it is written: *By the making of the sun, days, light, and years are separated by the knowledge of the Lord, whose command they keep, and they are divided by the wisdom of God,* *Ecclesiasticus 43:6-10*. So it is also said of Wisdom, *that she gives knowledge of the beginning, the end, and the middle of times, the changes of the solstices, the varieties of seasons, and the circuits of the years, etc.* *Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-19*. From the act and vitality of solar light—since its soul, namely Wisdom (according to Solomon), *is more mobile than any motion,* *Wisdom 7:24*—motion is generated, by whose power the Sun rises and sets, so that both day and night might be brought into the world for the benefit of man. This motion is procreated from the act of light; for the "Lucid Word" of God is the first actor both in the motion of the sun and of all other creatures. For light acts, and by its action produces motion in nature, which then afterward is the parent of heat—generating, fostering, and nourishing all things, as will be discussed more broadly below. Hence the wise man says: *Great is the Lord who made the sun, at whose word it hastened its path,* *Ecclesiasticus 43:5*. This indicates that not only was the creature of the sun created by the word and speech of Almighty God, but it also seems to have received life (which is light) and motion (which is the effect of acting light). Indeed, just as the hidden spirit of wisdom is the soul of the sun itself, and its beauty is sent down from the "Lucid Gate" of the Cabalists, <term>Tiphereth</term> <note>The sixth Sephirot in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, representing Beauty and often associated with the Sun as the balance point of the cosmos.</note>; so indeed, by the motion of this "vessel" (which is the admirable work of the Most High), the entire mundane spirit is ruled, quickened, moved, and governed—no differently than the whole mass of the human spirit and body is governed by the fiery power of the heart.

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

[The air] is stirred to fulfill the desire of the will, which is why Solomon says that by the turning of the sun the air hastens in its circuit, and returns according to its rounds, *Ecclesiastes 1*. And from this arises the saying that the winds are the infants of Titan, Astraea, and Aurora, insofar as they are born from solar motion and heat—as Aristotle himself says—yet we define winds simply as agitated air. Furthermore, that this solar motion is both a daily, "driven" motion <note>The "raptus" or "forced" motion refers to the daily rotation of the heavens from east to west.</note> and a natural motion governed by a single spirit operating in manifold ways, is taught to us because all things exist from and through Him, as the Apostle testifies. He, to give life to the world, acts voluntarily in the *Primum Mobile* <note>The "First Moved" sphere in classical astronomy which drives the other spheres.</note>, by whose motion the solar sphere is snatched along with all others from the rising to the setting, according to that word of David:

-> The sun, like a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber, shall rejoice as a giant to run his way; his going out is from the end of heaven, and his circuit even to the end of it, and there is none who can hide from his heat. *Psalm 19*. <-

And in this sense it is also said elsewhere that the sun knows its setting. But truly this celestial body has another motion appropriated to itself, insofar as it is a peculiar creature within the "Great Animal" <note>The *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, where the universe is viewed as a living organism.</note>. Thus we see that man, by his will (as an effect of the prime mover and as if in the *Primum Mobile* of the **Microcosm**), snatches the entire mass of the creature here and there; yet nevertheless, the heart in his center has its own peculiar and appropriated motion—namely in **systole and diastole** <term>contraction and expansion</term>—independent of the motion of the will, and yet depending on the will of the creating mind. In the same way, the Sun, insofar as it is a body, is seen to move slowly through its own resistance against the motion of the *Primum Mobile*—namely, from the setting toward the rising <note>The Sun's annual path through the Zodiac moves West to East, contrary to the daily East-to-West rotation.</note>—by which motion we measure and map the span of the year. In this motion, Solomon says the sun turns from the north to the south and back again to the north:

-> It circles, he says, through the south, and turns toward the North, etc. *Ecclesiastes 1*. <-

As if he had said: it goes toward the winter solstice or the **Tropic of Capricorn**, and returns to the summer solstice or the **Tropic of Cancer**, by which motion the annular circuit of the year is completed.

Finally, as motion is the most proximate and immediate effect of emanating light, so also heat proceeds immediately from motion as an effect, just as heat is produced by the friction of iron or any hard thing against another hard thing. We must therefore discuss solar heat succinctly, as it follows immediately from motion. **Ecclesiasticus** <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note> seems to attribute a triple property to the sun: namely, to scorch, to blow out fiery rays by reflection, and to blind the heavens with the brilliance of its rays, *Ecclesiasticus 43*. Regarding the heat coming from its motion, it is most certain that it comes either immediately from the solar nature (whose radical property is to blow out fiery rays from its body, not unlike the warm breath we see exiting the mouth of an animal) or because of the varied reflection of its rays against the earth or clouds, producing variations in intensity or weakness according to the angles of resistance. For direct rays striking perpendicularly produce stronger effects in heat due to stronger resistance; hence we read in express words that:

-> The sun at noon burns the earth, and who can stand before its heat? *Ecclesiasticus 43*. <-

By this we understand that for those to whom the sun is at the meridian or mid-heaven (especially when it passes near the Tropic of Cancer), it brings forth a more vehement heat because its rays strike more perpendicularly. Furthermore, wherever the sun’s rays strike in the summer season, whether from the rising to the meridian or from that point toward the setting, it burns greatly because of the perpendicularity of the rays relative to the climate. Thus it is said that:

-> the sun risen over the flower, with heat, dries the grass and its flower falls, *James 1:11*. <-

And elsewhere:

-> Tomorrow when the sun is hot, you shall have help, etc. *1 Samuel 11:9*. <-

From this it is clear that the sun's heat is present to creatures sometimes as a benefit and sometimes as a punishment, as it is a work full of the glory of the Lord, who acts either benevolently or severely according to His pleasure—but chiefly to serve man, for whose benefit and use all other things were created; whence it is written:

-> You commanded the splendor of the sun on the fourth day, to serve the man who was to come: *2 Esdras 6:40*. <-

This is why the sun was brought forth into the "dominion of the day," as the Psalmist says in *Psalm 136:8*, where by "day" one can understand life, both in the **Macrocosm** and the **Microcosm**; just as conversely, death and privation are understood by night and darkness. For the prince of darkness is the destroyer of life, while the commander of light is the author and creator of life. For this reason, the sun is called "fecund" by philosophers, and full of the power of generating many things. Although we receive many life-giving virtues from the other stars and planets, this nevertheless happens through the power of the sun, which warms them with its seed and life-giving virtue. For it is the opinion of the most excellent philosophers that the Sun is like a **celestial cock**, insofar as it makes the "army of the heavens" pregnant; for the celestial bodies are like "hens" <note>The author uses a rustic metaphor to explain how the Sun (the active/male principle) fertilizes the other planets and stars (passive/female principles).</note> in that they receive their seed and their generative and heating virtue from the Sun no differently than hens receive theirs from a cock. In a similar way, I say, this **cock of the ether** communicates and disperses the lucid virtue of life and generation everywhere—like the benevolent "seeds of divinity" (which **Hermes Trismegistus** said was abundantly full of the fecundity of both sexes)—into the stellar bodies. These act as wombs of various conditions, and consequently rain down various natures upon the earth according to the properties of those stars.

For it must be held as certain and determined: just as God, the author of light and of all acts, motions, and heats springing from it, is one and simple, yet is accustomed to operate in manifold forms according to the different nature of the recipient—just as human sperm cast into the womb of a cow, a dog, or a horse is observed to produce different effects—so also says the ***Novum Lumen*** <note>original: "Novum Lumen" — likely referring to the alchemical text "The New Chemical Light" by Michael Sendivogius.</note> that nature is simple and always the same, but all alteration is in respect to the places in which it operates uniformly in its being, yet in manifold ways in respect to the variety of the reception. We notice likewise that fire acts differently in respect to the variety of the resistance of the recipients.

Among these celestial matrices <note>In this context, a "matrix" is a womb-like environment or a formative source from which things are produced.</note>, the Moon is that common one which receives the seeds of life as much immediately from the Sun as mediately—that is, immediately from the higher stars. She distributes them everywhere to the air, water, and earth, for she is the common matrix of all things within the genus of the stars. Therefore, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians and theurgy.</note> and many others conclude that in Phoebus <note>A common poetic name for Apollo, the Sun god.</note>, shining with golden hair and holding the scepter and rudder of the world like a king, all the powers of the heavens reside. And Proclus <note>A later Neoplatonic philosopher (412–485 AD) known for his "Theology of Plato."</note> testifies that at the sight of the sun, all the forces of all the celestial bodies are gathered into one and, as it were, collected; these, we believe, are finally scattered into this lower world through fiery breathings. Is it not also proven by yearly experience that when the sun inclines toward us, the earth grows green and flourishes? When it stands perpendicularly above us, the earth is greatly heated and matures; and when it hastens toward the fourth winter quarter and departs, the plants and herbs lose their flowers and are seen to languish more and more every day, as if by a disease. He seems to do all this by means of his beneficial heat, which either fosters and quickens things by its moderation, or destroys and scorches them by its harshness; or finally, by its absence, the things—both vegetable and animal—that were quickened by it are noticed to languish and grow numb in the torpor of cold. According to this same sense, Plato says: "That the Sun is a celestial fire, cooking all things with its heat which belong to the food of the Great World Animal" <note>The *Magnum Animal Mundanum* is the universe itself, viewed as a living, breathing organism.</note>, where by "food" he understands the creatures of the world with which he wished to fill the world for its own preservation, which are brought to perfection and ripeness by solar "cooking" <term>concoctione</term> <note>Concoction is an alchemical and biological term for the process of refining or maturing a substance through heat.</note>. Sacred Scripture seems to agree with his words where it is said that the Sun guards the furnace in the works of heat—that is, in the refining of those things that are in the world. Indeed, its rays, with their mixed heat, are so effective and penetrating that they descend even to the bowels of the earth, and there they primarily cook and perfect the metals, which then afterwards that elementary fire purifies and cleanses in its trial. Because of this life-giving disposition and beneficial power, the ancients imagined him to be the inventor of medicine; and insofar as he is the parent of life (for by his heat he generates all things), he is called by the Platonists the **soul of the world** <note>original: *anima mundi*</note>.

We conclude, therefore, that just as Jehovah, in his own property, is inclined toward both severity and mercy in his bright gate of Tiphereth <note>In Kabbalah, Tiphereth is the sixth Sephirah, representing Beauty and the Sun, positioned between the pillars of Mercy and Severity.</note>—inasmuch as that property is in the middle between *Ehieh* <note>The Hebrew name of God associated with the highest crown, Kether.</note>, the Father or head of mercy, and *Adonai* <note>The Hebrew name of God often associated with the physical kingdom or judgment.</note> toward severity—he is nevertheless more inclined toward life than destruction. And nonetheless, since nothing under the sun is immortal, it is necessary that just as a creature is generated and preserved by the life-giving rays of life given from the "tabernacle in the sun" to mortals for their conservation, so indeed by their lack, or by a fiery and wrathful aspect, it is corrupted and perishes, or rather, is dissolved. But Hermes Trismegistus also elegantly confirms this: "The Sun and Moon have been allotted the increases and decreases of all bodies"; these are his words—not that these creatures usually perform these things in themselves, but insofar as they are the organs through which God does such things.

But now we shall proceed to describe his honor and dignity, which the wise man clearly expresses in these words: *The sun illuminating all things is the work of the Lord, full of his glory: Ecclesiasticus 43.* <note>Originally labeled Eccl. 43, referring to the book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus.</note> Whence also elsewhere he calls it an admirable vessel and the work of the Most High, inasmuch as (according to the witness of the Psalmist) that royal light of life placed its tabernacle in it, *Psalm 19:4*; that is, it is in that place as the soul is in the body; from which, according to the common laws of created nature, it distributes the benefits of life liberally and sumptuously to the creatures of the world in its circuit—for indeed in the Word was **life, and that life was the light of the world, as St. John teaches us.** Similarly, this Word strengthened the heavens, and his spirit brought forth all the powers of life into the light; which spirit, although it is not inclusively contained in the solar vessel, nevertheless that admirable vessel abounds with its presence and glory. Whence it is said to be the giver and distributor of life, growth, and increase not only to celestial but also to terrestrial bodies. Therefore, because of its surpassing glory and dignity, and because of its lordship over other creatures, it is called by the Platonists the **King and Emperor**, holding the scepter and government of the world—partly because he seems to sit on a throne of visible glory with a shining and golden mane, and partly because we, taught by experience itself, notice that all the powers of the heavens reside in him. Some others, wishing to make the nobility of the subject known to us in another way—and especially Orpheus and others of the Platonists following him—called that star the **Eye of the World**, since nothing in the world is more sharp-eyed than it; for in it, as if in a most bright mirror, all things are seen, and are brought out of darkness into light, and present themselves to the sight of the creature. Others, wishing to express the praises and dignity of the sun in a different way, called it the **heart of heaven** <note>original: *cor cœli*</note>, and this was not at all foolishly done. For, says Heraclitus: "If you take the sun out of the world, what is our little body if the soul be missing?" No pulsing vein would be felt there, no vital breath in it, and finally no motive, life-giving, or natural force throughout the entire human body. So indeed, in the sun, as the heart of the Macrocosm <note>The "Great World" or the universe.</note>, there seems to be the motion, growth, quickening, and preservation of all the members of the Microcosm <note>The "Small World" or the human being.</note>, both higher and lower. For it is accustomed to breathe life and heat in the manner of divine unity—or, let us say, from the center or middle point, or the uncreated light dwelling centrally in it, informing it and adorning it with rays of life—by means of its created light, or rather its illuminated spirit. And indeed, by reason of that divinity which dwells in it, there is nothing visible in the world that represents the image of the one God in three persons in a single essence more than this excellent vessel, full of divine glory; for in its entire essence, as if in a body, it has the icon of the Father; in the rays sent forth, the icon of the Son; and in the effect of both—namely, the life-giving heat...

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteorological Phenomena <note>In the 17th century, the term "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>

...the vivifying [force] of the Holy Spirit, from whom all the gifts of life arise; hence it is that Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note>, along with the Platonists, calls the Sun the "visible statue or image of God," and Iamblichus calls it the "image of divine intelligence." Furthermore, those Academic philosophers <note>Followers of Plato's Academy.</note> recognize it to be unique in itself—that is, in its essence and light—and yet multiple in its rays, after the pattern of the uncreated emanation, which is unique in itself, but is said to be multiple because its rays are scattered everywhere throughout the world into all creatures. By a similar reasoning, Wisdom, which is brighter than the sun, is simple and unique in its nature; yet, in respect to its manifold communication, it is called "multiple" by the wise man. *For he says: "Wisdom is a holy spirit of intelligence, unique or simple, yet multiple; more precious than the Sun and light, and compared to the arrangement of all the stars, she is found to be prior," Wisdom 7.* For this reason, then, Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher.</note> seems to observe that the Sun is called "Apollo" from *alpha* (meaning "without") and *poly* (meaning "multitude") <note>original: "α, id est sine & πολὺ multitudine"</note>, for he is the only one who seems to hold the power of the stars and heavens in his own authority. Yet Speusippus the Platonist says the Sun is called Apollo for a different reason: because his power consists of many fires; for in him alone are the luminous forces of all the stars radically hidden, so that the aspects of the stars can do nothing or bring nothing to completion until they have been made pregnant by the luminous seed of Apollo. And hence he is often called the "Rooster of the Heavens" <note>original: "cælorum gallas," likely a typo for "gallus" (rooster), the herald of the sun.</note>, by which it is indicated that in effect Apollo is both one and multiple, and thus both those philosophers can be reconciled into one. And the Latins call it *Sol* as if to say the "Sole" [Only] shining one, as some wish; and the Assyrians call it *Adad*, which in their language also signifies "One"; the Hebrews call it *Shemesh* <note>original: "Semei," a variant of "Shemesh."</note>, which can be interpreted as "Proper," because the light and the power of light are proper to it. But just as he is called Apollo as if he were "the only one," so also he is called Phoebus in the heavens from another perspective, namely from his appearance and brightness; on Earth, they call him Vulcan. In short, it is the visible tabernacle of the invisible God, or of the holy spirit of intelligence, made after the image of its creator or Lord, most full of the glory of the creating Lord, but not to be worshipped in place of the Lord dwelling within it.

Hence, we turn ourselves toward the rising Sun in our prayers, not as if to a statue or image, but to the uncreated Lord, after whose image the sun itself was made—the Lord dwelling in it and liberally pouring forth from it the necessary benefits of created nature. Him alone we ought to worship and revere; to Him be the highest glory and highest praise, and adoration from the whole human mind, for ages unto ages.

From this it is clear that this admirable work of the Most High is a creature that offers its obedience humbly to its creator or Lord—not only in this vessel of his, which abundantly shows his glory to the worldly, but by existing everywhere through his presence. By this, the error of those philosophers is clearly revealed who defend the idea that this eternal light, dwelling exuberantly in the sun, acts in nature out of necessity [by mechanical law]. On the contrary, we read that the obedience of the sun in observing the commands of its Lord is perfected in three ways: namely, by its duty and direct motion according to the laws of nature; by retrograde motion [moving backward] against the order of nature, or by standing still; or by celebrating its creator in praise and offering Him immense thanks for that glory with which it is endowed above all other worldly creatures. It explains its obedience in its direct motion in these words: *The Lord is great who made the Sun, at whose words it hastened its journey, Ecclesiasticus 43.* Furthermore, it obediently performs its duty in illuminating and heating according to the will of its creator. For *as the Sun was created for power over the day, as the Prophet says in Psalm 136:8*, or *for the ministry of light to all nations under heaven as is held elsewhere, Exodus 4*, so it is said that *the Sun proceeds like a bridegroom from his chamber—that is, from his rising—and rejoiced like a giant to run his way; his going forth is from the end of heaven and his circuit even to the end of it, nor is there anyone who can hide from his heat, Psalm 19:5.* By these words, its obedience is explained both in the duty of illuminating and in its daily and direct motion according to the will of Him who rotates the "First Mover" <note>The outermost sphere of the universe in traditional astronomy.</note>, and also in the property of heating. But even its obedience in its duty of heating, according to the will of its Lord, is explained by what is written: *The sun shall not burn thee by day, Psalm 121:6.* And elsewhere, with the opposite effect: *The sun at noon parches the earth, and who can endure in the sight of its heat?* From which it is manifest that this creature burns with its heat whenever its Lord pleases, and sometimes acts beneficially and vivifyingly without burning or drying things up. In this way we have seen how this solar creature obeys the pleasures of its creator in its duty, according to the ordinary laws of created nature. Furthermore, it is seen to act by divine command outside of and plainly against the ordinary laws of nature: hence, by the will of God, it sometimes moves backward against its ordered progress in its daily motion, and sometimes we read that it stood plainly fixed for the space of one entire day, as in *Joshua 10*. And elsewhere: *When God forbids it, the Sun does not rise, and He seals up the stars, Job 9:7.* Concerning its obedience in the former case, it is said in the Sacred Page: *The sun stood in the middle of heaven and did not hasten to set for the space of one day, Joshua 10.* In the latter case, we read: *The sun returned ten lines by the degrees which it had gone down on the sundial in the days of King Hezekiah, Isaiah 38.* Finally, it is not to be doubted that this glorious creature is endowed with an intellectual spirit within its great mass, no differently than a man is within his own body. For just as He breathed the breath of life into man's face, so in that Sun He placed a tabernacle; wherefore it is evident that each of them is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Consequently, it is within both the will and the power of the Sun—and those things which are animated by the sun through the incorruptible spirit—to pour out praises to its creator just as much as it is in the power of man. Hence says the Psalmist: *Praise the Lord, Sun and Moon; praise Him, all you stars and light, Psalm 148:3.*

### Section I, Port. IV, Part. II. Book IV. Member I.

Thus those three in the fiery furnace, glorifying God with one voice, said: *Sun and Moon, bless the Lord; praise him and exalt him above all forever* <note>original: "Benedicite Sol & Luna domino..." — This refers to the "Song of the Three Holy Children" found in the Greek additions to the Book of Daniel.</note>. So it is also said elsewhere, that *the Sun knows its setting, Psalm 104:19.* From these few examples, it is right to gather how great is the obedience of this solar creature toward its Creator. Therefore, man—a vessel most excellent in his creation but most perverse by nature—should long to offer his obedience and duty according to the will of his Creator. He should strive with the greatest effort to shine in such glory as the Solar creature radiates by its own justice. For according to the Evangelist, *the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father* <note>Matthew 13:43</note>. Indeed, we believe that before the Fall, the image of Adam living in Paradise was everywhere radiant and splendid, shimmering with the glory of the divine light dwelling within him, as a vessel formed by the very finger of God, the Father of Light. Have we not read that the stone tablets, inscribed by the finger of God and entrusted to Moses, gleamed with a sapphire-like brilliance in the eyes of those who beheld them? So too we read that the face of Moses (even though he was stained by the mark of mortality) so excelled in light that the Israelites could not look upon his face without a <term>peplum</term> <note>A veil or covering.</note> or veil. How much more, then, was Adam radiant, who was not in the least contaminated by the stain and blot of mortality before his disobedience?

Finally, we come to the **passion of the sun** <note>The word "passion" here refers to the Sun's suffering or its "eclipse" during the Crucifixion.</note>, by which we gather from the authority of both Holy Scripture and trustworthy authors that it has been affected many times in this world’s history. *The sun was darkened at its rising*, says the Prophet, *Isaiah 13*. And elsewhere: *Your sun shall no more go down, because the Lord shall be your light, Jerusalem: Isaiah 60.* We also find in Joel that *the sun shall be turned into darkness before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, Joel 2.* And elsewhere: *The sun and the moon are darkened, Joel 3*, so that in its place the "Sun of Righteousness" might rise for those who fear the Lord, as we have in the Prophet Malachi, *Malachi 4*. In Ecclesiastes we find that *the sun, the light, the stars, and the moon shall grow dark for man, Eccl. 12.* And in St. Matthew: *Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, Matt. 24.* Finally, at the "passion" of the primary Sun <note>Referring to Christ.</note>, or rather at the death and passion of His "tabernacle," the secondary and celestial sun lost its light and was darkened. It was as if, with the life of His fleshly tabernacle failing, the celestial sun also suffered death—or the deprivation of its luminous form—for a great span of time through an inseparable consensus. Regarding this deprivation of solar form or life, Eusebius writes: *In the 4th year of the 202nd Olympiad, a great and excellent failure of the sun occurred, beyond all that happened before; at the sixth hour, the day was turned into such a dark night that stars were seen in the sky, and there was an earthquake in Bithynia.* Thus says he; similarly, Lucian of Antioch, the Martyr, while in his torments, cried out to the judges of the infidels and the executioners: *Search your annals and you will find that in the times of Pilate, while Christ was suffering, the day was interrupted by darkness when the sun was hidden.*

Furthermore, it is most certain and confirmed by reasoning that this solar "passion" was wondrous and miraculous, far beyond ordinary solar eclipses (in which the Sun does not actually fail, but the body of the moon is placed between its sight and our eyes). The first reason is that this passion occurred contrary to the natural order of solar eclipses, which never happen when the moon is full—that is, when it is in opposition to the Sun—yet this failure of the Sun, a kind of <term>syncope</term> <note>A fainting or sudden loss of strength/light.</note>, occurred immediately after the opposition of the luminaries. Second, because the part of the sun toward the east was veiled and shadowed first, and that same part was afterward re-illuminated first, from which it is clear that it happened against the common laws of nature. Third (and what would seem monstrous and incredible to everyone), in the hour of the eclipse, the moon moved against its own natural course—namely from East to West—whereas its natural motion is from West to East; yet immediately after the passion ended, it was observed to travel in its natural motion. From these things we must conclude that this passion and failure was real, according to the nature of the Solar body itself, and not merely relative to us (as is the case in a normal eclipse, where the sun does not actually "suffer," as has been said).

And for this reason, this passion or failure was universal, which cannot happen to them through the mere interposition of the moon between the earth and the sun. We conclude, therefore, from these things, that in the first place, when the life of the tabernacle of the **uncreated sun** <note>Christ</note> on earth failed, the sun in heaven was also affected by a kind of "fainting" and seemed to be deprived of its life-force and luminous form. It was as if that luminous spirit, which established its temple and tabernacle in both subjects, held such an inhuman and cruel act in hatred and turned its radiant face away from both worlds for some space of time. We also see from this that this solar body is a creature subject to the **WILL OF GOD**, either for life or for the deprivation of its light; consequently, we see that God does not act in this world by necessity or as if forced into the ordinary course of nature, contrary to that foolish assertion of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed the universe operated by fixed, necessary laws.</note>.

Finally, the fact that the sun will be transfigured from its state on the Last Day and rendered seven times more splendid in its light—that is, casting off its corruptible garments to put on its incorruptible and immortal nature—seems first to be confirmed by the words of the Prophet: *The light of the moon* (he says) *shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, Isaiah 30.* And he teaches this more clearly when he says elsewhere: *Your sun shall no more go down, and your moon shall not wane, for the Lord shall be your light, Jerusalem, Isaiah 60.* John in the Apocalypse seems to agree with this speech, saying: *The city has no need of the Sun nor the Moon to shine in it, for the brightness of GOD shall illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb.* Here and there it is declared that the spirit of Wisdom will be far more excellent than any brightness of sun or star; by setting aside the solar creature which it put on when it "placed its tabernacle in the sun," it will reveal itself in its own inaccessible splendor and light, the sight of which no mortal in this state of mortality can behold; but

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...when the righteous shall shine like the sun (as Saint Matthew says) in that kingdom of their Father, then they shall see Him, their garments cast aside, as He truly is. Thus *Alpha* shall be turned into *Omega* <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the beginning and the end.</note>; the beginning shall meet its end. Just as things began in unity, so also shall they have their end in unity. All things are from God, and all things shall return to God, since in Him we live, move, and have our being (*Acts 17:28*). *From Him and in Him is the life of all (John 1).* He will then be all in all when Christ has obtained the Father’s kingdom. He is the Father from whom all things come, and as the beginning is, so is the end. He alone is the one who works all things in everyone; He is the Father of all, who is over all, through all, and in all. For He gives life to all things; indeed, He who lacks nothing gives life, breath, and all things to everyone. Finally, from Him, through Him, and in Him are all things, to whom be praise and honor forever (*1 Corinthians 15, 1 Corinthians 8, 2 Corinthians 5, Ephesians 4:6, 1 Timothy 6, Acts 17, Romans 11*). 

In this, many of the philosophers who were hidden in the more secret divine mysteries have agreed. Among them, the *Zohar* <note>original: "Zoar" — A fundamental work of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> says that all things are nothing but one in respect to GOD, though in respect to us, they are many. Plato and Parmenides say that what exists—insofar as it is in GOD and proceeds from Him—is nothing but one. Hermes, in his *Emerald Tablet* <note>original: "tabula sua Smaragdina" — A foundational text of alchemy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, says: "Just as all things were by the mediation of one, so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation." And Proclus, in his *Theological Elements* <note>original: "problematibus suis Theo-logicis"</note>, says: "As all things proceed from the one alone, so also they continually hasten to return to that one." And these things find all the greater peace and concord the closer they approach it and participate with it.

Plato also speaks thus in his *Epistles*: "All things proceed from the Most High, and they strive with all their might to return to Him again, as He is the one in whom their final rest and the protection of their essence consists," and so on in other places.

By these authorities, we have it confirmed that all things are in truth nothing but one, though they appear many in the imagination of common men. It is the way of such men to look at those things which appear in an external fashion—things which *seem* to be, but in the reality of the matter are nothing—rather than looking at central things, which are seen the least, yet are themselves the truth and the "One" and the same. This is no different than how infinite rays are continuous with the same solar body or essence, and are by no means divided from the identity of the sun.

Therefore, it is certain that although worldly people attribute the act of quickening and life, of heating and ripening, and of multiplying, illuminating, and nourishing to the solar creature—and even though the Holy Scriptures, speaking in the common tongue, sometimes attribute effects to it and other creatures—nevertheless, speaking truly, God works all these things that are done within His creatures. The creatures serve only in the place of instruments <term>organorum</term> <note>Literally "organs" or "tools" used to produce a specific effect.</note> to produce such effects. For example, we do not say that the flute produced this or that harmony, or that the sword wounded this or that person, but rather the blower or musician, or the soldier, or some other man doing the wounding. Nor do we say that the wagon transported such weights into the city, but rather the horses. Nor should it be said that the human body truly does this or that, but rather the internal agent, acting as the first mover who leads it according to his will and pleasure. A mirror does not burn things from a distance; rather, the rays emitted by the sun do. Nor does the sun emit its own rays; rather, He who informs and gives life to the sun does so—He who snatches it from its rising to its setting, and again from its setting to its rising, and again makes it stand still to fulfill His commands.

Therefore, the acts of angels, stars, and all other creatures are truly to be attributed to GOD, since it is from Him that they live, move, and exist, as the Apostles (agreeing with the Poets in this) affirm in *Acts 17*. And if you say that GOD moves nothing toward evil, I respond: if you can assign some other primary act co-eternal with GOD (and thus not one unique GOD, but two co-eternal Gods), then perhaps your objection might be given some credit; but we shall speak of these things more clearly below.
