### Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

By which discourse it is clearly manifest that God performs all these things; and although we say in our own speech that lightning and thunder "act," or in a more mystical sense, that angels inflame the air by their fiery presence, yet in truth it is God in the fiery angels, and God in the dense clouds or watery spirits, who brings all these things to their conclusion to fulfill his commands. Whence the Holy Scripture rightly said *that in God all things live, move, and have their being. Acts 17:28.* <note>original: "quod in Deo omnia vivant, moveantur & sint. Act. 17. 28."</note> And elsewhere, *God works all in all, 1 Corinthians 12.* And again, *God the father from whom are all things, 1 Corinthians 8.* 

Therefore, I leave it to be judged by you—looking into this matter with upright eyes and weighing it in the scales of justice—how foolish, tasteless, and overly subtle is the opinion and assertion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, who sought purely naturalistic explanations for weather.</note>, both of the Heathen and the Christian order. They presume to assert that lightning consists of hot and dry exhalations leaping from the earth, which are raised by the sun's power into the middle region of the air, and being enclosed there in a cloud and driven by the force of the cold in that place, are set on fire. I ask: Is this matter of lightning and thunder a thing of such small moment (as those Aristotelians think), or is it of a far higher depth and inscrutability, since the fires of God leaping from His mouth and throne, and the voices and sounds of God, are named as such everywhere in the Holy Scriptures? 

For this reason, certain philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of the lightning bolt, judged it to be not a work of nature but the immediate effect of the Most High God. Indeed, this work seemed so marvelous to the Heathens that they doubted greatly concerning its origin and disputed among themselves. For Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 490–430 BC) who proposed the theory of the four elements.</note> thought that the lightning bolt and the flash were fire generated by the rays of the sun descending downward and being intercepted by clouds. Anaxagoras <note>Another pre-Socratic philosopher who suggested that "mind" (nous) was the ordering force of the universe.</note> claimed that this fire was a portion of the ether, which he says is sent down from on high and struck into the place where the clouds consist. Although Aristotle himself and Seneca attempted to refute these opinions, they nevertheless seem far more probable and relevant to the matter than those of Aristotle and his sects. 

This is also declared clearly enough by arguments drawn from experience itself. For, good God! How destitute of reason are those who are accustomed to attribute the marvelous effects of thunder to the power of a terrestrial exhalation, or to the weak faculty of earthly fire? For by the action of a lightning bolt, we see wine drawn out of a cask by a sudden force while the vessel is not touched at all; a sword broken within its scabbard; gold and silver melted in a purse; and the bones crushed within the fleshy dwelling of a man. We see sudden winds created in the air, forests burned, stones ground to powder, huge towers suddenly torn up, and infinite other wonders performed, for which it is most difficult to give a ready reason. 

Indeed, there seems to be sense and reason in the lightning, by which it offers obedience to the Creator; and it is said to bless Him in the Holy Scriptures, thereby indicating to us Christians that there is within them a certain Angelic virtue, very near to divinity, by which they are governed. Having been sent out, they go forth violently, and returning, they say to the Creator, *Behold, here we are. Job 38:35.* <note>original: "en adsumus, Iob. 38. 35."</note> Indeed, so subtle are its spirits and so agile its life, that we have it written by one skilled in these mysteries: "Angels are much brighter and more splendid than spiritual bodies, which a man can hardly admit or comprehend; for by reason of their subtlety they can pass through and penetrate all things without any hindrance and without their own corruption, like lightning. Similarly, the human soul can do this, inasmuch as God likewise created it from the same [substance] from which the angels were created." Thus says the author of the *Book of the Secrets of Creation.* <note>original: "Lib. de secretis creationis." Likely a reference to a pseudo-epigraphical or Hermetic work on cosmogony.</note> By this he seems to hint that the substance of angels, of lightning, and of the human soul is of the same matter, which he is pleased to call the "sixth essence" in many places. And truly, just as the substance of an Angel is not seen at all except in its airy garment (which it illuminates in the manner of the spirit of the sun, which is illuminated by its internal soul), so also the internal part of lightning is an angelic power and essence, veiled in airy clothing. 

Hence it is that so many wonders arise from lightning, far surpassing the dull nature and disposition of a mere "exhalation." For experience has revealed here in England, in the county of Devon <note>original: "prouincia Deuienfi"</note>, that thunder coming from the North sent a "fiery stone" <note>A thunderstone or ceraunia, believed at the time to be a physical object cast down by lightning.</note> into the kitchen of a certain nobleman. Rolling from that place into the hall of that house and passing between the feet of a certain man of that house, it rendered him for a time demented and Raging. Passing from that place into a chamber, by its mere look all the glass of the windows of that part were perforated in infinite places, just as if they had been pierced by small needles. And so, penetrating through a thick wall and leaping out of the house, it buried itself in a marvelous way into a hard rock. 

Furthermore, in Ireland <note>original: "Hybernia"</note>, two women seeking a forest and traveling through a field were delayed on the way by a certain horrible thunder. One of them was struck with fear and trembling, and she called upon God and hurried quickly toward a tree. The other appeared not at all disturbed, but behaved herself in an impious manner; holding the voices of the thunder in derision and contempt, she struck her buttocks <note>original: "anum seu podicem"</note> with her hand and turned them toward the place from which the sounds were issued. Whereupon it happened that the first woman, moved by the fear of God and His voice, escaped safe; but the buttocks and the entire haunches of the other were immediately torn and mangled by the thunder, and so that blasphemous woman died miserably. 

But to come closer to the foolish assertions of these Peripatetics: one day certain merchants and others in the company of a certain Peripatetic (a youth of good character who lived in the city of Shrewsbury <note>original: "Salopienfem"</note>, where he applied himself to literary matters and was held in high esteem by all of that place for his knowledge in philosophy) were traveling together through the wide plain of Shrewsbury. They noticed dense clouds with sounds and thunder approaching them, and the greater part of them began to fear vehemently.

But that young man, wishing to show himself well-versed in the knowledge of **Peripatetic philosophy** <note>The school of philosophy following Aristotle, which the author is critiquing for its purely naturalistic explanations.</note>, consulted with them and persisted in boldly persuading them not to fear. He affirmed that this matter was common in nature and happened by chance through external circumstances, and that there was no danger in it. He asserted that it was caused solely by a hot and dry exhalation raised from the lap of the earth into the middle region of the air by the power of the sun's rays; he claimed this flame was produced through **antiperistasis** <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>A technical term in Aristotelian physics referring to the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being compressed and ignited by the surrounding cold of the upper atmosphere.</note>, which he said existed between the coldness of that place and the heat of the trapped exhalation. However, it happened quite differently for him than he had imagined; for while he was alone among the others, he was struck dead by a sudden flash of lightning. The rest, however, were only struck with stupor and fear and fell to the ground. In this way, the blasphemy of that man, deceived by Aristotelian arguments, was judged by the righteous judgment of God.

In the year 1623, near the town they call **Croydon**, only eight miles distant from the city of London, around the month of July, certain people were preparing hay in the field of a certain nobleman. As they were drying it in the sun, they noticed voices and thunder approaching with horrendous lightning. It happened that they divided themselves into two companies or groups, standing not much more than two cubits apart from each other, gathered together so that they might remain safer from the rage of the storm. Three maidservants sat with a certain boy under one tree; two or three men sat under another. As the storm approached—**wonderful to relate** <note>original: "mirabile dictu"</note>—the thunder could do nothing against those under the first tree while one of the aforementioned maidservants remained there, as if she alone had been sealed on her forehead by God so that the evil spirit might not bring any harm to her. 

Prompted by the instinct of I know not what spirit, while the thunder continued and very heavy rain was falling, she proposed to leave that tree and hurry to the other. Addressing the others, she said, "I shall hasten to the other tree; do you wish to come away with me?" But when the others refused, and she had gone only five or six paces, immediately the other two girls and the boy who remained under that tree and refused to leave with her were struck dead by lightning. No other sign appeared upon them except a tiny scraping of the bark. The maidservant who left escaped safely to the men hiding under the other tree. 

But what seemed an even greater miracle was a fire in the form of a globe <note>An early description of "ball lightning."</note> descending from the top of that tree to its root; it rolled upon the earth like a wheel and moved toward the other tree under which the maidservant and the men stood. Not only were those standing beneath it stunned and astonished by its presence and passage, but the tree itself, moved by a certain remarkable reverence, was seen to bow toward that wheel and humble itself in such a way that the back of a sturdy man who was leaning against its trunk seemed to him to be broken by the great bending of the tree. From this it is clear that there is a greater mystery in lightning and thunder than the **Peripatetics** could ever comprehend. Therefore, true Christians ought to apply themselves to the sense of the Holy Scriptures rather than to the vain and scarcely probable imagination of the Heathen Peripatetics, since the certainty of the former and the vanity and absurdity of the latter have been clearly declared in the preceding pages.

Furthermore, another wonderful example of this astounding meteor in nature presented itself last year, 1624, in the month of July, near the town of **Windsor** <note>original: "Windesor"</note>, where one may see the royal and well-fortified palace or castle, only eighteen miles from the city of London. For as two women and three girls were gathering ears of wheat scattered everywhere through the field after the harvest, a stupendous thunder suddenly came upon them. The eldest of the girls, seeing the lightning flying everywhere through the air and appearing before her eyes in an oblong shape with sharp tails, was moved and disturbed in spirit far beyond all the others, crying out to her mother, "Fie on this lightning and thunder! I cannot endure it; I wish I were home." 

When she was admonished by her mother and another honest woman—who before her marriage was my servant or handmaid in my house—to stop her frivolous and contentious talk and call upon God, she nevertheless neglected her prayers to God and continued her exclamations against the annoying appearances of the meteor. Consequently, the others attempted to protect themselves from the violence of the storm under the branches of two tall trees. But that girl, with a joking and cheerful face, leaning her back against the trunk of a very high oak, said she was placed as if on a royal throne above the others and was secure from the storm. 

The other woman, who was once my servant, had her arm resting in the lap of the said girl, and the girl's younger sister was not far from them, while the mother of the girl was under another tree five or six paces away. It happened suddenly that a certain globe of fire fell from a cloud onto that huge tree. With a most violent and sudden force, it stripped the bark in three places from the top to the root without any interruption of the parts, and scattered fragments of it everywhere for almost a mile's distance. Meanwhile, the substance of the trunk and the internal body was not immune from that triple wound; hollow wounds were inflicted to the depth of a finger, long and continuous from the highest branches down to the root, as if carved by **plowshares** <note>original: "vomeribus"</note>—working, without a doubt, by the finger of God or some administering angel. 

Thus it happened that the girl, who thought herself most safe and protected from all violence, was struck dead in the blink of an eye by a force that cannot be explained in words. The woman who was formerly my servant was deprived of the use and feeling of the arm that had been resting in the girl's lap; she ran through the street or way like one possessed, crying out in a loud voice and looking up at the clouds, "Holy God, open your clouds and your gates, that I may enter, nor..."

Just as the angels vary in their composition, they produce meteors of varying condition, property, and constitution. Thus, we observe some to be comets, fiery columns, glowing spears, or **chasms** <note>A term used for "openings" or streaks in the night sky.</note>, and others to be flashes of lightning, thunderbolts, or sulfurous rains. Nevertheless, there is but a single act: one God remaining in His essence, who acts variously—not by reason of Himself, but by reason of the object which receives His rays in different ways. This occurs in respect to the various angelic bodies which are distributed through the various portions of the worldly air by a primary internal act, and which differ in density, rarity, and quality, as trustworthy writers testify.

That **GOD** <note>original: "DEVS"</note> is the primary as well as the immediate cause (for there is no regard for either place or time before God, who is the **Alpha and Omega** <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, signifying the beginning and the end of all things.</note>), we gather from the Holy Scriptures. There we find it written that "God moves the earth from its place, so that its columns tremble; He moves the mountains," etc. (Job 9:5). And elsewhere: "The earth trembles at the look of God" (Psalm 104:32). And hence, in another place, the royal Psalmist said that "the deepest tracks of the earth are in the hand of God." Similarly, it is noted there that He induces this disturbance of the earth in His property of severity and wrath; for an earthquake is always an act in the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "Microcosm" or the human being.</note> that is "beyond nature." Thus it was said in the wrath of God against the Israelites: "The earth was shaken and moved, the foundations of the heavens were moved" (2 Samuel 22:8); they are shaken when His wrath is kindled. Furthermore, we gather from many places in Scripture that **Jehovah** <note>The Hebrew name for God.</note>, sometimes surrounded by a thick cloud and usually clothed in an angelic body, produces these stupendous meteors. "Behold," says Saint Matthew, "a great earthquake occurred, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and his appearance was like lightning," etc. (Matthew 28:2). By these words, it is implied that the Angel of God was the efficient cause of the earthquake. Thus, after he had expressed the effect in these words: "Behold, a great earthquake occurred," he explains the reason or efficient cause in the following words: "For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven." The manner through which he did this was his lightning-like appearance—that is, the essential lightning and splendor of God, shining out from the angelic composition. For angelic bodies are called mirrors receiving the splendor of divinity, as will be discussed more broadly below. Hence David said: "The earth trembled at the look of God," etc. (Psalm 104:32).

From these things, then, it appears clearer than the midday light how impious and profane is that opinion of the **Heathens** <note>Referring to non-Christian or secular philosophers like Aristotle.</note> who say that an earthquake is nothing other than a violent eruption of a multitude of winds trapped within the bowels of the earth. Here they wrongly mistake the wind or air—which is merely the instrument or vehicle of the divine "look" that produces such stupendous things—for the cause itself. Thus, they fall into a notable form of idolatry, wrongfully attributing the acts of the Creator to the creature. But truly, if they would look upon the mystery of this matter with eyes a little more accurate, they would perceive a matter of deeper significance, and...

# On the Efficient Cause of Atmospheric Phenomena <term>Atmospheric Phenomena</term> <note>Original: *Meteororum*. In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any phenomenon in the sky or earth, including rain, wind, and earthquakes.</note>

...as they themselves believed. For common experience teaches us what hidden events follow an earthquake, and with what great wonders its effects are accompanied—namely, plagues, famines, and sometimes the earth itself is observed to groan with fiery sighs and roar with a moan like a lion. To assign all these wonders to wind that is accidentally trapped within the earth will appear (to any rational person) quite absurd. Among a thousand examples, we shall produce only one from our own Europe that is worthy of wonder.

On the day of the **Conversion of St. Paul** <note>January 25th.</note> (says the *History of Venice*), around one o'clock in the afternoon, during the reign of **Andrea Dandolo** <note>The 54th Doge of Venice, who reigned from 1343 to 1354.</note>, the 54th Doge, a massive earthquake arose. It shook the city with such motion and violence that various structures, both public and private, collapsed under its force. The bell towers of the churches—namely, **St. Sylvester**, **St. Vitalis**, and **St. James of Lorio**—along with the roof of **St. Angelo** and the left side of **St. Basil**, fell to the ground and were leveled. 

This earthquake lasted for about fifteen days, more or less. By its shock, many pregnant women suffered miscarriages. Furthermore, a highly contagious disease followed, which began with a swelling in the groin <note>This refers to the "buboes" of the Black Death, which struck Venice in 1348.</note>. This was immediately followed by extreme heat, along with pain and heaviness in the head, so that their memory was taken from them. It was observed that those suffering from this infection commonly exchanged life for death within three days at most; indeed, out of a hundred people, barely ten were counted who escaped the scourge of death. Throughout the entire city, nothing was in use except tears, groans, funerals, doctors, and the visiting of the sick. 

Finally, a plague began to rage at the end, invading with such atrocity and severity that men, children, and women of every age who suffered the infection fell dead suddenly, even in the streets. Thus, kinsman dared not provide aid to kinsman, nor friend to friend; likewise, children were forced to refuse and avoid their parents, and parents their children. The doctors themselves took flight in terror. Funeral processions became unknown; instead, without ceremonies, even the nobles were dragged to the pit in a lowly manner. This contagion grew from the beginning of springtime until the first of May, and only then (with few survivors remaining) did it begin to decrease.

What then? Is this to be attributed to a brutal and empty wind trapped in the earth? Or is it rather the presence of the Lord, punishing the wicked and the proud through an angel (as in the time of **King David**, when he began to count the people against the command of God)? O, the vain invention of the Greek philosophers! Though they were almost eyewitnesses to the wonderful effects of earthquakes (for **Diodorus Siculus** and **Herodotus** narrated wonders concerning earthquakes happening in Greece), they still delight in assigning these stupendous effects to a cause so frivolous as mere air or wind trapped in the cavities of the earth.

But at this point, we shall begin to recite the various theories of the philosophers concerning earthquakes, so that you may more easily discern how inconsistent and unstable they are in their opinions. This usually arises because they are ignorant of the true foundation of "meteors" and the secret acts of the Divine Word.

**Posidonius** said the cause of this was wind trapped in the hollows of the earth. In this, he seems to agree with the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, who say it is caused by vapors obstructed in the bowels of the earth. These vapors, finding no way out and being expanded and thinned by the sun's rays during the day, shake the sides of the earth while seeking an exit, and thus, breaking out, cause an earthquake. 

The **Assyrians**, and the **Babylonians** above all others, want it to be produced by the power of a certain planet or by the aspect of its rays, meeting with the rays of the sun in the center of the earth. **Anaxagoras** thinks it is created by air retained in the earth over the course of time. 

And so you see that many have said many things, but have indicated nothing certain about its origin or efficient cause. In truth, **God** is the immediate cause of this thing, looking upon the earth from an angelic body with the appearance of His wrath; He performs and acts all these things in the strength of His arm, as was declared in the preceding pages. To Him alone, therefore, be the praise and glory of such a great miracle forever.

Sacred Scripture also teaches us that God is the sole efficient cause of springs and rivers, where we read:
> *He sends the springs into the valleys, which run among the hills, to give drink to every beast of the field.* (Psalm 104) <note>Original text cites Psalm 107.</note>
And elsewhere: 
> *When Jehovah strengthened the fountains of the deep, wisdom was with him, etc.* (Proverbs 8:28)
By these passages, it is clear that God or divine power is the cause that produces springs and rivers, and not the "vapors of the earth," as the Peripatetics falsely believed.

Finally, God is the unique worker of the sea storm, inasmuch as He acts from the whirlwind to produce such an effect—not unlike how He is said to have spoken to **Job** from the whirlwind. This also seems to be confirmed by these words of the Royal Psalmist:
> *Those who go down to the sea in ships, they see the works of Jehovah, and his wonders in the deep. For he speaks and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up the waves thereof. They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths, etc.* (Psalm 107:23-26) <note>Original text cites Psalm 107:33.</note>
Furthermore, we read elsewhere:
> *You break the ships of the sea with an East wind, etc.* (Psalm 48:7) <note>Original text cites Psalm 65.</note>

Therefore, having understood these things in the right way, we must first and foremost flee to God in all these tribulations, pray to Him, and acknowledge His power with trembling, so that in this way we may be de-

# Correlative to the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>

We have learned from the doctrine of both the Theosophers <note>Philosophers who seek knowledge of God through spiritual intuition or divine revelation.</note> and the more learned Philosophers that there are four things in the world created after the likeness of the Archetype <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original divine blueprint or "First Idea" in the mind of God.</note> and the first Idea. Two of these were created by the natural way by the best and greatest Creator: namely, the world and man. The others, however, were fabricated by the artifice of the human creature—namely, the Ark or Tabernacle of the Covenant built by Moses, and that distinguished Temple built by Solomon. Just as those natural things were created according to the image of the Archetype, so indeed were the artificial things fabricated according to the example of the natural ones. 

For thus in the world we have three regions, of which one excels the other in dignity: namely, the highest, which is the most excellent essence of all, called the Empyrean <term>Empyrean</term> <note>From the Greek 'empyros,' meaning fiery; the highest heaven, thought to be the realm of pure light and the residence of God.</note> from its fiery nature. And truly, just as fire is an element more eminent in dignity than all others, purer and simpler in essence, so also for that reason the Empyrean heaven is the head and prince over the other two lower regions. Whence it is assigned as the seat for the purest and simplest creatures of all—namely, the Angels and the Intelligences shimmering with divine splendor.

Then follows the middle region, participating in both extremes, which is called *Ether* <term>Ether</term>, because it seems to be composed of the highest fire and the lowest air; wherefore it is not as pure as that highest one, nor as impure, thick, and unclean as that lowest one, but consists in a middle state. 

Finally, the lowest is thicker in quantity than the higher ones, more imperfect in quality, and subject to all changes—namely, the agitation of winds, the procreation of clouds, the crying out of thunders, and the inflammation of lightnings, fire-storms <term>Presteres</term> <note>Original: "prestres," a Greek-derived term for a whirlwind accompanied by fiery bolts.</note>, and other shining meteors, the wetting of rains, the flooding of waters, the insane and raging violence of winds bursting from the earth, the power of whirlwinds, and infinite other accidents occurring beyond the laws of placid nature. 

Furthermore, in man, who is fabricated in the image of the world (whence he is also called the "Son of the World" by Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary author of the Hermetic Corpus, which explores the relationship between the divine, the cosmos, and humanity.</note>), we have an intellectual heaven assigned to the divine mind and its angelic sparks, whence his head is the seat, the "Holy of Holies." In the middle region or the celestial spirit is the seat of life and the living soul; and its thick air, along with the external seat of this human temple—namely, the body—is subjected to so many and such great changes and the effects of "meteors" <note>Recall that "meteors" here refers to any atmospheric or geological phenomena like rain or earthquakes.</note> tending toward both generation and corruption, that it ought most aptly to be compared to the lowest region of the world.

But indeed Moses in his method of constructing the Tabernacle, and Solomon in his building of the Temple, confirmed this same thing. For their first part is uncovered and left open to the common air, subject to winds, rains, hail, snow, and other atmospheric impressions observed to form beneath the lunar circle—and finally, it is subject to all alterations and changes. Wherefore, common men of every kind, as well as animals, approach this part, where by reason of continual sacrifices there is a constant alternation of life and death. Hence it is that this part is applied in accordance with the elemental disposition of the world, since it is composed of water as a fluid and unstable substance. For this reason the world is truly called a place of shadows and obscurity; and for this cause the tempter is sometimes called the Prince of Darkness, sometimes the Prince of the World, and sometimes the Prince having the power of the air. 

The second part of the Tabernacle or Temple is covered and shines within with gold, and is illuminated by a lampstand with seven branches, which without doubt denote as many planets. Whence this region of the Tabernacle undoubtedly represents the celestial world in the Macrocosm, participating in light and darkness—namely, fire and thin water. For this reason the heavens are called by the Hebrews *Eschamaim* <note>Original: *Eschamaim* from *Esh* (fire) and *majim* (water).</note>, from which it is clear that the substance of the heavens is truly a body, but incorruptible, imbued with a certain intellect by which it is governed and to which it is joined, so that this matter is neither free nor wandering. Such also is the relation of the rational soul in man, or the Microcosm, to his body. 

The third part of the Tabernacle or Temple was the Holy of Holies, presenting the image or likeness of the intellectual world, which is the seat and domicile of the fiery angels and abstract or separated Intelligences (who are the ministers of the living God). This is also signified therein because two golden Cherubim, with wings extended lengthwise, cover and overshadow the mercy seat <term>Propitiatorium</term> <note>The golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant, considered the place where God's presence rested.</note>. Furthermore, in the human temple we have all these regions, differing in every way in purity and impurity. Whence it happens that, just as in the greater world we have all influences from GOD through the most pure and fiery world into that which lies immediately beneath it—namely, by means of the Sephirot <term>Sephirot</term> <note>In Kabbalah, the ten emanations or attributes of God through which the universe is created and governed.</note> through the angelic or Empyrean region into the ethereal one, and likewise from the ethereal into the sublunary, elemental...

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors <note>In early modern science, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, lightning, and clouds, not just falling space rocks.</note>

...mentioned above, in which so many and such great changes occur in the world; so indeed in the human world, the mental force—through the intellect—exerts its influences upon the ethereal region, where the force of life resides. By these influences, the airy spirit <note>original: "spiritus aereus"; a subtle, vital substance believed to carry life through the body</note>—dispersed everywhere through the body and the blood channels—is ruled and governed for the completion and preservation of human life. Truly, we derive the essences of these internal regions from those of the Macrocosm <note>The Great World or Universe</note>. Furthermore, besides that double breath (namely, the common one which the Creator assigned to the world for its completion, and that specific one which He himself breathed into the face of Adam under the name of the **breath of life**), it is necessary that particles from every region of the Macrocosm attributed to man during his creation should concur toward the perfection of the regions of the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," i.e., the Human Being</note>.

Furthermore, by the same reasoning, it is clear that the lowest region of the Macrocosm, or the air—weighed down and disturbed by the presence of various meteors—also communicates constantly with the human air. This is because the common air, drawn in and breathed through the nostrils, the windpipe <note>original: "asperam arteriam"</note>, and the pores of the Microcosm, joins with the air enclosed within the man. Through this communication, the human air partakes in and possesses the natures and "impressions" <note>Influences or physical effects</note> previously generated in the Great Air, and then later dissipated through it and enclosed as if in seed-beds. 

And just as in the Macrocosm, God rains down influences—which procreate all meteors, both favorable and malevolent—through His "shining gates" into the angelic world, and from there into the celestial world, which finally disseminates them everywhere through the elemental world; so indeed is God the general actor in all these things. His act is the effect of His Word dispersed everywhere, or His Wisdom, or His radiant emanation and emission. 

Therefore, it is also manifest that all diseases produced in man proceed from God no differently than those meteors in the Great World. Just as the outflows of the divine will first descend through various orders of angels (according to the different nature of those outflows), who then pour them into the stellar bodies of the ether—from which they are finally rained down into the lower parts for the procreation of meteors and impressions of every kind—so indeed the winds, like spirits and angelic impressions, both occult and manifest, are the ministers of God. They act first in the open air so that they may then act in the human air in various ways and paths to execute the will or pleasure of GOD, whether for good or evil. 

Hence it is that, as was said of the Greater World, *clouds passed in the brightness of His presence: hail and coals of fire. And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave His voice and coals of fire. He sent out His arrows and scattered them; He multiplied lightnings and troubled them, etc. Psalm 17, verse 9.* <note>This corresponds to Psalm 18:12–14 in modern Bibles.</note> By "arrows" here, the rays of lightning can be understood, as it is said elsewhere: *The shafts of lightning shall go directly, and shall be driven to a specific place as if from the well-curved bow of the clouds. Wisdom 5:22.* <note>A reference to the deuterocanonical Book of Wisdom.</note> In the Microcosm, God acts in such a way by means of the human spirit; namely, by kindling a fire in his airy spirit no differently than in the Macrocosmic air.

Since the opportunity presents itself, we shall discuss their names, composition, distinctions, and properties, both in general and in greater detail.

As far as their names are concerned, these are not imposed upon them out of necessity or from their true essence—as if they were named and called upon openly according to how they truly are in their own natures. Rather, these names are merely "memorial signs" <note>original: "signacula memorativa"</note> handed down to the wise through revelation. It is through these signs that they are understood and held in the memory by human beings. For not all divine power is hidden within the spoken voice. For example, the name of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The "Four-Letter Name" of God in Hebrew, YHWH, considered too sacred to pronounce.</note> is ineffable; yet when Moses asked, "What is your name?", God answered him: *i. h. u. h.* <note>The author uses the Latinized characters for the Hebrew Yod-He-Vav-He.</note> saying, "This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation." Therefore, the Tetragrammaton is the name of eternity, but for mankind, it is only a "memorial," because no name can be composed of any voice that could equal the nature of the divinity. For this reason, **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> says that the names of God used by men are derived from His properties (His attributes) and are by no means to be uttered from His essence. For example: *Ehieh* <note>meaning "I Am"</note> comes from eternity; *Adonai* <note>meaning "Lord"</note> from His dominion; *El* <note>meaning "God"</note> from His strength, and so on.

By the same reasoning, it is difficult and impossible to name the **Angels** or **Intelligences** according to their own essences, as they are most full of the divine essence. But in truth, as the wise have come to know the angels through their works, they have imposed upon them names that are both general and particular. For example, by a general name, the first order of the highest hierarchy is called the **Seraphim**, named for their love and fiery heat. The **Cherubim** are named for wisdom and knowledge; the **Thrones** for Justice, and so forth. So too, the **Archangels** and **Angels** are named for their office as emissaries (messengers). Furthermore, specific names are assigned to specific angels for the same reason—that is, according to their condition, office, or virtue. For instance, **Raphael** is named for medicine and healing; **Gabriel** for manliness <note>or strength/might</note>; **Uriel** for his fiery nature, and so on. Nevertheless, it remains quite difficult to produce their proper and essential names, because we are ignorant of their essence. Consequently, human fragility denies and forbids us from finding it, except for what has been granted to us through divine revelation.

Because of this, the most contemplative sages formed the names of angels for themselves out of numbers and figures according to their intentions. They did this just as children are taught to compose words out of letters—whether Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Arabic, or Egyptian. It is not that the voices themselves *need* such letters, but rather that our own weakness is so great that such characters are required for the sake of memory, and such names are formed from letters and characters. Therefore, these names are like "notations" (as **Reuchlin** <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist and scholar of Hebrew and the Kabbalah.</note> holds) which primarily stimulate our senses either by their shape or by their sound. Then, the imagination is stirred by the senses, the imagination stirs the memory, the memory stirs the reason, the reason stirs the intellect, the intellect stirs the mind, and finally, the mind moves the angel.

From this it is clear that the angel is "aroused" by us in this way so that he might perform our pious will—and not that we are moved by the angels. For GOD and the angels are not moved by syllables, words, or the prayers familiar to the common people; rather, *we* are moved by them. These names lead us so that we might have confidence in them, as if they were an anchor. For example (to use Reuchlin’s words), when bringing a ship to port, sailors are accustomed to throw out a rope or extend a cable to pull themselves toward the land, even though the land is immovable. By this effort, they pull *themselves* to the land. In exactly the same way, through signs of this kind presented to our senses, we seem to pull the invisible Divinity to ourselves, when in reality we are pulling our own changeable selves toward the immovable Divinity.

This, then, is why we use signs, characters, voices, hymns, and other ceremonial rites in our invocations of GOD and the Angels for our aid: not, I say, to move them to us, but conversely, so that we may lift ourselves up to them by these means. But back to the point.

They are called *Daemons* and *Daemonia*, meaning those who are "knowing," "intelligent," or "wise," and especially those who are assigned to the care of lower affairs. The **separate intellect** is distinct not from matter, but from the Divine nature, insofar as that nature is **unity**, whereas the angelic essence is **alterity** <note>original: "alteritas." In Neoplatonic philosophy, "alterity" refers to "otherness" or the state of being distinct from the absolute oneness of God.</note>, as will be shown more clearly below. Moreover, by "intelligence" and "separate intellect," we mean an **intelligible substance**, free from all gross and decaying bodily mass; it is immortal, imperceptible to the senses, present to all things, and influencing all things. From this we can further conclude that **Intelligence, Daemon, and Spirit** are of the very same nature and condition.

Names are also assigned to them based on their origin and dignity, namely: **Saints**, the **Will of God** <note>original: "nutus DEI," literally "the nod of God," signifying divine command or intent.</note>, and **Divine Faces**. Indeed, they are even called **Gods**, and "Angels" is sometimes interpreted as "Gods." Furthermore, **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century Christian theologian and Neoplatonist.</note> calls them <term>agalmata</term> <note>original: "agalmata," a Greek term for "images," "statues," or "vessels of honor."</note>, that is, distinguished and polished mirrors in which the divine glory and splendor are received. On account of the omnipresence of such forms, the **Platonists** said that "all things are full of gods," though they referred these gods back to a single **Jupiter** as if to their own parent; for they were born from an uncreated lineage and received from it their radiant glory. Regarding the names given to them due to the names of the men they assisted, we read in the Holy Scriptures that such names are assigned: for instance, in the book of **Ezra**, the name of the Archangel **Jeremiel** is derived from the Prophet **Jeremiah**; **Zachariel** from **Zechariah**; and **Uriel** from the Prophet **Uriah**, whom Joachim killed. In the same way, **Samuel, Ezekiel, and Daniel** are names of both prophets and angels. Furthermore, **Phaniel** is the name of both an angel and the place where **Jacob** wrestled throughout the night. From these examples, it is clear that the names of spirits are never taken from the things over which they are set—whether stars, men, or places—but from their source.

Finally, they are called "good" or "evil" based on the contrariety of their natures. However, since we shall make more extensive mention of these in the following sections where we discuss the differences between Angels, we shall now descend with a light step to their composition.

## Chapter II.

### On the Essence and composition of an Angel: what is its external, and what is its internal?

A great dispute and discrepancy has arisen among the more skilled philosophers and theosophers regarding the **Angelic consistency**. Some (among whom I name **Damascene, Thomas Aquinas, and Dionysius**) affirm that an Angel is something absolutely incorporeal. However, **Basil, Origen, Gregory, and Hermes Trismegistus**, along with the entire **Academic School** <note>The "Academic School" refers to the followers of Plato's Academy.</note>, maintain that an angel is a corporeal substance. **Augustine**, in his commentary on Genesis, says in express words that it is no error to call Angels "bodies," and that daemons are "aerial and fiery animals." Consequently, he seems to assign **aerial bodies** to them; for elsewhere he does not hesitate to assert that angels, from the beginning of their creation, had aerial bodies formed from the purer part of the upper air, suited for acting but not for suffering <note>In this context, "suffering" means being acted upon or feeling pain/decay.</note>. He argues that the **evil angels** were changed by their fall, their bodies taking on the quality of thicker air, so that they might be able to suffer and be tormented by fire. **Basil** teaches us what kind of bodies were assigned to angels by God at creation: namely, that they are thin, aerial, and pure spirits. **Artesius** <note>Likely referring to a medieval or early modern alchemical/hermetic authority.</note>, in his *Key of Wisdom*, says that the **external** of a Devil is air, but his **internal** is fire; for this reason, he teaches that it is very easy for a Devil, by means of his external part, to join with the aerial spirit within a human being, and in this way produce "burning" diseases.

As for our own opinion, it is most certain and proven by clear reason that **Basil, Gregory, Origen**, and all the **Platonists** did not deviate from the truth when they said that daemons or angels are, as to their external part, embodied out of air. Thus, according to the thickening or thinning of the air, different orders of daemons are found in the world, differing in nature and condition. For just as it is observed in the order of nature that **subtle air** is nothing but pure fire, and **moderate air** is nothing but wind, and **thick air** migrates into the nature of water (the density of which is earth itself), so for this very same reason, some daemons are **fiery**, others **aerial**, others **watery**, and some **earthy**. Consequently, all are, in respect to their external part, merely aerial—that is, finely corporeal insofar as they are aerial.

For who, having some training in philosophy, can be ignorant of the fact that **rainwater** was first a dense cloud, and a **dense cloud** was derived from a kind of misty vapor? And that misty vapor, which is visible to the eyes, was once an **invisible vapor**, which is the first step in the progression from moderate, invisible air to that which is thick and visible. This alteration happens through degrees of thickness. By the same logic, it is necessary to consider the various constitutions of angels. From this arises the mystery of **angelic mutation** from one species to another, from a visible form to an invisible one, and vice versa. Thus, it is certain that angels, insofar as they are aerial, are to that extent corporeal; for unless air in its invisible nature were corporeal, it would be impossible for it to be condensed into a visible body. For that which makes something "such" is always "more such" in its beginning <note>A common scholastic maxim: *propter quod unumquodque tale, illud ipsum magis tale* (that because of which a thing is such, is itself more so).</note>; certainly nothing can give what it does not possess. But air, through the addition of density, becomes cloud, water, and earth; therefore, without doubt, it has a corporeal nature within itself, otherwise it would be impossible for it to be altered into a bodily form. This, therefore, was the reason why some daemons are **fiery**—namely, those who are clothed in the thinnest and rarest

**air;** <note>This is a catchword from the bottom of the original page to ensure continuity with the next.</note>

air: others are winds which are indeed clothed in moderate air, and are thicker in their bodies than those made of fire, and so it is with the rest: by which we conclude that, however angels are understood to be in their spheres, they must be accepted as having bodies, although they seem to differ among themselves in rarity and purity according to whether they participate more in this or that element.

For this reason, without a doubt, **Orpheus** <note>The legendary Greek prophet and musician, often cited in the Renaissance as a source of "Ancient Theology."</note> seems to recognize one body that consists only of fire—that is, one whose internal and external nature is both fiery—and these types of daemons he calls **super-celestial**. Another type is tempered by a mixture of fire and air, and these daemons are called **aerial** and **ethereal**. If water is added to these, a third genus of daemons arises, who are called **aquatic**, and these are sometimes visible to the sight. If a subtle earthy part is joined to these, they are called **terrestrial** daemons. By these descriptions, he seems to suggest to us that the bodies of angels appear to differ among themselves according to the various temperaments of the world-spirit <note>original: "spiritus mundani."</note> in its thinness or thickness.

But let us now be permitted to approach a clearer demonstration of this matter. In the entire universe, we have only two things proposed to us: namely, the **Universal Creator**, or the uncreated light that forms all things; and the **Creature**, which constitutes all things in heaven and on earth by means of the said uncreated light. **St. Peter** taught us that this creaturely medium is **water**, just as he called that light the **Divine Word**. Here, therefore, we have the external and internal of all creatures. The internal, I say, has its beginning from the incorruptible **Spirit of God**, which is said to be in every thing (*Wisdom of Solomon 12:1*) <note>The verse states: "For thy incorruptible Spirit is in all things."</note> so that life and being may be imparted to it—that is, to every creature. Among these, we establish that **angels** and **intelligences** are of the first order and intention: that is, closest to God in their essence and excellence, and touching upon God in the purity and thinness of their external consistency. 

Thus, just as God's essence is most simple, most free of all matter, and sufficient unto itself without any help from matter—and is therefore rightly called **Identity** and **Unity**—so too, insofar as an angel (besides the ray of that uncreated divinity which is its internal part) possesses a created external spirit for its consistency to fill the mass of its body (however subtle), it is to that extent a creature and not the Creator. For this reason, it is said to stand apart from the dignity of Identity; because it is fashioned out of two things, it is not inaptly called **Alterity** <term>Alterity (Otherness): A philosophical term meaning the state of being "other" than the absolute One (God).</term> by those most skilled in both philosophy and theosophy. 

Alterity presupposes the **number two** (the binary). From this it is evident that, just as God in His nature is absolute simplicity, so the angelic nature is the highest degree in composition—not unlike how the number two is the first "confusion of unities," or the first immersion of unity into multitude. That is, it is the primary degree in composition, just as the number ten (which is a "leading number" or *articulus*) is the root to a hundred (the square) and to a thousand (the cube). For the *articulus* is the first degree in the composition of numbers after the "digits," which are simple numbers, as will be seen more clearly in the following demonstration. 

Or look at it this way: This **angelic Alterity** is the number two, fashioned from the **Divine Unity** (which is its formal and internal light) and **Created Unity** (which is the subtle air, or the thinnest proportion of the primordial water, which is the angel's external and corporeal part). Therefore, it is certain that the number two is, as it were, the root of all composite things in the world. Since its square is four, it signifies those **four elements**, which, when multiplied in their root, produce the elements under the form of a cube; these are the final species in composition, just as the number one thousand is the final end of numbers. 

Furthermore, just as the pure unity or light of God (the Word) is the primary or angelic form in composition, so the angelic nature is the form for the **celestial composition**, which consists of the **number three** (the ternary). And that composition is likewise in the place of a "form" for the sublunary elements and those things constituted by them. This is the reason why the wise have said that every hidden work, every effect of a **meteor** <note>In the 17th century, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note>, and every property of animal, vegetable, or mineral has its own angelic virtue flowing into it from heaven and the stars themselves. 

Indeed, for this reason **Orpheus** and the **Pythagoreans** said that "all things are full of Gods," all of whom they referred back to the one **Jupiter**, the God of Gods. But the **Platonists** said, "All things are full of forms," which they likewise referred back to the single **Soul of the World**. The former group made their demonstration more *a priori* (from the cause), namely from the angels whom they related to the one God; the latter group more *a posteriori* (from the effect), namely from the Soul of the World, which they placed in the ethereal heaven. This soul is that angelic power infused by God, by which the heaven is animated, and which liberally rains down new forms continually into the various spheres of the elements and their species.

From these things, therefore, we see how angels are composed of an internal and pure part, which is **Divine Light** (with whose glory they are more or less filled), and of the thinnest **world-spirit** as their external part. This spirit also differs in thinness, purity, and subtlety; hence it happens that those who are purer and thinner are more capable of **Grace**, while those of denser bodies are less so. For the further matter stands from grossness, the nearer and closer it is to God. Hence we read in the more secret parts of the **Cabala** and **Theography** <note>The study of divine writing or the mapping of the divine.</note> that the angelic nature is very close to the **First Light** (which is God) because of its purity; and that it draws more from the fountain of light the closer it is, and receives more **Theophany** <note>original: "Theophaniã," the manifestation of God to man.</note>—that is, the light and splendor of God—the purer it is. Thus the First Light descends first into the angels of the first order from the **Father of Lights**, by whom it is then infused into those of the second order, and so on.

But so that these things may be more clearly understood, I would have you know the opinion of the **Archangel** <note>Likely referring to Archangelo de Burgonovo, a 16th-century Franciscan who wrote on the Cabala.</note> in his *Cabalistic Dogmas*: "Whatever," he says, "is distant from God in its first and purest act, must necessarily come under the heading of matter." For this reason, natural philosophers describing the breadth of beings placed the **Pure Act** without matter at the very summit...

# Concerning the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

In which you see the upper portion of the **material pyramid** occupies barely a third part, so that there appear to be three portions of the **formal pyramid** <note>The "Formal Pyramid" represents the descending Light of God or the spiritual "Form," while the "Material Pyramid" represents ascending gross matter.</note> for every one of the material.

Furthermore, from the third division in the highest region up to the seat of God, you see the material pyramid gradually diminished and decreased by degrees as it ascends; for it is most certain that the more an angelic creature is near to the divine nature, the more pure, thin, and rare the matter in its composition is rendered, and consequently, it is proportionally smaller. As you see in that demonstration, the more that pyramid tends toward the **apex** <note>original: "conum." In Fludd's diagrams, the "cone" or point of the material pyramid represents the point where matter is most refined.</note>, the more it is enclosed by the greater portion of the formal pyramid—the emanation sent forth by God. Thus, the order of an angel is such that the closer it approaches God in its nature—that is, the more subtle and rare it is in its matter—the fuller and richer it is in the **divine form**. From this sort of pyramidal proportion, it is permitted to gather the dignities, exaltations, and differences of the angels: for the more the internal nature of the angel (which shone forth from God as pure form) is submerged in a multitude of matter, the more it is lowered in rank and honor. 

Hence it happens that, according to the observations of **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential theologian whose works, like *The Celestial Hierarchy*, defined the nine orders of angels for the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, the Order of *Seraphim* excels that of the *Cherubim* in dignity and excellence, because the highest portion of the Seraphic material composition is at the apex of the material pyramid, which is contiguous with God Himself. For this reason, the angels of that order are those who are said to stand immediately in the presence of God, and consequently, they are the ones who immediately receive the fiery or luminous influxes from God, which they then later send down to the Cherubim, just as the Cherubim send them to the Thrones, and so on successively through the rest; so that the more the orders are removed downward in their position, the more remote they are from the dignity of the divine presence. Those deeper in **divine writing** <note>original: "theographia."</note> seem to argue this with even more expressive words, which are of this sort: "The simpler the substance of the angel, the further it stands from the dominion of matter; and the further the angelic order is from the multitude of matter, the more expressively the likeness of God shines back in it, as if in a most clear and polished mirror." Consequently, the Divine splendor is clearer in it, and the influence of happiness is more copious, more vivid, and more worthy. Hence Dionysius says: "Those who are of the superior order receive the light of God more copiously than those who are inferior, and these participate that light which they have received with others who are lower," for this law of participation is observed among the angels. Thus he speaks. 

But this is also explained more clearly through a certain demonstration in our physics, in the *History of the Microcosm* <note>original: "De Microcosmi historia." This refers to the second volume of Fludd's *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*, focusing on human anatomy, psychology, and the soul.</note>, where we made mention of the harmony of the internal man; which demonstration we have expressed here again in this place for a better understanding of this matter.

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

In this figure, therefore, the proportion is clearly explained by which any order of angels abounds in both matter and form, and also in what proportion the divine emanation immerses itself into multiplicity—that is, into the depth of the formal pyramid. Also, in the contemplation of this image, you will see with open eyes how all things have proceeded from God and how they will return to God, according to the words of the Apostle: "And consequently how one is all, and all finally are nothing but one." <note>Likely referring to the Neoplatonic interpretation of Colossians 1:16-17, "all things were created through him and for him... and in him all things hold together."</note> Furthermore, in the proper speculation of the formal pyramid, you will perceive what the Kabbalists understood by their great angel *Metattron* <term>Metatron: In Jewish mysticism, the highest of angels who serves as the celestial scribe and the mediator between the divine and the mundane.</term> or the emanation from *Ehieh* <term>Ehieh: Derived from "Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh" (I Am That I Am), the Hebrew name for God's absolute essence.</term>, which is that wisdom so often cited in the scriptures; and what that "soul of the world" <term>Anima Mundi: A concept from Plato and later Hermeticism describing an intrinsic spirit that connects all living things on Earth.</term> of the Platonists is, and what the *Pan* and *Panthea* of the poets are. You will see how an angel is an "otherness"—namely, composed from the created pyramid (which is material with respect to its exterior) and the uncreated or formal pyramid (with respect to its interior), which is why angels are called mirrors receiving divine lights. You will see, finally, what "created nature" is—namely, the material pyramid, which is made from primordial water—and what "uncreated nature" is—namely, the informing pyramid, which is nothing other than the emanation or flowing out of divinity into the spirit or "worldly water." This water was once overwhelmed by darkness and formless, but is now "informed" by the divine presence—that is, brought into the light. In conclusion, we can perceive that creation is nothing other than the mixing of the divine emanation with that which is to be re-created, without which it could not persist for even a moment of time. Hence it is said that *all things were made by the Word*, and *without Him was not anything made that was made* <note>original: "Omnia verbo fieri... sine eo nihil," quoting the Gospel of John 1:3.</note>; hence we say that God fills all things everywhere; hence the Apostle said, *In God we move, and in Him, through Him, and from Him all things are, etc.* <note>original: "In Deo nos mouere..." quoting Acts 17:28 and Romans 11:36.</note> Truly, however, the Angels are called creatures of the "first composition" because their matter, being the thinnest of all, first received the effects of the creative emanation, which is therefore called by the wise "the first of all creatures."

But lest you misunderstand me when I mention pyramids—because the word "pyramid" seems to sound mathematical, and furthermore we have described them in a mathematical manner (that is, with a base and a cone)—I wish you to understand that I mean a **physical pyramid**, and not a mathematical one. I have been forced to describe the former by the latter only because it is more commonly known. By "physical pyramid," I mean the worldly spirit which, ascending from the earth to the periphery of the world, always gradually makes itself thinner and more subtle in its ascent, until at its apex it reaches the extreme perfection of rarity, beyond which limit matter cannot ascend. But what is beyond the grasp of matter must necessarily belong to the divine essence. Does not experience itself seem to declare this same thing, since all coincide in this—both natural philosophers and those most skilled in theology—that water is subtler than earth, air than water, fire than air, ether than fire, and the Empyrean spirit <term>Empyrean: The highest part of heaven, thought in Fludd's time to be the source of pure light and the dwelling place of God.</term> than ether? This spirit also has its own degrees up to the cone of the physical pyramid. Here, therefore, we have expressed the material pyramid both physically and mathematically so that what we have said may be more easily grasped by you.

### In a similar way, we delineate the formal pyramid both physically and mathematically in this manner.

**No 1.**  **No 2.**
<note>The image depicts two diagrams showing the intersection of light and matter. The "formal" pyramid represents divine light descending, while the "material" pyramid (implied) represents substance ascending. The point where they meet creates the various levels of existence.</note>

Therefore, by the contraction of the parts of both physical pyramids—the formal as well as the material—they will stand by themselves and in their separate positions, as can be seen in number 2 of the aforementioned demonstration.

But indeed, the proportion of the mixture of the one formal pyramid, namely with the material one, is indicated according to God's decree by the place of intersection, through which the **sphere of equality** passes. For in that place, matter and form are equal, as is declared through the conforming adaptation of both in the second figure of the aforementioned demonstration.

You see, therefore, the reason clearly why the Kabbalists <term>Kabbalists: Practitioners of Jewish mysticism who explored the nature of the divine through symbolic systems, often influencing Renaissance thinkers like Fludd.</term> called an angel **Otherness**—namely, because he is composed of two <note>Referring to the mixture of spiritual form and spiritual matter.</note>—but called God **Identity** and unity, insofar as He is purely formal and self-sufficient, without any regard to matter. Hence, in respect to this property, He is frequently called *Sadai* <note>original: "Sadai" (Shaddai). A Hebrew name for God, often translated as "Almighty," but derived here by Fludd from "She-dai," meaning "He who is sufficient."</note>, that is, self-sufficient.

But Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and theologian.</note>, [John of] Damascus, and others of that sect will reply: "We acknowledge matter in the Angels, but we deny that this matter is corporeal; for we assert it to be purely spiritual." To them, we reply that a star is not to be removed from the designation of "body" simply because it is the denser part of the spirit of its own circle—which spirit is ethereal, and consequently, exceedingly thin and rare. Furthermore, even a body that is however rare and invisible is no more to be removed from the laws of bodies than that which is thick and visible. Yet we see that a star is a visible, dense body; should it then be denied that the ethereal spirit is likewise a body, even if invisible, since [it is composed] of its invisible parts...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 216 regarding the composition of spiritual beings. Fludd previously established that angels are considered "Otherness" because they are composed of two parts—spiritual matter and divine form—unlike the absolute "Identity" of God. Here, he defends the idea that spirits can be considered "bodies" in a subtle sense and explores their role as mirrors of divine light.</meta>

# On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.

...can a visible body be produced by addition? Therefore, whatever can be understood within the laws of rarity and density can be called (and not without justice) a body. Just as a cloud is a dense form of air, why shouldn't its rare form also receive the name of "body," since that which creates such a thing is itself of that nature? What then? Is it because it is a "natural body" that it cannot be a "spiritual body"? The Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44.</note> says: *The body that is sown in corruption rises in incorruption; the natural body will be changed into a spiritual body.* Therefore, it is no more impossible for a sublunary, ethereal, empyrean, or angelic spirit to be a **rare body**—and consequently for angelic creatures to be rendered corporeal by their presence—than it was for the physical body of our Savior. After His passion, His body was made incorruptible and was raised and sublimated by its purity and subtlety all the way to the throne of God, where He is said to sit at the right hand of the Father; and yet, nonetheless, He did not lose the name of "body." For this reason, we should not be faulted for assigning an external corporeal nature to angels of any order, because all matter—whether it is subject to corruption or is of a celestial and incorruptible nature—is contained within the limits of corporeal substance. For who can rightly deny that water reduced to vapor is a body, just as much as it is in the form of liquid water? Or that the tip of a material pyramid is any less a "body" than its base? The entire difference lies in **rarity and density** <note>In Fludd's philosophy, "rarity" refers to substance that is thin, light, and spiritual, while "density" refers to substance that is thick, heavy, and material.</note>. Truly, because a body is "dense," it does not follow that something "rare" is excluded from being a body. Therefore, I hope it has been explained more clearly than light that angels, as far as their external part is concerned, are corporeal and not incorporeal, as some have thought.

But as for their internal part, we say that it is **uncreated light**, such that the exterior of angels is like a highly polished, clear, and stainless mirror, receiving within itself the ineffable likeness of God. For in them, as if in a clean and pure mirror, the divine splendor emanating immediately from the Divine Majesty shines back. Whence (as was declared in the preceding pages) angels are called *Agalmata* <note>original: "Agalmata" (Greek: ἀγάλματα). While usually meaning "statues" or "images," Fludd follows the Neoplatonic tradition of Dionysius the Areopagite, treating them as "divine mirrors."</note>, that is, very clear mirrors receiving the light of God. For this reason, an angel is said to be the image of God, the revelation of hidden light, a mirror most polished and pure, without stain.

->*Dionysius, On the Divine Names, chapter 6.*<-

For they receive through influence the light of the Deity, which in itself is incomprehensible and invisible, and they show it, emit it, and reveal it to others of an inferior order. The angel is called a "mirror" because it is able to receive light, and a "most polished mirror" because of the complete purity of its substance. Another author says that angels are **intellectual lights**, receiving light from the First Light. That emanation, however, descending both into the bodies of angels and into other creatures through their mediation, is what the <term>Kabalists</term> call *Hochma* <note>original: "Hochma" (Hebrew: חָכְמָה). Translated as Wisdom.</note>, or Wisdom. This is why the wise man calls it the "first creature," as it proceeds immediately like a son from a father, from a shining fountain. Solomon describes this as a holy, intelligent spirit, more mobile than all mobile things, reaching everywhere because of its purity. He says that in its essence it is a vapor of the power of God, a certain pure emanation or flow of the brightness of the Almighty God, and the whiteness or splendor of eternal light, and a stainless mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of His goodness (*Wisdom 7*). From this, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalists, this spirit is that great angel **Metatron**, whose role it is to animate the entire universe, whom the Platonists were fond of calling the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "anima mundi." The principle of life and intelligence that permeates the physical universe.</note>. But they understood that divine brightness only insofar as it is mixed with created spirit. Therefore, we say that this brightness, first striking the angelic spirit, formed it by its presence. For this reason, it is also said that the **Name of God** is in the angel—that is, the Divine light or the Word that gives life to all things, moving primarily within the angelic composition. Hence angels are ministers, through whom, as if through instruments, the Word of God is perfected in this world. Wherefore the Psalmist says: *Angels of God, most mighty in strength, performing His word, listening to the voice of His speech, His ministers, doing His pleasure (Psalm 103).* And elsewhere: *Behold, I send my angel before you; listen to his voice, because my name is in him (Exodus 23).*

We conclude, therefore, that an angel is composed of **created spirit**, which is its external part and serves as its body, and **uncreated light**, shining immediately from God, which is its internal part by which it is animated. By means of this composition, an angel is sometimes called "Angel" or "Otherness" in Holy Scripture with respect to the whole composition of two parts (internal and external); and in another place, it is called **JEHOVAH** with respect to its internal part alone, which is the emanation of God. Thus, it is sometimes said that an "angel" was in the bush, and sometimes that "Jehovah" spoke to Moses from the bush. For this very reason, the Name of God is assigned to the angels of God, such as:
->**Gabriel, Michael, Raphael, etc.**<-
<note>The suffix "-el" in these names is the Hebrew word for God.</note>

Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Division II.

# CHAPTER III.

## On the General Difference of Angels, and Then Afterward on the Specific Division of Good Angels.

Since it is well known and common knowledge, not only from the experience of Christians themselves, but even from that of the Pagans, that there are demons both bad (which they call *cacodaemons* <term>cacodaemon: from the Greek "kakos" (evil) and "daimon" (spirit); an evil spirit or demon</term>) as well as good: we have first thought it worthwhile to distinguish these "intelligences" according to this general division based on the opposition of their properties and conditions. Therefore, we distinguish angels at their primary root in this way:

We distinguish Angels into:
*   Good or Luminous ones (see section A).
*   Bad and dark ones (concerning which, see the following chapter).

Such a great opposition in the Angelic condition consists in the diverse property of the Creator, which varies according to the ten names attributed to Him by the Hebrews according to the sense of the Holy Bible. According to the dispositions of these names, various influences flow into this world through the *sephiroth* <term>sephiroth: the ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself to the world</term>, or "enumerations," or "luminous gates." Some of these influences tend toward clemency and kindness, which are carried downward through the mediation of good angels; likewise, those which incline toward severity are referred to punishing angels, who strike with the blow of divine wrath, as will be discussed abundantly below. According to these two most opposite properties, worldly men have found diverse forms of knowledge: namely, the **Good**, which is occupied with God (the source of all goodness) and His good administrative angels; and the **Bad**, which concerns the Devil, who is the merchant of all malice or the effects of darkness. To delineate this for you methodically, we have compiled it into this distinction:

Knowledge in this world is either:
1.  **Of the Good**, and it is:
    *   **Theosophy** <term>theosophy: literally "divine wisdom"; knowledge of God and spiritual things</term>, which is concerned with two things:
        *   Knowledge of the word of God, and the ordering of life according to His word.
        *   Knowledge of the government of GOD through Angels (whom the holy page calls "Watchers" <note>original: *vigiles*; a reference to the Book of Daniel and the Book of Enoch</note>), as well as the discerning of the mystery of the angels themselves.
    *   **Androsophy** <term>androsophy: "human wisdom"; the study of man and the natural world</term> given to man, namely:
        *   The science of natural things.
        *   Prudence in human affairs.
2.  **Of the Bad**, and it is:
    *   **Cacosophy** <term>cacosophy: "bad wisdom"; the inversion of divine knowledge</term>, whose members are:
        *   Contempt for the word of God, and living according to the will of the evil spirit.
        *   Ignorance of God's government through Angels.
        *   Despising the protection of good Angels and embracing the society of malignant demons.
        *   Idolatry and Atheism.
    *   **Cacodaemonia** <term>cacodaemonia: the practical application of demonic knowledge or sorcery</term>, which also has two members:
        *   The science of sorcerers in nature and the use of it.
        *   Prudence in all arts inclined toward the destruction of the human race, and their practice to the insult of God and the harm and destruction of man.

But to the purpose: we distinguish good Angels in various forms, according to the various dimensions of the world, that is, according to the orders of the heavens, from which the world is composed.

<margin>B. The supercelestial angels are divided by:</margin>
- **Recent Theologians** into three distinctions which they call hierarchies or choirs, named as:

        - **Seraphim**
        - **Cherubim**
        - **Thrones**

        - **Powers**
        - **Dominations**

    - First: **Haioth Kadosh** <note>original Hebrew: "Holy Living Creatures"</note>, that is, the animals of holiness or lives.

    - Ninth: **Cherubim**.

Theologians have placed the **Seraphim**, **Cherubim**, and **Thrones** in the upper distinction or Hierarchy as supercelestial spirits. They contemplate the rank and condition closest to divine providence. The highest of these orders (Seraphim) regards God's goodness and fiery love; the second (Cherubim) regards His essence and wisdom; the third (Thrones) regards His prudence and justice. **Isaiah (Chapter 6)** mentions the Seraphim, and Holy Scripture describes them in many other places as spirits being closest to God in rank. To the Cherubim is assigned the guarding of Paradise, and elsewhere: *God ascended upon the Cherubim, and flew upon the wings of the wind* (**Psalm 17** <note>Modern Psalm 18:10</note>). Many holy biblical passages also speak of the Thrones, namely **Ezekiel Chapter 1**, the Apostle in **Colossians 1**, and the Book of Revelation in many places.

In the second Hierarchy are placed **Virtues**, **Powers**, and **Dominations**, acting as spirits of the world whose office is more adapted to the governance of the world. The highest of these (Dominations) commands and instructs the lower ones; the second (Powers) administers in the heavens and ordains the laws of fate; the third (Virtues) strives with great effort to prevent those things that presume to disturb divine law in any way. The Apostle speaks of principalities, powers, and dominations in the place cited above, namely, **1 Colossians 1:16**.

In the lower Hierarchy, they describe **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**, whose office is to descend to care for lower things. The first order of this distinction (Principalities) cares for public matters, namely Princes, Magistrates, and Provinces or kingdoms—each one to its own. Among these, 72 are numbered by the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalist: a practitioner of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</term>, to whom 72 portions of the earth are committed by Divine Providence, which are therefore called kingdoms.

The second order (Archangels) is involved in sacred matters and assists upright men on earth; they are said to offer prayers and sacrifices to **GOD**. Furthermore, seven of them are dedicated in the heaven of the wandering stars <term>wandering stars: the seven classical planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon)</term> to their governance and direction, as will be discussed more broadly below. Finally, it is the role of the **Angels** to care for those things which are of lesser...
