<header># Universal Experiment</header>

L. M. is the neck of the <term>matrass</term> <note>original: "matracei"; a long-necked glass bulb used in chemistry.</note>, the opening of which is submerged in water.
N. is the opening in the lid, through which the part of the neck submerged in water enters.
M. is the portion of the matrass divided into twelve equal parts.
O. is the body of the matrass, standing perpendicular and upright.

We believe it is worth the effort to proceed quickly to its properties and use. First, therefore, it must be observed that when the body of the matrass, O, is heated, the air contained within it is thinned by the external heating source. Once <term>rarefied</term> <note>original: "subtiliatus"; made thinner or less dense.</note>, the air requires a more spacious place to exist. Thus it happens that the greater portion of air—which had been gathered and contracted by the cold in the hollow of that body—now, having been more or less thinned and expanded by the heat, requires a larger space for its existence. For this reason, a portion of it is forced to exit into the open air while the vessel or body of the matrass is heating up.

This is why, when the opening of the neck of the matrass is placed in water (while the vessel is still warm), as that body gradually cools down, the water is raised higher and higher into the neck of the matrass—specifically from degree 1 to 2, and then later from 2 to 3. The reason for this is as follows: the action of cold is in every way the opposite of heat. Therefore, if it is the nature of heat to rarefy and require a larger or more spacious place for the thing it has thinned, it follows that, conversely, it is the nature of cold to thicken and gather together that which was dispersed and rarefied by heat, reducing it into a narrower space.

Thus it happens that as the vigor of the heat gradually vanishes and the power of the cold consequently grows stronger, a greater portion of air has been expelled from the cavity of the vessel by thinning. Because the barrier of the water prevents new air (sufficient to match the proportion of the growing cold spirit) from being drawn into the belly of the vessel, it is necessary that a portion of water supply the lack of air. The water is raised into the neck of the matrass in place of the air. This occurs because the rarefied air, which once filled the entire cavity of the body, is now contracted into a narrower place by the <term>styptic</term> <note>original: "stiptica"; contracting or binding.</note> and freezing faculty of the cold. Without the supplement of water filling that space, it would leave a vacuum in the vessel, which is in no way permitted by nature—as has been explained more extensively elsewhere.

Therefore, once the body of water has been drawn in and raised in this way due to the successive creeping in and abundance of cold, it will be necessary that every successive increase of cold or heat be discerned by the naked eye. For if either the air surrounding that vessel, or something more physical placed against or adhering to the vessel, grows warm, the water will decline downward toward the box. For example, if according to the state of the cold the water stood at degree 6 or 7 in the neck, it will descend by as many degrees as the proportion of heat has increased in the enclosed air, whether by the surrounding air or by the application of a hand or another object to the body.

The reason for this is readily apparent: namely, because the greater the proportion of heat (as has been said), the greater also will be the rarefaction or thinning of the enclosed air. And the thinner and more rarefied a thing is made, the larger and more free a place it seeks for its existence. For a single handful of water expanded into air requires ten times as much space to be contained as it would claim for itself in its consistency as water; the same ratio or proportion exists between air and fire, for air kindled by heat migrates gradually into the thinness of fire. This is why the air enclosed in the body of the vessel—once contracted by cold and reduced to a narrower place—is now expanded by the approach of heat and thrusts the water that had been raised in the neck downward, so that it may acquire a larger or narrower space for itself according to the greater or lesser degree of its rarefaction.

Are we not taught by experience that water, reduced into vapor by the violence of fire, requires a vaster place for its freedom? Whoever intends to equip themselves more exactly for the investigation of this matter, we wish them to refer to the experiments brought forth by us in Chapter 2, Experiments 12, 13, and 16, and in Tract 2, Part 7, Book 3, Chapter 1, Rules 6 and 7, where we have clearly expressed the infinite faculty of nature expanding itself. Furthermore, this same thing is explained even more evidently to the unlearned in <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "puluere Bombardali"; literally "bombard powder" or "cannon powder."</note>, a small portion of which in its earthy substance is accustomed to be converted into a great smoke like a huge cloud, snatching and shattering everything with it if its spacious freedom is hindered. So also in the extraction of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aquæ fortis"; nitric acid.</note> composed from <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "sale petræ"; potassium nitrate.</note> and <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitriolo"; sulfates.</note>, we observe the receiving vessel containing the greatest spirits leaping out from the mouth of the <term>retort</term> <note>original: "retortæ"; a glass vessel used for distillation.</note>. We conclude, therefore, that heat, by expanding, makes the air enclosed in the body repel the water raised in the neck, so that the expanded air itself may acquire a larger place, according to the greater or lesser dominance of the effect of heat in the enclosed air.

But indeed, as the effect of heat decreases and languishes, and as the cold gradually revives and predominates, it is necessary that all the power and operation of the preceding heat be removed, and that, on the contrary, the property of cold and that act contrary to heat be produced. Hence it is that just as in the act of heat the water raised in the neck was pushed downward, so now by the contrary affection of cold, the contrary effect is usually brought forth.

The reason for this matter is as follows: namely, just as it is the property of heat to thin and rarefy—in which act it requires a wider space to contain the thinned substance—

Just as heat thins the air, it is likewise the duty of the region of cold to thicken and make dense that which the heat has refined. In this capacity, cold contracts into a smaller space and quantity that which the heat had dilated. The more the effects of cold assault the air, the more the air is constricted and compressed into a narrower space.

Hence, it follows (lest a <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "vacuum"; at this time, many scientists believed nature "abhorred a vacuum" and would pull fluids in to fill any empty space.</note> be created) that the same water which the action of heat pushed downward is drawn upward by the action of cold as it contracts the air. The water is carried upward by as many degrees as the cold is exalted in its dominion over the power of heat.

As for the underlying reason for these properties, it has been explained by us at length in Book 1, Chapter 4 of the first part of this work, where we deal with the <term>accidental principles of meteors</term> <note>original: "principiis meteororum accidentalibus"; in this era, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon like rain, wind, or lightning.</note>, and we shall clarify the same even more brilliantly in the following sections.

## CHAPTER III.

### On the various uses of this experimental instrument.

Although the primary goal in demonstrating such an instrument is to derive the most fit speculation regarding "meteors" through its dual and contrary motions, it is also my secondary purpose here to speak—not irrelevantly to our following contemplation—of its common uses.

By its general action of constriction, or the pulling up of water through the contraction of air, we perceive the nature of **Density** or the thickness of any thing; this action of nature proceeds from cold (as you have seen recorded above). By the action of **Dilation**, through which the water is propelled downward because of the scattering and <term>resolution</term> <note>original: "resolutionem"; the breaking down of a substance into a finer state.</note> of the enclosed air, we perceive the cause of **Rareness** or subtlety in nature, a property derived from heat. From this, it is certain—and we are made more sure beyond all doubt—that nothing in the universal kingdom of nature can be <term>rarefied</term> or made subtle except by means of light or fire (whether visible or invisible), the effect of which is heat. Conversely, nothing can be condensed, constricted, or thickened where darkness does not hold dominion, as the effect of darkness is cold, as was brilliantly explained in the place cited above.

Its more specific use is manifold. First and most evidently, it is accustomed to indicate the natural state and <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperamentum"; the specific balance of qualities in the air.</note> of the external air in terms of heat and cold. For the higher the water tends to go through the degrees of the neck, the greater is the dominion of cold in the air. Thus, in any quarter of the year or day of the week, we can judge the levels of cold by the rising of the water. Indeed, even within the same day, we may perceive the conflict between solar heat and cold, along with many other things worthy of observation. Furthermore, by the same logic, we can determine the dominion of heat in any quarter, day, or hour through the contrary motion. These observations are matters of no small importance in the unfolding of nature and her mysteries.

Moreover, these effects are typically produced by the addition of heat or cold from outside sources. Thus, if we merely apply a hand to the bottom of the glass bulb, the enclosed air—refined by the heat of the limb—forces the water downward in the blink of an eye. When the hand is removed from the vessel, the water immediately yearns to rise back to its original place assigned to it by natural cold.

Finally, by diligent observation of this instrument and watchful attention to the movement of the water, we can measure the heat of **chemical furnaces**. If we have two such instruments ready—one exposed to the natural state of the air, and the other applied to the vent or breathing-hole of a furnace—they will provide a ratio for adapting the artificial heat of the one to the natural heat of the other. Thus, the one applied to the artificial heat will be "rectified" in its degree by the natural one. It will then be very easy to calculate a unified proportion for the artificial heat in this way: by adapting the degree of natural heat in the air to the artificial. For example, if the instrument in natural air reflects the water at only degree 7, but the heat of the instrument applied to the furnace depresses it to degree 4, I may then observe that the artificial fire exceeds the natural by exactly three degrees. Therefore, if the natural heat in the air later decreases and the water rises to degree 8 or 9, I will expect the water in the artificial instrument to rise by the same proportion to degree 5 or 6. Thus, it always maintains its distance of a triple proportion, which is to be ascribed to the artificial heat, and so on for the rest.

Now, however, I shall proceed to the second part of this book, where, with God’s favor, we shall discourse upon the strict contemplation of the generation of meteors, with respect to the action or property of this "spiritual" instrument.

# SECOND PART OF THIS
## Experimental Book.
### CHAPTER I.
->On the primary reason for condensation and freezing.<-

Just as we have abundantly declared to you in the previous sections that heat and its effects flowed forth from God in His revealed state, so too do we show that coldness and its effects originally drew their beginning from God in His hidden state. Nevertheless, coldness (though born from the womb of darkness and <term>hyle</term> <note>original: "hylæ"; a Greek term used in ancient philosophy to describe the primordial, unformed "stuff" or matter of the universe.</note>) was not prior to heat in either place or time in terms of its actual existence. For coldness is only known to exist in the world insofar as it is opposed in every way to heat in its nature and properties.

And yet, God in His hidden state is thought—at least in relation to us—to be older in time than God in His revealed state, because before the creation of the world He was unknown and, as it were, at rest in respect to human capacity. For this reason, He is called <term>Ain</term> <note>original: "A E N"; a Hebrew term meaning "nothing" or "non-being," used in the Cabala to describe the infinite God before He manifested as light.</note> by the Cabalists and Hebrew Rabbis, which means "nothing" and "non-being," since He was known only to Himself and existed within Himself. Indeed, those more skilled in the occult philosophy established that such Wisdom existed before the fabric of the world: namely, a dark principle, having action only in potentiality. On this account, they frequently called it the "Dark <term>Aleph</term>" <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Here it represents the "First Principle" of all things.</note>, meaning that which has not yet shone forth from the darkness, but has reflected its rays back into itself. Hence, <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of alchemy and Hermetic philosophy.</note> said: *The Monad generates the Monad and reflected its ardor into itself.*

If, therefore, all ardor and fervor come from revelation and from this outflow—that is, from the revealed divine act, namely the emission and emanation of divine splendor from the center of darkness to its circumference when the Hidden God is turned into the Revealed God (or the Dark Aleph into the Radiant one)—it follows that all chill and cold are produced by the opposite reasoning. That is, they come from the contraction of the divine rays into themselves. In this act, the aerial medium, being deprived of heat (which arises from the act of sending out light, not pulling it back), gives way to cold. This quality holds its name and dominion from the deprivation of heat, just as dryness arises from the absence of moisture.

And the more God contracts or hides His action within Himself or His center, the more cold abounds, and dense, earthly darkness holds dominion. Therefore, in such a case, the air is turned into thick and dark clouds, into frost, into snow, hail, and even into ice. For Wisdom (which is the life of the mundane spirit, and consequently of the entire world), by withdrawing itself from the circumference toward the center, also contracts the spirit. Wisdom is life to this spirit just as the soul is to the body. Moreover, there is such an immense appetite in created matter for the central forming Creator that it follows Him by a certain natural instinct and is obedient to Him, both in dilating and in contracting, according to the will of the creating spirit—as if it greatly feared that by deserting the benevolent rays of its Creator, it would be rendered deformed and clearly nothing, just as it was in the beginning.

It is from this, therefore, that we have so many contraries in this world consisting of a binary nature (for which reason the number two is called the "number of confusion and imperfection" by the Pythagoreans): namely, darkness and light, night and day, the Devil and God, death and life, rest and motion, nothing and something, sin and justice. The prince of light presides over some of these, and the prince of darkness over others. Nonetheless, in reality, from a central consideration, all these things are but one. Hence it is certain that "one is all," or as we have it in the Sacred Scriptures: Christ (or Wisdom) is all, the beginning and the end, the Alpha and Omega, the center and the circumference.

Nevertheless, in respect to the variety of actions—without which there would be no mutability in the world, and no generation or corruption in the nature of things—this "One" seems to be divided and distributed into various things as far as we mortals are concerned. For by an absolute, general contraction of the divine rays that create all things within themselves, it is necessary that the world be reduced to nothing. By a particular contraction, it is necessary that the individual creature affected by that deprivation or withdrawal should suffer death, or tend toward death the more effectively God calls back or contracts the rays of His kindness into Himself. This is also to be gathered clearly enough from these words of the Royal Prophet:

> *When God hides his face, the creatures are troubled; when he takes away their breath, they die and return to their dust; when he sends forth his spirit, they are created anew. Psalm 104:29.* <note>original: "Deo abscondente faciem suam creatura conturbantur..."; the author is quoting the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note>

Whereby "the hiding of His face" is understood to be the turning away or contraction of His life-giving rays into Himself, more or less. From this "taking away" and absolute contraction comes the complete deprivation of life, the removal of vital motion, the fixation of the body, and its reduction to dust. But truly, by the "sending forth of His spirit," the dead rise again, the sick are restored to their former health, they are refreshed with good, and they are observed to remain in a state of unity and specific being.

And hence the Royal Psalmist says: *Life is in the benevolence of Jehovah. Psalm 30:6.* And elsewhere: *The fountain of life is with thee. Psalm 36:9.*

And elsewhere, the prolongation of life is the kindness of God <note>original: "benignitas DEI"</note>, as in Psalm 90:14. And Job said, *Thy visitation hath preserved my spirit*, Job 10:12. And Moses, *The Lord Jehovah thy God himself is thy life, and the length of thy days*; but of these things, we shall speak more secretly elsewhere.

From these things, therefore, it appears more clearly than the midday light (unless I am mistaken) that coldness arises by the contraction or reflection of the divine rays into Himself—that is, the absence of heat. And from cold comes freezing, and rest, and the removal of motion, and consequently death or the deprivation of life. It is from this that the earth, which is the last or furthest order in the nature of things, rests the most; it is immobile and fixed, being drenched in a thickening and contracting coldness. Therefore, the primary origin of freezing and constriction is from God lurking centrally, contracting and reflecting the rays of His goodness into Himself (as <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, a series of sacred texts on philosophy and magic.</note> holds), or as the prophet David suggests, by hiding His face or receiving His spirit back into Himself in Psalm 104. Conversely, the primary beginning of resolution and expansion <note>original: "dilatationis"</note> is from God opening Himself, emitting the rays or spirits of His goodness here and there everywhere according to His pleasure. This is according to the words of the royal prophet: that creatures are recreated when God emits His spirit. Or, as Hermes Trismegistus has it: *When Poimandres wished to reveal himself, all things were turned into a most pleasant light*, etc. But regarding this revealed principle, or the primary light brought into the light, we shall deal more extensively in the following sections.

## CHAPTER II.

### On the primary occasion and origin of thinning and expansion.

We have indicated that the primordial cause of condensation and thickening was the effect of the hidden God—namely, coldness. Now, however, we think it necessary to demonstrate that the cause of thinning <note>original: "subtiliationis"; the process of making matter less dense.</note> and expansion flowed originally from the efficacy of the active, revealed God. Thus, according to the meager capacity of humans, the <term>Dark Aleph</term> <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"; the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet used here to represent God in His primordial, unmanifested state.</note> or hidden God is considered by the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that explores the nature of the divine and the universe.</note> to be at rest—that is, idle and not at all active, and consequently existing only in potentiality. This state has regard to nothing, which is why it is called **NOTHING** <note>original: "NIHIL"; a translation of the Hebrew term "Ain" or "Ayin."</note> by the Cabalists. Likewise, on the opposite side, they understood the **Light Aleph** to be the revealed God—that is, the acting God, revealing Himself, illuminating and creating all things by His emanation and His luminous Word. Similarly, just as it is the nature of cold to condense, thicken, rest, and act very little (unless it is by reacting—that is, by repelling the attacks of active heat), so indeed we see that, by a contrary turn, the nature of heat is to thin, and never to rest, but to always be engaged in action. Its contrary, therefore, is coldness.

From these things it will be right to consider that heat is the offspring and firstborn of the acts of the revealed God, just as coldness is the immediately proceeding child of the hidden God. Cold holds its place and sequence during that progress which occurs from the hidden God to the revealed God—that is, between God having regard for nothing, and God Himself intent on the formation of the world or His creatures. Thus it happens that the fountain of cold is potentiality alone; for although it is a quality, it is nonetheless potential in itself, and is not brought into action except in respect to heat. Hence its name is defined in relation to heat, and it does not usually act except insofar as it suffers in return, and as it were, reverberates the actions arising from heat. Cold, therefore, rests with darkness by a natural instinct, while heat reigns and acts with light. 

And from this, it is observed that just as heat is most conducive to the generation of things, so also coldness is always the companion of deprivation. Yet it is certain that both these contrary qualities emanate from a single God in essence, though differing in property, which is why the Wise Man says in Ecclesiastes 7:14: *Good and evil, life and death, poverty and riches are from God.* For that same nature which is the author of generation is also the author and occasion of corruption. Therefore, when God hides His face—that is, leaning toward His hidden nature—cold reigns and heat grows faint; but when He emits His spirit—that is, manifesting or revealing Himself—the effect of heat is increased. 

By "God" in His simple essence, considered without any regard for creation, we understand the "hidden God." But by the "Word," the Holy Scriptures signified the Second Person, the first emanation into the world, the uncreated light in the world, by means of which all things were made and without which nothing was made (as is found in John). The Word, therefore, acts in its power, and the effect of its action produces heat. Heat, in imitation of its divine parent, always desires to move and never rests from action, but labors by expanding and thinning, and strives to destroy those things which coldness has built. Hence come death and life, generation and corruption; hence the thick and the thin, hence heaven and earth, hence the bright and the dark, hence motion and rest. The royal prophet taught us clearly the different disposition of these qualities, along with the primordial principle of each, in these words: *He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold? He sendeth out his word and melteth them; as soon as he bloweth with his wind, the waters flow.* Psalm 147:17. From this speech, one may gather that God, in His cold property, thickens the thin air into ice and snow and frost (as was clearly explained in the preceding verse). But truly, through His Word—that is, through the revelation of Himself—those things so thickened and condensed by cold are again resolved by thinning, and are led back from earthly thickness into water, and from water into air.

### Corollary from the Demonstration.

All these things, which have just been narrated concerning cold and heat, are best demonstrated by the effect observed through our experimental machine <note>This refers to the "weather glass" or an early thermoscope, a device Robert Fludd famously used to demonstrate the physical effects of temperature changes.</note>. For as far as the nature of coldness is concerned, we observe that when it predominates in the open air or in the body of the flask, the water is raised higher and higher. We have the reason for this at hand: namely, because the enclosed air, which was previously expanded by external heat, is now—with the arrival and assault of cold—contracted more and more according to the intensity and dominance of that cold. This contraction happens by natural necessity and instinct; but since a vacuum is not permitted in the nature of things, it is necessary that the water touching this enclosed air should fill the place which the air previously occupied due to its expansion. Thus, the water is visibly raised upward because of the presence of intense coldness, and the more that coldness dominates, the more the water will be lifted higher by degrees. Conversely, when heat predominates in the external air or on the surface of the vessel, the internal air (enclosed in the vessel) will expand for the reasons we alleged above. In its expansion, it requires a larger place to be contained. Therefore, the water—which had previously been drawn up by the predominating cold—now descends to give place to the expanding air; it is seen to humble itself by as many degrees as the heat is observed to prevail over the cold. Take this as a general consideration of this machine in relation to natural reality. Now, however, we shall move on to more particular matters.

# PART III.

## On the strict investigation of Meteors from the observation of those properties of the machine.

### CHAPTER I.

### On the Origin of Winds.

<margin>B</margin>
Elsewhere we have declared abundantly, and this according to the doctrine of the Sacred Page <note>The "Sacred Page" refers to the Holy Scriptures or the Bible.</note>, that God is the Act of acts, the Creator of creatures, the Light of lights, and the fountain of life and motion. This fountain of all things—this primary Spirit of spirits, Unity of unities, or the center of the universal circle—sent forth His Word. That is to say, He manifested His light which was once contracted and hidden within Himself (centrally). Through this emanation of His divine light or Word—which is the power of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often considered in Renaissance philosophy to be the source of all creative power.</note>, or the divine Word itself, or the light in the world which the world did not comprehend—He wonderfully brought all things existing only in potentiality into light and Being. This is according to that saying of the royal Psalmist: *By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth* (Psalm 33:6). Or as Saint Peter has it in 2 Peter 3:5: *The heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God.* Therefore, this light, creating all things and moving all things from the center, having completed the third day of creation, placed its tabernacle in the sun—that is, in the central habitation of the sun, as the most beautiful of all creatures and the most worthy in its cleanliness and purity. From the fountain of the sun, therefore, is the spring of life, the emanation of light both celestial and elemental, and the soul and act of the universal spirit. Thus, all other stars obey the sun like an emperor holding his throne and scepter. But even the Wise Man <note>Refers to Solomon, the traditional author of Ecclesiastes.</note> seems to recognize the sun's power over the worldly spirit, expressing it in these very words:

> After the sun sets, it pants again toward its place from whence it rises; it hastens to the south and circles toward the North; and circling in its conversion, the air (or as Jerome interprets it, the spirit) hastens on; but Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino (1470–1541), a prominent Hebraist and translator whose version of the Bible was highly regarded for its literal accuracy.</note> has it here: "The Wind, by circling continually, returns to its circuits."

This is from Ecclesiastes, Chapter 1. And indeed, since the soul and act of the world comes from the invisible or internal sun—which establishes its tabernacle in the visible sun—there is no doubt that all the force and motion of the worldly spirit derives its origin from that fountain. Consequently, every motion or agitation of the universal air comes from the central sun, acting as the intimate principle of all things. But they are said to obey the commands of <term>Juno</term> <note>In the alchemical and hermetic tradition, Juno often represents the element of Air.</note> insofar as they do not blow except in the aerial medium,

...which is called Juno <note>In classical mythology and alchemy, Juno often personifies the element of Air.</note>. From this, it is demonstrated clearly enough that Aristotle and Solomon agree on this point: namely, that the air or the wind is governed by the rays and motion of the sun. Indeed, it is certain and proven by the experience of skilled astronomers that the variety of the movements of the winds happens because of the various aspects or reflections of the sun and the other wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note>. Since all the stars receive their life and luminous being from the sun, it follows that all the actions of the planets—flowing from their influences upon one another due to their diverse aspects—originally proceed from the soul of the Sun or its central unity. This is not surprising, since we see diverse effects arising from the same fire. For example, fire warms gently, it parches and burns without mercy, it moistens by accident (which happens by thinning the substance), and yet, through the dry removal of moisture from the calcined earth, it both gives life and destroys; through reflection, it torments bodies more severely; contracted into a corner, it penetrates vividly; but when spread out, it vanishes. In the same way, the sun acts in different ways according to the various media through which it passes. For example, in the air it warms gently; in water, its heat is more tempered; sometimes it nourishes the earth and makes the grass, herbs, and trees grow; and sometimes it burns and cracks the earth and its fruits with its excessive heat. Nevertheless, the sun is always the same in its essential temperature and is not seen to vary except because of the diversity of the media and bodies it acts upon. For in the open air it nourishes mildly, but by means of a burning mirror it burns cruelly; yet it is always the same in itself and of the same power. It is only observed to act differently according to the nature of the passive receiver. For example, in the heavens, it communicates its rays to the planetary bodies, which in turn—by secondary or tertiary reflection, that is, from one planet to another according to the diversity of their distance, the difference of their bodies, and the variety of their aspects—produce various effects in the elements. From this, therefore, it follows that when God wishes to create this or that effect in the earth or air according to His pleasure and the order of nature, He then looks to this or that planet; by whose aspect the other planets also look upon one another, and from this, various winds arise. The "souls" of these winds are nothing other (as has been copiously declared before) than spirits or <term>daemons</term> <note>Fludd uses "daemons" in the classical sense of intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not necessarily evil "demons."</note> sent down by hidden influences from the various worlds or planetary orbs of heaven. Hence we said in the preceding pages that the Angel presiding over the sun is <term>Metattron</term> <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Kabbalistic tradition, often described as the celestial scribe or the mediator between the divine and the created world.</note>, whom we have explained to be nothing else, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalists, than that primary emanation or that radiant Wisdom created before all things, by which all things were afterwards created. All good angels are accustomed to obey and comply with him, just as the other stars are secondary to the sun in power, light, and dignity; and consequently, so are all those angelic presidents or <term>intelligences</term> to whom the command of those bright orbs is attributed. When Wisdom looks out from her central palace, existing in the very heart of the visible sun, these intelligences carry out the commands and will of the invisible sun as divine and universal lords.

### *Correlation to the property of that machine of ours.*

GOD, the source and supernatural origin of Light and consequently of heat (which is the effect of light), placed his tabernacle in the sun. From this natural source, He gives fiery power to the heavens and the elements, and then to the "elementated" things—both the celestial ones, such as the wandering and fixed stars, and the sublunary ones, among which lightning-fire and terrestrial fire claim the primary place for themselves. If, therefore, the airy spirit is altered by immediate fiery heat, or by violent agitation or motion (as is clear in the collision of two bodies or the revolution of a wheel), it originates primarily from the Sun in respect to its natural principle. The Sun received its central power—both moving and agitating as well as heating—from God, by means of His angel Metatron. We see, therefore, that by means of Heat (whose father is the sun), the air or universal spirit—and consequently the particular spirit—is governed, and is moved and led around by expansion, just as the human breath is drawn in and breathed out by means of the human soul. Therefore, the particular spirit enclosed in the glass or <term>matrass</term> <note>A matrass is a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck, used in early chemistry and physics experiments.</note> is expanded by the presence of heat, and in its expansion, it requires a larger place; thus, its thickness, which the cold had gathered together, is now dissipated and driven to the part opposite the seat of the heat.

<margin>Note Well</margin>
Thus also in the generation of winter winds, it is certain that the sun itself holds the first place. The reason is at hand: namely, because when the sun predominates in the regions beyond the equator and heats those places in a wonderful way because of the perpendicularity of its rays, it is necessary that the air—which was condensed by cold during our summer time (namely, when the sun dwells in Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo)—should now (in our winter time) be dissolved again by the nearby presence of the sun. It is thinned out, and because of its thinness, it requires a larger place to be contained; therefore, the thicker part of the air tends for the most part toward the opposite pole of the world, from the South toward the North, and this happens with more or less violence according to the greater or lesser action of the sun in the air in that open region. From this it happens that Southern winds are so frequent in our winter time, namely because of the thinning of the air in the Antarctic part of the equator, which happens by the presence of the sun, whence it also happens that the air of that quarter or region is so rarefied...

## CHAPTER II.
### *On the origin of Clouds and consequently of rains.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'E' with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>The creation of clouds and rains is brought about by clearly the same reasoning. The dissipated parts are forced toward the Temperate Zone, which is already made cold—and consequently condensed—due to the long absence of the sun. From this it happens that this thinned air, driven by the thinning of the South wind and animated by the attenuating solar spirit, mixes itself with the air of the Temperate and Cold Zones. Through the compression of its parts, it changes that air into a dense vapor, which then passes into a mist, a small cloud, or the substance of a cloud. This, in turn, because of the central heat of the thinned air inspired into it by the sun, is ready to be liquefied into droplets of water and converted into the nature of rain. But if, while this thinned air is seeking the northern part, a stronger wind (from which it claims its name) blows from the Northern region, then by the overabundance of dry cold, they are converted into snow...

### Correlation.

We see in our experimental instrument <note>The thermoscope or weather glass.</note> that the air itself, enclosed in a flask <note term="matracium">A 'matrass,' a long-necked glass flask used in chemistry.</note>, dilates itself at the contact of heat; in its dilation, it requires a larger and more spacious place. Thus, it tends downward against the quarter of the heat dilating it, with a motion so strong—indeed, contrary to the nature of the lightness of its body—that it even compels and urges the dense mass of water before it. By this we are taught that air dilated by solar heat moves for the most part either to the right or to the left in the world, and recedes on light wings from the seat of heat (namely, the solar position). This happens many degrees faster than in the glass, both because of the immense motion of the sun in the open air, and because the dilated air is not as strongly opposed or repelled by thickened air as it is by thick and dense water.

It follows, therefore, that if air applied or joined to air usually procreates a denser air, it is necessary that such a thickening of the air creates a middle composition between water and earth, of a moderate substance. For it must be a medium between two extremes: namely, water and air. Indeed, those more skilled in natural philosophy have frankly acknowledged the condensation of air into water, and again the rarefaction <note term="rarefaction">The process of becoming less dense; the opposite of condensation.</note> of water into air. Therefore, the medium between these terms is vapor; and a vapor, whether denser or looser, usually procreates a cloud of the same nature as itself, which cloud is finally resolved into drops of water. Thus, thinned air, mixed with thick air, passes into a cloudy vapor, which is finally seen to distill into rain. And even if some were ignorant of the opposite, we can prove this by ocular experience, moving from the lesser to the greater in this way: If a part of the subtlety of the air is usually transmuted into an aqueous substance, how much more so when that air is joined to thicker air? But that a part of thinned air is usually transformed into an aqueous substance is the major evidence; the minor is explained by the following experiment.

Take a glass that is sufficiently round, filled only with air and hermetically sealed; bury it almost

# Universal Experiment

<margin>Note</margin> Let the whole [vessel], except for its top, be covered, and let a gentle fire be lit beneath it, whether of coals or a lamp, it matters not. You will perceive with your eyes that when the lower part of the vessel is heated, the air contained within the glass will be thinned <note original="attenuabitur">Rarefied or made less dense.</note> due to the heat of that place. But since a larger or vaster space cannot be had for the body of the thinned air because of the solid composition of the glass, it is necessary that in the colder part of the vessel—namely the top—it reveals itself in a denser and more visible form than it was before. Wherefore, it will first change into a white smoke, and then gradually into drops, which indeed has been proven by me quite often. By a clearly similar logic, in the dissolution of water into air, which happens through its strong boiling, we notice first a wind is stirred up, and that wind accompanies a vapor, which then afterwards vanishes into the air. So also (since the logic of contraries or opposites is the same) air heated by the sun’s warmth is easily condensed into a cloud in the cold alongside dense air—much more so because of the abundance of material to be condensed—since the aforementioned experiment shows that this same thing is usually achieved by the simple condensation of air. From this it is clear how absurd is that opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, whose "Peripatetic" school dominated university learning for centuries.</note> asserting that the cause of clouds is the freezing of vapors [rising] from the earth and water in the middle region of the air due to the quality of that place. Similarly, we are taught by experience that clouds and rains are so rare in the summer time because of the strong dominion that the solar rays have in our air; because the air is more subtle and thinned, it is further removed from thickening into a cloud. But if by chance the thinned air is gathered by opposing blasts and migrates into the existence of a cloud, then it is for the most part mixed with such great fiery spirits <note>In this context, 'spirits' refers to active, energetic gaseous substances.</note> that thunder and lightnings arise from it.

### CHAPTER III.

### *On the origin of springs and consequently of rivers.*

<margin>Note</margin> From the preceding points, both by speculation resting on philosophical reasons and by experimental practice, we consider it demonstrated more than enough that the air filling all things in this world is expanded in its regions by the power of heat (whose common source we have said is the sun itself). By this expansion, it requires a larger place to receive its expanded substance—upwards and downwards, as well as to the right and left, and before and behind. But conversely, we have explained that this same universally dispersed air is condensed more or less by the presence of cold, according to the greater or lesser predominance of the aforementioned quality, and is gathered and contracted into one. We also noted that just as expanded air requires a larger place for itself, so indeed, with its members contracted, it is content with a narrower place. This being the case, it follows that in the summer time, the reason for the diminishing and drying up of springs and rivers is not due to the evaporation of their water into the air, according to the opinion of the Peripatetics. For if this were so, it would follow that solar heat was not the cause of the thinning of the air, but rather its thickening. For if the aquatic substance of the springs and rivers were evaporated into the air, then it would be necessary for the air to be thicker in the summer time; and consequently, the sun by its proximity and the direction of its rays would not rarefy the air, but rather make it thick. But we are taught that the property of heat is to rarefy and not to thicken, which we gather from the property of our aforementioned experiment: for in the presence of heat, the air contained in the matrass <note original="matraceo">A long-necked glass flask used in chemistry and physics.</note> is expanded, just as, on the contrary, it is thickened again by the assault of cold.

But to make a further inquiry into this matter, let us see, I pray, if the substance of rivers and springs is converted into air in the summer time, what then becomes of that superfluous air, since the extreme heat of the sun always intends the thinning of the air? Certainly it is not converted into clouds, because in the summer time, and especially when the sun is heating in an extreme way, clouds are not so frequent, nor is there rain in such abundance. Nay, indeed, as it is held in the Sacred Page <note>The Bible, specifically referencing Deuteronomy 28:23.</note>, "the heavens shall be as brass and dry" if any [clouds] were present they would be sterile. From which it follows that, contrary to the doctrine of the ancient philosophers, there is another cause for this flowing out of rivers, springs, and pools, and another path for them, though invisible and quite hidden. Namely, the air of the hemisphere being greatly thinned and requiring a wider and vaster place for its existence, thrusts the waters of the springs downward into their depths and causes the moisture to descend into the bowels of the earth. Is not this same thing indicated by the ocular demonstration of our machine? In which we see that by the presence of heat, the air contained in the matrass requires a larger place for itself by expansion; where the heat in its expansion does not convert the nature of the vessel of water below (which had been raised through the neck) into dense air—since such a sublimation would be in every way against the laws of the nature of heat—but visibly thrusts it downward to its deep hiding places and recesses (from which it had been primarily raised upward by the effort of the cold).

But perhaps someone will raise a question about the place where that water, so depressed in our region during the summer, moves while its waves are hidden from us—since without doubt it is necessary that the waters of springs are always in motion. We answer him with the Holy Bible: that they return to the sea from which they previously came, and yet the sea does not seem to grow. For the sea distributes that portion of water which the hotter quarter of the world refused to the wintry quarter of the world; for without any controversy, by as many degrees as the Northern hemisphere of the world excels in heat and dryness, by just as many does the Southern [hemisphere] prevail in coldness and moisture <note original="humilitate">Likely a typo for 'humiditate' (moisture/humidity), as it contrasts with dryness.</note>.

The author further proposes that rivers dry up in summer because expanding warm air pushes the water deep into the earth toward the colder hemisphere, rather than the water evaporating.</summary>

And this is the reason why the sea always seems to claim for itself the same portion in quantity, according to that saying of the wise man: *All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again. Ecclesiastes 1, verse 7.* From this, you can easily see how foolish is that opinion of the philosophizing Pagans <note>Fludd refers to the ancient Greek philosophers, like Aristotle, who lived before the Christian era.</note>, who hold the view that the material for springs and rivers is vapor resolved and liquefied into water by heat and cold together within the earth, just like clouds, snow, and rain. Therefore, either the Holy Scriptures are false, or this opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> is plainly imaginary. And yet, Christian followers or disciples of these men are so intoxicated by the magical cups of the Pagans philosophizing in this way, that they delight in preferring their false opinions over the true and infallible spirit of the whole truth.

I shall bring a single example vividly to light. Velcurius <note>Johannes Velcurius (died 1559), a widely read commentator on Aristotle’s physics whose textbooks were standard in European universities.</note>, a Doctor of Philosophy among Christians and held in no small esteem in the Academies of Europe, speaks as follows in the place where he treats the nature of springs and rivers: *“The Sacred Scriptures do not plainly agree with the Philosophers regarding the origin of springs and rivers; for Ecclesiastes, in chapter 1, says they flow from the sea through various channels and passages and flow back to their sources: ‘All rivers enter into the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers go out, they return that they may flow again.’ But the physicists,”* he says, *“claim the material of these things is vapor resolved into water and liquefied by cold and heat together within the earth.”* 

Thus he speaks, and yet in his teaching he departs from this fountain of truth, and, neglecting Solomon <note>Traditionally regarded as the author of Ecclesiastes.</note>, takes his philosophy or instruction from the Pagan philosopher Aristotle. From this it happens that in all the sciences depending on natural philosophy—and indeed even in commonly practiced Theology—we find so many contradictions, so much so that truth itself seems to be imprisoned away from us Christians by deceptive clouds and darkness.

But let us return to the matter. It is most certain, contrary to the doctrine of the Peripatetics and supported by the sacred page, that the nourishment of springs is from the sea, and not from vapor or air enclosed in the earth, condensed there into vapor by the cold as they would have it. For what is the need for many operations when a thing is usually perfected by nature through fewer? For this is an invincible axiom published to the world by those very men: namely, *that what can be done through fewer means is done in vain through more.* <note original="quod frustra fiat per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora">This is a phrasing of the principle of parsimony, commonly known as Occam's Razor.</note> For without the conversion of air into vapor and vapor into water, water—by its own simple nature—is carried upward through the recesses of the earth and the hidden veins of its bowels from the deep abyss of the sea. This is done solely by the water's astringent nature and the power of cold to gather air, moving it through the pores and veins of the earth. This is precisely indicated both by philosophical reasons and by this practical experiment of ours. 

For unless there were such a tight contiguity between the elements of water and air that one cannot be separated from the other, that monster in the nature of things—namely, a Vacuum <term>scil.</term> <note original="scilicet">That is to say / namely.</note>—would be admitted. From this it necessarily follows that where air retreats through vessels closed on all sides, water follows it because of the natural embrace of one with the other. This has been exactly demonstrated by us in the conclusion of Rule 7, Tract 2, Part 7, Book 3, of the *Technical History of the Macrocosm*, where the motion of the elements is discussed. The Rule is as follows: *The substance of the element of water is contiguous to air by a tenacious mingling, so that there is no distance between them.* Therefore, it happens from this that water is raised upward with the air. And at the end of that rule, an experimental demonstration follows, which we have expressed in this place.

[An illustration showing a man conducting a pneumatic experiment with a large barrel, a pipe, and a basin of water. He appears to be drawing air from a tube to demonstrate how water follows the air to fill a void.]

Furthermore, it is explained through the eighth rule of the same work how great the bond is between water and air. In that rule, a pot is shown that is perforated with many holes in the bottom and provided with a single hole at the top. If this is filled with water to half its capacity, the water adheres to the air filling the other half in such a way that, if the hole at the top is plugged, not even a drop of water can flow out through the holes in its bottom or base. The experiment follows.

This is clearly explained and demonstrated from many of **Hero’s** <note>Hero of Alexandria (c. 10–70 AD), an ancient engineer whose works on pneumatics—the study of air pressure—greatly influenced Renaissance science.</note> pneumatic experiments, and especially in the observation of our experiment at the end of chapter 6, book 1, Treatise 1, *On the Principles of the Macrocosm*, where globe **A** is filled with air.

Conversely, however, the role of heat is to rarefy <note>To make less dense or "thin out."</note> and expand the air, as is indicated by the preceding demonstration. This air, seeking a wider space in its rarefaction, does not seem to draw waters upward from the innermost parts of the earth, but rather appears to press them further downward from that region, so that the air may acquire a broader range for its existence. 

Indeed, we have said that the universal source of these waters is the sea, which also seems to be suggested by the Holy Bible in these words: <term>Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear</term> <note>original Latin: "Congregentur aquæ quæ sunt infra cælum in locum vnum vt conspiciatur arida"</note> and it was so (Genesis 1:9). Moreover, God called the dry land "Earth," but the gathering together of the waters He called "Seas." 

But in passing, some might object to these things we are writing: that if this were true, then the winds would tend to blow more abundantly and copiously at that time when the cold in our Zone is most intense; yet truly, in the time of frost and rime <note>Frost formed on cold objects by rapid freezing of water vapor.</note>, the air is found to be coldest. Therefore, in these times, the air would be more centrally contracted, and consequently, the rivers would be more abundant, and the springs more affluent and full. 

To these people we respond that the cause of the outflow and the more copious flow of springs is not solely from the cold of the region in which they flow (contracting the air of the place and consequently drawing upward the waters hidden in the earth due to the proximity and connection of water with air), but also the heat of the opposite region, which rarefies the air, is quite suitable. For example: in the winter season among us, when the sun occupies the spaces beyond the equinoctial region—namely toward the Antarctic pole, traveling through Scorpio, Sagittarius, and especially Capricorn—the air of that place or space of the earth is rarefied due to the direction of the solar rays. It seeks a more spacious place on all sides (that is, circularly) for its expanded existence. From this, it happens that the springs of that place are thrust down toward the bowels or center of the earth. For this reason, that hot action very easily provides the "hot material" for the multiplication of Northern springs. This material, having been offered in such a way, is then carried upward by its own absence—or rather by the weakness of the solar heat in the Northern parts (that is, because of the slant and feebleness of the rays striking them, with the dominion of cold contracting the air)—and it fills the springs copiously. 

But truly it is certain <note>Latin: "At vero certú est, q" (where q is an abbreviation for quod)</note> that no more water can be raised by the northern cold than in that same proportion which the southern heat has pressed down into the earth. <note>original Latin: "q" abbreviation for "quod"</note> Indeed, if it happened otherwise, then a vacuum would be left in the nature of things, which is most absurd and abominable to Nature itself. And hence it is that although rivers (according to the words of the Wise One <note>A reference to King Solomon in Ecclesiastes 1:7.</note>) flow into the sea, yet the sea does not overflow, nor is it fuller at one time than another; for there is in nature a <term>circular motion</term> <note>Latin: "circularis motus." Fludd views the Earth's water system as a closed circulatory system, similar to blood in the body.</note>, but it admits no increase or decrease itself. And although we see that floods occur and rivers overflow from their channels in their northern parts, we are nevertheless taught that this usually happens more abundantly from rains. These rains occur because of the extreme rarefaction of the air in southern places, in which a great portion of that air so rarefied is conducted into the northern parts by means of the southern wind. There, it is reduced back into clouds by the cold of the place, and finally, by its own inherent heat—which it receives from the solar rays by way of thickening—it is immediately dissolved into rains; for the heat enclosed therein naturally seeks the open...

### Corollary.

What need is there for more words? Do we not see in the observation of our present machine <note>Fludd is referring to his "weather-glass" or thermoscope, an early type of thermometer.</note> that upon the approach of heat to the **matrass** <note>A matrass is a long-necked glass flask used in alchemy and early chemistry.</note>, the air is dilated, and that in this dilation it requires a more ample space for its existence? This is proven by the fact that we perceive with our own eyes that the water—which had been raised many degrees in the neck of the vessel by the presence of cold—is gradually driven back by the dilation of the air. 

Indeed, this experience has been very costly and laborious, and even truly dangerous, for certain common chemists. For in the making of **aqua fortis** <note>literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid.</note> from salt of nitre and vitriol, the spirits leaping forth from the small mass contained in the **retort** <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note>, because of the dilation of the air, could not be contained within the vastest glass container or receiver. Instead (and I speak from experience), they wretchedly tore that vessel into infinite particles, accompanied by a horrific sound like that of a **musket** <note>original: *sclopeti*</note>, so that they might acquire a broader field in the air for their existence. 

Hence, therefore, is the reason for the diminishing of springs in the summer time: because, namely, by the presence of solar heat, the air in our **Zone** is thinned, as may be seen through diligent intuition of the properties of our machine. Wherefore the dilated air does not pull the waters upward to itself, but on the contrary, thrusts the terrestrial waters downward. 

Thus we see in paralytics that the nerves, relaxed by this thinning <note>original: *attenuatione*</note>, do not stretch or pull the limbs toward motion to perform their functions, but conversely, we note them falling toward the earth, that is, being pressed downward toward the ground. Do we not observe this very same thing in the action of this instrument of ours, whose water, raised by cold, is gradually driven downward by the presence of heat and the **rarefaction** <note>The process of a substance becoming less dense; the opposite of condensation.</note> of the air? 

In like manner, we see in the winter time the air contracted by cold, and in its contraction, the springs overflowing with water and the rivers swelling with waves. This, we have said, happens because of the constriction of the air, which for its own motion also moves the water itself, which is like its servant and handmaid. It moves it, I say, either by driving it from the center toward the circumference (and this in its hot and dilated condition), or by contracting it from the circumference toward the center (and this in its cold or contractive and gathering nature). 

Behold in our machine the wood <note>Likely referring to the wooden frame of the weather-glass.</note>, where by the contact of cold, the air contained in the matrass is so condensed that it raises the water many degrees high into the neck of the matrass, through which it is intended to be colder in its nature; whence it is clear that this is the reason why waters are raised high from the central hidden places of the earth: namely, by the presence of winter’s cold.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the origin of Luminous Meteors, and how they are procreated in rarefied air.

Since, therefore, ocular experience teaches us that the more the air is heated, the rarer and subtler it becomes, it follows conversely that the rarer and purer the air is, the more closely it approaches the nature of the element of fire and of the **luminous and fiery spirit**. Just as it is clear from the opposite side that as the air grows cold, it is rendered more dense; wherefore the first degree of condensing air is into the consistency of **vapor**, the second into the consistency of **mist**, the third of **cloud**, the fourth of **rain**, the fifth of **snow**, and the last of **hail and ice**. 

Such also is the respect of the degrees in the thinning of the air from its mediocre state toward its extreme, even unto the sphere of fire: namely, **wind**, **will-o'-the-wisp** <note>original: *ignis fatuus*</note>, **falling star**, **lightning**, **flashing**, **pillars of fire**, and other kinds of **comets**. All these fiery meteors possess air that has been rarefied by fiery heat.

<margin>NB.</margin> Here, however, we think it must be diligently observed by us that the **occult**—that is, the greatest spiritual part of the air—is **light**. This light vivifies the air itself no differently than a soul vivifies an animal, and agitates it everywhere according to its will. Therefore, the occult or internal part of the air, which inhabits its center, is **pure fire**, just as its manifest or external part is a certain moist substance, covering and enclosing that occult light no differently than a body encloses a soul. 

A dense cloud [enclosing] lightning is such; for the fiery or central substance of the air is pure fire, which God, in the first creation when He said **"Let there be light"** <note>original: *Fiat lux*</note>, breathed into the universal spirit of the world. By stripping off its moist garment (or by manifesting the occult and occulting the manifest), the moist invisible air is changed into invisible fire. 

But truly, just as we see the external and manifest (but invisible) air itself first take on the appearance of visible vapor by contraction, and then of a dense cloud, so also we shall perceive the occult or fiery invisible air change first into the substance of flashing and lightning, and then, in a tighter contraction, into a visibly fiery meteor, namely a comet, a falling star, a will-o'-the-wisp, and other things of this sort. 

The "point from which" the air tends from its mediocre nature by thinning is a fiery existence; but the "point toward which" it is accustomed to migrate from its mediocre nature is the nature of a dense cloud. Whence it is clear that in mediocre air there is an aptitude either toward a dark nature by virtue of thickening, or toward a luminous existence by the way of rarefaction. And in this way, both dark and luminous meteors are produced into the world, from which then afterwards both the internal and the external—that is, both the soul and the body of any thing, whether simple or composite—is derived.

Let whoever prefers it accept that view; for his will in this matter shall be pleasing to me. Similarly, some Christian theologians who are followers of the Peripatetic school do not blush to make a distinction between Theology and sacred Physics; by separating the rays of divinity from created nature, they assert that God is not in nature at all. Thus, with their Aristotle, they want fire, the sun, the stars, and their influences to be the actors and authors of all lower things, even though the sacred scriptures acknowledge that the one and only God does all things, in and out of all these things. These same theologians, with their master, report that the winds proceed from exhalations rising from the earth by the power of the sun and stars; and yet the sacred page makes God the author of the wind. 

It is the same in infinite other matters. Our fellow Christians have learned all these errors with such labor and weariness, and over such a long duration of time from Aristotle’s *Physics*, that even if they find the opposite in the sacred writings, they are nevertheless unable to uproot and cast them out from the treasure chest of their minds and memories, where they are so firmly impressed. They do not know the method for correcting them and they scorn being taught. 

And yet, both among Christian philosophers and those skilled in **theosophy** <term>Divine wisdom or mystical insights into the nature of God and the universe.</term>, there are some who frankly acknowledge the crookedness and weakness of Aristotelian doctrine, yet they do not know how to correct it properly. For **Freigius** <note>Joannes Thomas Freigius (1543–1583), a German humanist scholar.</note>, a man very well-versed in Aristotelian philosophy, after he had mentioned the efficient causes of windy meteors, immediately departed from Aristotle’s opinion and broke out into these words: 

*“Although the entire dispute concerning winds, as with other meteors, is full of the wonderful works of God—for which no firm and sufficient causes in nature can be put forward—nevertheless it is profitable to see how far human reason can progress. Indeed, the sacred scriptures say that God produces the winds from His treasures, from whence we hear their blasts, but we know not whence they come or whither they go.”* <note>original: "Quanquam tota disputatio de ventis... nos nescimus"</note> 

This is what Freigius wrote in book 25 regarding the cause of winds. And the *Margarita Philosophica* <note>A famous 16th-century encyclopedia by Gregor Reisch, used as a university textbook.</note>, in the chapter on lightning and thunder, writes thus: 

*“Certain philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of lightning, have judged it to be not a work of nature, but an immediate effect of the supreme God.”* 

And **Johann Velcurio** <note>Johannes Velcurio (1490–1559), a commentator on Aristotle’s physics.</note>, a man quite profound in Peripatetic philosophy, says this in book 3, chapter 6 of his commentary on Physics: 

*“The sacred writings do not clearly agree with the natural philosophers regarding the origin of springs and rivers; Ecclesiastes chapter 1 testifies that these flow from the sea through various channels and passages and flow back to their sources, saying: ‘All the rivers enter into the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return to flow again.’ However, Aristotle and the Peripatetic philosophers say that the matter of these is likewise vapor resolved into water and liquefied by cold and heat together within the earth, etc.”* 

And so it is in many other things which would be too long and tedious to recount here. By these examples, those still moved by a good conscience seem to argue that all meteors come immediately from God, and that Aristotelian doctrine is in every way most opposed to that fountain of all truth.

<margin>Note Well</margin>

But I advise that everyone use their own judgment in this matter. 

The second benefit which a diligent regard for this kind of philosophy will seem to bring to the reader is that it is impossible for one not to creep, slowly and step by step, into the true mysteries of theology through the study of this philosophy. Thus, one will feel oneself very well and radically versed not only in the foundations of Philosophy but also in **theographia** <term>A term Fludd uses for the "writing" or "mapping" of God's presence and actions within the physical world.</term>. For the reader will find this Philosophy to be as natural to a Christian—united by spiritual instinct and connected by the light of the intellect, and prone to the true knowledge of God—as that philosophy of Aristotle is suited to a Heathen and his faith, bound to his vain fantasies and least of all to the mind, and consequently prone to producing idolatry in the world. 

For the philosophy proposed by us teaches and warns to attribute uniquely to the Creator of all what is His. But this Aristotelian philosophy attempts to ascribe to its own "nature" the divine right by arrogantly stealing it; and thus it desires to claim for creatures those things which belong to the Creator alone, falsely detracting from God His right and His action. 

He [Aristotle] writes that all the meteors of his philosophy proceed not from the immediate power of God, but in a manner accidental to their nature: namely, that winds come from a hot and dry exhalation raised by the power of heat and pushed downward by the action of cold; clouds from vapors exhaled from water and earth by that same action and condensed by the cold of the middle region of the air; thunder from a conflict made between the water of a cloud and the fire from an exhalation enclosed in the cloud, arisen through **antiperistasis** <term>An ancient scientific theory that a quality (like heat) intensifies when surrounded by its opposite (like cold).</term>; stormy whirlwinds, both in the sea and the air, from dry but not at all inflamed exhalations (the same material he imagines for earthquakes); and horrendous **presters** <term>A fiery whirlwind or waterspout described in ancient meteorology.</term> from easily flammable fiery exhalations. He even affirms the matter of comets to be such. He makes the actors of all these things either the rays of the stars or the accidental meeting of contrary qualities in the elements. In all of these, he makes no mention at all of the true Author of all these wonders. And so, he seems not only to distract his Christian followers from divine worship but also causes them, through his false doctrine, to forget God in the hardships and dangers of storms—He who is in truth the ordainer of such weather on account of human sins, and the immediate efficient cause acting through angels...

<summary>Fludd argues that Aristotelian physics is a "heathen" distraction that misleads doctors and theologians by attributing natural phenomena to elemental qualities rather than divine will. He cites several scholars who admit discrepancies between Aristotle and the Bible, asserting that his "Mosaic" philosophy provides a direct path to understanding God's presence in nature.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Peripatetics, Mosaic philosophy, meteorology, divine agency, Freigius, Velcurio, Margarita Philosophica, theographia, antiperistasis, four humors</keywords>

--- Page 315 ---
<meta>This page concludes Fludd's discussion on the origins of weather, moving from the physical mechanics of the atmosphere to a theological argument. He transitions from "Macrocosmic" meteors (actual storms) to "Microcosmic" meteors (diseases within the human body), setting the stage for his next volume on "Sacred Medicine."</meta>

### On the Generation of Meteors.

Hence it happens that because of ignorance of this world, many people—not knowing the true author of these evils <note>Fludd refers here to destructive weather events like storms or lightning.</note>—ignorantly fail to call upon Him for His mercy and help with the prayers that are due. Consequently, they are destroyed by **Jehovah** the Destroyer or His wrathful Angels, who disturb the air, seas, and earth in a stupendous manner, and are exterminated in various ways. However, it is the purpose of the philosophy brought forth by us to attribute all these things justly to God, as is right. We recognize, led by the authority of the sacred page, that He acts through the mediation of Angels—that is, in the angels and through the angels—as the instruments and vehicles of His will. 

We say without hesitation, supported by the testimony of Scripture, that the air is moved, led, and governed by the word of God, insofar as it floats within the word of God that encompasses all things. It is guided by the Angels of God appointed for this purpose (whose role it is, as **David** <note>A reference to the Psalms, traditionally attributed to King David.</note> testifies, to carry out the word of God) whenever, wherever, and however God wills. And although this very idea might seem absurd and trivial to some disciples of **Aristotle**, nevertheless, Christians—weighing all these things in the scales of truth and penetrating the mysteries of divinity with sharper eyes—will perceive that this matter is profound and of the greatest importance. 

Indeed, it concerns divine honor itself: that Christians truly and fundamentally know and understand that tempests and other related operations do not arise from their own motion, or from "Aristotelian nature," or by mere chance, or in such an inept manner as the **Peripatetics** <term>Followers of Aristotle, who sought purely naturalistic explanations for weather rather than divine ones.</term> have imagined. Rather, they proceed from divine providence and from the storehouses of divine treasures hidden in the air, and are sent down upon this lower world. Thus, if dangerous storms should arise, people may be able to invoke God, so that He (as the sole producer of storms) might be willing to mercifully turn away the danger of the storm and grant kind rain instead, while simultaneously defending, protecting, and preserving the fruits of the earth along with humans and cattle from all evil—and so that they might also consider whatever else may redound to the honor of God.

The same should be thought concerning **Microcosmic** <term>The "Small World," referring to the human body as a reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</term> meteors and their effects. Regarding these—since they concern health and disease within the Microcosm—we shall treat them more extensively in the following volume (if the supreme Divine Power is favorable). We have proposed to correctly title that volume *The Final Cause of Meteors, or Sacred Medicine*. In the first part, the **Citadel** or fortification of health is described; in the second, the siege, assault, and invasion of that health-fortress by the "diseased enemy" is expressed; and in the third, we discuss the expulsion of the diseased enemy who has violently entered the fortress of health, and the restoration of that same violated or weakened bulwark. In the meantime, let us be allowed to catch our breath for a little while, so long as the Creator of the world is favorably present for you and for us; I shall never cease to trumpet His praises with both heart and pen.

> *Under your wings, therefore, O **JEHOVAH**, mighty **GOD**, I beseech you to keep me safe and sound from the viperous tongues of **Momus** <note>The Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism; Fludd is praying for protection against his academic and religious rivals.</note> and the envious, so that while I remain among the living, I may serve your divine Majesty with a sound mind and an upright soul; for Yours is the virtue, the praise, and the power forever.*
